Property Description Sequence The task sequence it runs, one a [TaskSequenceMethod] makes. Clock The clock its sequence runs by (below). Data Data its sequence runs with, loaded last (Data packets). A burst's sequence runs its course, and a lasting one's runs until its cue ends. It goes by the clock its Clock picks, else the sequence's own, else that of the one it plays on.

guides/cues/handlers/sound-cue.html.title: Sound cue | PlayForge
guides/cues/handlers/sound-cue.html.summary: Sound cue A Sound cue plays its clip where its Placement says (Placement). Property Description Clip The clip it plays. Placement Where it plays, and on whom. Volume How loud it plays, from 0 to 1. An attached sound plays from a source of its own under them, and follows them as it plays.

guides/cues/handlers/writing-your-own-ha.title: Writing your own handler | PlayForge
guides/cues/handlers/writing-your-own-ha.summary: Writing your own handler Write a handler of your own by deriving from AbstractCueHandler. Each of its hooks does nothing until you override it. Override the moments it plays at: OnApplied, OnTicked and OnRemoved. Or override Burst to play every burst one way, reading the moment from cue.Moment. Override Begin and End for a lasting one. Burst plays OnTicked for an effect's tick, OnRemoved for its removal, and OnApplied for any other moment.

guides/cues/index.html.title: Cues | PlayForge
guides/cues/index.html.summary: Cues A cue is what something shows and sounds, apart from what it changes: a spark as a hit lands, a hum while a shield holds, a shake as a giant falls. Effects, abilities, entities and items each list their cues, and a game's own code raises one where it likes. Every cue plays through ForgeCues, after Unreal's gameplay cues. A cue plays in one of two ways: a burst at a moment, as a hit's spark; a lasting cue's beginning and its end, which share a key, as a shield's hum. In this guide Where cues are raised: Effects, abilities, entities and items raise their cues through a Cues component, and code raises them through ForgeCues. Handlers: Each cue in a list is a handler, its kind picked from the list. Placement: A cue that places something, a Prefab or a Sound, says where with its Placement. Floating text: A Floating Text cue floats a text where its Placement says, 2 units above the one the cue is on by default. Routes: A Cue Tag cue names a tag, as Cue.Hit.Fire, in place of what it shows. Raised: The Cue Library's inspector lists under Raised each cue tag the project's assets raise through it, by a Cue Tag cue, in tag order. Pooling: A Prefab cue with Pooled takes its objects from ForgeCuePool and gives them back, in place of making and destroying one each time. Data packets: A cue that runs a process or a sequence hands it a data packet of its own, loaded for what raised the cue: CuePackets.For(cue, data). Raises and sinks: Each raise of a list of cues names what the list belongs to, its CueSource Silencing and listening: You can silence cues, or listen to each one as it plays. Built-in kinds: The kinds PlayForge ships for this guide's pickers, each with its menu and what it does, as its picker says. In the API The types of this guide's area: AbstractCueHandler, CameraShakeCue, CueContext, CueLibrary, CuePackets, CuePlace, CuePlacement, CuePoolInstantiator, CueRaise, CueReceiverEntityComponent, CueRoute, CuesAbilityComponent, CuesEffectComponent, CuesEntityComponent, CuesItemComponent, CueSource, ECueAt, ECueAttach, ECueEvent, ECueFacing, ECueMoment, ECueSource, EFloatingValue, FloatingTextCue, FloatingTextLook, FloatingTextMotion, FloatingTextStacking, FloatingTextValue, ForgeCuePool, ForgeCueRoutes, ForgeCues, ForgeCues.CuePlayedDelegate, ForgeCueSink, ForgeFloatingText, ICameraShaker, IPooledCue, PrefabCue, ProcessCue, SequenceCue, SoundCue, TagCue, TaggedCues, TaggedCueWatch.

guides/cues/placement.html.title: Placement | PlayForge
guides/cues/placement.html.summary: Placement A cue that places something, a Prefab or a Sound, says where with its Placement. Property Description At On whom it's placed (below). Socket A child of theirs it's placed at, by name, found at any depth, as a hand or a weapon's tip. Offset Moves it, in the space of what it's placed at. Scatter Moves it by a random amount, up to that much either way on each axis, in the same space. Attach Whether it follows them: a lasting cue's only, by default; always; or never. Facing Which way it faces (below). At has five options: At Where it places it Self On the one the cue is on: an effect's target, an ability's caster, the entity, or an item's holder. Where its raiser gave a point, as a hit's, it's there. Source On who's behind it, as an effect's source or a death's killer. Target On an ability's first target, or the place it targeted. For another's cue, on the one it's on. Each Target One at each of an ability's targets. Point At the cue's point, or the place an ability targeted. Facing has five options too: as what it's placed at faces, or along the cue's normal at a point; along the cue's normal; away from its source; toward its source; the world's way. An attached sound plays from a source of its own under them. Scatter draws from ForgeCues.Random, the cues' own random numbers. So a cue never moves the game's rolls: a server that plays no cues and a client that plays them must draw alike.

guides/cues/pooling.html.title: Pooling | PlayForge
guides/cues/pooling.html.summary: Pooling A Prefab cue with Pooled takes its objects from ForgeCuePool and gives them back, in place of making and destroying one each time. It gives an object back as its cue ends, or a burst's after its Lifetime. The pool makes Preallocate of them ahead, as the cue first plays. An IPooledCue on the prefab is told as it's taken and as it's given back, to reset it. A Process cue with Pooled does the same through CuePoolInstantiator, the instantiator its process's registration gives. Each object comes from the pool, placed where the cue's packet says, and goes back as its process ends.

guides/cues/raised.html.title: Raised | PlayForge
guides/cues/raised.html.summary: Raised The Cue Library's inspector lists under Raised each cue tag the project's assets raise through it, by a Cue Tag cue, in tag order. Each tag shows what plays it: "plays its own route", "plays Cue.Hit's route" or "plays nowhere". Under it, a row for each asset that raises it opens the asset in The Forge. The section's header counts the tags, and how many of them play nowhere. It follows the project as it changes, and the library's routes as they're edited. The Problems view notes a Cue Tag cue that plays nowhere: one that names no tag; one whose project names no Cue Library; one whose tag the library routes nowhere, neither its own route nor a parent's. It's a note, not a warning, as an entity's Cue Receiver may play the tag its own way. An edit to the library, or to the library a project names, checks every asset again.

guides/cues/raises-and-sinks.html.title: Raises and sinks | PlayForge
guides/cues/raises-and-sinks.html.summary: Raises and sinks Each raise of a list of cues names what the list belongs to, its CueSource: an effect, an ability, an entity or an item, by its asset; a cue tag raised from code, as ForgeCueRoutes.Burst(cue); or a game's own code, where it names nothing. Code can name one: ForgeCues.Burst(cues, cue, CueSource.Of(effect)). Before any cue of a raise plays, its world's sink is asked, once: ForgeCueSink.WillPlay(event, raise). The raise holds the cue and its source. The default sink plays everything. A world of its own takes a sink of its own with ForgeCues.UseSink(world, sink). ForgeCues.Sink is the one every other world asks. The sink is asked whatever mutes a cue. So a server that plays none can still send them on, as a network layer's sink does. A cue tag raised from code asks once. Its routes, and a Cue Tag within them, play inside that raise, unasked. An effect's applier can say where it hit, before applying it: spec.WithHit(point, normal, magnitude). Its cues then play at the point, facing the normal, with the magnitude, as a sword's spark where the blade struck.

guides/cues/routes.html.title: Routes | PlayForge
guides/cues/routes.html.summary: Routes A Cue Tag cue names a tag, as Cue.Hit.Fire, in place of what it shows. So an effect, an ability and an entity can each raise Cue.Hit.Fire, and one place says how it looks. That place is the project's Cue Library, an asset from Create > PlayForge > Cue Library. Project Settings > PlayForge names it under Forge Project. Each of the library's routes is a cue tag and the handlers it plays: A tag plays its own route, or else its nearest parent's. With no route for Cue.Hit.Fire, Cue.Hit's plays. A route that doesn't Override plays its parent's after it, so Cue.Hit.Fire's flames add to Cue.Hit's spark. Code can give a library of its own, ForgeCueRoutes.Library, in place of the project's. An entity's Cue Receiver component plays a tag its own way first, in place of the library's. With Pass Through, it plays its own way before the library's route, not in place of it. Its Variant plays the library's route under its name, as Cue.Hit.Golem for Cue.Hit, where the library has one. So a golem's hit sounds of stone.

guides/cues/silencing-and-listening.html.title: Silencing and listening | PlayForge
guides/cues/silencing-and-listening.html.summary: Silencing and listening You can silence cues, or listen to each one as it plays. Code What it does ForgeCues.Enabled = false Silences every cue, as on a server or while a simulation runs ahead. ForgeCues.Mute(entity, true) Silences one entity's, as one off screen. A lasting cue that began still ends. ForgeCues.Played Hears each cue as it plays, for a debugger or a recorder.

guides/cues/where-cues-are-raised.html.title: Where cues are raised | PlayForge
guides/cues/where-cues-are-raised.html.summary: Where cues are raised Effects, abilities, entities and items raise their cues through a Cues component, and code raises them through ForgeCues. Effects: an effect's Cues component plays its cues (Effects: Cues): as it lands, and as an application it takes in lands; as each tick executes, and as an impact it deals lands; as it comes off, and while it lasts; as an application is refused, and as its stacks change. Abilities: a Cues component plays an ability's as it activates, as it commits, while it's active, as it ends and as one is refused (Abilities: Components: Cues). A Play Cue task plays them at a stage's exact moment, on the caster, on the target or at the point. Entities: a Cues component plays an entity's as it spawns, dies and comes back (Entities: Components: Cues). It plays lasting ones while the entity holds a tag, as stars over its head while it's Stunned. Items: a Cues component plays an item's as it's equipped, while it's equipped and as it's used (Items: Components: Cues). Code: ForgeCues.Burst(sparks, new CueContext(entity, ECueMoment.Raised, point: hit.point)) plays sparks where a ray hit. ForgeCues.Begin and ForgeCues.End begin and end a lasting one. A cue's context, CueContext, says what raised it, and where and for whom it plays: Member What it holds Moment What raised it, as Applied, Activated or Died. Target and Source Its target, the entity it plays on, and its source, who's behind it. Spec and Origin The effect or the ability behind it. Point and Normal Where it plays, and which way it faces. Without a point, it plays at its target's place. Magnitude A magnitude its raiser gives it, as a hit's damage. Key For a lasting cue, the key its beginning and its end share.

guides/editor/build-verification.html.title: Build verification | PlayForge
guides/editor/build-verification.html.summary: Build verification BuildVerification proves that PlayForge's runtime compiles and links in a player, with no editor code in it, as a build server would check. This section covers running it. In this section Running a verification build: Run BuildWindowsPlayer from the command line, in batch mode What it builds: BuildWindowsPlayer builds a 64-bit Windows player in Build/Verification.

guides/editor/build-verification/running.title: Running a verification build | PlayForge
guides/editor/build-verification/running.summary: Running a verification build Run BuildWindowsPlayer from the command line, in batch mode: Unity -batchmode -nographics -projectPath <project> -executeMethod FarEmerald.PlayForge.Editor.BuildVerification.BuildWindowsPlayer ForgeValidator.LogAll checks the assets the same way (The validator).

guides/editor/build-verification/what-it.title: What it builds | PlayForge
guides/editor/build-verification/what-it.summary: What it builds BuildWindowsPlayer builds a 64-bit Windows player in Build/Verification. It builds the scenes enabled in Build Settings. With none enabled, it makes an empty scene for the build, and deletes it after. It then exits Unity with a code that says how the build went: Exit code Meaning 0 The build succeeded. 1 The build failed. 3 The build threw.

guides/editor/editor-helpers.html.title: Editor helpers | PlayForge
guides/editor/editor-helpers.html.summary: Editor helpers The types in this section are public pieces PlayForge's editor builds on, which an editor script of your own can use too. In this section Inspector building blocks: These types build inspector parts, and read what a serialized field is. Asset and number helpers: These types work out what an asset or a number field holds, as the editor shows it.

guides/editor/editor-helpers/asset-and-n.title: Asset and number helpers | PlayForge
guides/editor/editor-helpers/asset-and-n.summary: Asset and number helpers These types work out what an asset or a number field holds, as the editor shows it. Type Does AttributeStartValues What each attribute an attribute set gives starts at, at each level, worked out as the runtime does. Of(set) gives an AttributeStartValues.Result, with an AttributeStartValues.Start for each attribute. The Attribute Set and Entity inspectors' tables read it. NumberFields, NumberLimits What the number fields know: which properties are numbers, a field's unit, limits and context, the kinds a field's menu offers and where it files them, and what a number's kind reads. NumberFields.ScalersIn walks into the scalers it holds, as a NumberFields.Walk says. ScalerActions The number field's kind menu and field menu in code (Number fields). ForgeAssetLines An asset's one line, as its header and The Forge's Summary show it.

guides/editor/editor-helpers/inspector-b.title: Inspector building blocks | PlayForge
guides/editor/editor-helpers/inspector-b.summary: Inspector building blocks These types build inspector parts, and read what a serialized field is. Type Does ForgeDrawerStyles Builds inspector parts: sections, fields and rows. PropertyFieldExtensions OnPopulated: runs code once a PropertyField has built its contents. SerializedPropertyExtensions GetFieldInfo, GetAttribute<T> and HasAttribute<T>: the field a serialized property is, found through managed references along its path, and its attributes. TypePickerCache The concrete classes a type allows, kept for the session, which a kind field's picker lists. ForgeDrawerStyles ForgeDrawerStyles builds inspector parts. Besides sections, it also makes fields and rows. Member Description CreateCollapsibleSection Makes a section, with its Import, Clear and Help, from a ForgeDrawerStyles.SectionConfig. It gives a ForgeDrawerStyles.SectionResult: the section's header, content, summary and buttons. ForgeDrawerStyles.SectionConfig A section's name, title and help topic, and the serialized object and property paths Import and Clear act on. ForgeDrawerStyles.Colors, ForgeDrawerStyles.Icons Its colors and text icons. CreateMainHeader A header PlayForge's own inspectors don't use. ForgeDrawerStyles.HeaderConfig and ForgeDrawerStyles.HeaderResult belong to it.

guides/editor/fields-and-drawers.html.title: Fields and drawers | PlayForge
guides/editor/fields-and-drawers.html.summary: Fields and drawers PlayForge's property drawers draw its fields wherever they're shown: in its own inspectors, in the Inspector of a component, and in an inspector of your own built with UI Toolkit. Most draw in UI Toolkit alone. This section covers the kinds of field they make, then lists the drawers. In this section Asset fields: An asset field holds a PlayForge asset, a Value Pipeline, Crowd Control Rules or an Effect Modifier. Kind fields: A kind field holds an object of one of several classes, such as an ability task, a worker, a component, a cue handler or a purge's filter. Tag fields: A tag field shows its tag by its display name: its parents in secondary text and its leaf in strong text. Lists: PlayForge's lists are Unity's reorderable lists. PlayForge's dropdown: PlayForge's dropdown is the menu every PlayForge picker opens: a kind field's, the tag picker, an asset field's, Set Template..., a sequence reference's, and a number field's kind menu and field menu. The drawers: PlayForge's drawers build on these base classes. Asset reference drawers: These drawers draw a field that names an asset. Ability drawers: These drawers draw an ability's parts: its behaviour, stages, tasks, checks and costs. Effect drawers: These drawers draw an effect's parts, and an Effect Modifier's change. Attribute and entity drawers: These drawers draw attributes, attribute set elements, roles and an entity's parts. Worker and component drawers: These drawers draw workers, worker groups and components. Tag drawers: These drawers draw tags, tag queries and tag requirements. Other drawers: These drawers draw the rest of PlayForge's fields, and the classes with no drawer of their own.

guides/editor/fields-and-drawers/ability.title: Ability drawers | PlayForge
guides/editor/fields-and-drawers/ability.summary: Ability drawers These drawers draw an ability's parts: its behaviour, stages, tasks, checks and costs. Drawer Draws AbilityBehaviourDrawer An ability's behaviour (AbilityBehaviour) drawn whole, where an asset or a component of your own holds one: its targeting, its asset loaders, what cancels it and what it blocks, and its stages. AbilityTaskBehaviourStageDrawer An ability's stage: a row named by its place, such as Stage 1, with Critical while a task commits the ability to it. It folds to a line of what it holds. Open, it shows its policy, its usage effects, its condition, what cancels it and what it blocks, then its tasks. AbilityStageConditionDrawer A stage's condition: its tag. Once it names one, it shows where the stage looks for it, and whether the stage runs while the tag is missing instead. AbilityTaskDrawer An ability task (AbstractAbilityTask). TargetingTaskDrawer An ability's targeting task (AbstractTargetingAbilityTask). AssetSetterDrawer An ability's asset loader (AbstractSetAssetsTask). AbilityValidationRuleDrawer An ability's check (IAbilityValidationRule). Each list is offered the checks of its side, the caster's or the target's, and those of either. IProxyStagePolicyDrawer An ability stage's policy (IAbilityProxyStagePolicy). SequenceInjectionDrawer An Inject task's injection (ISequenceInjection). TaskSequenceReferenceDrawer A sequence reference: a pick of the project's [TaskSequenceMethod] methods by name, None first. Each class's methods sit under its name where more than one class holds them. A method the project no longer has shows as missing. ClockChoiceDrawer A clock picked in an inspector, such as a Run Sequence task's Clock: Caster's, Game's, Unscaled, Scaled, or one of your own. ChargeRechargeDrawer A Charges component's Recharge: Each Charge, All At Once, or one of your own. AttributeCostDrawer An attribute cost: the attribute it spends, or the role whose attribute it spends, and how much. CrowdControlRuleDrawer A crowd control rule: its tag, what it stops, and the tags of the abilities it stops where it stops some.

guides/editor/fields-and-drawers/asset-f.title: Asset fields | PlayForge
guides/editor/fields-and-drawers/asset-f.summary: Asset fields An asset field holds a PlayForge asset, a Value Pipeline, Crowd Control Rules or an Effect Modifier. It's Unity's object field, with a button beside it. Button Shown What it does Open While the field names an asset Shows the asset in a window of its own, so the asset that holds the field stays in the Inspector. New While the field is empty Opens the New Asset window, its name starting as the holder's and the field's, such as "Goblin Attribute Set". Then it makes the asset where The Forge makes its type, and puts it in the field. While the Unity project has a Forge Project, the field's picker offers the active project's assets alone, in PlayForge's dropdown. An effect field's levels An effect field has a line under it that says how the effect takes its levels. The line says Button Linked to the asset that holds the field, with its levels — Linked to another asset Link Here Not linked Link Link and Link Here make the effect take the holder's levels, as one Undo step. An effect New makes takes them too. An effect field's right-click menu Item What it does Copy the Cost Effect Template On an ability's Cost: makes a copy of the project's Cost Effect named for the ability, such as "Fireball Cost Effect", taking its levels. Use the Cost Effect Template On an ability's Cost: puts the project's Cost Effect itself in the field. Pick an Unlinked Effect... A pick of the project's effects that take no asset's levels. New Linked Effect... Names a new effect in the New Asset window, and makes it take the holder's levels. An ability's Cooldown has the same two items for the project's Cooldown Effect.

guides/editor/fields-and-drawers/asset-r.title: Asset reference drawers | PlayForge
guides/editor/fields-and-drawers/asset-r.summary: Asset reference drawers These drawers draw a field that names an asset. Drawer Draws AbilityDrawer, GameplayEffectDrawer, ItemDrawer, EntityDrawer, AttributeDrawer, AttributeSetDrawer A reference to an ability, effect, item, entity, attribute or attribute set. ValuePipelineDrawer, CrowdControlRulesDrawer, EffectModifierDrawer A reference to a Value Pipeline, Crowd Control Rules or an Effect Modifier. LevelProviderDrawer A [LinkedSource] field: Unity's object field of the assets that give levels, and a line of the levels the one named gives.

guides/editor/fields-and-drawers/attribu.title: Attribute and entity drawers | PlayForge
guides/editor/fields-and-drawers/attribu.summary: Attribute and entity drawers These drawers draw attributes, attribute set elements, roles and an entity's parts. Drawer Draws AttributeSetElementDrawer An attribute set element: a row of its attribute, folding to a line of what it starts at. Open, it shows what it starts at at each level, its Base and Current, its bounds, its constraints, its retention group and its collision. A typed magnitude is kept within its bounds. AttributeOverflowDataDrawer An attribute's bounds: its policy, then the floor and the ceiling it reads. A bound's right-click menu sets it to no limit. AttributeConstraintsDrawer An attribute's constraints: Auto Clamp, Scale With Base and Rounding, with Snap Interval under Rounding while it snaps. AttributeValueDrawer An attribute value: its Current and Base side by side. AttributeRoleDrawer A project's role on one row: its tag, then the attribute that plays it. StartingItemDrawer An entity's starting item on one row: the item, then Equip, which equips it as it's given. RespawnPlaceDrawer A Respawn's place: Home, Where It Died, Point, or one of your own.

guides/editor/fields-and-drawers/effect-.title: Effect drawers | PlayForge
guides/editor/fields-and-drawers/effect-.summary: Effect drawers These drawers draw an effect's parts, and an Effect Modifier's change. Drawer Draws GameplayEffectDurationDrawer An effect's duration: its policy, then what the policy uses. GameplayEffectImpactDrawer An effect's impact: its attribute, operation and magnitude, its delivery, its impact types and whom it affects. Then its additional impacts, with Add Impact, and its contained effects. AttributeImpactEntryDrawer An additional impact: a row of its attribute and a remove button, folding to a line, such as "Mana −10 · Continuous". Its delivery offers what the effect's duration can make, and says so where it can't. ContainedEffectPacketDrawer A contained effect on one row: when it's applied, then the effect. AttributeTransferDrawer A transfer: when it moves, who gives and of what, who gets and in what, which of the values, and how much. EffectPurgeDrawer An effect's Purges: a foldout of its fields, its arrow in line with the lists' around it. PurgeFilterDrawer A purge's filter (AbstractPurgeFilter), such as Except Tagged. StackBehaviourDrawer A stacking effect's stack behaviour (AbstractStackingConfig). EffectChangeDrawer An Effect Modifier's change (AbstractEffectChange).

guides/editor/fields-and-drawers/kind-fi.title: Kind fields | PlayForge
guides/editor/fields-and-drawers/kind-fi.summary: Kind fields A kind field holds an object of one of several classes, such as an ability task, a worker, a component, a cue handler or a purge's filter. Its box shows the kind it holds: the name its [ForgeMenu] gives, or its class's name spaced out, without the ending its kind shares. For example, ApplyEffectsAbilityTask shows as Apply Effects. Picking a kind Pressing the box opens PlayForge's dropdown of the kinds the field can hold. They sit under the submenus their [ForgeMenu] paths name, such as Effects for Apply Effects. None comes first, where the field may be empty. The kind the field holds is checked. The search finds a kind in any submenu. The Context says the kind's description. Picking a kind makes a new object of it for each selected asset, as one Undo step. What the field shows The kind's own fields show under it. A field marked [ShownWhen] shows only while the field it names says so. A class Unity can't find, such as after it's renamed, shows as missing, and keeps its data. Workers, components, cue handlers and the other kinds that fold show one line of their values when closed. They keep their fold for the session as the object moves in its list. A component kind an asset can hold once isn't offered while its list holds one.

guides/editor/fields-and-drawers/lists.h.title: Lists | PlayForge
guides/editor/fields-and-drawers/lists.h.summary: Lists PlayForge's lists are Unity's reorderable lists. What a list adds depends on what it holds: List What it adds A list whose field holds its objects by reference, such as a stage's tasks or a worker group's workers An empty element, for its kind to be picked. A list whose elements hold such objects, such as a Group's members A copy of the last element, with copies of its objects of its own. As an element is removed or dragged, each element keeps its fold.

guides/editor/fields-and-drawers/other-d.title: Other drawers | PlayForge
guides/editor/fields-and-drawers/other-d.summary: Other drawers These drawers draw the rest of PlayForge's fields, and the classes with no drawer of their own. Drawer Draws ProcessInstantiatorDrawer A mono process's instantiator (AbstractMonoProcessInstantiator), or None. CueHandlerDrawer A cue's handler (AbstractCueHandler). ValueStageDrawer A Value Pipeline's stage (AbstractValueStage). ChanceRollDrawer How a chance rolls: Pseudo Random, Own Luck, and Luck while Own Luck is on. DataWrapperDrawer A Local Data row: its key, its value's kind and its value, each a column of its own. ForgeFlagsDrawer A flags field of PlayForge's: EPurgeRelation, EEffectCategory, ESpreadMoment or ECombatLogRecords. It stores only the flags picked, and writes nothing as it's drawn. TextureItemDrawer An asset's texture on one row: its tag, then the texture. AlignedFoldoutDrawer PlayForge's classes with no drawer of their own, such as an ability's definition and tags, an On Hit entry, a cue's placement or a project's settings. It draws a foldout of their fields, its arrow in line with the lists' around it. A field marked [ForgeShowWhen] shows only while the field it names says so. It draws in an IMGUI inspector too.

guides/editor/fields-and-drawers/playfor.title: PlayForge's dropdown | PlayForge
guides/editor/fields-and-drawers/playfor.summary: PlayForge's dropdown PlayForge's dropdown is the menu every PlayForge picker opens: a kind field's, the tag picker, an asset field's, Set Template..., a sequence reference's, and a number field's kind menu and field menu. It holds a title, a search field, and the choices in their submenus. At its foot, a Context says more of the choice the pointer or the keys are on. It grows no wider than Menu Width nor taller than Menu Height (Preferences → PlayForge). A longer list scrolls. Key What it does Up, Down Move between the choices. Enter Picks the choice. Right Opens a submenu. Left Goes back out of a submenu. Escape Closes the dropdown.

guides/editor/fields-and-drawers/tag-dra.title: Tag drawers | PlayForge
guides/editor/fields-and-drawers/tag-dra.summary: Tag drawers These drawers draw tags, tag queries and tag requirements. Drawer Draws TagDrawer A tag field (Tag fields). TagQueryDrawer A tag query: its tag and which tags match it, then how many it counts, as a comparison and a number on one row. EffectTagRequirementsDrawer An effect's tag requirements on one side, the target's or the source's, as a table. Its rows are Applying, While On and Removed By, each with what it requires and what it must not have. A cell opens its list under the table, with its group's template. AbilityTagRequirementsDrawer An ability's tag requirements as the same table: the caster's, the caster's while the ability runs, and the target's. AvoidRequireTagGroupDrawer A requirement group of its own, such as a targeting task's or a Requirement Template's, as the same table of one row.

guides/editor/fields-and-drawers/tag-fie.title: Tag fields | PlayForge
guides/editor/fields-and-drawers/tag-fie.summary: Tag fields A tag field shows its tag by its display name: its parents in secondary text and its leaf in strong text. While Show Full Tag Paths is on, it shows the whole path. Pressing the field opens the tag picker. It offers the tags the field's context offers in the active project, with None, and New Tag… where the field may make one. Its right-click menu holds None, New Tag…, Make It a Child Of… and Copy Path. Tags covers tag fields in full.

guides/editor/fields-and-drawers/the-dra.title: The drawers | PlayForge
guides/editor/fields-and-drawers/the-dra.summary: The drawers PlayForge's drawers build on these base classes. Base class Draws AbstractForgeObjectDrawer<T> An asset field, with Open and New. A drawer made from it adds its own items to the field's right-click menu. AbstractTypeRefDrawer<T> A kind field. A drawer made from it chooses which kinds the picker offers, how they're named, and whether the field may be empty. AbstractGenericDrawer<T> A kind field that folds to a line of its values. AbstractWorkerDrawer<T> A folding kind field that's always of some kind, such as a worker. AbstractComponentDrawer<T> A component. It offers a kind an asset can hold once only while its list holds none. InlineFieldsDrawer A field's own fields, drawn where it's held, with no foldout of their own. The drawers themselves are grouped by what they draw: Asset reference drawers, Ability drawers, Effect drawers, Attribute and entity drawers, Worker and component drawers, Tag drawers and Other drawers. The number fields' drawers are listed in Number fields.

guides/editor/fields-and-drawers/worker-.title: Worker and component drawers | PlayForge
guides/editor/fields-and-drawers/worker-.summary: Worker and component drawers These drawers draw workers, worker groups and components. Drawer Draws AttributeWorkerDrawer, FocusedAttributeWorkerDrawer, RelativeAttributeWorkerDrawer An attribute worker, of each kind. ImpactWorkerDrawer, ContextImpactWorkerDrawer, EffectWorkerDrawer, TagWorkerDrawer, AnalysisWorkerDrawer An impact, effect, tag or analysis worker (Workers). StandardWorkerGroupDrawer A worker group: its four lists of workers. TagWorkerRequirementsDrawer, TagWorkerRequirementPacketDrawer A tag worker's requirements: a row for each, with its tag, its policy and the weight it requires. EffectComponentDrawer, AbilityComponentDrawer, EntityComponentDrawer, ItemComponentDrawer An effect's, ability's, entity's or item's component. AuraEntryDrawer, EffectAreaDrawer An Aura component's aura and an Area component's area, drawn as the component's own fields.

guides/editor/forge-projects.html.title: Forge Projects | PlayForge
guides/editor/forge-projects.html.summary: Forge Projects A Forge Project (ForgeProject) holds one game's PlayForge assets and its settings. The project is an asset, and the assets in its folder are the project's. This section covers the project asset and its folder, which assets belong to which project, the active project, and moving assets between projects. In this section The project and its folder: A Forge Project lives in a folder of its own under the PlayForge Folder, with a folder inside for each type's assets. The project's inspector: The project's inspector (ForgeProjectEditor) shows the project's fields, and a line in place of its catalog's entries. Which assets belong to which: Each asset belongs to one project, or to none, by the folder it's in. The active project: The active project is the one The Forge shows. Moving and copying: Move to Project and Copy to Project, in the asset menu, put assets into another Forge Project.

guides/editor/forge-projects/moving-and-.title: Moving and copying | PlayForge
guides/editor/forge-projects/moving-and-.summary: Moving and copying Move to Project and Copy to Project, in the asset menu, put assets into another Forge Project. Select the assets in The Forge's list. Right-click them, and choose Move to Project or Copy to Project. Choose a project. The menu lists the projects other than the active one. Each selected asset goes into its type's folder in the chosen project. A number is added to its file's name where another file has the name. Action The catalogs Move The asset is named in its new project's catalog, and stays named in its old one's. Copy The copy is named in its new project's catalog.

guides/editor/forge-projects/the-active-.title: The active project | PlayForge
guides/editor/forge-projects/the-active-.summary: The active project The active project is the one The Forge shows. You choose it in The Forge's project menu, or in the Creator Lab's Project. Each user keeps their own active project, for each Unity project. Until one is chosen, it's the project at the root of Assets where there is one. Otherwise it's none, and The Forge shows the assets in no project. While the Unity project has no Forge Project, every asset counts as the active project's. What the active project decides Area What the active project decides Lists What The Forge lists, what its Tags view and its counts of uses read, and what the Creator Lab's library holds. Picks of assets What each pick of assets offers: an asset field's picker, Set Template..., a number field's Scaler Assets, the Import window's sources, Import Values… and Pick an Unlinked Effect.... Tag pickers Which tags a tag picker offers. New assets Where a new asset goes. Settings Whose settings Project Settings → PlayForge shows and edits.

guides/editor/forge-projects/the-project.title: The project and its folder | PlayForge
guides/editor/forge-projects/the-project.summary: The project and its folder A Forge Project lives in a folder of its own under the PlayForge Folder, with a folder inside for each type's assets. Make a Forge Project In The Forge's project menu, choose New Project…. Enter a Name. It starts as the game's product name, from Player Settings, without its spaces. Select Create. New Forge Project. PlayForge makes the project in a folder of its own under the PlayForge Folder, such as Assets/PlayForge/Arena/Arena.asset, and makes it the active one. With it, PlayForge makes: the project's Game Root entity, in its GameRoot folder. It's the game's own entity, on the System side, which the project's GameRoot runs as. the Bootstrapper, GameRoot and ProcessControl prefabs, in the PlayForge Folder's Bootstrap folder, where they're missing. A Bootstrapper that plays no project plays the new one. Bootstrap, the prefabs' folder, can't be a project's name. Two other commands make a project: Command What it makes Create Forge Project, where the Unity project has none The same as New Project…. Create → PlayForge → Forge Project The project's asset alone, in the folder the Project window shows. The PlayForge Folder The PlayForge Folder is Assets/PlayForge until Project Settings → PlayForge sets another. Where it's the folder PlayForge's own code is in, or a folder inside it, projects and Bootstrap go in a folder beside the code's, named for it, such as Assets/PlayForge Projects. That way the code's folder never holds a project's files. Type folders A type's new assets go in its folder within the project's folder. The folder is made as the first asset of the type is. Until Project Settings → PlayForge says otherwise, the folders are: Type Folder Ability Abilities Gameplay Effect Effects Item Items Attribute Attributes Attribute Set AttributeSets Entity Entities Scaler Asset Scalers Requirement Template Requirements Value Pipeline Pipelines Effect Modifier Modifiers Crowd Control Rules Rules A type The Forge doesn't list, such as a Tag Library, goes in the project's folder itself.

guides/editor/forge-projects/the-project.title: The project's inspector | PlayForge
guides/editor/forge-projects/the-project.summary: The project's inspector The project's inspector (ForgeProjectEditor) shows the project's fields, and a line in place of its catalog's entries. A Forge Project's inspector. Property Description Description What the project is for. Settings The project's settings, which its game reads as it runs: its attributes' roles, and the crowd control rules an entity follows where it names none (Preferences and Project Settings). Game Root Entity The entity the game's GameRoot runs as. The project's GameRoot folder holds it. Keep Catalog Current Keeps the catalog current as assets are made, copied, moved and deleted. The catalog's line reads, for example, "Names 166 assets for saves, kept current as they're made, moved in and deleted". The catalog A project is the asset catalog its saves read (Saving and Loading: The Asset Catalog). Each PlayForge asset made, copied or moved into the project's folder is named in the catalog by its GUID, as it lands. A deleted file's entries go. An asset moved out stays named, so a save made before still finds it. A project also catches up on the assets it doesn't name yet as it's imported, and once each editor session. With Keep Catalog Current off, the catalog is left as it is.

guides/editor/forge-projects/which-asset.title: Which assets belong to which | PlayForge
guides/editor/forge-projects/which-asset.summary: Which assets belong to which Each asset belongs to one project, or to none, by the folder it's in. An asset belongs to the innermost project whose folder holds it, so one project's folder can hold another's. A project at the root of Assets holds every asset no other project does. An asset in no project's folder is in no project. Whose settings apply The Problems view checks each asset against its own project's settings. For example, it reads the project's roles for an ability's attribute costs, and its Cue Library for a Cue Tag cue. A game as it runs reads its settings from ForgeProject.Current. That's the project code passes to ForgeProject.Use, or else the one the game's GameRoot names. Note A running game never reads the editor's active project, so Play mode reads what a build does.

guides/editor/import-and-clear.html.title: Import and Clear | PlayForge
guides/editor/import-and-clear.html.summary: Import and Clear A section's Import copies chosen fields into the asset from another, and its Clear resets the section. The asset menu's Import from Another Asset... imports the whole asset. This section covers the Import window (ForgeImportWindow) and Clear (SectionClearUtility). In this section The Import window: The Import window copies chosen fields into an asset from another. Clear: A section's Clear resets the section's fields at once, with no question.

guides/editor/import-and-clear/clear.htm.title: Clear | PlayForge
guides/editor/import-and-clear/clear.htm.summary: Clear A section's Clear resets the section's fields at once, with no question. It sets each of the section's fields to a new asset's value and empties its lists, as one Undo step. SectionClearUtility.Clear(serializedObject, sectionName, paths) does the same in code.

guides/editor/import-and-clear/the-impor.title: The Import window | PlayForge
guides/editor/import-and-clear/the-impor.summary: The Import window The Import window copies chosen fields into an asset from another. It's titled for what it imports, such as Import Leveling, and names the asset it imports into. It goes in three steps: Choose a source. The type's Defaults come first: the assets Project Settings → PlayForge lists first for it. Then come the active project's other assets of the type, by name. Choose what to import. Each field that differs has a row, checked, with its value now and the source's. Uncheck a field to leave it. Select Import N Changes. It imports the checked fields as one Undo step, and closes the window. Choosing a source The search finds a source by its name or its asset tag. A Workers section's Import lists any PlayForge asset with the same fields at the same paths, whatever its type. So an item's workers are a source for an ability's. Choosing what to import A list is replaced, unless its row's Add is on. With Add on, the source's items go after its own. Show matching lists the fields that are the same as well. Otherwise, a line names them. Importing a whole asset Import from Another Asset... offers every field but those that make the asset itself: its name, description, textures and asset tag, its template, and its level link. The Import window in code Member Description ForgeImportWindow.ShowFor(serializedObject, what, paths) Opens the window for fields of your own choosing. ForgeImportWindow.ShowForAsset(serializedObject) Opens it for a whole asset. Choose(source) Picks the source. Changes Lists what the import would change, each a ForgeImportWindow.Field. Import() Imports them. Each ForgeImportWindow.Field has its Path, its Label, whether it IsList, and whether it's included (Include) or added to (Append).

guides/editor/index.html.title: The Editor Tools | PlayForge
guides/editor/index.html.summary: The Editor Tools PlayForge's editor tools make a game's assets, check them and watch them at work. This guide covers each tool in depth, with the editor types behind it. Tool What it does The Forge Lists a Forge Project's assets beside their inspectors. Inspectors and their fields Edit the assets. The Problems view Says what's wrong with the assets. The Debugger Shows the entities and processes as the game plays. The editor types are in FarEmerald.PlayForge.Editor, and the Creator Lab's are in FarEmerald.PlayForge.Lab.Editor. The Tooling tour in Getting Started: Tooling tour is the short version. In this guide Menus and shortcuts: This section lists where each tool opens from: Unity's menus, a keyboard shortcut, and the tools' own window menus. The Forge: The Forge (TheForge) is PlayForge's main window. Forge Projects: A Forge Project (ForgeProject) holds one game's PlayForge assets and its settings. New assets and presets: The Forge's Create makes an asset of any type it lists, blank or from a preset, ready to fill in. Templates: An asset can take another asset of its type as its template, as a prefab instance takes its prefab. Renaming, duplicating and deleting: This section covers what a rename changes, and what Duplicate and Move to Trash do. The Tags view: The Forge's Tags shows the active project's tags in place of its assets. Inspectors: PlayForge draws an inspector of its own for each of its assets. Import and Clear: A section's Import copies chosen fields into the asset from another, and its Clear resets the section. Fields and drawers: PlayForge's property drawers draw its fields wherever they're shown: in its own inspectors, in the Inspector of a component, and in an inspector of your own built with UI Toolkit. Number fields: Every number a PlayForge asset authors is a number field, a ScalableFloat or a ScalableInt, which ScalableFloatDrawer and ScalableIntDrawer draw. The Problems view and validation: PlayForge's validator checks every PlayForge asset in the Unity project as it changes, and keeps what it finds. The Debugger: The Debugger (RuntimeDebugger, Window → PlayForge → Debugger) shows the game as it plays, and changes its entities as it shows them. Preferences and Project Settings: PlayForge has two settings pages. Spreadsheets: Spreadsheets write a project's numbers by level, or its items' stats, to CSV, and read a sheet back. The Creator Lab: The Creator Lab is a scene for trying a project's own assets: units, test dummies, and its time in your hands. Build verification: BuildVerification proves that PlayForge's runtime compiles and links in a player, with no editor code in it, as a build server would check. Editor helpers: The types in this section are public pieces PlayForge's editor builds on, which an editor script of your own can use too. In the API The types of this guide's area: AbilityBehaviourDrawer, AbilityComponentDrawer, AbilityDrawer, AbilityEditor, AbilityStageConditionDrawer, AbilityTaskBehaviourStageDrawer, AbilityTaskDrawer, AbilityValidationRuleDrawer, AbstractComponentDrawer<T>, AbstractForgeObjectDrawer<T>, AbstractGenericDrawer<T>, AbstractMonoProcessEditor, AbstractTypeRefDrawer<T>, AbstractWorkerDrawer<T>, AlignedFoldoutDrawer, AnalysisWorkerDrawer, AssetSetterDrawer, AttributeConstraintsDrawer, AttributeCostDrawer, AttributeDrawer, AttributeEditor, AttributeImpactEntryDrawer, AttributeOverflowDataDrawer, AttributeRoleDrawer, AttributeSetDrawer, AttributeSetEditor, AttributeSetElementDrawer, AttributeStartValues, AttributeStartValues.Result, AttributeStartValues.Start, AttributeTransferDrawer, AttributeValueDrawer, AttributeWorkerDrawer, AuraEntryDrawer, BasePlayForgeEditor, BuildVerification, ChanceRollDrawer, ChargeRechargeDrawer, ClockChoiceDrawer, ContainedEffectPacketDrawer, ContextImpactWorkerDrawer, CrowdControlRuleDrawer, CrowdControlRulesDrawer, CrowdControlRulesEditor, CueHandlerDrawer, CueLibraryEditor, DataWrapperDrawer, EffectAreaDrawer, EffectChangeDrawer, EffectComponentDrawer, EffectModifierDrawer, EffectModifierEditor, EffectPurgeDrawer, EffectTemplateRegistry, EffectWorkerDrawer, EntityComponentDrawer, EntityDrawer, EntityIdentityEditor, FocusedAttributeWorkerDrawer, ForgeAssetLines, ForgeComponentRule<TComponent>, ForgeDrawerStyles, ForgeDrawerStyles.Colors, ForgeDrawerStyles.HeaderConfig, ForgeDrawerStyles.HeaderResult, ForgeDrawerStyles.Icons, ForgeDrawerStyles.SectionConfig, ForgeDrawerStyles.SectionResult, ForgeFlagsDrawer, ForgeImportWindow, ForgeImportWindow.Field, ForgeLint, ForgeLogSettingsBridge, ForgeNewAssetWindow, ForgePreset, ForgePresetMaking, ForgePresets, ForgeProblem, ForgeProblemSeverity, ForgeProblemsWindow, ForgeProjectEditor, ForgeQuickFix, ForgeRenames, ForgeRenameWindow, ForgeTagLibraryEditor, ForgeTemplateConfig, ForgeTemplatePropagator, ForgeTemplatePush, ForgeValidationRule, ForgeValidator, GameplayEffectDrawer, GameplayEffectDurationDrawer, GameplayEffectEditor, GameplayEffectImpactDrawer, IForgeComponentRule, ImpactWorkerDrawer, InlineFieldsDrawer, IProxyStagePolicyDrawer, ItemComponentDrawer, ItemDrawer, ItemEditor, LevelProviderDrawer, PlayForgeGASProfilerModule, PlayForgePreferences, PlayForgeProcessesProfilerModule, PlayForgeSettings, ProcessInstantiatorDrawer, PropertyFieldExtensions, PurgeFilterDrawer, RelativeAttributeWorkerDrawer, RequirementTemplateEditor, RespawnPlaceDrawer, RuntimeDebugger, ScalerAssetEditor, SectionClearUtility, SequenceInjectionDrawer, SerializedPropertyExtensions, StackBehaviourDrawer, StandardWorkerGroupDrawer, StartingItemDrawer, TagWorkerDrawer, TagWorkerRequirementPacketDrawer, TagWorkerRequirementsDrawer, TargetingTaskDrawer, TaskSequenceReferenceDrawer, TextureItemDrawer, TheForge, TypePickerCache, ValuePipelineDrawer, ValuePipelineEditor, ValueStageDrawer.

guides/editor/inspectors.html.title: Inspectors | PlayForge
guides/editor/inspectors.html.summary: Inspectors PlayForge draws an inspector of its own for each of its assets. It's the same in the Inspector and in The Forge's detail pane. An effect's inspector, its sections with their help buttons. This section covers the layout the inspectors share, each one's sections, and BasePlayForgeEditor, the base of the six asset inspectors. Fields and drawers covers the fields inside them. Each inspector takes Unity's own controls and PlayForge's style sheet, in the editor's light or dark theme. Each asset type has an icon in a color of its own, which is where the type's color shows. In this section The header: An inspector opens with a header that stays at the top of the Inspector while the content scrolls under it. Sections: Under the header, an inspector's content is in sections. The six asset inspectors: Six inspectors edit PlayForge's main assets, with their sections in one order: Identity, Leveling and Tags, then the type's own, then Components, Workers and Local Data, and last Used By. The other inspectors: PlayForge's other assets, and every MonoBehaviour process, have inspectors of their own too. BasePlayForgeEditor: BasePlayForgeEditor is the base of the six asset inspectors, a UnityEditor.Editor.

guides/editor/inspectors/baseplayforgeed.title: BasePlayForgeEditor | PlayForge
guides/editor/inspectors/baseplayforgeed.summary: BasePlayForgeEditor BasePlayForgeEditor is the base of the six asset inspectors, a UnityEditor.Editor. It builds the header, and hands the content to BuildInspectorContent. There an inspector adds its sections with CreateSection, each section's open state kept for the inspector's type. Its overridable members say what the header and its menu offer: Member Description GetDocumentationTopic The guide Help opens. ShowImportButton Whether the menu offers Import from Another Asset.... ShowTemplateButton Whether the menu offers the template's items. SupportsMultipleObjects Whether it edits several assets at once. OnAssetChanged hears each change to the asset, an Undo among them. BasePlayForgeEditor.TemplatesFor(asset) lists the assets an asset can take as its template, as Set Template... offers them.

guides/editor/inspectors/sections.html.title: Sections | PlayForge
guides/editor/inspectors/sections.html.summary: Sections Under the header, an inspector's content is in sections. Each is drawn as Unity's foldout headers are: its arrow, its title, and, while it's collapsed, its one-line summary, such as Leveling Levels 1–5. A click on a section's header opens or closes it. Each inspector type keeps which of its sections are open, so collapsing Tags on one ability keeps it collapsed on the next. Section buttons A section's buttons sit on its header and always show, where it has them. Button What it does Import Opens the Import window for the section's fields (Import and Clear). Clear Resets the section's fields to a new asset's values, and empties its lists, at once. Undo takes it back. Help (?) Opens the part of the asset's guide that covers the section, such as the Leveling section of Abilities: Leveling for an ability's Leveling. The help buttons open PlayForge's documentation site in the browser. The site is built from the pages of the package's Documentation folder, which ship with it, to read offline.

guides/editor/inspectors/the-header.html.title: The header | PlayForge
guides/editor/inspectors/the-header.html.summary: The header An inspector opens with a header that stays at the top of the Inspector while the content scrolls under it. Part What it shows or does Icon The type's icon, or the asset's own texture where it has one: the one under its Primary tag, else its first. Name The asset's name. Under it are its type, its asset tag and its template, such as "Gameplay Effect · Effect.Burning". One line The asset's one line, where it has one. Problem count A count such as 2 problems, while the validator finds any. Its tooltip lists them, and a click opens the Problems view on the asset. Open in The Forge Shows the asset there. In The Forge's detail pane, it's Show in Project, with the asset's file name under it. Help (?) Opens the asset type's guide. Asset menu (⋮) Import from Another Asset... (Import and Clear); Set Template..., Unassign Template "Name" and Push to Its Children (Templates); then The Forge's asset menu (The asset menu). The one line The one line sums up the asset, by its type: Asset Its one line Ability Its effects by their first impact at each level, then its costs and its cooldown, such as "-450/-600/-750 Health; 280/420/680 Mana; 70/60/50 s". Item What it changes while equipped, and the ability it grants, such as "+20 Armor; Blink". Entity Its first three attributes as it starts, and its starting abilities. Effect Its first impact at each level. A * marks a number that reads what the editor can't give it, such as a target. Several assets selected With several assets selected, the header says how many. It leaves out what acts on one asset: the line, Open in The Forge and the template's items. Other assets' headers The inspectors of the other assets, such as a Scaler asset's, a Value Pipeline's or a Tag Library's, open with the same header. They have no Help and no template's items. For a type The Forge doesn't list, Open in The Forge is Show in Project.

guides/editor/inspectors/the-other-inspe.title: The other inspectors | PlayForge
guides/editor/inspectors/the-other-inspe.summary: The other inspectors PlayForge's other assets, and every MonoBehaviour process, have inspectors of their own too. Inspector Shows ScalerAssetEditor A Scaler asset: its Name, which renames it as the menus and The Forge list it; its Description; its Values; Try; and Used By, each field that shares it, by asset and field, a row opening the asset in The Forge (Scalers: Scaler assets). ValuePipelineEditor A Value Pipeline: its Description, a line of its stages, its Stages, and Try (Value Pipelines: Trying a pipeline). EffectModifierEditor An Effect Modifier: its Description, a line that says its rule, such as "Outgoing, effects tagged Status.Chill: …", and its Rule. EffectModifierEditor.Describe(rule) gives the line. CueLibraryEditor A Cue Library: its Routes, and Raised, each cue tag the project's assets raise through it (Cues: Raised). CrowdControlRulesEditor, RequirementTemplateEditor Crowd Control Rules and a Requirement Template: the header, then their fields. ForgeProjectEditor, ForgeTagLibraryEditor A Forge Project (Forge Projects) and a Tag Library (The Tags view). AbstractMonoProcessEditor Every MonoBehaviour process, made from AbstractMonoProcess, a GameplayAbilitySystem among them. The process inspector AbstractMonoProcessEditor draws every MonoBehaviour process. It edits several at once, and shows a prefab instance's overrides (Processes). It shows a Process section, then the component's own fields. Each choice's tooltip says what it does. Property Description Lifecycle How the process runs and ends. Timing The update loops it steps in. Priority Method Where it steps among the other processes. Shown while it steps. Priority Its step priority: a lower one steps earlier. Shown while the method is Manual. Instantiator Makes and destroys the process's object. With none, Object.Instantiate and Object.Destroy do. Participate In Sibling Cascade Pauses and ends it as its siblings do. Off, a sibling's pause or end leaves it be.

guides/editor/inspectors/the-six-asset-i.title: The six asset inspectors | PlayForge
guides/editor/inspectors/the-six-asset-i.summary: The six asset inspectors Six inspectors edit PlayForge's main assets, with their sections in one order: Identity, Leveling and Tags, then the type's own, then Components, Workers and Local Data, and last Used By. Inspector Sections AbilityEditor Identity, Leveling, Tags, Activation, Stages, Requirements, Components, Workers, Local Data, Used By (Abilities) GameplayEffectEditor Identity, Leveling, Tags, Duration, Impact, Requirements, Components, Workers, Local Data, Used By (Effects) ItemEditor Identity, Leveling, Tags, Effects, Abilities, Components, Workers, Local Data, Used By (Items) EntityIdentityEditor Identity, Leveling, Tags, Attributes, Abilities, Items, Death, Components, Workers, Local Data, Used By (Entities) AttributeSetEditor Identity, Leveling, Attributes, Sub-Sets, Collision Settings, All Attributes, Workers, Local Data, Used By (Attribute Sets) AttributeEditor Identity, Local Data, Used By (Attributes) Each of the six edits several selected assets at once. The parts that hold each asset's own objects, such as an ability's components, ask you to select one asset instead. Identity and Used By Section What it holds Identity The asset's Name and its Description. For an ability, effect, item, entity or attribute set, it also shows the asset tag its name gives, which can be selected and copied. Used By The PlayForge assets whose data refers to the asset, each by its type icon and name, in name order. It follows the project as it changes, and a row opens its asset in The Forge. Where the stored tag isn't the one the name gives, Identity shows the tag in warning text, with Update, which stores it. Other marks A template's child marks each field it overrides (Templates). An ability's inspector shows the warnings and errors a component rule finds, under its Components list (A rule of your own).

guides/editor/menus-and-shortcuts.html.title: Menus and shortcuts | PlayForge
guides/editor/menus-and-shortcuts.html.summary: Menus and shortcuts This section lists where each tool opens from: Unity's menus, a keyboard shortcut, and the tools' own window menus. In this section Opening the tools: Each PlayForge tool opens from Unity's Window menu, from a settings page, or with a shortcut. The Create menu: Create → PlayForge, in the Project window, makes PlayForge's assets. Window menus: Two tools add items to their window menu, the ⋮ on the window's tab.

guides/editor/menus-and-shortcuts/openin.title: Opening the tools | PlayForge
guides/editor/menus-and-shortcuts/openin.summary: Opening the tools Each PlayForge tool opens from Unity's Window menu, from a settings page, or with a shortcut. Where Opens Window → PlayForge → The Forge The Forge (The Forge) Window → PlayForge → Debugger The Debugger (The Debugger) Window → PlayForge → Problems The Problems view (The Problems view and validation) Window → PlayForge → Creator Lab The Creator Lab, in a new scene that it plays (The Creator Lab) Project Settings → PlayForge The settings a project shares (Preferences and Project Settings) Preferences → PlayForge Your own preferences Alt+Shift+F The Forge, with its search focused, from anywhere in the editor Tip To rebind Alt+Shift+F, find PlayForge/The Forge in Unity's Shortcuts Manager.

guides/editor/menus-and-shortcuts/the-cr.title: The Create menu | PlayForge
guides/editor/menus-and-shortcuts/the-cr.summary: The Create menu Create → PlayForge, in the Project window, makes PlayForge's assets. It lists them in four groups: Forge Project. Ability, Gameplay Effect, Item, Attribute, Attribute Set and Entity. Scaler, Requirement Template, Value Pipeline, Effect Modifier, Crowd Control Rules, Tag Library and Cue Library. Lab Rules and Lab Driver. Unity's Create menu and The Forge's Create put a new asset in different places: Menu Where it makes the asset Create → PlayForge, in the Project window In the folder the Project window shows. The Forge's Create Where its project's settings put the asset's type, named and tagged (New assets and presets).

guides/editor/menus-and-shortcuts/window.title: Window menus | PlayForge
guides/editor/menus-and-shortcuts/window.summary: Window menus Two tools add items to their window menu, the ⋮ on the window's tab. Window Its window menu holds The Forge Problems…, Project Settings…, Preferences…, Spreadsheets and Documentation (The window menu) The Debugger Samples a Second (The Debugger)

guides/editor/new-assets-and-presets.htm.title: New assets and presets | PlayForge
guides/editor/new-assets-and-presets.htm.summary: New assets and presets The Forge's Create makes an asset of any type it lists, blank or from a preset, ready to fill in. This section covers the New Asset window, what a new asset starts as, PlayForge's presets and a project's own templates. In this section Create: Create, on The Forge's toolbar, lists each type The Forge lists. The New Asset window: The New Asset window (ForgeNewAssetWindow) names a new asset and says where it goes. What a new asset starts as: A new asset is made in four steps PlayForge's presets: PlayForge's presets fill a new effect, item, ability or entity with a common setup. The project's templates: A project can keep assets of its own that new assets start as copies of.

guides/editor/new-assets-and-presets/cre.title: Create | PlayForge
guides/editor/new-assets-and-presets/cre.summary: Create Create, on The Forge's toolbar, lists each type The Forge lists. Each item opens the New Asset window. A type with presets opens a submenu. It holds: Blank; PlayForge's presets; after a line, the project's own templates. Make an asset from a preset In The Forge's toolbar, select Create. Choose the asset's type, then a preset, or Blank. The New Asset window opens. Enter a Name. To put the asset somewhere other than its type's folder, select Choose… beside Folder. Select Create. The Forge shows the new asset.

guides/editor/new-assets-and-presets/pla.title: PlayForge's presets | PlayForge
guides/editor/new-assets-and-presets/pla.summary: PlayForge's presets PlayForge's presets fill a new effect, item, ability or entity with a common setup. Create lists them under their types. Preset What it makes Gameplay Effect → Damage An instant −10 to the attribute playing the project's Health role, on those of other sides. Gameplay Effect → Damage over Time 5 seconds of −4 Health, a tick a second, on those of other sides. Applied again, it replaces the one before. Gameplay Effect → Buff +10 to an attribute you choose, for 10 seconds, on its own side. Applied again, it replaces the one before. Gameplay Effect → Debuff −10 to an attribute you choose, for 10 seconds, on those of other sides. Applied again, it replaces the one before. Gameplay Effect → Stun 1.5 seconds under the tag of the first rule in the project's Crowd Control that stops every ability, such as Stunned. Gameplay Effect → Aura An infinite effect with an Aura component, which reaches its holder's allies within 5. The aura's effect is yours to choose. Item → On-Hit An item with an On Hit entry, which lands on the one hit. Its effects are yours to name. Item → Active An item that grants an ability of its own, named for the item: one stage that applies its effects, and a Cost and a Cooldown effect, named for it and taking its levels. Ability → Passive An ability that activates as it's granted, with implicit targeting, so the effects its one stage applies land on its holder. Entity → Hero An entity with an attribute set of its own, named for it, such as "Goblin Attributes" for Goblin. The set holds the attributes playing the project's roles, Health first, at 100, the rest at 0. An Active item's Cost and Cooldown An Active item's Cost and Cooldown are copies of the project's Cost Effect and Cooldown Effect, where Project Settings → PlayForge names them. Otherwise they're a Cost of −10 to an attribute you choose, and a Cooldown of 5 seconds. Where a preset's other assets go The assets a preset makes besides its own go in their types' folders. Where the window names a folder that isn't the new asset's type's folder, they go in that folder instead. Presets in code ForgePresets holds the presets in code. Member Description For(type) Lists a type's presets: PlayForge's, then the project's templates. Each is a ForgePreset. Make(preset, name) Makes an asset from a preset. A ForgePreset holds: Property Description Name Its name in the menu. Type The type it makes. AssetName The name a new one starts as. Description What it makes. Template For a template, the asset it copies. As a preset fills a new asset, it reaches a ForgePresetMaking: Member Description Name, Folder The new asset's name and folder. Project The project. Health The project's Health attribute. Make<T> Makes another asset the preset needs. Then Acts once the new asset is saved.

guides/editor/new-assets-and-presets/the.title: The New Asset window | PlayForge
guides/editor/new-assets-and-presets/the.summary: The New Asset window The New Asset window (ForgeNewAssetWindow) names a new asset and says where it goes. It's titled for what it makes, such as New Damage Effect. The New Asset window. Control What it does Name The new asset's name, which gives its asset tag. It starts as "New" and the preset's name or the type's. Folder The type's folder in the active project. Choose… picks another in Assets. File line Says the file it will be, such as File: IronSword.asset. Create Makes the asset, and The Forge shows it. Enter does the same. Cancel Closes the window. Escape does the same. A field's New button opens the same window, its name starting as the holder's and the field's, such as "Goblin Attribute Set" (Asset fields). In code, ForgeNewAssetWindow.Show(type, onCreated) opens the window, and CreateAsset() makes the asset as Create does.

guides/editor/new-assets-and-presets/the.title: The project's templates | PlayForge
guides/editor/new-assets-and-presets/the.summary: The project's templates A project can keep assets of its own that new assets start as copies of. Project Settings → PlayForge → Templates lists them. Create lists each under its type, by its name, after PlayForge's presets. A new asset made from one is a plain copy that takes its own name and tag. It doesn't follow its template afterwards, as a child of Set Template... does (Templates). An ability's Cost and Cooldown fields take the project's Cost Effect and Cooldown Effect from their right-click menu (Asset fields).

guides/editor/new-assets-and-presets/wha.title: What a new asset starts as | PlayForge
guides/editor/new-assets-and-presets/wha.summary: What a new asset starts as A new asset is made in four steps: It starts as a copy of its type's New Asset default, where Project Settings → PlayForge names one. Its preset fills it, or it becomes a copy of its template. It's named, with the asset tag its name gives. The tag is the type, then the name's words capitalized and joined, punctuation left out, such as Item.IronSword for Iron Sword. An attribute takes no asset tag. A Scaler asset's name is its scaler's, and a Requirement Template's is its requirements'. It's saved in the folder, its file named for it. Its spaces, and any character a file can't have on any platform, are left out. A number is added where the folder has the name already. The first asset made while the Unity project has no Forge Project makes one, named for the game, in a folder of its own under the PlayForge Folder.

guides/editor/number-fields.html.title: Number fields | PlayForge
guides/editor/number-fields.html.summary: Number fields Every number a PlayForge asset authors is a number field, a ScalableFloat or a ScalableInt, which ScalableFloatDrawer and ScalableIntDrawer draw. This section covers the field in the editor, its menu and the windows it opens, and the Try sections. Scalers: A magnitude field covers the kinds and what each reads. In this section The field: A number field shows its name, its kind (Constant or another), its number or the range it gives, such as "6–8 s", and its field menu (⋮). Its windows: The field menu opens three windows: Save as Scaler Asset, Import Values and Quick Fill. Try: A Scaler asset's inspector and a Value Pipeline's have a Try section, which reads the asset at each level of a range. The drawers: These drawers draw number fields and the scalers in them.

guides/editor/number-fields/its-windows..title: Its windows | PlayForge
guides/editor/number-fields/its-windows..summary: Its windows The field menu opens three windows: Save as Scaler Asset, Import Values and Quick Fill. Save as Scaler Asset Save as Scaler Asset (SaveScalerAssetWindow) saves the field's scaler as a Scaler asset, and makes the field share it. It waits for one selected asset. Control What it does Name The Scaler asset's name. It starts as the asset's and the field's, such as "Burning Duration". Folder The Scaler type's folder in the active project. Choose… changes it. Save and Use Saves the field's scaler as a Scaler asset, and makes the field share it. Import Values Import Values (ScalerValuesWindow) copies values per level into the field. Choose Import Values… in the field menu. Pick a source. The window lists the active project's Scaler assets, then the fields of its other assets with values per level. Compare its values with the field's, level by level, with both curves. Select Copy Values. It copies them as one Undo step. Quick Fill Quick Fill (QuickFillWizard) fills the field's values, or the points of one spread over levels, from a pattern. Setting Options Pattern, a QuickFillWizard.EFillPattern Same Value, Straight Line, Slow Then Fast, Fast Then Slow, Steps, Add Each Level, Multiply Each Level, Ease In and Out or Custom Curve. Rounding, a QuickFillWizard.ERounding None, Whole Numbers or Nearest Step. A preview shows the values as the table will, with their curve. Apply writes them as one Undo step. Number field actions in code ScalerActions does in code what the kind menu and the field menu do. Each call is one Undo step that reaches every selected asset: SetKind, MakeConstant, CanMakeConstant, UseScalerAsset, SaveAsScalerAsset and CopyValues.

guides/editor/number-fields/the-drawers..title: The drawers | PlayForge
guides/editor/number-fields/the-drawers..summary: The drawers These drawers draw number fields and the scalers in them. Drawer Draws ScalableFloatDrawer, ScalableIntDrawer Every ScalableFloat and ScalableInt: the number field. ScalerDrawer A scaler field on its own, such as an effect's Delta Time Scaler or a Group member's scaler: its kind, the range it gives and its settings, with a number field's menu. ScalerBehaviourDrawer A scaler's behaviour (AbstractScalerBehaviour). The list's − removes one. VarianceDrawer A Randomized scaler's variance: Percentage, Flat, Multiplier, or one of your own. ConditionDrawer A condition (GameplayCondition), such as a Conditional's When: its kind, a project's own among them, its line, then its fields. LevelThresholdDrawer A Threshold scaler's threshold: its level and its tier's name on one row, then what the scaler reads from there. MagnitudeModifierGroupMemberDrawer, CachedMagnitudeModifierGroupMemberDrawer A Group's member: how its result joins the members' before it, then its scaler. NumberSiblingFieldDrawer The field a Relative to a Field number reads, picked from the other number fields of its object. A field that reads it back stays out, so a loop can't be picked.

guides/editor/number-fields/the-field.ht.title: The field | PlayForge
guides/editor/number-fields/the-field.ht.summary: The field A number field shows its name, its kind (Constant or another), its number or the range it gives, such as "6–8 s", and its field menu (⋮). The kind menu The kind menu files the kinds by category. It offers only those the field's context can work out, as its code declares with [NumberContext]. Where fields of several selected assets have different kinds, the kind shows as mixed. Choosing one gives it to each. Kinds other than Constant A kind other than Constant shows these on a shaded block under the field: a line of what the field reads, such as "0.3 × Target's Health (base)"; Combine, how the field joins its number with the kind; a whole-number field's Rounding; the kind's own settings. Messages and limits A field that reads its scaler and has none says it reads 0, with Make It Constant. A kind the field's context can't work out says so, and the field reads its number. A field whose unit is "%" shows and takes its number as a percentage. A field with limits keeps its constant within them, on a slider where they're a range. The field menu The field menu is the ⋮ beside the number. Item What it does Save as Scaler Asset… Saves the field's scaler as a Scaler asset, to share (Its windows). Scaler Assets A submenu of the active project's Scaler assets to share. The one shared is checked. Import Values… Copies values per level from a Scaler asset or another field. Quick Fill… Fills the field's values from a pattern. Make Constant Makes the field's kind Constant. Each change is one Undo step, and reaches each selected asset's own field. A scaler field of its own, such as a Group member's scaler, has the same menu.

guides/editor/number-fields/try.html.title: Try | PlayForge
guides/editor/number-fields/try.html.summary: Try A Scaler asset's inspector and a Value Pipeline's have a Try section, which reads the asset at each level of a range. The range is 1 to 5 to start. It reads against a stand-in caster and target, and the values a caller sets. Each value is typed, or filled from an Entity. What's typed is kept for the session, never in the asset (Scalers: Scaler assets, Value Pipelines: Trying a pipeline). ScalerTry ScalerTry does the same in code. Member Description From, To The levels. Caster, Target Each a ScalerTry.Side, holding a ScalerTry.AttributeRow for each attribute a read asks of it. Caller A ScalerTry.CallerRow for each key. SetCaller, UnsetCaller Give a caller key, or take it. Read(scaler) Gives a ScalerTry.Reading: the value at each level, and the parts behind each. A side's attribute is given with Set, taken with Lack, or filled from an entity with FillFrom. ValuePipelineTry ValuePipelineTry puts a Value through a pipeline, against its Numbers, a ScalerTry. Its chances come up or miss as ChancesComeUp says. Read(pipeline) gives a ValuePipelineTry.Reading: a ValuePipelineTry.Run for each level. A run holds each stage's step, what came out, and the stop that stopped the hit, where one did.

guides/editor/preferences-and-project-se.title: Preferences and Project Settings | PlayForge
guides/editor/preferences-and-project-se.summary: Preferences and Project Settings PlayForge has two settings pages. Project Settings → PlayForge holds the settings a project shares, kept in assets under version control. Preferences → PlayForge holds each user's own. This section covers both, and the logging level. In this section Project Settings → PlayForge: Project Settings → PlayForge holds the settings a project shares: the PlayForge Folder, and the active Forge Project's settings. Preferences → PlayForge: Preferences → PlayForge holds each user's own preferences, kept in EditorPrefs. The log level: The log level is the quietest message PlayForge logs, which Minimum Log Level sets.

guides/editor/preferences-and-project-se.title: Preferences → PlayForge | PlayForge
guides/editor/preferences-and-project-se.summary: Preferences → PlayForge Preferences → PlayForge holds each user's own preferences, kept in EditorPrefs. Preferences → PlayForge. Tag preferences The Tags group sets how tag fields and the tag picker show tags. Property Description Show Full Tag Paths Shows a tag's whole path in strong text, in place of its parents in secondary text before its leaf. Off to start. Group Tags by Root Groups the tag picker's tags under their root. On to start. Menu preferences The Menus group sets the most a PlayForge dropdown grows to, a picker's or a field's menu. A longer list scrolls. Property Description Menu Width 360 to start, from 220 to 1200. Menu Height 420 to start, from 160 to 1600. Logging preferences The Logging group sets how much PlayForge logs. Property Description Minimum Log Level The quietest message PlayForge logs. Info to start. Level Logs Verbose Every trace. Info Notable events. Warning, Error Problems alone. None Nothing. Use Defaults Use Defaults puts every preference back, the tables' column widths and hidden columns and the log level among them. PlayForgePreferences holds the preferences, and its UseDefaults() does what Use Defaults does.

guides/editor/preferences-and-project-se.title: Project Settings → PlayForge | PlayForge
guides/editor/preferences-and-project-se.summary: Project Settings → PlayForge Project Settings → PlayForge holds the settings a project shares: the PlayForge Folder, and the active Forge Project's settings. Project Settings → PlayForge. About this PlayForge The page opens with which PlayForge this is: its version, package name and the Unity it needs, as its package.json says. A row of links follows. Each site link's tooltip is its address. Link Opens Guides The documentation site. Editor Tools This guide. API Reference The API reference. Changelog The package's CHANGELOG.md. The folder setting The PlayForge Folder is the Unity project's own setting, kept in ProjectSettings/PlayForge.asset. Property Description PlayForge Folder Where a new Forge Project goes, each in a folder of its own, and the Bootstrap prefabs. It's Assets/PlayForge to start. … picks a folder in Assets. The active project's settings The rest of the page is the active Forge Project's, kept in its asset, so each game has its own. Each edit is saved in the project's asset, and Undo takes it back. With no project active, the page says so. Choose one in The Forge. While the Unity project has none, Create Forge Project makes one named for the game. Forge Project Forge Project holds what the project's game reads as it runs, through its GameRoot. Property Description Roles The attribute playing each role, by its tag (Attributes: Roles). Crowd Control The rules an entity follows where it names none (Abilities: Requirements: Crowd Control). Cue Library The project's Cue Library (Cues: Routes). Resolve Order The order an area's effects land on those it takes, by the tags they carry (Effects: Workers: Resolve Order). Combat Log What each entity's combat log writes, and how many entries it keeps (Entities: Combat Log). Purge Levels The tiers a purge reaches, and what a death keeps (Effects: Purging). Workers Every entity's workers (Workers: Where workers come from). Fill Roles by Name gives each of PlayForge's roles no attribute plays the project's attribute of that name, as one Undo step. The roles are Health, Luck and Movement Speed, and Movement Speed takes Move Speed too. New Assets New Assets sets each type's folder within the project's folder. The Forge and a field's New put the type's new assets there. Control What it does A type's folder Where its new assets go. … picks one inside the project's folder. Use Default Folders Puts each folder back to its default. Defaults Defaults sets two things for each type. Property Description New Asset The asset a new asset of the type starts as a copy of. Import The assets the Import window lists first. Cost and Cooldown Cost and Cooldown names the project's Cost and Cooldown effects. Property Description Cost Effect The effect an ability's Cost field offers to copy or use, and an Active item copies. Cooldown Effect The effect an ability's Cooldown field offers to copy or use, and an Active item copies. The Templates list The page's last group, Templates, lists the project's own templates.
