Property Description Templates The project's own assets that Create offers to start a new asset as a copy of. Project settings in code PlayForgeSettings reads and writes the project's authoring settings. Member Description FolderFor(type) The folder a new asset of the type goes in. NewAssetDefault(type) The asset a new asset of the type starts as a copy of. ImportDefaults(type) The assets Import lists first for the type. UsageEffect(key), SetUsageEffect(key, effect) Get or set the Cost or Cooldown effect, by "Cost" or "Cooldown". SetNewAssets Sets where a type's new assets go. SetDefaults Sets a type's defaults. UseDefaultFolders() Puts every type's folder back to its default. DefaultFolder(type) The folder a type's new assets go in until a setting says otherwise. UseProject(project) Reads another project's settings in place of the active one's, and gives back the one it replaced. EffectTemplateRegistry gets and sets the Cost and Cooldown effects by their keys, "Cost" and "Cooldown". The settings themselves are the project's ForgeProjectSettings, and the authoring ones its ForgeAuthoringSettings.

guides/editor/preferences-and-project-se.title: The log level | PlayForge
guides/editor/preferences-and-project-se.summary: The log level The log level is the quietest message PlayForge logs, which Minimum Log Level sets. ForgeLogSettingsBridge keeps the log level, and gives it to ForgeLog.MinimumLevel after each domain reload. Its members are CurrentLevel, SetLevel(level) and ResetLevel(). A build logs Info unless code sets ForgeLog.MinimumLevel (Getting Started: Logging). A double click on a message ForgeLog wrote, in the Console, opens the code that logged it, not ForgeLog.

guides/editor/renaming-duplicating-and-d.title: Renaming, duplicating and deleting | PlayForge
guides/editor/renaming-duplicating-and-d.summary: Renaming, duplicating and deleting This section covers what a rename changes, and what Duplicate and Move to Trash do. In this section Renaming: You rename an asset from the asset menu's Rename…, with F2 on The Forge's list, or in its inspector's Name. Duplicating: Duplicate copies an asset beside it. Deleting: Move to Trash moves assets to the trash, where they can be restored.

guides/editor/renaming-duplicating-and-d.title: Deleting | PlayForge
guides/editor/renaming-duplicating-and-d.summary: Deleting Move to Trash moves assets to the trash, where they can be restored. Select the assets in The Forge's list. Press Delete, or choose Move to Trash in the asset menu. Read the question. It asks once for every asset selected, and names the assets, prefabs and scenes that refer to any of them: their references will break. Select Move to Trash to move the assets to the trash. The question names up to eight of the assets, prefabs and scenes that refer to them, and counts the rest.

guides/editor/renaming-duplicating-and-d.title: Duplicating | PlayForge
guides/editor/renaming-duplicating-and-d.summary: Duplicating Duplicate copies an asset beside it. The copy is named as a copy, such as "Fireball Copy", with the tag that name gives. Where the copy shows depends on where you chose Duplicate: Chosen from The copy The Forge's list The Forge shows it. An inspector's header, while The Forge has the keyboard The Forge shows it. An inspector's header, otherwise The Project window selects it.

guides/editor/renaming-duplicating-and-d.title: Renaming | PlayForge
guides/editor/renaming-duplicating-and-d.summary: Renaming You rename an asset from the asset menu's Rename…, with F2 on The Forge's list, or in its inspector's Name. To rename an asset in The Forge: Select the asset in The Forge's list. Press F2, or choose Rename… in the asset menu. The Rename window (ForgeRenameWindow) opens, titled for the asset's type, such as Rename Ability. It holds the asset's name selected, to type over. Type the new name. Select Rename, or press Enter. Cancel, or Escape, leaves the name as it was. The Rename window. A rename is one Undo step. What a rename changes Asset What a rename changes An ability, effect, item, entity or attribute set It takes the name, and the asset tag the name gives. An attribute It takes the name. A Scaler asset The name goes to its scaler, which the lists that offer it show. A Requirement Template The name goes to its requirements, which the lists that offer them show. An asset with no name of its own, such as a Value Pipeline It's named by its file, so renaming renames the file, its spaces kept. Undo doesn't take that back. The old tag Where a rename changes an asset tag, every PlayForge asset that stored the old tag stores the new one. That includes a requirement's tag query, a trigger or a filter. The exception is where another asset still has the old tag as its own, such as the one it was duplicated from. The file The asset's file takes the name too, as a new asset's file does. Its spaces, and any character a file can't have, are left out. A number is added where another file in its folder has the name. Undo and Redo bring the file back with the name. Renaming in the inspector In an inspector, leaving the Name field of an ability, effect, item, entity or attribute set renames it this way, its file with it. Each one's tag comes from its own name, so a selection of several can't be renamed at once. Renaming in code ForgeRenames renames in code. Member Description CanRename(asset) True for an asset that's its file's main asset. NameOf(asset) Its name, as The Forge lists it. Rename(asset, name) Renames it. ForgeRenameWindow.Show(asset) opens the Rename window. A tag is renamed in The Forge's Tags view (The Tags view).

guides/editor/spreadsheets.html.title: Spreadsheets | PlayForge
guides/editor/spreadsheets.html.summary: Spreadsheets Spreadsheets write a project's numbers by level, or its items' stats, to CSV, and read a sheet back. This section names the editor's parts. Spreadsheets covers them in full. In this section The Spreadsheets menu: The Forge's window menu holds the spreadsheet commands under Spreadsheets. Spreadsheets in code: ForgeSpreadsheets writes and reads sheets in code.

guides/editor/spreadsheets/spreadsheets-.title: Spreadsheets in code | PlayForge
guides/editor/spreadsheets/spreadsheets-.summary: Spreadsheets in code ForgeSpreadsheets writes and reads sheets in code. Member Description NumbersOf(assets) Gives a sheet's text of the assets' numbers. StatsOf(items) Gives a sheet's text of the items' stats. Read(csv) Gives what a sheet would change: a SpreadsheetImport of SpreadsheetChanges. A SpreadsheetImport's Apply() makes those chosen.

guides/editor/spreadsheets/the-spreadshe.title: The Spreadsheets menu | PlayForge
guides/editor/spreadsheets/the-spreadshe.summary: The Spreadsheets menu The Forge's window menu holds the spreadsheet commands under Spreadsheets. Item What it does Export Numbers… Writes the project's numbers by level. Export Selected Numbers… Writes the selected assets' numbers. Export Item Stats… Writes the project's items' stats. Export Selected Item Stats… Writes the selected items' stats. Import… Lists a sheet's changes in a window of their own (ForgeSpreadsheetWindow). There, Import makes those ticked, as one Undo step.

guides/editor/templates.html.title: Templates | PlayForge
guides/editor/templates.html.summary: Templates An asset can take another asset of its type as its template, as a prefab instance takes its prefab. The asset is the template's child: it takes the template's fields when the template is pushed, and keeps the fields it overrides. This section covers setting a template, pushing it, overrides and what a push leaves. It's apart from the project's templates that Create copies (New assets and presets). In this section Setting a template: You set an asset's template from the asset menu in its inspector's header. Pushing: A push gives a template's children its fields. Overrides: An override is a field a child holds as its own, which a push leaves as it is. In code: Three editor types handle templates in code, and BaseForgeAsset holds an asset's side.

guides/editor/templates/in-code.html.title: In code | PlayForge
guides/editor/templates/in-code.html.summary: In code Three editor types handle templates in code, and BaseForgeAsset holds an asset's side. ForgeTemplatePush ForgeTemplatePush does what the menus do. Member Description ChildrenOf(template) The assets that name the template as their template. PushToChildren(template) Pushes the template to its children, and gives back the assets it changed. RevertToTemplate(property) Takes a child's field back to its template's value. ForgeTemplatePropagator ForgeTemplatePropagator is the push's engine. It records no Undo of its own. Member Description PropagateToChild(template, child) Gives one child the template's fields. PropagateToAllChildren(template) Gives each child the template's fields, then their children. FindChildAssets(template) The assets that use the template as their template. ChildrenByTemplate(type) Every asset of a type, by the template it names. IsUsedAsTemplate(asset) Whether any asset uses the asset as its template. WouldPropagationModifyAny(template, children) Whether a push would change at least one child. UpdateOverrides(child) Marks overridden the fields that differ from the template, and clears the rest. CaptureInitialListSnapshots(child) Records the template's lists as the child's starting point, so a push adds only what the template adds after it. ForgeTemplateConfig ForgeTemplateConfig says which fields a push leaves. Member Description IsExcluded(path, type) Whether a push leaves the field at a property path, for an asset type. GetAllExclusions(type) Every path a push leaves, for an asset type. SupportsTemplates(type) True for an ability, effect, item, entity or attribute set. The asset's side The asset's side is BaseForgeAsset's: Template, HasTemplate, SetTemplate, ClearTemplate and its overrides.

guides/editor/templates/overrides.html.title: Overrides | PlayForge
guides/editor/templates/overrides.html.summary: Overrides An override is a field a child holds as its own, which a push leaves as it is. An edit to a child's field makes the field an override. The edit can be in the child's inspector, through Import, or through a script's SerializedObject. The inspector marks an override with a bar at its left and its label in bold, as Unity marks a prefab instance's override. Undo of the edit takes its mark back too. Some edits override more than the field, or nothing: Edit What it overrides An edit inside a [SerializeReference] object The whole object. An edit inside a list Nothing, as lists merge. An edit to a field a push leaves, such as the name Nothing. Revert an override Right-click the marked field. Choose Revert to Template "Name". The field takes the template's value and is the template's again, as one Undo step.

guides/editor/templates/pushing.html.title: Pushing | PlayForge
guides/editor/templates/pushing.html.summary: Pushing A push gives a template's children its fields. Note Saving a template changes no child: only a push does. In the template's inspector header, open the asset menu (⋮). Choose Push to Its Children. It reads Push to Its Child or Push to Its 3 Children, by how many children it has. The push gives each child the template's fields, and each of their children theirs, as one Undo step. What a push does to each field Field What a push does A plain field Takes the template's value, unless the child overrides it. A [SerializeReference] field, such as an ability task or a worker Is copied whole, as a new object of its own, unless the child overrides it. A list Is merged. The elements the template added since the last push are added, and those it removed since are removed. Those the child added itself stay. What a push leaves A push leaves each asset's identity: its name, description, textures and asset tag, and its own template. It leaves an ability's, effect's, item's or entity's level link too.

guides/editor/templates/setting-a-templa.title: Setting a template | PlayForge
guides/editor/templates/setting-a-templa.summary: Setting a template You set an asset's template from the asset menu in its inspector's header. In the asset's inspector header, open the asset menu (⋮). Choose Set Template.... Pick the template from the searchable list of the active project's other assets of the type. An asset that takes this one as its template, itself or through others, isn't listed, so no loop can be made. Unassign Template "Name", in the same menu, takes the template away. Either is one Undo step, and starts the asset with no overrides. The line under the asset's name in its header names its template.

guides/editor/the-creator-lab.html.title: The Creator Lab | PlayForge
guides/editor/the-creator-lab.html.summary: The Creator Lab The Creator Lab is a scene for trying a project's own assets: units, test dummies, and its time in your hands. This section names its editor parts, in FarEmerald.PlayForge.Lab.Editor. The Creator Lab covers the lab. The Creator Lab: a quick battle, a unit selected. The lab's assemblies are left out where PLAYFORGE_NO_LAB is defined. In this section Opening the lab: CreatorLabMenu opens the lab from Window → PlayForge → Creator Lab. The lab's library: EditorLabLibrary is the lab's library in the editor. The lab's inspectors: LabRulesEditor and LabDriverEditor are the inspectors of the Lab Rules and Lab Driver assets.

guides/editor/the-creator-lab/opening-th.title: Opening the lab | PlayForge
guides/editor/the-creator-lab/opening-th.summary: Opening the lab CreatorLabMenu opens the lab from Window → PlayForge → Creator Lab. It makes a new scene and plays it. First it saves the scenes open before, if you want. CreatorLabMenu.Open(play) does the same in code. In Play mode, it makes the lab in the scene playing.

guides/editor/the-creator-lab/the-labs-i.title: The lab's inspectors | PlayForge
guides/editor/the-creator-lab/the-labs-i.summary: The lab's inspectors LabRulesEditor and LabDriverEditor are the inspectors of the Lab Rules and Lab Driver assets. Each shows the shared header, then the asset's fields.

guides/editor/the-creator-lab/the-labs-l.title: The lab's library | PlayForge
guides/editor/the-creator-lab/the-labs-l.summary: The lab's library EditorLabLibrary is the lab's library in the editor. It holds the active Forge Project's assets by kind. While the Unity project has no Forge Project, it holds every asset in the project's own folders. Its Project switch changes the active project, as The Forge's does. Given folders, it plays their assets alone.

guides/editor/the-debugger.html.title: The Debugger | PlayForge
guides/editor/the-debugger.html.summary: The Debugger The Debugger (RuntimeDebugger, Window → PlayForge → Debugger) shows the game as it plays, and changes its entities as it shows them. This section covers its four views, Entities, Processes, Tags and Timeline, and the Profiler's PlayForge modules. The Debugger's Entities view in play mode, an entity selected. Outside Play mode, the Debugger says so, with Enter Play Mode. In Play mode, it follows ProcessControl: its lists change as processes register and leave. Their values change in place, as often as Samples a Second, in its window menu, says: 2, 4, 10 or 30 times a second, 4 to start. While the Debugger reads them, ProcessControl times each process's steps. In this section The toolbar and status bar: The Debugger's toolbar and status bar frame each of its views. Entities: Entities lists the hubs ProcessControl runs, GameplayAbilitySystem and RuntimeGameplayAbilitySystem alike. Processes: Processes lists every process ProcessControl holds. Tags: Tags shows every tag the listed entities hold, as a tree of their paths. Timeline: Timeline shows what the entities' abilities and effects did over the last seconds. Profiler modules: Two modules chart PlayForge's counters in Unity's Profiler.

guides/editor/the-debugger/entities.html.title: Entities | PlayForge
guides/editor/the-debugger/entities.html.summary: Entities Entities lists the hubs ProcessControl runs, GameplayAbilitySystem and RuntimeGameplayAbilitySystem alike. The Debugger's Entities view: an entity's attributes, effects, abilities and tags. Column Shows Name The entity's name. A MonoBehaviour hub goes by its GameObject's name, which tells two of one asset apart. Hub Mono or Runtime. Lvl Its level. Effects The number of effects on it. Finding an entity The toolbar's hub filter shows Both hubs, Mono hubs or Runtime hubs. With Follow Selection on, selecting an entity's GameObject, or a child of it, in the scene shows that entity. A double click selects a MonoBehaviour hub's GameObject. The entity's detail The detail's header names the entity, such as "Entity · Goblin Raider · Mono hub · Level 3". It has Select in Scene, and Open Asset, which opens its asset in a window of its own. Each of its sections has a table. A click selects a row, and a foot row acts on the row selected and adds to the table. The Attributes section Attributes shows each of the entity's attributes. Column Shows Base, Current The attribute's values. The current's tooltip breaks it down by retention group. Changed by Each source of what it took in the last second, such as "Burning -8/s", then each effect that holds a modifier on it. To set an attribute's value: Select the attribute's row. Type the value in the foot row's Base or Current. Press Enter. The change is one the entity makes on its own account, an unworkable one (Workers: Workable and unworkable). A double click on a value goes to its field. The Effects section Effects shows each effect on the entity. Column Shows Left The time it has left. Stacks Its stacks. From Where it's from, such as "Player · Fireball". Remove takes the selected effect off, where its source applied it. To apply an effect: Pick the effect in the foot row's field. Select Apply. The effect lands from the entity itself. The Abilities section Abilities shows each of the entity's abilities. Column Shows Lvl The ability's level. State Its state, such as Stage 2/3, Active, Cooldown or Ready. Cooldown The cooldown it has left. Activate sets the selected ability off as the entity would, and Interrupt stops its run. To grant an ability: Pick the ability in the foot row's field. Set its Level. Select Grant. The ability is granted at that level. The Tags section Tags shows each tag the entity holds. Column Shows Count Its count, by weight. From What it's from. Remove takes back the selected tag, where it's a loose one. To grant a loose tag: Type a tag in the foot row's field, or pick one from the project's with its button. Select Add Tag, or press Enter. The Combat Log section Combat Log shows the entity's combat log, newest first, as its project writes it. A click on an entry shows its hit's run through its pipeline and its steps (Entities: Combat Log).

guides/editor/the-debugger/processes.htm.title: Processes | PlayForge
guides/editor/the-debugger/processes.htm.summary: Processes Processes lists every process ProcessControl holds. Each column sorts. The Debugger's Processes view, a process selected. Column Shows ID Its ID. Process Its name. Handler Its handler. Lifecycle Its lifecycle. Timing The update loops it steps in. State Its state, with the state it moves to next where something has asked, such as "Running → Terminated". Lifetime Its lifetime. Step Its average time a step, over the last second. The toolbar's filter shows All states, Running or Waiting. Its ProcessControl menu sets ProcessControl's own state, from Ready to Terminated Immediately. The process's detail The detail names the process, its ID, and whether it's a Mono or a Runtime process. A Mono one has Select in Scene. Button What it does Pause Pauses it, and the processes it handles. Resume Resumes it, and the processes it handles. Terminate Ends it, and the processes it handles, as its lifecycle allows. Terminate Now Ends it, and the processes it handles, at once. Its sections say how it runs: Section Shows Process Its lifecycle, step timing, step priority and handler, with Show, which selects the handler's process in the list. State Its state, the state it's queued to move to, and its Run. Time Its lifetime, its time running, its step time and its peak step. A Run is going, held by a pause, not started, cancelled, or ended. Once it's cancelled, Resume starts a new one. Processes covers processes.

guides/editor/the-debugger/profiler-modu.title: Profiler modules | PlayForge
guides/editor/the-debugger/profiler-modu.summary: Profiler modules Two modules chart PlayForge's counters in Unity's Profiler. Turn them on in its list of modules. Module Charts PlayForge Processes (PlayForgeProcessesProfilerModule) Processes Running, Processes Waiting, Processes Created, Registrations, Terminations, Steps, State Changes, Step Time, Sequences Running and Stages Started. PlayForge GAS (PlayForgeGASProfilerModule) Mono Entities, Runtime Entities, Effects Active, Effects Applied, Effects Removed, Impacts, Activations, Refused Activations, Tag Compiles and Recomputes. The details of PlayForge Processes list the selected frame's costliest processes, each by ID, type and step time. PlayForge writes them into the capture as the Profiler records, so a saved capture shows them too. Getting Started: Profiling lists PlayForge's profiler markers and counters.

guides/editor/the-debugger/tags.html.title: Tags | PlayForge
guides/editor/the-debugger/tags.html.summary: Tags Tags shows every tag the listed entities hold, as a tree of their paths. The hub filter applies. The Debugger's Tags view: the tags the entities hold, and who holds the one selected. Column Shows Entities How many entities hold it. Weight Their weight. A parent counts its children's. Held By A tag's detail lists who holds it under Held By. Column Shows Entity The entity that holds it. Weight Its weight. Granted by What grants it. Source The source of what grants it. A Source is one of these: its attribute set; an effect, and who applied it; an ability's asset tag, or its passive or active tags; an item; the entity's own asset tag, affiliation or granted tags; a loose tag, granted directly.

guides/editor/the-debugger/the-toolbar-a.title: The toolbar and status bar | PlayForge
guides/editor/the-debugger/the-toolbar-a.summary: The toolbar and status bar The Debugger's toolbar and status bar frame each of its views. Bar Holds Toolbar The views to switch between, the search, each view's own tools, and, in Play mode, the frame count. Status bar ProcessControl's state; the processes, and how many run, wait or are being created; and the entities by hub. On its right, it says what the window's last action did, such as "Applied Burning" or "Burning was refused". In a narrow window, such as a docked column, each view's list sits above its detail, and the frame count moves to the status bar. Each detail's sections keep their fold for the session.

guides/editor/the-debugger/timeline.html.title: Timeline | PlayForge
guides/editor/the-debugger/timeline.html.summary: Timeline Timeline shows what the entities' abilities and effects did over the last seconds. The Debugger's Timeline view: each track's runs, and an effect's applications and journal. What it records While the Debugger is open in Play mode, the Timeline records, whatever view shows: each ability's runs, stage by stage; each refused activation; each effect's time on the shelf; each refused effect; an effect journal of the entities it lists. It starts afresh each time Play mode does. Timeline tools Control What it does Record Stops and starts recording. Clear Forgets what it recorded. Last 10 s Picks how far back the strips reach: 5, 10, 30 or 60 seconds. Tracks The Timeline's list has a track for each entity's ability or effect, the newest first. A track shows its number of Runs, and a strip of its spans: a bar for a run, or for an effect's time on the shelf; a tick for an instant effect or a refusal. The search finds a track by its entity or its asset. A track keeps its last 100 spans. An ability's track An ability's track shows its Stages: each with its policy and its tasks, when the selected run reached it and how long it stayed, or that it didn't. Then it shows its Runs, the latest first. A click on a run shows its stages. Column Shows Start When the run started. Length How long it ran. Stages The stages it reached. Outcome Running, Ended, Stopped, or the refusal and why. An effect's track An effect's track shows its Applications, its refusals among them, each with its Start, End and Length. Then it shows its Journal, newest first: each landing, tick, hit and removal of the effect on the entity, and each worker that ran. The journal keeps its last 1,000 entries. A click on an entry shows its parts: a number's trace, a hit's breakdown, or what a worker queued and what came of it (Entities: Effect Journal).

guides/editor/the-forge.html.title: The Forge | PlayForge
guides/editor/the-forge.html.summary: The Forge The Forge (TheForge) is PlayForge's main window. It lists the active Forge Project's assets beside a detail pane that shows the one selected. The Forge: the Demo project's assets beside the one selected, its summary above its inspector. Open it from Window → PlayForge → The Forge, or press Alt+Shift+F to open it with its search focused. The Forge follows the project as assets are made, edited, moved and deleted, so it has no Refresh. In code, TheForge.ShowWindow() opens The Forge as the menu does. TheForge.OpenToAsset(asset) opens it on an asset, with its type's filter on and the asset selected, as an inspector's Open in The Forge does. This section covers The Forge's toolbar, its list, its detail pane, the asset menu, the window menu and its keys. In this section Your first Forge Project: While the Unity project has no Forge Project, The Forge asks you to make the first one, in place of its list (Forge Projects). The toolbar: The toolbar runs along the top of The Forge. The list: The list shows the active project's assets that the toolbar's filters and search let through, one row each. The detail pane: The detail pane shows the selected asset's Summary above its inspector. The asset menu: The asset menu acts on the selected assets. The window menu: The window menu is the ⋮ on The Forge's tab. Keys: These keys work in The Forge and its dialogs.

guides/editor/the-forge/keys.html.title: Keys | PlayForge
guides/editor/the-forge/keys.html.summary: Keys These keys work in The Forge and its dialogs. Key What it does Alt+Shift+F Opens The Forge with its search focused. Alt+Left, Alt+Right Back and Forward, except while a text field has the keyboard. The mouse's back and forward buttons do the same. F2 Renames the selected asset. In the Tags view, it renames the selected tag. Delete, or Cmd+Backspace on a Mac Moves the selected assets to the trash, asking first. Enter, Escape In The Forge's dialogs (New, New Project and Rename), does the dialog's action, or cancels.

guides/editor/the-forge/the-asset-menu.h.title: The asset menu | PlayForge
guides/editor/the-forge/the-asset-menu.h.summary: The asset menu The asset menu acts on the selected assets. It opens from a right-click on The Forge's list, and from the ⋮ in an inspector's header, which adds the asset's own items (The header). Item What it does Show in Project Selects the asset in the Project window. Open in a Window Shows its inspector in a window of its own. Rename… Asks for its new name (Renaming, duplicating and deleting). Duplicate Makes a copy beside it, and shows the copy. The copy is named as a copy, such as "Fireball Copy", with the tag that name gives. Move to Project, Copy to Project Move or copy every selected asset into another Forge Project, each into its type's folder there. Move to Trash Moves every selected asset to the trash, asking first. Move to Project, Copy to Project and Move to Trash act on every selected asset. The others act on the first selected asset.

guides/editor/the-forge/the-detail-pane..title: The detail pane | PlayForge
guides/editor/the-forge/the-detail-pane..summary: The detail pane The detail pane shows the selected asset's Summary above its inspector. The Forge filtered to abilities, an ability's summary and inspector beside the list. The summary The summary follows the asset's edits. From the top, it holds these lines: Line Shows Description The asset's description, where it has one. A line for each inspector section The section's one-line summary, such as Leveling Levels 1–5. Kind, Reads, Used By For a Scaler asset: its kind, what it reads, and what uses it. Requires, Must Not Have For a Requirement Template: what it requires, and what it must not have. Problems Last: what the validator finds. The inspector The inspector under the summary is the asset's own, as the Inspector shows it (Inspectors). In The Forge it differs in two ways: Its header's Open in The Forge is Show in Project. The header of an ability, effect, item, entity, attribute or attribute set shows the asset's file name under it, since the list shows its name alone.

guides/editor/the-forge/the-list.html.title: The list | PlayForge
guides/editor/the-forge/the-list.html.summary: The list The list shows the active project's assets that the toolbar's filters and search let through, one row each. Column Shows Name The asset's type icon and its name: its own, or its file's where it has none. Its tooltip is the asset's path. Type Its type. Asset Tag Its asset tag, for an ability, effect, item, entity or attribute set. Levels The levels it uses, such as 1–5, for an asset with levels of its own. Summary Its one line, as its inspector's header shows it (The header). Its tooltip holds the whole line. (unnamed) A warning glyph where the validator finds problems in the asset, in the destructive color for an error. Its tooltip says the problems. In code, ForgeAssetLines.Of(asset) gives an asset's one line. Sorting A click on a column's title sorts the list by that column. It sorts in natural order, so 9 comes before 10, then by name. Selecting assets Action Result Click Shows the asset in the detail pane. Select several Selects them to move, copy or trash together. The first one shows in the detail pane. Double-click Shows the asset in the Project window. Right-click Opens the asset menu (The asset menu). What the list keeps The list's width, its columns' widths and the columns its header's menu hides are kept for each user. Its sort is kept through a domain reload. The status bar The status bar under the list counts what the list shows, of how many, in which project, and the problems. For example: "12 of 40 assets in Arena · 3 problems".

guides/editor/the-forge/the-toolbar.html.title: The toolbar | PlayForge
guides/editor/the-forge/the-toolbar.html.summary: The toolbar The toolbar runs along the top of The Forge. The Forge's toolbar. From left to right, it holds these controls: Control What it does Back, Forward Go over the assets the detail pane has shown, as a browser's buttons do, up to 50 back. Going to an asset the list hides clears the search and turns its type's filter on. Project menu Switches between the Forge Projects. It's named for the active one. Create Makes a new asset of any type The Forge lists (New assets and presets). Type filters A filter for each PlayForge asset type, shown by its icon: Ability, Gameplay Effect, Item, Attribute, Attribute Set and Entity. On, a filter shows its type alone. Off again, the list shows every type. More Holds the filters of the other types The Forge lists: Scaler Asset, Requirement Template, Value Pipeline, Effect Modifier and Crowd Control Rules. It shows the name of the one chosen. Tags Shows the project's tags in place of its assets (The Tags view). Search Shows the assets whose name, file name or asset tag holds its text. Problem count Reads No problems, or a count such as 3 problems. It opens the Problems view. Help (?) Sits at the toolbar's end. It opens this guide's section on The Forge on the documentation site. The project menu The project menu switches the active Forge Project. It reads the active project's name, No Project while none is active, and All Assets while the Unity project has none. Item What it does Each project Makes that project the active one. The active one is checked. No Project Shows the assets in no project. It's listed where no project sits at the root of Assets. New Project… Makes a project (The project and its folder). Show in Project Selects the active project's asset.

guides/editor/the-forge/the-window-menu..title: The window menu | PlayForge
guides/editor/the-forge/the-window-menu..summary: The window menu The window menu is the ⋮ on The Forge's tab. It opens PlayForge's other windows, its spreadsheets and its documentation. Item What it does Problems… Opens the Problems view. Project Settings… Opens Project Settings → PlayForge. Preferences… Opens Preferences → PlayForge. Spreadsheets → Export Numbers…, Export Selected Numbers…, Export Item Stats…, Export Selected Item Stats…, Import… Write numbers and item stats to a spreadsheet, and read one back (Spreadsheets). Documentation → The Forge Opens this guide's section on The Forge. Documentation → The Editor Tools Opens this guide. Documentation → All Guides Opens the documentation site's guides. Documentation → API Reference Opens the API reference, a page for each public type. Each Documentation item opens the documentation site in the browser.

guides/editor/the-forge/your-first-forge.title: Your first Forge Project | PlayForge
guides/editor/the-forge/your-first-forge.summary: Your first Forge Project While the Unity project has no Forge Project, The Forge asks you to make the first one, in place of its list (Forge Projects). Open The Forge. In place of its list, it shows Make your first Forge Project. Enter a Name. Select Create Forge Project. This makes the project as New Project… does (The project and its folder).

guides/editor/the-problems-view-and-vali.title: The Problems view and validation | PlayForge
guides/editor/the-problems-view-and-vali.summary: The Problems view and validation PlayForge's validator checks every PlayForge asset in the Unity project as it changes, and keeps what it finds. The Problems view lists it. This section covers the view, fixing problems, the severities, PlayForge's rules, the validator, and adding a rule of your own. In this section The Problems view: The Problems view (ForgeProblemsWindow) lists what the validator finds. Fixing problems: A problem that one step fixes has a quick fix in the Problems view, which you apply with one click. Severities: A problem's severity is a ForgeProblemSeverity, which says how much the problem matters. PlayForge's rules: Each of PlayForge's rules finds what an inspector warns about in place, in the same words. The validator: ForgeValidator runs every ForgeValidationRule on each asset it checks. A rule of your own: A rule of your own adds a check to the validator.

guides/editor/the-problems-view-and-vali.title: A rule of your own | PlayForge
guides/editor/the-problems-view-and-vali.summary: A rule of your own A rule of your own adds a check to the validator. In an editor assembly, write a class that derives from ForgeValidationRule, with a public constructor that takes nothing. Override Check(asset, problems). Override Name and Reads(asset) where their defaults don't fit. The validator finds the rule. Member Description Check(asset, problems) Adds a ForgeProblem for each problem it finds in the asset. Name The name By Rule groups its problems under. Unless the rule says, it's its class's name, spaced out, without "Rule". Reads(asset) True for an asset it reads to check others, so an edit to that asset has every asset checked again. Example using System.Collections.Generic; using FarEmerald.PlayForge; using FarEmerald.PlayForge.Editor; using Object = UnityEngine.Object; public class AbilityDescriptionRule : ForgeValidationRule { public override string Name => "Abilities with no description"; public override void Check(Object asset, List<ForgeProblem> problems) { if (asset is Ability ability && string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(ability.GetDescription())) problems.Add(new ForgeProblem(asset, ForgeProblemSeverity.Warning, "It has no description.")); } } A quick fix of your own A problem one step fixes carries the step as its Fix. The step writes through a SerializedObject of the asset, or records Undo, so the Undo step the view opens around it takes it back. A rule about components A rule about one kind of component derives from ForgeComponentRule<TComponent>. It hears each component of its kind an asset holds, with its place in the list. It's an IForgeComponentRule, whose warnings and errors an ability's inspector shows under its Components list. Extending PlayForge covers writing rules.

guides/editor/the-problems-view-and-vali.title: Fixing problems | PlayForge
guides/editor/the-problems-view-and-vali.summary: Fixing problems A problem that one step fixes has a quick fix in the Problems view, which you apply with one click. To fix a problem with a quick fix: Open the Problems view from Window → PlayForge → Problems, or from a problem count. Select By Rule. Find the problem under the rule it breaks. Select its quick fix, the button named for the step, such as Store the Tag. To fix every problem of a rule that has a quick fix, select the rule's Fix All, or Fix 2 and so on. Each is one Undo step. PlayForge's rules lists each rule's quick fix.

guides/editor/the-problems-view-and-vali.title: PlayForge's rules | PlayForge

guides/editor/the-problems-view-and-vali.summary: Severities A problem's severity is a ForgeProblemSeverity, which says how much the problem matters. guides/editor/the-problems-view-and-vali.title: The Problems view | PlayForge
guides/editor/the-problems-view-and-vali.summary: The Problems view The Problems view (ForgeProblemsWindow) lists what the validator finds. It follows the validator, so it has no Refresh. The Problems view, listing each problem by asset. Opening the view From Opens Window → PlayForge → Problems The view. The Forge's problem count, or its window menu The view. An inspector header's problem count The view, searching for that asset. In code, ForgeProblemsWindow.ShowWindow() opens the view, and ForgeProblemsWindow.ShowFor(asset) opens it on an asset. Toolbar Control What it does List, By Rule Switch between the view's two views. Errors, Warnings, Notes Each is a filter that counts its problems, such as 2 Errors. Search Finds a problem by its asset or its words. List view List has a row for each problem: the errors first and the notes last, then by asset. A row shows its severity, its asset by type icon and name, and what's wrong. The columns sort. Action Result Click Selects the asset and shows it in the Project window. Double-click Opens the asset in a window of its own. By Rule view By Rule groups the problems under the rule each breaks, a rule with errors first. A rule's arrow folds it. The Problems view, By Rule. A problem that one step fixes has a quick fix: a button named for the step, such as Store the Tag. Its rule has Fix All, or Fix 2 where only two of its problems have one. Each is one Undo step. Status bar The status bar says how many problems there are, in how many assets, and the notes beside them. It also says how many are shown, and, in By Rule, how many have a quick fix.

guides/editor/the-problems-view-and-vali.title: The validator | PlayForge
guides/editor/the-problems-view-and-vali.summary: The validator ForgeValidator runs every ForgeValidationRule on each asset it checks. It checks every PlayForge asset, Scaler asset, Requirement Template, Value Pipeline, Effect Modifier and Crowd Control Rules (Checks(asset)). When it checks The validator follows the project, so nothing polls. An edit checks its asset again. An import checks what it brought. A delete or a move has every asset checked again, as they're next asked for. So does an edit to what one asset gives others, such as the impact types an effect deals or a Cue Library's routes. A rule that throws doesn't keep the others from checking. Members Member Description Check(asset) Runs every rule on an asset, saved or not. ProblemsOf(asset), NotesOf(asset) What it found in one asset. All, Notes What it found in every asset. Changed Raised as what it knows changes. Problems and quick fixes Each problem is a ForgeProblem. Property Description Asset The asset it's in. Severity Its severity. Message What's wrong. PropertyPath The field it's about. Rule The rule that found it. Fix Where one step fixes it, a ForgeQuickFix. A ForgeQuickFix has its Name, as its button says, and the step it applies, Apply. On a build server On a build server, run the validator in batch mode: Unity -batchmode -quit -projectPath <project> -executeMethod FarEmerald.PlayForge.Editor.ForgeValidator.LogAll LogAll checks every asset afresh, and writes to the Console, in this order: each problem, an error as an error and a warning as a warning, each starting "[PlayForge problems]" and its asset's path; each note as a plain line, so a build that fails on warnings passes them; how many there are.

Callbacks.EffectRemoved(spec), the tag recompile Note over S,A: OnApply and Periodic commits never reverse Note over S,P: Its cues play through its Cues component, as the components hear Lend, Land, Tick, End and TakeBack From GenerateEffectSpec through the shelf's gates, the commits or the modifiers, the impact relay to the dealer, the ticks and the removal. An entry holds { AttributeTarget, Delivery, Operation, TargetSlot, MultiplyBehaviour, SortOrder, Magnitude, RetentionGroupOverride, ImpactTypes }. One effect may carry many entries across many attributes: "+10% speed while active AND 5 HP per tick" is one asset. The first entry is derived from its impact's fields, then each of its AdditionalImpacts follows (§7). Delivery decides everything. There is deliberately no separate "retained?" or "reverse on removal?" switch: Delivery Kind When Reversal Continuous Modifier — transient, derived registered on apply, while the carrier lives automatic & exact: unregister + recompute. The ONLY reversal mechanism. OnApply Commit — permanent once at application never Periodic Commit — permanent once per execute tick never Modifier = "while this carrier is present": item stat bonuses, auras, durational %-buffs. Its magnitude is re-evaluated on every recompute, and removing the carrier recomputes without it. A ×1.2 buff can never leave residue, because its value is never stored, always derived. Commit = an event that permanently changed the attribute: damage, heals, DoT/HoT ticks. The post-constraint delta is recorded into per-group committed history and survives everything. Retention groups (Tag) are pure attribution. Every contribution (root value, modifiers, commits) belongs to a group: an entry's override, or else the effect's Definition.RetentionGroup; for attribute-set roots, their element's RetentionGroup. Groups partition one pool for queries and UI (base vs bonus health, base vs bonus damage). They never change the math. Validation: Continuous requires a durational or infinite effect, and Periodic requires ticks (AttributeImpactEntry.IsDeliveryValidFor).

guides/effect-pipeline/2-attribute-state.title: 2. Attribute state (CachedAttributeValue) | PlayForge
guides/effect-pipeline/2-attribute-state.summary: 2. Attribute state (CachedAttributeValue) Each attribute's runtime state is a CachedAttributeValue, whose ActiveValue is derived from that state: ActiveValue = ConstrainValue( ← element clamp + rounding ModifierPipeline( ← Add → Multiply → FlatBonus → Override root ← Blueprint.GetActiveValue(cache), re-derived + Σ committedByGroup ) ) ← fresh every recompute (or generic seed) The state has three parts: modifiers: ordered (carrier, impacter, group) entries. Presence == contribution. There are no alive-flags and no zombie state. Re-registering a carrier replaces its entries: an idempotent refresh, which the stacking path relies on. Removed entries are kept spare and reused, so a refresh allocates nothing. committedByGroup: permanent history per retention group. Only CommitImpact writes it. Attribution: rebuilt on every Recompute, as per-group slices that sum exactly to ActiveValue. In this section 2.1 Recompute pipeline: Recompute rebuilds the value in this order 2.2 Commit math: CommitImpact(carrier, impacters) runs each impacter as a sequential mini-step against the live value (op → clamp → round). 2.3 Query surface: Two pairs of calls read an attribute's groups and its breakdown

guides/effect-pipeline/2-attribute-state.title: 2.1 Recompute pipeline | PlayForge
guides/effect-pipeline/2-attribute-state.summary: 2.1 Recompute pipeline Recompute rebuilds the value in this order: Baseline = the root value. Add: additive modifier impacters, per slot (Current / Base / CurrentAndBase) → DirtyValue. The sums come first. Then each add that diminishes, on what's left: 1 − (1 − x)(1 − v). Every add on a Resistance attribute diminishes, unless its Add Behaviour says Sum, and so does any add whose Add Behaviour says Diminishing. Multiply: Multiplicative impacters compound (×1.5, ×1.5 → ×2.25). AdditiveBonus impacters pool (eval − 1) into one ×(1 + Σ) (+50%, +50% → ×2.0). FlatBonus: post-multiplication additive. Committed history: all of it, where it was measured. It comes after the modifiers, so a transient % modifier doesn't scale it. 50 base × 1.5 aura + 10 tome = 85, and a 30 hit under the aura takes 30. Override: per-slot, lowest SortOrder wins. It comes after the committed history, so an override ("stun: speed = 0") still pins the value. Constrain: element overflow clamp (AttributeOverflowData.Clamp) + rounding policy. Attribution is captured during the walk, so GetBreakdown() always sums to ActiveValue: the root → its group; commits → their groups; each modifier → the value swing its op produced; pooled multiplies → proportional shares; the constraint shift → the unattributed slice.

guides/effect-pipeline/2-attribute-state.title: 2.2 Commit math | PlayForge
guides/effect-pipeline/2-attribute-state.summary: 2.2 Commit math CommitImpact(carrier, impacters) runs each impacter as a sequential mini-step against the live value (op → clamp → round). It records each step's post-constraint delta into its group: a +50 heal clamped to +30 commits +30. Then it runs one canonical Recompute. Reproducibility invariant: ActiveValue is always exactly Recompute(state), since every mutation path ends in a recompute. There is no second bookkeeping system to drift.

guides/effect-pipeline/2-attribute-state.title: 2.3 Query surface | PlayForge
guides/effect-pipeline/2-attribute-state.summary: 2.3 Query surface Two pairs of calls read an attribute's groups and its breakdown: Calls On GetGroupValue(Tag) / GetBreakdown() CachedAttributeValue TryGetGroupValue(attr, group, out v) / GetBreakdown(attr) AttributeSystemComponent Consumer pattern: UI splits a health bar by group slices. A damage formula reads GetGroupValue(damage, Group.Base) vs GetGroupValue(damage, Group.Bonus) and applies different outgoing calculations. Group-specific math lives in consumers, not the pipeline.

guides/effect-pipeline/3-the-four-verb-a.summary:
3. The four-verb attribute API (AttributeSystemComponent) Every attribute mutation funnels through one shared 4-phase pipeline (CommitWithCarrier): flowchart TD classDef general fill:#FFE86D,stroke:#CBB333,color:#574900 classDef decision fill:#A0C4FB,stroke:#6A8BBF,color:#14315E classDef terminator fill:#DDDDD8,stroke:#A8A8A0,color:#434339 v(["a verb: RegisterModifier (Continuous), UnregisterModifier (its reversal),
CommitImpact (permanent) or ModifyAttribute (a Commit with no impacters)"]):::terminator c1["CommitWithCarrier(attr, smav, runEvents, mode, impacters)"]:::general m{"mode?"}:::decision f["freeze the impacters: ScalerImpacter.Evaluate,

then CachedAttributeValue.PreviewCommit makes the ChangeValue"]:::general pre["Callbacks.AttributePreChange(attr, change)
then, when runEvents, the PreChange attribute workers:

that may edit the change, or DeferredIntercept actions"]:::general soak["Commit only: a workable loss soaks into the Barrier-role
attributes that absorb for it, and a workable gain
is scaled by GainsScaledBy"]:::general arc["apply: Register adds the modifier, Unregister removes it,
Commit records it under its retention group
Recompute: root, Adds, Multiply, FlatBonus, the commits,
Override (the lowest SortOrder wins)
constrain: overflow clamp, rounding, AutoScaleWithBase"]:::general post["the PostChange attribute workers,
then Callbacks.AttributePostChange"]:::general id["ImpactData.Generate: the target's RecordFrameImpactReceived
(FrameSummary, OnImpactReceived, the combat log, IMPACT_TAKEN),
then the dealer's ProvideFrameImpactDealt"]:::general cb["Callbacks.AttributeChanged, AttributeBaseChanged,
AttributeCurrentZero or AttributeCurrentFull

the dependents and runs their post-change workers and callbacks"]:::general eof(["at the end of frame: the deferred actions,
the analysis workers and WatchProjectHealth"]):::terminator v --> c1 --> m m -->|Commit| f --> pre m -->|Register or Unregister| pre pre --> soak --> arc --> post --> id --> cb --> eof What one change runs through, from the verb to the end of frame. Register and Unregister keep the transport value; only a Commit previews its delta. pre-change workers; PHASE-2 dispatch; post-change workers; impact relay (ImpactData, frame summaries, source-side TrackImpact, AttributeChanged). Four verbs make up the API, each with its own dispatch: Verb Dispatch Used by RegisterModifier(attr, smv, impacters) register/refresh in modifiers + recompute Continuous entries on apply / stack refresh / replace UnregisterModifier(attr, smv) remove carrier's entries + recompute removal & replacement (see below) CommitImpact(attr, smv, impacters) permanent per-group commit OnApply / Periodic entries ModifyAttribute(attr, smv) CommitImpact; a delta-only carrier's delta commits as constant Adds in its retention group init pulse, EnforceScaling propagation, external systems (TryModifyAttribute) UnregisterModifier fires callbacks like any change, so regulated attributes refresh. Removal used to be silent, which left stale derived values. It's no hit, though: its ImpactData.Ends holds. So: its effect's workers and components hear no impact; its dealer's impact workers don't run; no Impact Taken or Dealt is sent. Registration and unregistration are identity-based on the carrier instance. They are never wrapped in synthetic carriers. Pre-change phase (commits). Before the pre-change callback and workers run, a commit evaluates its impacters once. They are frozen as constants, so a randomized scaler can't roll differently twice. The commit then previews the incoming delta: ops in order, no bounds or rounding. That delta is what ChangeValue holds, since effect specs arrive as (0,0) transport. An Inline worker's edit is what commits: untouched → the frozen impacters commit as authored (op semantics, per-impacter groups); adjusted → the new delta commits as one constant Add in the impacters' shared group (mixed groups fall back to the carrier's retention group). Either way §2.2 applies: post-constraint delta recorded, then Recompute. Armor therefore acts on incoming damage and the clamp comes after: 20 HP, −30 hit, 50% armor → −15 → 5 HP. Raw deltas (ModifyAttribute) preview as themselves. Register/Unregister are observe-only here, because modifiers are re-derived every recompute, so a one-off adjustment has nowhere to live. A commit allocates nothing, adjusted or not. It rents its ChangeValue and its frozen impacters and gives them back when it's done. It rents one set for each commit in progress, since a worker or a listener can commit inside another. An adjusted delta's Adds are frozen in the same impacters. So: a ChangeValue belongs to its commit. A callback or an Inline worker reads it during the call, or copies its Value, and doesn't keep it; a Deferred worker's actions may keep it. A change handed to one is left to them, and its commit takes a new one for the next; the source-side TrackImpact keeps a total, the last impact and a count, not every impact. A raw delta allocates nothing on its way through either. Its delta's Adds are frozen in the same impacters, and a SourceAttributeImpact keeps the origin it makes. GenerateSimple makes a new carrier on every call. So a raw delta made every frame keeps its carrier, made once with IAttributeImpactCarrier.GenerateSourceDerivation(source, attribute). The changes the system makes on someone's behalf, EnforceScaling's rescale and the lifesteal worker's heal, allocate nothing either: each is carried by a carrier kept for its source and attribute, in a table keyed weakly by source, so a source that's gone isn't held; each deferred one is queued in a ModifyAttributeAction that the system takes back once the queue has run it: so a listener of OnActionQueued or OnActionExecuted reads an action during the call; one the queue invalidates isn't taken back; the queue walks its priority buckets by index, and EnqueueRange reads a list or an array by index, so taking an action off allocates nothing. Null or undefined attribute targets early-out safely: pure tag-grant effects are legal.

Magnitudes are always evaluated freshly by the impacter pipeline. In this section 4.1 Re-application (ReApplicationPolicy): The re-application policy decides what an application does when the target already has the effect 4.2 Loop-safety invariants (do not undo): The effect shelf relies on these invariants for its correctness and its cost

guides/effect-pipeline/4-effect-lifecycl.title: 4.1 Re-application (ReApplicationPolicy) | PlayForge
guides/effect-pipeline/4-effect-lifecycl.summary: 4.1 Re-application (ReApplicationPolicy) The re-application policy decides what an application does when the target already has the effect: Policy Behavior DoNothing absorbed; only the interaction runs ReplaceOldContainer ReverseImpact() old spec → container adopts new spec (+durations; stack count preserved) → register new spec's Continuous entries. Old commits stay: commits never reverse. AppendNewContainer fresh container + distinct spec instance → modifiers coexist (stacking by coexistence; MultiplyBehaviour controls composition) StackExistingContainers Stack(n) on the found container → re-register Continuous entries so stack-aware magnitudes recompute now Under StackExistingContainers, ScalerImpacter evaluates container-aware via spec.RuntimeContainer. A stack lost when its time runs out re-registers the same way, as does the stack Extend adds to independent durations. ReApplicationInteraction (Refresh/Extend + re-fire TickOnApplication) runs only when absorbed. The append path would double-tick otherwise.

guides/effect-pipeline/4-effect-lifecycl.title: 4.2 Loop-safety invariants (do not undo) | PlayForge
guides/effect-pipeline/4-effect-lifecycl.summary: 4.2 Loop-safety invariants (do not undo) The effect shelf relies on these invariants for its correctness and its cost: All finish paths go through MarkFinished, exactly once: a duplicate OnRemove would be a double reversal. A set mirrors the finished list, so marking a container and skipping a finished one never walk it. TickEffectShelf iterates by index over the frame-start count, since contained effects add to the shelf mid-loop. Already-finished containers are skipped. ClearFinishedEffects snapshots-and-clears. Then it takes the whole pass off the shelf and out of the index, in one walk of each, before any OnRemove. Taken off one at a time, each a linear remove, ending n containers cost n². A spec builds its impacters once, with each delivery's attributes and each attribute's impacters. GetImpactersFor returns the spec's own list: read it, don't change it. A tick's lookups, its contained effects and a recompute allocate nothing. Walk the lists by index or with a foreach over the concrete type, since one through an interface boxes. Scaler-driven execute-tick counts are evaluated once per batch, never per loop iteration. An effect asked for again on an entity before its own application there is over is refused, with one warning per entity and effect. Before this rule, an effect that contained itself, directly or through other contained effects or what applying it set off, recursed until the stack overflowed. Any change to a container's stack count re-registers its Continuous entries, gained or lost. Applying never walks the shelf: its requirements wait for one pass at the next tick; a container's tags count from the moment it is shelved; re-application finds its containers in an index by asset tag, which Shelve and Unshelve keep. Before, each application re-checked every container and rebuilt all tags, so it cost as much as the entity carried.

guides/effect-pipeline/5-recalculation-r.title: 5. Recalculation (regulated attributes) | PlayForge
guides/effect-pipeline/5-recalculation-r.summary: 5. Recalculation (regulated attributes) A regulated attribute is recomputed when an attribute it depends on changes. Blueprint cached scalers register contact → dependent edges at attribute registration (ProvideAttribute → RegulateContactWith). Any commit or modifier registration or unregistration then sets off this chain: The change fires AttributeChanged, whose handler runs RefreshRegulatedAttributes(contact). The dependents Recompute. Each re-derives its root from the contact's fresh ActiveValue, and its own modifiers and committed history are preserved. A dependent whose value changes fires a chained AttributeChanged, cycle-guarded. A dependent's refresh is the system's own change. It takes the post-change half of the pipeline: EnforceScaling, post-change workers and AttributePostChange. It is recorded in the frame summary as received and dealt, self to self. Its carrier is the attribute's root, typed DisallowImpact, so a worker that checks impact types passes it by. Effect-magnitude scalers that read attributes capture snapshots at apply time, by design. Only blueprint scalers create live dependencies.

guides/effect-pipeline/6-initialization-.title: 6. Initialization & auto-scaling | PlayForge
guides/effect-pipeline/6-initialization-.summary: 6. Initialization & auto-scaling Attributes initialize as their set is provided, and an auto-scaling attribute's Current follows its Base: ProvideAttributeSet: register attributes → initialize each cached value (first recompute) → zero-delta ModifyAttribute pulse per attribute. Callbacks observe initial values. No worker does, as the pulse runs none and is unworkable. The pulse commits nothing. EnforceScaling (AutoScaleWithBase): Base changes, a dependent's refresh included, enqueue a deferred proportional Current adjustment. The adjustment goes through a synthetic carrier, kept for whoever changed Base, and lands as ordinary committed history. The carrier is typed DisallowImpact and unworkable, as the pulse is, so no worker that checks impact types sees it. The adjustment is a share of Current before the bounds, where it lands, so the bounds clamp the result once. Under ZeroToBase, an 80/100 attribute that loses half its Base ends at 40/50.

guides/effect-pipeline/7-entry-derivatio.title: 7. Entry derivation (no asset migration) | PlayForge
guides/effect-pipeline/7-entry-derivatio.summary: 7. Entry derivation (no asset migration) The first entry is derived, never serialized. The effect's impact quad + duration flags are its authored surface. GameplayEffectImpact.RebuildEntries re-derives that entry on every Generate(). So inspector edits (magnitude, attribute target, duration policy, tick flags) always take effect on the next application. Magnitude on the derived entry references the live ScalableFloat, so even already-registered modifiers re-evaluate new magnitudes on their next recompute. Note Serializing the derived entry was tried and reverted: OnValidate froze half-authored state into assets (null targets, stale magnitudes, deliveries minted while the policy was still Instant) and never re-synced. Additional impacts are authored entries. GameplayEffectImpact.AdditionalImpacts holds AttributeImpactEntry values that the impact drawer edits, each naming its own delivery. RebuildEntries appends them, live, after the derived entry. It skips one with no attribute, and one whose delivery the duration can't make (IsDeliveryValidFor), which the drawer flags in place. ResolveDelivery derives the first entry's delivery from the authored shape: Authored shape Derived delivery Instant OnApply Durational/Infinite, no ticks Continuous + periodic ticks Periodic (ReverseImpactOnRemoval flagged: rollback no longer exists) TickOnApplication-only trap Continuous for Multiply/Override (flagged), else OnApply Window → PlayForge → Problems lists each effect that has one of the shapes above, among the validator's other problems. It's read-only: nothing is written. Deleted outright: IsSustainedModifier(); the Mode A/B inference; TickAttribute; RollbackCommittedDelta; tick-rollback via TrackedImpact, which is analytics-only now.

guides/effect-pipeline/8-verification.ht.title: 8. Verification | PlayForge
guides/effect-pipeline/8-verification.ht.summary: 8. Verification The golden tests in Assets/PlayForge/Tests/Editor/PlayForgeGoldenTests.cs pin this pipeline. Run them from the Test Runner's EditMode tab, FarEmerald.PlayForge.Tests.Golden, or in batchmode with -executeMethod FarEmerald.PlayForge.Tests.PlayForgeGoldenTests.RunAll. Their scenarios pin: multiplicative/pooled buff add/remove ordering (the 50→60→72→60→50 case); item modifier reversal; HoT permanence through expiry; clamp + history reproducibility; committed history landing after the modifiers; stack-aware magnitudes; regulation propagation on removal; null-target effects; replace idempotency; group attribution sums; pre-change workers adjusting the committed delta (armor before the clamp).

guides/effect-pipeline/index.html.title: Gameplay Effect & Attribute Pipeline | PlayForge
guides/effect-pipeline/index.html.summary: Gameplay Effect & Attribute Pipeline This page describes how a GameplayEffect becomes an attribute change, stays correct while it lives, and reverses when it dies, under the two-kind impact model. It is the authoritative description of the runtime pipeline. If code and doc disagree, one of them has a bug: file it either way. All paths are relative to Assets/PlayForge/Runtime/PlayForge/. In this guide 1. The model in one page: Every authored impact is an AttributeImpactEntry on GameplayEffectImpact.Entries, and its delivery makes it one of two kinds of change: a modifier or a commit. 2. Attribute state (CachedAttributeValue): Each attribute's runtime state is a CachedAttributeValue, whose ActiveValue is derived from that state 3. The four-verb attribute API (AttributeSystemComponent): Every attribute mutation funnels through one shared 4-phase pipeline (CommitWithCarrier) 4. Effect lifecycle (EffectSystemComponent): One shared component owns the shelf. 5. Recalculation (regulated attributes): A regulated attribute is recomputed when an attribute it depends on changes. 6. Initialization & auto-scaling: Attributes initialize as their set is provided, and an auto-scaling attribute's Current follows its Base 7. Entry derivation (no asset migration): The first entry is derived, never serialized. The effect's impact quad + duration flags are its authored surface. 8. Verification: The golden tests in Assets/PlayForge/Tests/Editor/PlayForgeGoldenTests.cs pin this pipeline.

guides/effects/built-in-kinds.html.title: Built-in kinds | PlayForge
guides/effects/built-in-kinds.html.summary: Built-in kinds The kinds PlayForge ships for this guide's pickers, each with its menu and what it does, as its picker says. A project's own kinds join them in the same pickers. In this section Components Changes Stacking Purge filters

guides/effects/built-in-kinds/changes.ht.title: Changes | PlayForge
guides/effects/built-in-kinds/changes.ht.summary: Changes Kind Menu What it does AddContainedEffectChange — Adds a contained effect, landing as it lands, each tick, or as it ends. AddOverflowChange — Adds an overflow effect, landing as an application would pass its most stacks. ChanceChange — Changes its chance to apply. ChangeImpactChange — Changes the numbers of its impacts by a Value Pipeline stage. DurationChange — Changes how long it lasts. GrantTagsChange — Adds tags it grants while it's on. StacksChange — Changes its most stacks, and how many a landing gives.

guides/effects/built-in-kinds/components.title: Components | PlayForge
guides/effects/built-in-kinds/components.summary: Components Kind Menu What it does AreaEffectComponent — Lands the effect on others near its target too. AuraEffectComponent — Gives those near the target an aura's effects while the effect lasts. CuesEffectComponent — Shows and sounds the effect's moments: as it lands, ticks, stacks or comes off, while it lasts, and as it's refused. SideChangeEffectComponent — Changes the target's sides while the effect lasts, as a mind control. SpreadEffectComponent — Spreads the effect, or another, from its target to those near it. TransferEffectComponent — Moves an amount of an attribute from the caster or the target to either.

guides/effects/built-in-kinds/purge-filt.title: Purge filters | PlayForge
guides/effects/built-in-kinds/purge-filt.summary: Purge filters Kind Menu What it does ExceptTaggedPurgeFilter — Spares the effects carrying one of its tags.

guides/effects/built-in-kinds/stacking.h.title: Stacking | PlayForge
guides/effects/built-in-kinds/stacking.h.summary: Stacking Kind Menu What it does InitializationOperation — The stacks a new effect starts with. StackAmountOperation — How many stacks an application adds. StackBoundsConfig — The fewest and the most stacks the effect holds, and what happens at the most.
