Property Description Policy End (default): as it dies, its hub ends it at its frame's end, as an entity always did. Stay: keeps it, dead, until it revives, for a MOBA hero or anyone who dies and comes back. Dies At Zero Health On by default: where no death watcher watches, the entity dies as the attribute playing its project's Health role reaches 0. Off, as for a training dummy, that attribute doesn't kill it. Purges On by default: a staying entity's death purges its effects, all but those it keeps. Keeps As Project On, it keeps what its project's Purge Levels keep on death. Keeps Tiers More tiers it keeps. Keeps Categories More categories it keeps, whatever their effects' tiers. On Death The effects it takes as it dies. On Revive The effects it takes as it revives, such as its health back. Body A MonoBehaviour process, a prefab, that it spawns where it is as it starts and as it revives, and ends as it dies. In this section How an entity dies: An entity dies as a death watcher among its analysis workers, or its attribute set's, says it does. Staying dead: An entity whose Policy is Stay dies at its frame's end and stays registered, with its items, levels and lasting effects. Purging on death: A staying entity's death purges its effects, all but those it keeps, as the games' deaths do (Effects: Purging). On Death and On Revive: A staying entity takes the effects these two lists hold as it dies and as it revives. Body: An entity's Body is a MonoBehaviour process, a prefab, that it spawns where it is as it starts and as it revives, and ends as it dies. Reviving: Revive(at) on either hub brings a staying entity back, at a point or where it was.

guides/entities/death/body.html.title: Body | PlayForge
guides/entities/death/body.html.summary: Body An entity's Body is a MonoBehaviour process, a prefab, that it spawns where it is as it starts and as it revives, and ends as it dies. A runtime entity takes its position from its body, so an area search finds it there. GetBody() returns the body. UseBody(process) gives a running entity a body of its own at runtime: a process running already, or one registered for it there. The entity follows it, and it ends with the entity as the entity dies, as its identity's Body does. A revive spawns the identity's Body, where it has one. The body the entity had ends first. UseBody(null) lets one go, ending it. A dead entity takes none.

guides/entities/death/how-an-entity-dies.title: How an entity dies | PlayForge
guides/entities/death/how-an-entity-dies.summary: How an entity dies An entity dies as a death watcher among its analysis workers, or its attribute set's, says it does. Where none watches, and an attribute plays its project's Health role (Attributes: Roles), it dies as that attribute reaches 0. Dies At Zero Health, on by default, says it does. Off, as for a training dummy, that attribute doesn't kill it.

guides/entities/death/on-death-and-on-re.title: On Death and On Revive | PlayForge
guides/entities/death/on-death-and-on-re.summary: On Death and On Revive A staying entity takes the effects these two lists hold as it dies and as it revives. On Death holds the effects it takes as it dies. A respawn timer is a durational effect with a Revive On Removal worker: as it ends, the entity revives, where it was or at a point. On Revive holds the effects it takes as it revives, such as its health back.

guides/entities/death/purging-on-death.h.title: Purging on death | PlayForge
guides/entities/death/purging-on-death.h.summary: Purging on death A staying entity's death purges its effects, all but those it keeps, as the games' deaths do (Effects: Purging). Purges, on by default, turns the purge on. It keeps the categories it keeps, whatever their effects' tiers, and the tiers it keeps. The categories are: Category What it holds Cooldown An ability's cooldown. Lent What an equipped item, a set bonus, an aura or a passive lends. A passive is an ability that activates as it's granted, and what applied an effect can claim it so too, through spec.Claimed. Toggle A Toggle component's effect, or one an ability's component claims as a toggle's. Own The rest it applied to itself. Three fields say what it keeps: Keeps As Project, on, keeps what its project's Purge Levels keep on death: each tier's Kept On Death, and their Kept On Death categories. Keeps Tiers keeps more tiers. Keeps Categories keeps more categories. A project starts with cooldowns, lent effects and toggles as its Kept On Death categories, and those are what a death keeps with no project. An effect at no tier goes, unless a category it's of is kept. Note The purge took the place of Ends Effects Tagged, which ended effects by their tags.

guides/entities/death/reviving.html.title: Reviving | PlayForge
guides/entities/death/reviving.html.summary: Reviving Revive(at) on either hub brings a staying entity back, at a point or where it was. It re-arms the entity's analysis workers, so its death watcher sees its next death. Callbacks hear OnEntityRevived, as they hear OnEntityDied.

guides/entities/death/staying-dead.html.title: Staying dead | PlayForge
guides/entities/death/staying-dead.html.summary: Staying dead An entity whose Policy is Stay dies at its frame's end and stays registered, with its items, levels and lasting effects. Its abilities are refused while it's dead. A dead entity takes no one else's effects, as the dead in the games are untargetable. An effect another applies to it while it's dead is refused. Its own effects still land, as its On Death respawn timer and its On Revive effects do.

guides/entities/effect-journal.html.title: Effect Journal | PlayForge
guides/entities/effect-journal.html.summary: Effect Journal An EffectJournal keeps the life of each effect on the entities it listens to. The Creator Lab's bottom panel reads one, and so does the Debugger's Timeline. In this section Listening: An effect journal records only while it listens, and an entity no journal listens to pays nothing. Reading the journal: An effect journal keeps its entries in order, and counts each one it writes. Journal entries: Each entry in an effect journal is an EffectJournalEntry.

guides/entities/effect-journal/journal-e.title: Journal entries | PlayForge
guides/entities/effect-journal/journal-e.summary: Journal entries Each entry in an effect journal is an EffectJournalEntry. It holds its Kind, its Time and Frame, the Entity it happened on, the Effect, its Spec and its Source, and what its kind tells. Kind What it tells Applied The effect landed, with its first impact's number read as it landed, part by part (Trace, a NumberTrace). Refused It didn't land, and its Refusal says why. Ticked Its ticks executed, Ticks of them. Impact A change it made, to its Attribute, by its Change, with its Breakdown through its pipeline. Removed It came off. Worker One of its workers heard one of its moments, or one of its dealer's impact workers ran for its hit. An entry reads as a line: "Burn landed on Target, from Caster", "Poison refused by Target: immunity", "Burn's Noting heard it tick on Target, queuing Ticked". Refusals A refused entry's Refusal is one of these: Dead: the entity is dead. Affiliation: its affiliation policy doesn't take the entity. Requirements: its requirements don't hold. Immunity: an immunity names it. Chance: its chance missed. Stopped: a Block or Evade stopped it. Cycle: it was asked for again inside its own application. Callbacks hear each refusal as OnEffectRefused(spec, refusal). Worker entries A worker entry holds: the Worker, and its WorkerName; the Hook: Application, Tick, Removal or Impact; the Side it ran on: the Target, or the Dealer for a hit, as Workers: The map says; the Actions it queued, each Queued, Ran or Dropped.

guides/entities/effect-journal/listening.title: Listening | PlayForge
guides/entities/effect-journal/listening.summary: Listening An effect journal records only while it listens, and an entity no journal listens to pays nothing. Method What it does Listen(gas) Listens to one entity. Follow(list) Listens to these entities and no others. Forget(gas) Stops listening to one entity. Dispose() Stops listening to all of them. What it wrote stays.

guides/entities/effect-journal/reading-t.title: Reading the journal | PlayForge
guides/entities/effect-journal/reading-t.summary: Reading the journal An effect journal keeps its entries in order, and counts each one it writes. Its Entries run oldest first: its last Keep of them, 500 unless it's told otherwise. Of(effect) and On(entity) filter them. Written counts every entry it wrote. Wrote is raised as each is written.

guides/entities/identity.html.title: Identity | PlayForge
guides/entities/identity.html.summary: Identity The Identity section names the entity, shows its asset tag and holds its icons. sequenceDiagram autonumber participant B as Bootstrapper participant PC as ProcessControl participant W as ProcessWorld participant PCB as ProcessControlBlock participant H as GAS hub participant C as GASCore participant S as Subsystems B->>B: Bootstrap(), TagRegistry.Initialize, AttributeRegistry.Add B->>PC: instantiate ProcessControlPrefab if there is no Instance B->>PC: Bootstrap(deferStartState true) PC->>W: ResetProcessControl(Ready), ApplyTickRate() B->>PC: Register(GameRootPrefab).With(Default()).Run(out relay) B->>PC: EnterStartState, BootstrapOverrides(), DeferredInit() PC->>PC: CollectSceneProcesses(), by priority then depth PC->>W: Register(p).With(Default()).In(this).Run() Note over PC,W: The taker is the given world, else the Instance's World. The handler is the given one, else the packet's source, else GameRoot W->>W: refuse AlreadyRegistered or ProcessControlClosed W->>PCB: ProcessControlBlock.Generate makes the ProcessRelay W->>W: HandlerSubscribeProcess(relay), SetProcess, ConfigureWrapper W->>PCB: Initialize() PCB->>H: SendProcessData(data, relay), WhenInitialize() alt Mono hub H->>C: new GASCore(this, Callbacks) H->>C: Initialize(new RuntimeEntityIdentity(EntityData), affiliation) else Runtime hub Note over H,C: Its constructor already built and initialized the GASCore. WhenInitialize applies a registration AFFILIATION end C->>C: localData.Init(identity), ForgeEntities.Add(owner) C->>S: Setup each subsystem, AttributeSystem.Setup(AttributeSet) C->>C: InitializeEndOfFrame() makes ActionQueue, FrameSummary, AnalysisCache C->>S: SetDeferredContext C->>S: InitWorkers of the identity, the AttributeSet, the project's Every-Entity group C->>S: LevelSystem.Register(AssetTag), AbilitySystem.Initialize(StartingAbilities) C->>S: AttributeSystem.Initialize(), a CachedAttributeValue each, a zero pulse C->>S: ItemSystem.Initialize(StartingItems), CompileGrantedTags() C->>S: ActivateImmediateAbilities(), SpawnBody(), components Register C-->>H: Callbacks.SystemInitialized() W->>W: Callbacks.OnProcessRegistered W->>PCB: the default transition for its lifecycle Note over W,PCB: SelfTerminating, RunThenWait and Synchronous go to Running. RequiresControl waits for relay.Run() From the Bootstrapper to a registered entity. The runtime hub initializes in its constructor, the Mono hub when it registers. Property Description Name The entity's display name, which also gives the asset tag. Renaming the entity changes its tag, so update anything that names the old tag. Description Free text for your UI. Asset Tag Read-only, made from the Name: punctuation is dropped, and each word is capitalised and joined. Textures Icons, each paired with a tag. The texture tagged Primary is the entity's icon; without one, the first texture is used. The asset tag is stored when you edit the Name, and the inspector header shows it after the entity's type. If the stored tag differs from the one the Name gives, it shows in warning text with an Update button that stores the new one.

Both hubs implement it and forward to one internal GASCore, which reads only a RuntimeEntityIdentity. The asset is the entity's starting setup: its attributes, abilities, items, tags, level and workers. Many entities can share one asset. At runtime, a GAS hub reads the asset when it initializes. The hub is either the GameplayAbilitySystem component on a GameObject, or a RuntimeGameplayAbilitySystem made from code. As it initializes, the hub: Subscribes the entity's workers. Registers its level. Gives its Starting Abilities. Builds its attributes from its Attribute Set. Gives its Starting Items. Applies its tags. Tags are names, such as State.Stunned, that an entity carries and that requirements check. Each asset stores a tag made from its Name: Hero gives Entity.Hero. The entity carries this tag and keeps its own level under it. Each section below matches the inspector section of the same name. A collapsed section shows one line about what it holds, such as the level range or how many starting items the entity equips. The inspector's header shows the entity's one-line summary, as The Forge's Summary column does. The line gives the first three attributes of the entity's attribute set as it starts, at its starting level, then its starting abilities: "Health 500, Mana 300, Armor 5; Fireball, Blink". In this guide Identity: The Identity section names the entity, shows its asset tag and holds its icons. Leveling: The Leveling section sets the entity's level range. Tags: The Tags section sets the entity's sides and the tags it carries. Attributes: The Attributes section names the entity's attribute set and the attribute its time runs at. Abilities: The Abilities section sets the abilities the entity starts with, how many it can hold, and what its abilities do while another is busy. Items: The Items section sets the items the entity starts with and the limits on its inventory. Components: An entity's components are features it carries, each a class with hooks into the entity's life. Workers: Workers are reusable behaviours, picked from a list, that react to what happens to an entity. Death: The Death section sets what the entity's death does. Combat Log: Each entity keeps a combat log of what happens to it. Effect Journal: An EffectJournal keeps the life of each effect on the entities it listens to. Local Data: Local Data is a list of named values stored on the asset. Used By: The Used By section lists the PlayForge assets that refer to this entity, each with its type icon, such as the abilities and items linked to it. Built-in kinds: The kinds PlayForge ships for this guide's pickers, each with its menu and what it does, as its picker says. guides/entities/items.html.title: Items | PlayForge
guides/entities/items.html.summary: Items The Items section sets the items the entity starts with and the limits on its inventory. Property Description Starting Items Items the entity is given when its GAS initializes, one row each. A row's Equip equips the item as it is given. Max Items The most items the inventory can hold, 99 by default. Max Equipped Items The most items equipped at once, 99 by default. Allow Duplicates Lets the inventory hold the same item more than once. Off by default. Equipped Too Lets more than one copy of the same item be equipped at once. Off by default; it needs Allow Duplicates, since an inventory that holds one of each item has no second copy to equip. Each Max field is a number or, by its kind, a scaler that changes the limit with the entity's level, with its rounding (Scalers). A give or equip that breaks a limit fails.

guides/entities/leveling.html.title: Leveling | PlayForge
guides/entities/leveling.html.summary: Leveling The Leveling section sets the entity's level range. An entity's level is kept under its asset tag. A level provider is an asset whose level range another asset follows. Property Description Link Mode Standalone (default): keeps the entity's own range. Linked To Provider: shows a provider's range instead. Starting Level The entity's level when its GAS initializes, 1 by default. It's also the entity's lowest level. Max Level Its highest level, 99 by default. The level always stays within this range. Level Provider Shown while linked: the asset whose range the section shows, an Entity, Ability, Effect, Item or Attribute Set. Right-click the Level Provider field to pick from one type. A link that would make a loop is refused, with an error in the Console. While no provider is set, a warning says the entity uses its own range. Two buttons link the entity's Starting Items and Starting Abilities to it, or unlink them. Each asks first, and one Undo takes it back. Link Items & Abilities links this entity's Starting Items and Starting Abilities to it, so their per-level values follow its range. Unlink Items & Abilities removes the links that point at this entity. The entity's level feeds per-level values: the effects it applies as an origin; its Max Abilities and item limits; the cached scalers in its attribute set. Code changes the level through the GAS, with SetLevel or ModifyLevel and the entity's asset tag. Note At runtime, the entity's level range comes from its own Starting Level and Max Level, even while it is linked.

guides/entities/local-data.html.title: Local Data | PlayForge
guides/entities/local-data.html.summary: Local Data Local Data is a list of named values stored on the asset. Each row has a Key (a tag) and a value of a kind. Column Description Key A tag that names the row. Kind The kind of value: Float, Int, String, Bool, Tag, Attribute, Effect, Ability, Entity, Object, MonoBehaviour or ScriptableObject, or a kind of your own. Value The row's value. A row saves its own value alone. A kind of your own is a [Serializable] class made from LocalDataValue<T>, such as a point or a colour. The row's kinds offer it beside PlayForge's. Object fields take project assets, not scene objects. Code reads a value by its type, with data.TryGet(out float range) or data.TryGet(out MyPoint point). A number, a Float or an Int, can scale. Code reads it with data.Value.TryReadNumber(context, out float number). When a GameplayAbilitySystem component initializes, it loads the entity's Local Data into a store of its own. A RuntimeGameplayAbilitySystem loads its identity's rows the same way: the entity asset's, where it's made from one. Code and workers read and write that store through the GAS, with TryGetLocalData and SetLocalData. Threshold analysis workers, for example, note there that they have fired.

guides/entities/tags.html.title: Tags | PlayForge
guides/entities/tags.html.summary: Tags The Tags section sets the entity's sides and the tags it carries. Property Description Affiliation The entity's team or faction tags. An effect's Affiliation check compares its origin's affiliation with its target's. Context Tags Tags that describe the entity, such as Undead. Changes the entity makes as an origin itself carry them as context, and workers can filter by them. Granted Tags Tags that are always applied to the entity. In this section Affiliation at runtime: An entity's affiliation can change as the game runs, from code or from an effect. Hearing tag changes: Code hears an entity's tags change through its tag cache.

guides/entities/tags/affiliation-at-runt.title: Affiliation at runtime | PlayForge
guides/entities/tags/affiliation-at-runt.summary: Affiliation at runtime An entity's affiliation can change as the game runs, from code or from an effect. Code that starts a GAS can pass affiliation tags in its registration data. Those replace the asset's list. As the game runs, SetAffiliation on either hub sets them, for a side switch or a scripted betrayal. The GAS also applies these tags to the entity, on either hub. An effect's Side Change goes over them while it lasts (Effects). GetSides says which side changes the entity is under.

guides/entities/tags/hearing-tag-changes.title: Hearing tag changes | PlayForge
guides/entities/tags/hearing-tag-changes.summary: Hearing tag changes Code hears an entity's tags change through its tag cache. gas.GetTagCache().Listen(tag, onChange) hears the tag, and every tag under it, come and go, as it happens. Pass ETagChangeKind.AnyCount to hear every change to a tag's weight. Each change says the tag, and its weight before and after. TagChanged hears every change to any tag. When the entity rebuilds its tags from their sources, it tells only what the rebuild changed. It rebuilds them as an ability starts or ends, as an item changes, or as a loose tag is granted. The listener below drives an animator's Stunned flag. Dispose the listener to stop it. var listener = gas.GetTagCache().Listen(stunned, change => animator.SetBool("Stunned", change.Added)); listener.Dispose(); A tag worker is evaluated at the end of a frame in which the entity's tags changed. One whose ValidateWorkFor reads more than the tags overrides EvaluateEveryFrame to be evaluated every frame.

guides/entities/used-by.html.title: Used By | PlayForge
guides/entities/used-by.html.summary: Used By The Used By section lists the PlayForge assets that refer to this entity, each with its type icon, such as the abilities and items linked to it. Click a row to select the asset. The list follows the project as it changes.

guides/entities/workers.html.title: Workers | PlayForge
guides/entities/workers.html.summary: Workers Workers are reusable behaviours, picked from a list, that react to what happens to an entity. This group is subscribed when the entity's GAS initializes, and stays for the entity's lifetime. The attribute set's workers are subscribed at the same time. Property Description Name Labels the group. Attribute Workers that run before or after an attribute changes, for example to reduce incoming damage. Impact Workers that inspect the changes the entity deals. Tag Workers that react when the entity's tags change. Analysis Workers that examine the frame at its end, for example to detect death. Each list's + adds an empty worker to pick a kind for. The section's import button copies a worker group from another asset. Above the worker group, the section holds the entity's Modifiers. In this section Threshold: A Threshold, an analysis worker, acts as an attribute crosses a value, without code. Can't Fall Below and Return Damage: Two attribute workers keep the common rules. Modifiers: Modifiers, above the workers, change other effects as they're made, for as long as the entity lives. Lifesteal: An entity's own lifesteal is its Lifesteal: the attribute its project's Lifesteal worker names as its Share.

guides/entities/workers/cant-fall-below-.title: Can't Fall Below and Return Damage | PlayForge
guides/entities/workers/cant-fall-below-.summary: Can't Fall Below and Return Damage Two attribute workers keep the common rules. Worker What it does Can't Fall Below Holds its attribute at its Floor: a loss that would take it lower takes it to the floor. Return Damage Sends its Share of each workable loss its attribute takes from another back to the one who dealt it, as Blade Mail does. Shallow Grave keeps its target at 1 Health with a Can't Fall Below, in a buff's worker group while it lasts. What Return Damage sends back is typed Returned. So a return on the other side doesn't send it back again, and no lifesteal heals from it.

guides/entities/workers/lifesteal.html.title: Lifesteal | PlayForge
guides/entities/workers/lifesteal.html.summary: Lifesteal An entity's own lifesteal is its Lifesteal: the attribute its project's Lifesteal worker names as its Share. Its value is its set's value for that attribute, which the Lifesteal worker heals by (Workers: Lifesteal). Note The entity's Lifesteal list is gone.

guides/entities/workers/modifiers.html.title: Modifiers | PlayForge
guides/entities/workers/modifiers.html.summary: Modifiers Modifiers, above the workers, change other effects as they're made, for as long as the entity lives. They change its own effects, such as a Frost Mage's every Chill granting Frozen. They change those landing on it. Each entry is a rule of its own, or names a shared Effect Modifier asset (Effects: Workers: Modifiers).

guides/entities/workers/threshold.html.title: Threshold | PlayForge
guides/entities/workers/threshold.html.summary: Threshold A Threshold, an analysis worker, acts as an attribute crosses a value, without code. Megaera rages as her Health falls past half, and Ice Blast shatters below 13%. Property Description Target The attribute it watches. Groups Which retention groups' parts it reads: all of them, the whole value, by default; only these; or all but these. What What it reads of the attribute: Current, Base, Missing (what's missing of it) or Share (its share of its base). On its share, a Threshold of 0.5 is half. Threshold The value it watches for, read at the entity's level. Crossing When it fires: While It Holds: while its Comparison holds, as it always did. Falling: as what it reads falls to the threshold or below. Rising: as what it reads rises above it. Either: either way. Comparison How what it reads compares with the threshold, where it fires while that holds. Trigger Once Fires at its first crossing alone. Off, it fires each time. Effects The effects it applies to the entity as it fires. Applied By Whom the effects come from: the entity itself, or, set to Crosser, the one whose change crossed it this frame. So a shatter is its caster's, kill and all. Event A gameplay event it sends as it fires, which its abilities' triggers hear. Its source is the one who crossed it, and its subject the entity. It checks at the frame's end, as the death watcher does, so the frame's hits and heals net out. The death watcher is a Threshold that kills. An entity that revives re-arms it. Its first check after the revive notes its side again.

guides/extending/a-games-own-objects.htm.title: A game's own objects | PlayForge
guides/extending/a-games-own-objects.htm.summary: A game's own objects PlayForge asks a game's own objects for a few things through interfaces: turning, moving, shaking the camera, and a pooled cue's comings and goings. This section covers each. In this section Turners: A turner turns an entity's object as PlayForge orders, in place of PlayForge setting the object's rotation. Movers: A mover is a caster's own movement, which PlayForge's movement tasks hold and stop while they move the caster. Camera shakers: A camera shaker shakes the game's camera for PlayForge's Camera Shake cue. Pooled cues: A pooled cue hears its pool hand it out and take it back (Cues: Pooling).

guides/extending/a-games-own-objects/cam.title: Camera shakers | PlayForge
guides/extending/a-games-own-objects/cam.summary: Camera shakers A camera shaker shakes the game's camera for PlayForge's Camera Shake cue. Implement ICameraShaker, and set it as ForgeCues.Shaker. Hooks Hook When PlayForge calls it Shake(float strength, float duration) As the Camera Shake cue plays, which calls it through ForgeCues.Shaker.

guides/extending/a-games-own-objects/mov.title: Movers | PlayForge
guides/extending/a-games-own-objects/mov.summary: Movers A mover is a caster's own movement, which PlayForge's movement tasks hold and stop while they move the caster. Implement IForgeMover on a caster's object. Hooks Hook When PlayForge calls it Hold(bool held), Stop() While a movement task, as Dash, moves the caster: it calls them on the caster's own movement.

guides/extending/a-games-own-objects/poo.title: Pooled cues | PlayForge
guides/extending/a-games-own-objects/poo.summary: Pooled cues A pooled cue hears its pool hand it out and take it back (Cues: Pooling). Implement IPooledCue on a pooled Prefab cue's prefab. Hooks Hook When PlayForge calls it Taken() As its pool hands it out, placed and active. Returned() As it goes back.

guides/extending/a-games-own-objects/tur.title: Turners | PlayForge
guides/extending/a-games-own-objects/tur.summary: Turners A turner turns an entity's object as PlayForge orders, in place of PlayForge setting the object's rotation. Implement IForgeTurner on an entity's object. Hooks Hook When PlayForge calls it Face(Vector3 direction, float degreesPerSecond, float deltaTime) At each step of a turn PlayForge orders, as an ability's turn to face its target. Example This turner turns its object toward the direction PlayForge asks, at the speed it asks: using FarEmerald.PlayForge; using UnityEngine; namespace MyGame { // On an entity's object: turns it toward the direction PlayForge asks, at the speed it asks public sealed class SmoothTurner : MonoBehaviour, IForgeTurner { public void Face(Vector3 direction, float degreesPerSecond, float deltaTime) { direction.y = 0f; if (direction.sqrMagnitude < 0.0001f) return; var goal = Quaternion.LookRotation(direction); transform.rotation = degreesPerSecond <= 0f ? goal : Quaternion.RotateTowards(transform.rotation, goal, degreesPerSecond * deltaTime); } } } An animated character's turner sets its animator's turn here instead, and lets the animation turn the object. Traps PlayForge reads how far is left from the object's rotation, so that's what the turner turns.

guides/extending/ability-tasks.html.title: Ability tasks | PlayForge
guides/extending/ability-tasks.html.summary: Ability tasks An ability task is a step of an ability's stage: it's picked in a stage's Tasks, runs with the stage, and is handed the activation's data. Task instances belong to the asset and are shared. This section covers writing one; Abilities: Stages covers stages. In this section Stage tasks: A stage task is one step of an ability's stage, as applying an effect to the target several times. Asset loaders: An asset loader puts assets in the activation's data for its tasks to read.

guides/extending/ability-tasks/asset-loa.title: Asset loaders | PlayForge
guides/extending/ability-tasks/asset-loa.summary: Asset loaders An asset loader puts assets in the activation's data for its tasks to read. Derive from AbstractSetAssetsTask, whose Activate does nothing. A loader overrides IsCriticalSection, and does its work in Prepare(data), with data.AddPayload(tag, asset). Hooks Hook When PlayForge calls it Prepare(data) Once an activation, after its targeting and before its first stage. The loader's work goes here. IsCriticalSection Required, as for every ability task. An ability's loaders run once an activation, after its targeting and before its first stage. Each is prepared, activated and cleaned at once, so a loader's Activate isn't awaited. In the picker An ability's Asset Loaders offer every class derived from AbstractSetAssetsTask.

guides/extending/ability-tasks/stage-tas.title: Stage tasks | PlayForge
guides/extending/ability-tasks/stage-tas.summary: Stage tasks A stage task is one step of an ability's stage, as applying an effect to the target several times. Derive from AbstractAbilityTask (from AbstractAbilityRelatedTask). Its hooks are handed the activation's data, an AbilityDataPacket, which holds the activation: Member Holds data.EffectOrigin The ability's spec, whose GetSource() is the caster. data.AbilitySpec The same, as an AbilitySpec. data.TryGetFirstTarget(out ITarget target), data.TryGetTarget(EDataTarget policy, out target) The entities its targeting picked, filed under Tags.TARGET_REAL. data.GetTargetingPacket(Tags.TARGET, out var packet, autoInterrupt: false) The pick's place, an entity's or a point's. With autoInterrupt on, its default, a missing pick interrupts the run. data.TryGet(Tags.POSITION, EDataTarget.Primary, out Vector3 point), data.AddPayload(key, value), data.TryGetFirst(key, out T value) Anything filed under a tag. data.GetTaskState<T>(this) What the task keeps for this activation. Its helpers are protected and static: Read(number, data): a ScalableFloat or ScalableInt read at the ability's level. EntityOf(data, NumberSide.Caster) and NumberSide.Target: its caster, or the activation's first target. ApplyTo(data, target, effect): applies an effect from the activation, with the magnitudes its caller set. Hooks Hook When PlayForge calls it IsCriticalSection Required. True holds the ability's claim while its stage runs. Prepare(data) Before its stage's tasks run. Activate(data, token) Required: its work, awaited. An interrupt cancels the token. Clean(data) After it ends, however it ended. Description Its line in the ability's breakdown. While a critical stage holds the claim, the entity's other activations wait or are refused, as their When Busy says. The run takes only the injections its critical policy allows, an interrupt by default. A run with no critical stage lets its claim go as it starts. In the picker A stage's Tasks offer every class derived from AbstractAbilityTask (How a kind is found). The example's [ForgeMenu("Effects")] files it under the Effects submenu, where the picker shows PulseTask as Pulse. Example This task applies its effect to the target several times, a pause apart: using System; using System.Threading; using Cysharp.Threading.Tasks; using FarEmerald.PlayForge; using UnityEngine; namespace MyGame { [Serializable] [ForgeMenu("Effects", Description = "Applies its effect to the target several times, a pause apart.")] public class PulseTask : AbstractAbilityTask { [Tooltip("The effect each pulse applies to the activation's target")] public GameplayEffect Effect; [Tooltip("How many pulses, read at the ability's level")] [NumberMin(1f)] public ScalableInt Pulses = 3; [Tooltip("The pause between pulses, in seconds of the run's time")] [NumberMin(0f)] public ScalableFloat Interval = 0.5f; public override bool IsCriticalSection => false; public override string Description => "Pulses its effect on the target"; public override async UniTask Activate(AbilityDataPacket data, CancellationToken token) { if (Effect == null || !data.TryGetFirstTarget(out var target)) return; int pulses = Read(Pulses, data); float interval = Read(Interval, data); for (int i = 0; i < pulses; i++) { // The library's wait counts the run's clock and holds while the run is paused if (i > 0) await SequenceTaskLibrary.Delay(interval, token); if (!ApplyTo(data, target, Effect)) return; } } } } Traps Wait through the task library or the run's clock. SequenceTaskLibrary.Delay(seconds, token) and the library's other waits hold while the run is paused. A loop of its own reads TaskSequenceRuntime.ClockOfRun(token, data) for the run's clock, and awaits ForgeTick.Next(clock, token) or ForgeTick.NextFrame(token). Await with the token. An interrupt cancels it, and a task that ignores it runs on after its ability has ended. One task serves every activation: keep what one activation counts in data.GetTaskState<T>(this). A stage's policy is All or Any. An ability compiles only those two. A stage policy of another type (IAbilityProxyStagePolicy) runs as All, with a warning.

guides/extending/before-you-start.html.title: Before you start | PlayForge
guides/extending/before-you-start.html.summary: Before you start This section covers what every kind of a game's own shares: the assembly it lives in, how the editor finds it, how its picker names and files it, how its fields show, where it keeps what it counts, and how it's renamed. In this section The assembly: A kind of a game's own compiles in an assembly that references PlayForge's. How a kind is found: The editor finds a kind of a game's own by its base, so nothing registers a kind: writing the class is enough. How a kind is named and filed: [ForgeMenu] on a kind's class says where its picker files it and what it's called. How its fields show: A kind's fields draw under its picker as Unity draws their types. One object for every holder: A kind is one object on its asset, shared by every entity the asset reaches. Renaming a kind: A kind is saved by its class's name, assembly and namespace, so renaming one needs care.

guides/extending/before-you-start/how-a-.title: How a kind is found | PlayForge
guides/extending/before-you-start/how-a-.summary: How a kind is found The editor finds a kind of a game's own by its base, so nothing registers a kind: writing the class is enough. A field a designer picks a kind for is a [SerializeReference] field of an abstract base or an interface. An asset's Components, a stage's Tasks, a worker group's lists and a number field's Kind are such fields. The field's picker lists every class that derives from the field's type, in any assembly the editor loads. It leaves out a class that's abstract or an open generic. Give each kind of your own these two things: A public constructor that takes nothing. The picker makes the kind with it as it's picked. The number, condition and Local Data menus list only classes that have one. Another picker lists a class without one, and fails as it's picked. [Serializable], as PlayForge's own kinds are. The condition menu lists only serializable classes. The constructor runs once for each pick, so it can set defaults of its own over its base's, as CantFallBelowAttributeWorker sets its timing and its sign. Field initializers run with it.

guides/extending/before-you-start/how-a-.title: How a kind is named and filed | PlayForge
guides/extending/before-you-start/how-a-.summary: How a kind is named and filed [ForgeMenu] on a kind's class says where its picker files it and what it's called. Argument What it does A path, as [ForgeMenu("Effects")] Files the kind under a submenu. A slash nests them, as "Effects/Areas". Name = "..." Replaces the class's name in the picker and in the field. Description = "..." What the picker says while the kind is highlighted. A path holds for the classes made from the one that names it. So a kind of AbstractScaler's is filed under its Scaler submenu, unless it names another. [ForgeMenu("")] puts a kind at the top, whatever its base names. Without a Name, a picker shows the class's name spaced out, with its family's word taken off its end: Family Words taken off Example Components EffectComponent, AbilityComponent, EntityComponent, ItemComponent, Component BountyMarkEffectComponent is Bounty Mark Ability tasks AbilityTask, Task PulseTask is Pulse Targeting tasks TargetTask, Task ClickNearestEnemyTargetTask is Click Nearest Enemy Workers, cue handlers, value stages, and the other kinds drawn as workers are Worker, Scaler, Handler, Behaviour, Policy, Rule, Config, Settings, Task, Cue, and a few more GainOnHitWorker is Gain On Hit, AnimatorCue is Animator Scaler behaviours ScalerBehaviour, Behaviour RoundToStepScalerBehaviour is Round To Step Variances Variance TwoDiceVariance is Two Dice Respawn places RespawnPlace NearHomeRespawnPlace is Near Home Injections Injection SkipIfTaggedInjection is Skip If Tagged A number kind takes the name its [NumberKind] gives, and a condition the one its [GameplayCondition] gives (Scalers, number kinds and conditions).

guides/extending/before-you-start/how-it.title: How its fields show | PlayForge
guides/extending/before-you-start/how-it.summary: How its fields show A kind's fields draw under its picker as Unity draws their types. The picker draws a kind's public fields and its [SerializeField] ones, each with its [Tooltip]. [HideInInspector] keeps one out. Two attributes show a field only while another field of the same object says so: Attribute Shows the field while Read by [ShownWhen(nameof(UsePhysics))] A bool is on Tasks, components, workers, cue handlers and the other kinds a picker makes [ShownWhen(nameof(Mode), (int)EMode.Area)] An enum holds one of the values given The same kinds [ForgeShowWhen(nameof(Mode), EMode.Curved)] The same as the two above Scalers, number kinds and conditions A number field of a kind's own is a ScalableFloat or a ScalableInt. Limit it with [NumberMin], [NumberMax] or [NumberRange]: Unity's own [Min] and [Range] don't work on one (Scalers: A number field in your own code). A tag field takes [ForgeTagContext(...)] to say which tags its picker offers (Tags in code).

guides/extending/before-you-start/one-ob.title: One object for every holder | PlayForge
guides/extending/before-you-start/one-ob.summary: One object for every holder A kind is one object on its asset, shared by every entity the asset reaches. One Burn effect's component serves every burning entity, and one ability's task serves every activation of it. So a kind keeps nothing for one holder in its own fields. Each family hands it a place to keep that: Family Where it keeps what it counts for one holder Components ctx.GetState<T>(this): one effect application's, one entity's ability's, one entity's, one entity's item's Effect workers ctx.GetState<T>(this) in its hooks, spec.GetWorkerState<T>(this) elsewhere: one application's Ability tasks data.GetTaskState<T>(this): one activation's Targeting tasks, sequence tasks Locals of their run, or the run's data packet Tag and analysis workers The entity: an entity service, or its Local Data Cue handlers A dictionary keyed by cue.Key ?? cue.Spec A [NonSerialized] field that caches something of the kind's own, made from its settings, is fine, as Cast Range keeps its Check Range.

guides/extending/before-you-start/renami.title: Renaming a kind | PlayForge
guides/extending/before-you-start/renami.summary: Renaming a kind A kind is saved by its class's name, assembly and namespace, so renaming one needs care. Renaming or moving the class needs Unity's [MovedFrom], or every asset that holds one loses it. The Problems view lists an asset that holds a class it can't find.

guides/extending/before-you-start/the-as.title: The assembly | PlayForge
guides/extending/before-you-start/the-as.summary: The assembly A kind of a game's own compiles in an assembly that references PlayForge's. Code Where it lives What it references Runtime code Unity's default assembly, or a game's own assembly definition FarEmerald.PlayForge, and UniTask for anything async: an ability task, a wind-up, a process or a sequence task Editor code, as a validation rule or a drawer An editor-only assembly FarEmerald.PlayForge.Editor as well The runtime assembly, FarEmerald.PlayForge, is referenced automatically, so scripts in Unity's default assembly see it. A game's own assembly definition lists it among its references. Two of PlayForge's names clash with others: Attribute. PlayForge's attribute asset is FarEmerald.PlayForge.Attribute, and System.Attribute shares its name. A file with both using System; and using FarEmerald.PlayForge; that writes Attribute doesn't compile. The examples here alias it: using ForgeAttribute = FarEmerald.PlayForge.Attribute;. Editor. The editor's namespace is FarEmerald.PlayForge.Editor. In code inside a namespace under FarEmerald.PlayForge, a bare Editor names that namespace, so write UnityEditor.Editor in full there.

guides/extending/components.html.title: Components | PlayForge
guides/extending/components.html.summary: Components A component is a feature an asset carries in its Components section: an effect's, an ability's, an entity's or an item's. It hears its asset's moments through hooks, each a no-op it may override. It's the way to add a feature that needs more than one moment, as a mark that pays its caster when the marked one dies. Each family is a base in the runtime assembly, in FarEmerald.PlayForge: Base Held by Its context AbstractEffectComponent an effect's Components EffectComponentContext AbstractAbilityComponent an ability's Components AbilityComponentContext AbstractEntityComponent an Entity asset's Components, or a runtime entity's EntityComponentContext AbstractItemComponent an item's Components ItemComponentContext Every component also has these members, from AbstractForgeComponent: Hook When PlayForge calls it AllowsSeveral As the Components list offers kinds. False, for a kind that makes no sense twice, has the list offer it only while the asset holds none. Describe() As The Forge's summary and the breakdowns show the component: what it does in one line with its numbers, as "Range 6", beside its name. Null shows its name alone. Its protected NameOf(asset) gives an asset's name for that line: its PlayForge name, its file's, or "nothing". Each kind lists its own traps, and Traps, last in this section, lists those every component shares. In this section Effect components: An effect component adds a feature to an effect, heard at each moment of the effect's life. Ability components: An ability component adds a feature to an ability: it can refuse an activation, make it wait as it winds up, and take over how its cost and cooldown apply. Entity components: An entity component adds a feature to an entity: it hears the entity register, die, revive and end, and can make its abilities wait as they wind up. Item components: An item component adds a feature to an item: it hears the item given, equipped, unequipped, removed and used. State a component keeps: A component keeps what it counts for one holder through its context, never in its own fields. Capabilities other code finds: A component can implement an interface that other code asks an asset for. Traps: These traps apply to every kind of component.

guides/extending/components/ability-comp.title: Ability components | PlayForge
guides/extending/components/ability-comp.summary: Ability components An ability component adds a feature to an ability: it can refuse an activation, make it wait as it winds up, and take over how its cost and cooldown apply. Derive from AbstractAbilityComponent. An ability holds it in its Components, and its hooks are called with an AbilityComponentContext: Member Holds Spec The ability as its entity holds it. Data The activation's data packet. It's null as the ability is granted or removed. Source The entity that holds it. GetState<T>(this) What the component keeps for this entity's ability. Hooks Hook When PlayForge calls it Granted(ctx), Removed(ctx) As an entity learns the ability, and loses it. CanStart(ctx) As an activation is asked for, after the ability's own Caster Checks. A reason refuses it, nothing of it paid; null lets it go on. CanTakeTarget(ctx) As its targeting ends, whichever task picked. A reason ends the activation there, before its wind-up, its cost and its stages. RefusedAs As a refusal from CanStart or CanTakeTarget is told: the refusal kind it's told as. It's Rule unless it says, as Cast Range says Range. WindUp(ctx, token) After its targeting and its Target Checks, before its cost and its first stage. The activation waits on it, with its entity's components' wind-ups and its other components', all together. Start(ctx) As an activation starts, its claim taken. ApplyUsage(ctx) In place of the ability applying its cost and its cooldown: true says it did, and false leaves it to the ability. Build one from ctx.Spec.PayCosts(data) and ctx.Spec.SpendCooldown(data). Waives(ctx) The checks of its use it waives for this activation: EUsageCheck.Cost, EUsageCheck.Cooldown or both. A Toggle that's on waives them, so it can always turn off. Commit(ctx) As an activation's cost and cooldown apply. CategoryOf(ctx, effect) As a purge finds an effect its ability put on: the purge categories it's of, beside the ability's own. End(ctx, how) As an activation ends: EAbilityEnd.Done, Cancelled or Failed. Refused(ctx, refusal) As an activation is refused, nothing of it paid. DescribeUsage() What it adds to the ability's Activation line after its cost and cooldown, as "3 charges". TargetCheck, CasterCheck A check it stands behind, shown among the ability's Target Checks or Caster Checks while the ability holds it (Validation rules). In CanTakeTarget, the pick is in Data under Tags.TARGET, not yet resolved to an entity, as a picked point has none. In the picker An ability's Components list offers every class derived from AbstractAbilityComponent (How a kind is found). One whose AllowsSeveral is false, as the example's, is offered only while the ability holds none. Example A component that enforces a rule says so in the ability's checks by returning an AbstractComponentValidationRule<T> from TargetCheck. The check is the rule's place in the list, and it passes: the component does the refusing. This example is a minimum range, the mirror of Cast Range: using System; using FarEmerald.PlayForge; using UnityEngine; namespace MyGame { [Serializable] [ForgeMenu(Description = "How near the caster the ability's target may not be.")] public sealed class MinimumRangeAbilityComponent : AbstractAbilityComponent { public const string TooClose = "Its target is inside its Minimum Range"; [Tooltip("How near its caster its target or point may not be, read at the ability's level")] [NumberMin(0f)] public ScalableFloat Least = 3f; // Its place among the ability's Target Checks, made as it's first asked for and kept with it [NonSerialized] private CheckMinimumRangeValidation check; public override bool AllowsSeveral => false; public override string Describe() => $"Minimum range {NumberText.Of(Least)}"; public override IAbilityValidationRule TargetCheck => check ??= new CheckMinimumRangeValidation(this); // The pick its targeting made, whichever task made it, refused inside the range public override string CanTakeTarget(AbilityComponentContext ctx) { if (ctx.Data is not AbilityDataPacket data || !data.TryGetFirst(Tags.TARGET, out AbstractTargetingPacket picked) || picked == null || ctx.Source?.GetTargetingPacket() is not { } caster) return null; float least = ctx.Spec.Read(Least, data); var offset = picked.position - caster.position; offset.y = 0f; return offset.sqrMagnitude < least * least ? TooClose : null; } } [ValidationSide(EValidationSide.Target)] [ForgeMenu(Name = "Check Minimum Range", Description = "The Minimum Range component's check. It comes and goes with the component.")] public sealed class CheckMinimumRangeValidation : AbstractComponentValidationRule<MinimumRangeAbilityComponent> { public CheckMinimumRangeValidation(MinimumRangeAbilityComponent component) : base(component) { } public override string Describe() => Component == null ? null : $"Its target at least {NumberText.Of(Component.Least)} from its caster"; } } Tip A target or a point an AI hands in its request is refused soonest in CanStart, before targeting. Read Tags.TARGET_REAL and Tags.POSITION from the data, as Cast Range does: the request is then refused at once, with nothing of it run. Traps CanStart and CanTakeTarget are asked often, an AI's every request among them. Keep them quick and free of allocation, and of side effects: a refusal must leave nothing behind. A wind-up is cancelled through its token. Await with it, and let OperationCanceledException pass: it ends the activation as cancelled, its cost unpaid. Any other exception fails the activation, which is written to the Console. Granted and Removed have no data: ctx.Data is null there.

guides/extending/components/capabilities.title: Capabilities other code finds | PlayForge
guides/extending/components/capabilities.summary: Capabilities other code finds A component can implement an interface that other code asks an asset for. Other code finds a component through its asset's Find<T>(), by its class or by an interface it implements, as ability.Find<IAbilityReach>() or spec.Find<ICooldownModel>(). Interface What it answers Who asks IAbilityReach How far its ability reaches: bool TryReadReach(AbilitySpec spec, ProcessDataPacket data, out float range, out bool flat). Targeting tasks, the Creator Lab's bots and a game's AI, through ForgeReach. ICooldownModel How many uses its ability holds and how one is spent, in place of the single cooldown, as Charges does. AbilitySpec.CooldownModel finds it. The Cooldown check and the ability's usage go through it. IAuraComponent is PlayForge's own components' mark, and nothing reads it. An aura of a component's own is given from its Lend through ForgeAuras.Provide, and taken back from its TakeBack through ForgeAuras.Remove.

guides/extending/components/effect-compo.title: Effect components | PlayForge
guides/extending/components/effect-compo.summary: Effect components An effect component adds a feature to an effect, heard at each moment of the effect's life. Derive from AbstractEffectComponent. An effect holds it in its Components, and its hooks are called with an EffectComponentContext: Member Holds System The entity of the moment. Spec The effect's application. ExecuteTicks For a tick, how many ticks it executes. ImpactData For a hit, its impact. GetState<T>(this) What the component keeps for this application (State a component keeps). Hooks Hook When PlayForge calls it Lend(ctx) As a lasting effect starts to last on the one it's on: as it lands, before Land; as it takes another's place under its tag; and as a load or a move puts it back, where it doesn't land again. An instant effect lends nothing. TakeBack(ctx) As a lasting effect stops lasting there, matching each Lend: as it comes off, before End; as another takes its place; and as a load clears it or a move takes it away. Land(ctx) As the effect lands, with its workers' Application. Tick(ctx) As a lasting effect executes its period's tick. It isn't called on a tick that doesn't execute. Hit(ctx) As an impact the effect deals lands. System is then the dealer, the effect's caster. End(ctx) As the effect comes off: an instant one as it's done, a lasting one as it's removed. Death(ctx) As the one it's on dies while it's on them, before what the death ends comes off. Reapply(ctx) As another application lands on one it's on already and is taken in: a stack, a refresh, an extension or a replacement. Spec is the application that came. Refused(ctx, refusal) As an application is refused, as by an immunity or a missed chance. Nothing else of it is heard. StacksChanged(ctx, before, after) As its stacks change while it lasts. It isn't called as the effect lands, comes off or is loaded. Lend and TakeBack are for what an effect gives while it lasts and must give back exactly once, as an aura. A load calls them where Land and End aren't called. In the picker An effect's Components list offers every class derived from AbstractEffectComponent, as How a kind is found describes. The picker shows BountyMarkEffectComponent as Bounty Mark, and [ForgeMenu] can name and file it otherwise. Example This component gives the effect's caster an effect as the one it's on dies while it lasts: using System; using FarEmerald.PlayForge; using UnityEngine; namespace MyGame { [Serializable] [ForgeMenu(Description = "Gives the effect's caster an effect as the one it's on dies while it lasts.")] public sealed class BountyMarkEffectComponent : AbstractEffectComponent { [Tooltip("The effect its caster takes as the marked one dies, from the marked one, so it reads the marked one's level")] public GameplayEffect Reward; public override bool AllowsSeveral => false; public override string Describe() => $"{NameOf(Reward)} to its caster as the marked one dies"; public override void Death(EffectComponentContext ctx) { var marked = ctx.System; if (Reward == null || marked == null || ctx.Spec?.Source is not IGameplayAbilitySystem caster || ReferenceEquals(caster, marked) || caster.IsDead) return; var origin = IEffectOrigin.GenerateSourceDerivation(marked); caster.ApplyGameplayEffect(caster.GenerateEffectSpec(origin, Reward)); } } } Traps A load calls Lend and TakeBack on a lasting effect's components. What a component applied as its effect landed comes back from the save on its own.

guides/extending/components/entity-compo.title: Entity components | PlayForge
guides/extending/components/entity-compo.summary: Entity components An entity component adds a feature to an entity: it hears the entity register, die, revive and end, and can make its abilities wait as they wind up. Derive from AbstractEntityComponent. An Entity asset holds it in its Components, or a runtime entity does, and its hooks are called with an EntityComponentContext: Member Holds System The entity. Killer For its death, the source of the last loss it took from another. Identity Its settings as its GAS uses them. GetState<T>(this) What the component keeps for this entity. Hooks Hook When PlayForge calls it Register(ctx) As the entity registers, its systems set up. Death(ctx) As it dies, whether it stays or ends. Revive(ctx) As a staying entity revives. End(ctx) As it ends. WindUp(ctx, ability, token) As an activation of one of its abilities winds up, with the ability's own components' wind-ups. ability is that activation's context. In the picker An Entity asset's Components list offers every class derived from AbstractEntityComponent (How a kind is found). Example This component makes each of its entity's abilities wait a moment before its first stage, as a heavy unit braces: using System; using System.Threading; using Cysharp.Threading.Tasks; using FarEmerald.PlayForge; using UnityEngine; namespace MyGame { [Serializable] [ForgeMenu(Description = "Each of its abilities waits a moment before its first stage, as a heavy unit braces.")] public sealed class BraceEntityComponent : AbstractEntityComponent { [Tooltip("How long it braces, in seconds of its own time, read at its level")] [NumberMin(0f)] public ScalableFloat Seconds = 0.25f; public override bool AllowsSeveral => false; public override string Describe() => $"Braces {NumberText.Of(Seconds)} s before each ability"; public override async UniTask WindUp(EntityComponentContext ctx, AbilityComponentContext ability, CancellationToken token) { if (ctx.System == null) return; float wait = Seconds?.Evaluate(NumberContext.Of(ctx.System)) ?? 0f; var clock = ctx.System.GetClock(); for (float waited = 0f; waited < wait; waited += clock.DeltaTime) await ForgeTick.Next(clock, token); } } } The wait counts the entity's own clock, so a slow on the entity slows its brace. ForgeTick.Next(clock, token) steps with the game's fixed tick where one is on. Traps A wind-up is cancelled through its token, as an ability component's is. Await with it, and let OperationCanceledException pass.

guides/extending/components/item-compone.title: Item components | PlayForge
guides/extending/components/item-compone.summary: Item components An item component adds a feature to an item: it hears the item given, equipped, unequipped, removed and used. Derive from AbstractItemComponent. An item holds it in its Components, and its hooks are called with an ItemComponentContext: Member Holds Container The item as its entity holds it. Source The entity. Restoring True where the moment comes from a load. GetState<T>(this) What the component keeps for this entity's item. Hooks Hook When PlayForge calls it Given(ctx) As an entity is given the item in a slot of its own. Equipped(ctx), Unequipped(ctx) As it's equipped and unequipped. Also as a load puts it back worn or takes it off, with Restoring true. Removed(ctx) As it's taken away. An equipped item is unequipped first. Used(ctx) As its holder's use of the item's ability ends, having paid what it costs. In the picker An item's Components list offers every class derived from AbstractItemComponent (How a kind is found). Example A load puts back what a component's earlier moments did, the effects it applied and the loose tags it added among them. So a component does nothing of that kind where Restoring is true, as this one shows: using System; using FarEmerald.PlayForge; using UnityEngine; namespace MyGame { [Serializable] [ForgeMenu(Description = "Its holder carries a tag while the item is equipped.")] public sealed class TagWhileEquippedItemComponent : AbstractItemComponent { [Tooltip("The tag its holder carries while it's equipped")] [ForgeTagContext(ForgeContext.Granted)] public Tag Tag; public override string Describe() => Tag.IsValid ? $"{Tag} while equipped" : null; public override void Equipped(ItemComponentContext ctx) { // A load puts back the loose tags its save held, this one among them if (ctx.Restoring || !Tag.IsValid || ctx.Source is not IGameplayAbilitySystem holder) return; holder.AddLooseTag(Tag); } public override void Unequipped(ItemComponentContext ctx) { if (ctx.Restoring || !Tag.IsValid || ctx.Source is not IGameplayAbilitySystem holder) return; holder.RemoveLooseTag(Tag); } } } Traps A load calls Equipped and Unequipped on an item's components, with Restoring true. What a component applied comes back from the save on its own.

guides/extending/components/state-a-comp.title: State a component keeps | PlayForge
guides/extending/components/state-a-comp.summary: State a component keeps A component keeps what it counts for one holder through its context, never in its own fields. ctx.GetState<T>(this) makes a T the first time it's asked for, and keeps it for that holder: Component Its holder An effect's One effect application An ability's One entity's ability An entity's One entity An item's One entity's item A state that needs more than a constructor with no parameters is made and kept through the holder's ComponentStates, which AbilitySpec, GameplayEffectSpec and ItemSpecContainer each have: TryGet<T>(this, out state) finds the state, where it's kept already. Where it isn't, make it, then Keep(this, state). A save keeps no component state.

guides/extending/components/traps.html.title: Traps | PlayForge
guides/extending/components/traps.html.summary: Traps These traps apply to every kind of component. A component is shared. A field it sets as one entity's moment comes is every entity's. Keep it in the context's state. Describe() runs as The Forge draws, often: no side effects.

guides/extending/cue-handlers.html.title: Cue handlers | PlayForge
guides/extending/cue-handlers.html.summary: Cue handlers A cue handler plays feedback, a shake, a sound, an animation, at an effect's, an ability's, an entity's or an item's moments, or where a cue tag routes. This section covers writing one; Cues: Handlers covers where cues are raised and PlayForge's handlers. Traps, last in this section, lists the traps of handlers and sinks. In this section Writing a cue handler: A cue handler of a game's own plays feedback its own way, as setting a trigger on the Animator of the one it plays on. Sinks: A sink decides whether a raise plays at all, as a server's that plays none, or a client's that plays only its own player's. Traps: These traps apply to every cue handler and sink.

guides/extending/cue-handlers/sinks.html.title: Sinks | PlayForge
guides/extending/cue-handlers/sinks.html.summary: Sinks A sink decides whether a raise plays at all, as a server's that plays none, or a client's that plays only its own player's. Derive from ForgeCueSink. raise.Cue is the cue, and raise.Source what raised it. Hooks Hook When PlayForge calls it WillPlay(ECueEvent cueEvent, in CueRaise raise) Once for each raise of a list of cues, before any of them plays: whether it plays. In the picker No picker offers a sink. It's given every world as ForgeCues.Sink, or one world with ForgeCues.UseSink(world, sink). ForgeCues.Enabled = false plays none.

guides/extending/cue-handlers/traps.html.title: Traps | PlayForge
guides/extending/cue-handlers/traps.html.summary: Traps These traps apply to every cue handler and sink. A handler is shared: one keeps what a lasting cue placed under cue.Key ?? cue.Spec, which its End hands back, as PlayForge's Prefab cue does. Two lasting cues on one entity each begin and end. So a bool the first End turns off is off for the second too, as in the example: count them where that matters. End can come with no Begin. A muted entity's cues, and every cue while ForgeCues.Enabled is off, don't begin, and still end, so what began before the mute is taken down. End does nothing where it finds nothing. A sink is asked for End too: it answers an End as it answered its Begin. A cue is presentation alone. A server may play none, so game state never depends on a cue. Rolls come from ForgeCues.Random, the cues' own random numbers, so a cue never moves the game's. A handler that throws is caught and written to the Console, and the cues after it play.

guides/extending/cue-handlers/writing-a-.title: Writing a cue handler | PlayForge
guides/extending/cue-handlers/writing-a-.summary: Writing a cue handler A cue handler of a game's own plays feedback its own way, as setting a trigger on the Animator of the one it plays on. Derive from AbstractCueHandler. Its hooks are handed a CueContext: Member Holds Target The entity it plays on. Moment The moment that raised it. Tag The cue's tag, where one raised it. Source Who's behind it: the effect's or the ability's caster, or the entity itself. Origin What raised it: an effect's origin, an ability's spec, an item's, or the entity. Spec, Ticks For an effect: its spec, and for a tick's burst, how many of its ticks executed. Data An activation's data, for an ability's cue. Magnitude, Point, Normal Where its raiser gave a hit: a number to scale with, as the hit's damage, and the hit's point and normal. Key What pairs a lasting cue's beginning with its end. Lasting Whether it was raised to last. Transform, Position The target's object, and where it plays. NumberContext.Of(in cue) reads a handler's numbers for it. Hooks Each hook is a no-op it may override. Hook When PlayForge calls it Burst(cue) At a moment that plays once. By default it calls OnTicked for a tick, OnRemoved for a removal and OnApplied for any other moment. OnApplied(cue), OnTicked(cue), OnRemoved(cue) From Burst. Begin(cue), End(cue) As a lasting cue begins and ends, as a While Active one does. In the picker Handlers sit in the Cues components' lists, the Play Cue task's, and a cue library's routes. The picker shows AnimatorCue as Animator. Code plays one with ForgeCues.Burst, ForgeCues.Begin and ForgeCues.End, handed a handler or a list and a CueContext. Example This handler sets an Animator trigger on the one the cue plays on, and a bool while a lasting cue lasts: using System; using FarEmerald.PlayForge; using UnityEngine; namespace MyGame { [Serializable] [ForgeMenu(Description = "Sets an Animator trigger on the one the cue plays on, and a bool while a lasting cue lasts.")] public class AnimatorCue : AbstractCueHandler { [Tooltip("The trigger set as it bursts")] public string Trigger = "Hit"; [Tooltip("The bool on while a lasting cue lasts")] public string WhileActive = "Stunned"; public override void OnApplied(CueContext cue) { if (!string.IsNullOrEmpty(Trigger) && AnimatorOf(cue) is { } animator) animator.SetTrigger(Trigger); } public override void Begin(CueContext cue) { if (!string.IsNullOrEmpty(WhileActive) && AnimatorOf(cue) is { } animator) animator.SetBool(WhileActive, true); } public override void End(CueContext cue) { if (!string.IsNullOrEmpty(WhileActive) && AnimatorOf(cue) is { } animator) animator.SetBool(WhileActive, false); } private static Animator AnimatorOf(in CueContext cue) => cue.Transform != null ? cue.Transform.GetComponentInChildren<Animator>() : null; } } Note A runtime entity has no object, so Transform is null on one.

guides/extending/deferred-actions.html.title: Deferred actions | PlayForge
guides/extending/deferred-actions.html.summary: Deferred actions A deferred action is a piece of work queued to an entity that runs at its end of frame, by priority. Deferred workers return them, and any code queues one with entity.GetActionQueue().Enqueue(action). This section covers writing one; Workers: The action queue covers when the queue runs and what it tells. In this section Writing an action: An action of a game's own does a piece of work at an entity's end of frame, as sending it an event once the frame's changes have run. PlayForge's own actions: PlayForge's own actions are each usable from a game's code.

guides/extending/deferred-actions/playfo.title: PlayForge's own actions | PlayForge
guides/extending/deferred-actions/playfo.summary: PlayForge's own actions PlayForge's own actions are each usable from a game's code. Action Does ModifyAttributeAction(target, attribute, value, runEvents = true, priority = null) Changes an attribute by a SourcedModifiedAttributeValue. ApplyEffectAction(target, effect, origin, priority = null) Applies an effect from an origin. RemoveEffectAction(target, effect, priority = null) Removes an effect. LambdaAction(action, description, priority, isValid) Runs a function, while its validity check, if it's given one, holds. LogAction Writes a line through ForgeLog. DeathAction(system) Kills the entity, at Critical.

guides/extending/deferred-actions/writin.title: Writing an action | PlayForge
guides/extending/deferred-actions/writin.summary: Writing an action An action of a game's own does a piece of work at an entity's end of frame, as sending it an event once the frame's changes have run. Implement IRootAction. For an action that holds only while its carrier's origin is active, derive from EffectScopedAction instead: an ability's holds while a run of it is active; an item's holds while it's equipped; an entity's holds always. EffectScopedAction takes the carrier in its constructor, keeps it as carrier, and leaves Description and Execute to its kind. Hooks IRootAction has four members: Hook When PlayForge calls it int Priority { get; } As the queue orders its actions. Higher runs first, and within one priority, in the order queued. bool IsValid { get; } As its turn comes. False drops it unrun. string Description { get; } Its line in the logs, the debugger and the effect journal. void Execute(ISource system) As its turn comes, where it's valid: its work. system is the entity whose queue runs it. ActionPriority names the levels: Critical (100), High (50), Normal (0), Low (-50), TagWorker (-100), Analysis (-200), Cleanup (-300). Enqueue(action, priorityOverride) queues one at another priority. In the picker No picker offers an action. A deferred worker returns it, or code queues it with entity.GetActionQueue().Enqueue(action). Example This action sends an entity a gameplay event once the frame's changes have run: using FarEmerald.PlayForge; namespace MyGame { // Sends an entity a gameplay event once the frame's changes have run public sealed class SendEventAction : IRootAction { private readonly IGameplayAbilitySystem to; private readonly Tag eventTag; public SendEventAction(IGameplayAbilitySystem to, Tag eventTag, int priority = ActionPriority.Low) { this.to = to; this.eventTag = eventTag; Priority = priority; } public int Priority { get; } public bool IsValid => to != null && !to.IsDead && eventTag.IsValid; public string Description => $"Send {eventTag}"; public void Execute(ISource system) => to.SendGameplayEvent(eventTag); } } Traps The queue runs in the entity's end of frame, which a Mono hub runs as it steps in LateUpdate. Its process timing takes LateUpdate, as Update And Late does, or its queue never runs. An action queued to another entity runs at that entity's end of frame: this frame if it's still to come, by the order the entities step in, or the next. An action that throws is caught: it's told as failed, written to the Console, and the rest of the queue runs. An action the system makes for itself is used again once the queue has run it. So a listener of the queue's events reads it during the call, and keeps nothing of it. An action that queues another for good is cut off at 10,000 a pass, with an error.

guides/extending/entity-services.html.title: Entity services | PlayForge
guides/extending/entity-services.html.summary: Entity services An entity service is an object of a game's own each entity keeps as it runs, as a combo count, a cooldown of the game's own or a respawn's wait. It's made the first time it's asked for, and stepped by the entity's own time. This section covers writing one. Writing a service A service of a game's own keeps something for each entity, stepped with the entity. Derive from AbstractEntityService. System is the entity it's for. Hooks Hook When PlayForge calls it Step(float deltaTime) Each frame of the entity's step, with its own clock's time, after its effects. Revive() As a staying entity revives. End() As the entity ends, after which it keeps none. In the picker No picker offers a service. entity.GetService<T>() gives an entity's T, making it the first time. entity.FindService<T>() gives it only where it's made, or null. Example A combo count each entity keeps, back to 0 after a pause between hits and as it revives: using FarEmerald.PlayForge; namespace MyGame { // A combo count each entity keeps, back to 0 after a pause between hits and as it revives public sealed class ComboService : AbstractEntityService { public float Window = 2f; public int Count { get; private set; } private float sinceLast; public void Hit() { Count++; sinceLast = 0f; } public override void Step(float deltaTime) { if (Count == 0) return; sinceLast += deltaTime; if (sinceLast >= Window) Count = 0; } public override void Revive() => Count = 0; } } A worker or a component counts a hit with ctx.System.GetService<ComboService>()?.Hit(). A number kind reads it with context.SystemOf(NumberSide.Caster)?.FindService<ComboService>()?.Count ?? 0. Traps A service has no inspector: it's made with its constructor that takes nothing, and its settings come from code. A save keeps no service. A loaded entity makes its services again as it's asked for them. Step runs every frame for every entity that has the service. Keep it quick, as above, which returns at once while there's nothing to count down. See Time, Input and Logging for PlayForge's other services.

guides/extending/index.html.title: Extending PlayForge | PlayForge
guides/extending/index.html.summary: Extending PlayForge This guide covers each place a game's own code plugs into PlayForge. PlayForge's rules are kinds a designer picks in an inspector: components, workers, tasks, scalers, conditions, stages, cue handlers and more. A game adds its own by writing a class of the same base. The editor finds the class, and its picker offers it beside PlayForge's own. It runs where they run, handed what they're handed. Each extension point here follows the same order, leaving out what doesn't apply to it: What it's for, in a sentence. The base to derive from, and what its hooks are handed. Its hooks, and when PlayForge calls each. How the kind reaches the inspector's picker. A complete example. Its traps. Code that only uses PlayForge, as a script that casts an ability or reads an attribute, needs none of this. The kinds here plug into what Workers, Scalers, Processes and Task Sequences explain. I want to… Read Know what every kind of my own needs: its assembly, its constructor, its name, its fields Before you start Give effects, abilities, entities or items a feature of my own Components React to an attribute's change, a hit, a tag, a frame's events or an effect's life Workers Make a change wait for the entity's end of frame Deferred actions Give an ability a step of my own Ability tasks Choose an ability's target my own way Targeting tasks Build sequences in code with tasks, injections and stage rules of my own Sequence tasks, injections and stage policies Run something over time under ProcessControl Processes Work out a number my own way, or test a condition Scalers, number kinds and conditions Reshape a hit's value on its way in Value stages Play feedback: an animation, a sound, a shake Cue handlers Keep something for each entity as it runs Entity services Refuse an activation by a rule of my own Validation rules Choose where an entity respawns, how charges come back, what a purge takes, a Local Data type Smaller kinds Let my own character controller turn, move, shake the camera or pool a cue A game's own objects Show an entity's state in my UI Readers Drive PlayForge's time, random numbers or pointer input Time, randomness and input Save data PlayForge's snapshot doesn't hold Saving a game's own data Name tags in code and offer them to the pickers Tags in code Check assets, draw a base type of my own, or start assets from templates The editor Test what I wrote Testing your extensions Drive the Creator Lab's units my own way The Creator Lab In this guide Before you start: This section covers what every kind of a game's own shares: the assembly it lives in, how the editor finds it, how its picker names and files it, how its fields show, where it keeps what it counts, and how it's renamed. Components: A component is a feature an asset carries in its Components section: an effect's, an ability's, an entity's or an item's. Workers: A worker is a small rule that reacts to what happens: an attribute's change, a hit it deals, its tags, its frame's events, an effect's life. Deferred actions: A deferred action is a piece of work queued to an entity that runs at its end of frame, by priority. Ability tasks: An ability task is a step of an ability's stage: it's picked in a stage's Tasks, runs with the stage, and is handed the activation's data. Targeting tasks: A targeting task picks what an activation acts on before its stages run. Sequence tasks, injections and stage policies: A task sequence runs stages of tasks, built in code with TaskSequenceBuilder (Task Sequences). Processes: A process is anything that runs over time under ProcessControl: a MonoBehaviour or a plain C# object stepped from Unity's player loop. Scalers, number kinds and conditions: A number field's Kind says how its number is worked out, and a Conditional's or a rule's condition says whether it holds. Value stages: A value stage reshapes a hit's value on its way to its attribute, as one of a Value Pipeline's Stages, which an effect's impact names as its Pipeline (Value Pipelines: Stages). Cue handlers: A cue handler plays feedback, a shake, a sound, an animation, at an effect's, an ability's, an entity's or an item's moments, or where a cue tag routes. Entity services: An entity service is an object of a game's own each entity keeps as it runs, as a combo count, a cooldown of the game's own or a respawn's wait. Validation rules: A validation rule refuses an ability's activation, as one of the ability's Caster Checks, asked of the caster, or its Target Checks, asked of the target once its targeting has picked one. Smaller kinds: This section covers the smaller kinds a game picks in one field each: where an entity respawns, how charges come back, what a purge takes, how a modifier changes an effect, a Local Data value's type, and the clock a run… A game's own objects: PlayForge asks a game's own objects for a few things through interfaces: turning, moving, shaking the camera, and a pooled cue's comings and goings. Readers: A reader is a MonoBehaviour process that shows an entity's state, as a bar or a counter. Time, randomness and input: PlayForge reads its time, its random numbers and its pointer through sources a game can replace, so a game can run it on a fixed step, repeat its rolls, or aim with a gamepad. Saving a game's own data: A ForgeSnapshot holds what PlayForge saves of an entity, and nothing of a game's own: a game saves its own data beside it. Tags in code: A game's code names tags for its kinds to read: a data key, an event, a state its components grant. The editor: A game's editor code can check PlayForge's assets, draw a base type of its own as PlayForge draws its kinds, and start new assets from its own templates. Testing your extensions: PlayForge's test kit runs a game's own kinds in a world of entities stepped frame by frame, in Unity's Test Runner. The Creator Lab: The Creator Lab plays a project's assets on units of its own (The Creator Lab).
