In the API The types of this guide's area: AbilityComponentContext, AbilityReader, AbstractAbilityComponent, AbstractEffectComponent, AbstractEntityComponent, AbstractForgeComponent, AbstractItemComponent, AbstractReader, AbstractTagRequirements, AttributeReader, AvoidRequireTagGroupColor, BaseForgeAsset, BaseForgeLevelProvider, BasicEffectOrigin, ComponentStates, DataWrapper, DeferredContextSystem, EAbilityEnd, EEffectLinkMode, EffectComponentContext, EntityComponentContext, EUsageCheck, ForgeContext, ForgeEffectTemplateAttribute, ForgeLog, ForgeLog.ELevel, ForgeLog.ESystem, ForgeLogEntry, ForgeMenuAttribute, ForgeShowWhenAttribute, ForgeTagContext, ForgeTagDefault, ForgeTagExcludeUniversal, ForgeTagExposed, ForgeTagGroup, ForgeTagLockedCountAttribute, ForgeTagLockedIndicesAttribute, ForgeTagNoCreate, ForgeTagPrefix, ForgeTagReadOnly, ForgeTagRequired, ForgeTagTooltip, ForgeUtils, IHasIntentToTarget, ILevelProvider, ILocalDataSource, ILocalDataUser, ItemComponentContext, LinkedSourceAttribute, LocalAbility, LocalAttribute, LocalBool, LocalDataStructure, LocalDataValue, LocalDataValue<T>, LocalEffect, LocalEntity, LocalFloat, LocalInt, LocalMonoBehaviour, LocalObject, LocalScriptableObject, LocalString, LocalTag, ShownWhenAttribute, TemplateListSnapshot, TextureItem.

guides/extending/processes.html.title: Processes | PlayForge
guides/extending/processes.html.summary: Processes A process is anything that runs over time under ProcessControl: a MonoBehaviour or a plain C# object stepped from Unity's player loop. This section covers writing one; Processes covers lifecycles, registering, pausing and groups. Writing a process A process of a game's own does work over time, as a regeneration that runs until its entity dies. Derive from one of four bases: Base Is AbstractMonoProcess A MonoBehaviour process, whose lifecycle and timing are fields of its inspector. LazyMonoProcess A MonoBehaviour process whose run lasts until it's paused or ended. AbstractRuntimeProcess A plain C# process, whose name, timing, priority and lifecycle are given to its base's constructor. LazyRuntimeProcess A plain C# process whose run lasts until it's paused or ended. A process reads its packet as regData, or Data, and its handle as Relay. Hooks Each hook is virtual. Hook When PlayForge calls it RunProcess(token) The run, which ProcessControl awaits for a process that isn't Synchronous. Required under AbstractMonoProcess and AbstractRuntimeProcess. WhenInitialize() As it's registered. WhenUpdate(), WhenLateUpdate(), WhenFixedUpdate() At its timing. WhenWait() As it goes to Waiting. WhenTerminate() As it ends. WhenTerminateQueued() As a Terminate is asked of it while it runs. WhenDestroy() In place of OnDestroy, as a mono process's object is destroyed. TryHandlePause(), TryHandleResume() As it's paused and resumed. True holds a run through a pause (Processes: Pausing). In the picker No picker offers a process: code registers it with ProcessControl. ProcessControl.Register(new RegenProcess(hero, health, 5f)).HandledBy(hero).Run(out ProcessRelay relay) starts the example, and relay.Terminate() ends it. Example This process gives an entity an amount of an attribute each second of its own time, until it dies or the process ends: using FarEmerald.PlayForge; using ForgeAttribute = FarEmerald.PlayForge.Attribute; namespace MyGame { // Gives an entity an amount of an attribute each second of its own time, until it dies or the process ends public sealed class RegenProcess : LazyRuntimeProcess { private readonly IGameplayAbilitySystem entity; private readonly ForgeAttribute attribute; private readonly float perSecond; private float waited; public RegenProcess(IGameplayAbilitySystem entity, ForgeAttribute attribute, float perSecond) : base("Regen", EProcessStepPriorityMethod.First, 0, EProcessStepTiming.Update, EProcessLifecycle.Synchronous) { this.entity = entity; this.attribute = attribute; this.perSecond = perSecond; } public override void WhenUpdate() { if (entity == null || entity.IsDead || attribute == null) { Relay.Terminate(); return; } waited += entity.GetClock().DeltaTime; if (waited < 1f) return; waited -= 1f; entity.TryModifyAttribute(attribute, SourcedModifiedAttributeValue.GenerateSimple(entity, attribute, perSecond, 0f)); } } } It changes the attribute once a second, not each frame. A change each frame would make a new change, and run the attribute's workers, every frame. Traps Call the base in an override of WhenInitialize or WhenTerminate. WhenDestroy stands in for OnDestroy, which a MonoBehaviour process of its own would hide. A Synchronous process isn't awaited: its run is its steps. A mono process's object comes from an instantiator, an AbstractMonoProcessInstantiator, as a pool hands one out (Processes: Registering one).

guides/extending/readers.html.title: Readers | PlayForge
guides/extending/readers.html.summary: Readers A reader is a MonoBehaviour process that shows an entity's state, as a bar or a counter. This section covers writing one. Writing a reader A reader of a game's own shows a piece of an entity's state in the game's UI. Derive from AbstractReader, a LazyMonoProcess. Assign(gas) gives it its entity: it keeps the entity as Source, and calls SubscribeIfOnChangePolicy(). PlayForge's AttributeReader and AbilityReader are readers. Hooks Hook When PlayForge calls it SubscribeIfOnChangePolicy() As Assign gives it its entity. A reader implements it to hear the changes it shows through the entity's callbacks, or leaves it empty to read the entity in WhenUpdate. WhenUpdate At its timing, as for any process. WhenTerminate, WhenDestroy As it ends, and as its object is destroyed: where a reader that subscribed unsubscribes. In the picker No picker offers a reader: it's a MonoBehaviour process on an object, which code gives its entity with Assign(gas). Example This reader tells its listeners a tag's weight on its entity as it changes, as a stack counter shows it: using FarEmerald.PlayForge; using UnityEngine; using UnityEngine.Events; namespace MyGame { // Tells its listeners a tag's weight on its entity as it changes, as a stack counter shows it public class TagWeightReader : AbstractReader { [ForgeTagContext(ForgeContext.Granted)] public Tag Tag; public UnityEvent<int> Changed = new(); private int shown = -1; public override void WhenUpdate() { if (Source == null || !Tag.IsValid) return; // An absent tag's weight is -1 int weight = Mathf.Max(0, Source.GetTagWeight(Tag)); if (weight == shown) return; shown = weight; Changed.Invoke(weight); } protected override void SubscribeIfOnChangePolicy() { } } } Traps A reader that subscribes unsubscribes, in WhenTerminate or WhenDestroy, and Assign called again subscribes again. A lambda subscribed can't be taken off: subscribe a method. A reader runs as a process: ProcessControl registers one already in a scene as it starts.

guides/extending/saving-a-games-own-data.title: Saving a game's own data | PlayForge
guides/extending/saving-a-games-own-data.summary: Saving a game's own data A ForgeSnapshot holds what PlayForge saves of an entity, and nothing of a game's own: a game saves its own data beside it. This section covers how, and what a save leaves out; Saving and Loading covers saving and loading. A snapshot is plain serializable types, so a class of the game's own holds it with the rest: using System; using FarEmerald.PlayForge; using UnityEngine; namespace MyGame { [Serializable] public class GameSave { public ForgeSnapshot Hero; public int Gold; public int BestCombo; public static string Write(IGameplayAbilitySystem hero, ForgeAssetCatalog catalog, int gold, int bestCombo) => JsonUtility.ToJson(new GameSave { Hero = ForgeSave.Capture(hero, catalog), Gold = gold, BestCombo = bestCombo }); public static GameSave Read(string json, IGameplayAbilitySystem hero, ForgeAssetCatalog catalog) { var save = JsonUtility.FromJson<GameSave>(json); if (save?.Hero != null) ForgeSave.Restore(hero, save.Hero, catalog); return save; } } } What a save leaves out, which a game that needs it saves itself: Local Data, an entity's and its assets'. Entity services, which a loaded entity makes again. Component states, what ctx.GetState<T>(this) keeps. What a game's code hears of a load: gas.GetCallbacks().OnRestored fires once a load is done (Saving and Loading: What a load does). An effect component's Lend and TakeBack, and an item component's Equipped and Unequipped with Restoring true (Components). An asset made at run time, or one of the game's own a save names, goes in the catalog with catalog.Add(id, asset) (Saving and Loading: The Asset Catalog). An effect from another entity is saved by that entity's id, through an IForgeEntityIds the game gives Capture and Restore (Saving and Loading: Effects from other entities): Hook When PlayForge calls it IdOf(entity) As Capture saves an effect from another entity: that entity's id, or null where it has none. Find(id) As Restore puts the effect back: the entity the id names, or null where there's none.

guides/extending/scalers-number-kinds-an.title: Scalers, number kinds and conditions | PlayForge
guides/extending/scalers-number-kinds-an.summary: Scalers, number kinds and conditions A number field's Kind says how its number is worked out, and a Conditional's or a rule's condition says whether it holds. This section adds to Scalers: Writing your own scaler, which covers the kinds' names, their inspectors and a number field in a class of a game's own. Here are their members, the variances and behaviours, and an example of each. Traps, last in this section, lists the traps they share. In this section Number kinds: A number kind is the simplest way to a number of a game's own: it reads its site through a NumberContext. Conditions: A condition says whether something holds, as a Conditional's or a rule's does. Scalers: A scaler of the full kind holds values for each level and behaviours, for a number that reads levels in a way of its own. Cached scalers: A cached scaler works out an attribute set element's Scaling from the entity's cached attribute values. Variances: A variance varies a Randomized scaler's value, handed a roll from 0 to 1. Scaler behaviours: A scaler behaviour adjusts the value a scaler works out, as one of the scaler's Behaviours, in order. Traps: These traps apply to every kind in this section.

guides/extending/scalers-number-kinds-an.title: Cached scalers | PlayForge
guides/extending/scalers-number-kinds-an.summary: Cached scalers A cached scaler works out an attribute set element's Scaling from the entity's cached attribute values. Derive from AbstractCachedScaler. PlayForge's own, as CachedAttributeScaler, show its shape. Hook When PlayForge calls it EvaluateActiveValue(blueprint, cache) Required. It gives the value.

guides/extending/scalers-number-kinds-an.title: Conditions | PlayForge
guides/extending/scalers-number-kinds-an.summary: Conditions A condition says whether something holds, as a Conditional's or a rule's does. Derive from GameplayCondition, which has the same shape as a number kind. condition.Holds(context) reads it, and one that can't be worked out where it's read doesn't hold. Hooks Hook When PlayForge calls it Evaluate(in NumberContext context), protected As it's read: whether it holds. Describe(), Reads, CanEvaluate, WhyNot, Explain As a number kind's. Initialize(carrier) As an effect's spec is made. It passes the spec on to the numbers it holds. In the picker A condition is offered wherever one is picked: a Conditional, an effect's requirements, an On Hit, a modifier's rule, an ability's Condition check. [GameplayCondition("Name", Reads = ...)] names a condition. The condition menu lists only [Serializable] classes with a constructor that takes nothing. Example using System; using FarEmerald.PlayForge; using UnityEngine; namespace MyGame { [Serializable] [GameplayCondition("Behind Target", Reads = NumberReads.Caster | NumberReads.Target)] [ForgeMenu("Space", Description = "Holds while the caster stands behind the target.")] public class BehindTargetCondition : GameplayCondition { [Tooltip("How wide the arc behind the target is, in degrees")] [NumberRange(0f, 360f)] public ScalableFloat Arc = 120f; protected override bool Evaluate(in NumberContext context) { var caster = context.Caster?.GetTargetingPacket(); var target = context.Target?.GetTargetingPacket(); if (caster == null || target == null) return false; var toCaster = caster.position - target.position; toCaster.y = 0f; var facing = target.rotation * Vector3.forward; facing.y = 0f; if (toCaster.sqrMagnitude < 0.0001f || facing.sqrMagnitude < 0.0001f) return false; float arc = Arc?.Evaluate(in context, this) ?? 120f; return Vector3.Angle(-facing, toCaster) <= arc * 0.5f; } public override void Initialize(IAttributeImpactCarrier carrier) => Arc?.Initialize(carrier); public override string Describe() => $"the caster within {NumberText.Of(Arc)}° behind the target"; } } A kind or a condition reads its own numbers with itself as their owner, Arc.Evaluate(in context, this), so a number of the Relative to a Field kind can read its other fields.

guides/extending/scalers-number-kinds-an.title: Number kinds | PlayForge
guides/extending/scalers-number-kinds-an.summary: Number kinds A number kind is the simplest way to a number of a game's own: it reads its site through a NumberContext. Derive from NumberKind. A kind is a scaler, so it works in an effect's magnitude and inside a Group or a Conditional too. Its scaler Evaluate methods are sealed, and it reads none of a scaler's levels unless its Parts say. Hooks Hook When PlayForge calls it Evaluate(in NumberContext context), protected As the field is read: its number. Describe() Its line in the field's summary, as "the distance to the target". Reads What it reads of the site, from its [NumberKind]: NumberReads.Level, Caster, Target, Caller, LocalData, Carrier, Data, Owner. A field offers it only where its site provides them. CanEvaluate(in context) Whether the site has what it reads. Where it hasn't, the field reads Fallback, 0 unless it says, and logs why. WhyNot(in context) Why it can't be worked out, for that line. It's protected internal, so an override in another assembly is protected override. Explain(in context, NumberTrace trace) What its explanation lists, as the numbers it read. In the picker A number field's Kind menu lists a number kind with a public constructor that takes nothing. [NumberKind("Name", Reads = NumberReads.Caster | NumberReads.Target)] names it and says what it reads. Example using System; using FarEmerald.PlayForge; using UnityEngine; namespace MyGame { [Serializable] [NumberKind("Distance to Target", Reads = NumberReads.Caster | NumberReads.Target)] [ForgeMenu("Space", Description = "How far the target stands from the caster.")] public class DistanceToTargetKind : NumberKind { [Tooltip("Measures along the ground, leaving height out")] public bool Flat = true; protected override float Evaluate(in NumberContext context) { var from = context.Caster?.GetTargetingPacket(); var to = context.Target?.GetTargetingPacket(); if (from == null || to == null) return 0f; var offset = to.position - from.position; if (Flat) offset.y = 0f; return offset.magnitude; } public override string Describe() => Flat ? "the distance to the target, along the ground" : "the distance to the target"; } } A number read in code is number.Evaluate(context), with a NumberContext made Of what the code has: an effect's spec, an activation's data, a worker's context, an entity, a cue or a process. NumberContext.For(caster, target, level) makes one with nothing else, for a test.

guides/extending/scalers-number-kinds-an.title: Scaler behaviours | PlayForge
guides/extending/scalers-number-kinds-an.summary: Scaler behaviours A scaler behaviour adjusts the value a scaler works out, as one of the scaler's Behaviours, in order. Derive from AbstractScalerBehaviour. Its overloads that take a stacking container are never called. Hooks Hook When PlayForge calls it Initialize(IAttributeImpactCarrier spec) Required. At each read, handed the carrier the value is read for. Evaluate(float magnitude, IAttributeImpactCarrier spec) Required. Next, handed the value so far: the value after it. In the picker A scaler's Behaviours offer every class derived from AbstractScalerBehaviour. The picker shows RoundToStepScalerBehaviour as Round To Step. Example using System; using FarEmerald.PlayForge; using UnityEngine; namespace MyGame { [Serializable] [ForgeMenu(Description = "Rounds the number to a step, as 5 for multiples of 5.")] public class RoundToStepScalerBehaviour : AbstractScalerBehaviour { [Tooltip("The step it rounds to; 0 leaves the number as it is")] [Min(0f)] public float Step = 1f; public override void Initialize(IAttributeImpactCarrier spec) { } public override float Evaluate(float magnitude, IAttributeImpactCarrier spec) => Step > 0f ? Mathf.Round(magnitude / Step) * Step : magnitude; } }

guides/extending/scalers-number-kinds-an.title: Scalers | PlayForge
guides/extending/scalers-number-kinds-an.summary: Scalers A scaler of the full kind holds values for each level and behaviours, for a number that reads levels in a way of its own. Derive from AbstractScaler. Its protected helpers read its levels: EvaluateFromSpec(carrier): its values at the carrier's level, exactly or spread, through its behaviours. ApplyBehaviourEvaluation(carrier, value): a value through its behaviours. Its behaviours apply only where its Evaluate calls one of these two. EvaluateAtLevel(level, relativeLevel), GetEffectiveMaxLevel(carrier), GetEffectiveRelativeLevel(carrier) and EvaluateScalingAtRelativeLevel(relativeLevel), for one that reads its levels itself. Hooks Hook When PlayForge calls it Initialize(IAttributeImpactCarrier carrier) As an effect's spec is made. It readies the scaler for the spec. Evaluate(IAttributeImpactCarrier carrier) As its number is read: its value. Parts Which of every scaler's parts its inspector draws (Scalers: Writing your own scaler). IsEmpty True reads it as no scaler at all. In the picker A kind of AbstractScaler's is filed under its Scaler submenu, unless it names another (How a kind is named and filed). Example using System; using FarEmerald.PlayForge; using UnityEngine; namespace MyGame { [Serializable] [ForgeMenu(Description = "Its values per level, eased toward a cap so each level adds less.")] public class SoftCapScaler : AbstractScaler { [Tooltip("The value it nears and never reaches; 0 or less, no cap")] public float Cap = 100f; public override void Initialize(IAttributeImpactCarrier carrier) { } public override float Evaluate(IAttributeImpactCarrier carrier) { float raw = EvaluateFromSpec(carrier); return Cap <= 0f ? raw : Cap * raw / (Cap + Mathf.Abs(raw)); } } }

guides/extending/scalers-number-kinds-an.title: Traps | PlayForge
guides/extending/scalers-number-kinds-an.summary: Traps These traps apply to every kind in this section. A number is read often, as an effect's magnitude for every application and a tooltip each time it draws: no allocation and no side effects in Evaluate. A kind is saved by its class's name (Before you start). Draw rolls from ForgeRandom, never UnityEngine.Random, so a test or a replay that puts in a seeded source repeats them (Time, randomness and input).

guides/extending/scalers-number-kinds-an.title: Variances | PlayForge
guides/extending/scalers-number-kinds-an.summary: Variances A variance varies a Randomized scaler's value, handed a roll from 0 to 1. Derive from AbstractVariance. Its protected Read(number, carrier, fallback) reads one of its numbers for the carrier, with itself as their owner. The roll comes from ForgeRandom, once for each spec where the scaler's Roll Once Per Spec is on. Hooks Hook When PlayForge calls it Vary(value, roll, carrier) The value varied by the roll. Lowest(value, carrier), Highest(value, carrier) The range a tooltip shows. Initialize(carrier) It readies its numbers for a spec. Numbers() Its numbers with their roles, for an explanation. In the picker A Randomized scaler's Variance offers every class derived from AbstractVariance. The picker shows TwoDiceVariance as Two Dice. Example using System; using System.Collections.Generic; using FarEmerald.PlayForge; using UnityEngine; namespace MyGame { [Serializable] [ForgeMenu(Name = "Two Dice", Description = "Up or down by a share of the value, the middle likeliest, as two dice fall.")] public class TwoDiceVariance : AbstractVariance { [Tooltip("The most it varies by either way, as a share of the value: 0.2 for 20%")] [NumberMin(0f)] public ScalableFloat Share = 0.2f; public override float Vary(float value, float roll, IAttributeImpactCarrier carrier) { // The roll through a triangle's inverse, from -1 to 1, the middle likeliest float centred = roll < 0.5f ? Mathf.Sqrt(2f * roll) - 1f : 1f - Mathf.Sqrt(2f * (1f - roll)); return value * (1f + centred * Read(Share, carrier, 0f)); } public override float Lowest(float value, IAttributeImpactCarrier carrier) => value * (1f - Read(Share, carrier, 0f)); public override float Highest(float value, IAttributeImpactCarrier carrier) => value * (1f + Read(Share, carrier, 0f)); public override void Initialize(IAttributeImpactCarrier carrier) => Share?.Initialize(carrier); public override IEnumerable<(string Role, ScalableFloat Number)> Numbers() { yield return ("Share", Share); } } }

guides/extending/sequence-tasks-injectio.title: Sequence tasks, injections and stage policies | PlayForge
guides/extending/sequence-tasks-injectio.summary: Sequence tasks, injections and stage policies A task sequence runs stages of tasks, built in code with TaskSequenceBuilder (Task Sequences). This section covers what a game writes for one: a task, an injection that changes a run as it goes, a stage policy that says when a stage ends, and a method the inspector's sequence pickers list. In this section Tasks: A sequence task is one step of a sequence's stage, run in an async sequence or a synced one. A sequence the inspector lists: A method marked [TaskSequenceMethod] offers its sequence to an ability's Run Sequence task and a Sequence cue. Injections: An injection changes a run as it goes, as a skip, a jump or an interrupt. Stage policies: A stage policy says when a stage ends.

guides/extending/sequence-tasks-injectio.title: A sequence the inspector lists | PlayForge
guides/extending/sequence-tasks-injectio.summary: A sequence the inspector lists A method marked [TaskSequenceMethod] offers its sequence to an ability's Run Sequence task and a Sequence cue. Those two pick a sequence from a dropdown of the project's methods marked [TaskSequenceMethod]. Such a method is: static; taking no parameters; returning a TaskSequence, a TaskSequenceChain or a TaskSequenceDefinition. In the picker The dropdown names each by its [TaskSequenceMethod("...")] name, or its method's. Example using System.Threading; using FarEmerald.PlayForge; namespace MyGame { public static class GameSequences { [TaskSequenceMethod("Short Pause")] public static TaskSequence ShortPause() => TaskSequenceBuilder.Create("Short Pause") .Stage(stage => stage.Task((CancellationToken token) => SequenceTaskLibrary.Delay(0.25f, token))) .BuildSequence(); } }

guides/extending/sequence-tasks-injectio.title: Injections | PlayForge
guides/extending/sequence-tasks-injectio.summary: Injections An injection changes a run as it goes, as a skip, a jump or an interrupt. Implement ISequenceInjection. Its hook is handed the run, a TaskSequenceRuntime, which gives it Data, StageIndex, CurrentStage, IsRunning, IsPaused, Pause(), Resume() and Inject. The skips, jumps and interrupts themselves are the built-in injections': SkipStageInjection, JumpToStageInjection, InterruptSequenceInjection and the rest. An injection of a game's own composes them. Hooks Hook When PlayForge calls it bool Apply(TaskSequenceRuntime runtime) As it's injected into a run. It acts on the run, and says whether it took effect. In the picker An injection reaches a run four ways: runtime.Inject(injection), into one run; sequence.Inject(injection), into every run of a sequence; the builder's InjectWhen; an ability's Inject task, whose picker lists a [Serializable] injection with a constructor that takes nothing. It shows SkipIfTaggedInjection as Skip If Tagged. Example This injection skips the current stage where the caster carries a tag: using System; using FarEmerald.PlayForge; using UnityEngine; namespace MyGame { [Serializable] [ForgeMenu(Name = "Skip If Tagged", Description = "Skips the current stage where the caster carries a tag.")] public class SkipIfTaggedInjection : ISequenceInjection { [Tooltip("The tag on the caster that skips the stage")] [ForgeTagContext(ForgeContext.Granted)] public Tag Tag; public bool Apply(TaskSequenceRuntime runtime) { if (!Tag.IsValid || runtime?.Data is not AbilityDataPacket data) return false; var caster = data.EffectOrigin?.GetSource(); if (caster == null || caster.GetTagWeight(Tag) <= 0) return false; // This injection passed the run's checks as it came in; the skip it composes is part of it return runtime.Inject(SkipStageInjection.Instance, overridePermission: true); } } } Traps Permissions name injections by their exact type. A sequence or a stage that lists its allowed injections, AllowInjections(typeof(SkipIfTaggedInjection)), takes only those types, not types made from them. A critical section takes only an interrupt unless its critical policy lists more. An injection is one object every run shares: what it keeps for one run goes in the run's data.

guides/extending/sequence-tasks-injectio.title: Stage policies | PlayForge
guides/extending/sequence-tasks-injectio.summary: Stage policies A stage policy says when a stage ends. Implement ISequenceStagePolicy. A policy of a game's own is handed a token source of its own, linked to the stage's, so cancelling it cuts off the stage's tasks and not the stage. Hooks ISequenceStagePolicy has one member: Hook When PlayForge calls it UniTask AwaitCompletion(TaskSequenceRuntime runtime, SequenceStage stage, UniTask[] taskUnits, CancellationTokenSource stageCts) While the stage's tasks run. It awaits them as it sees fit, and the stage ends as it returns. In the picker No picker offers a stage policy: stage.WithPolicy(policy) gives a stage one in code. TaskSequenceBuilder.Create("Search").Stage(stage => stage.Task(a).Task(b).WithPolicy(FirstSuccessStagePolicy.Instance)) gives a stage the example's. Example This policy ends the stage as its first task finishes well. A task that throws ends it only where every task fails. using System; using System.Threading; using Cysharp.Threading.Tasks; using FarEmerald.PlayForge; namespace MyGame { // The stage ends as its first task finishes well; a task that throws ends it only where every task fails public sealed class FirstSuccessStagePolicy : ISequenceStagePolicy { public static readonly FirstSuccessStagePolicy Instance = new(); public async UniTask AwaitCompletion(TaskSequenceRuntime runtime, SequenceStage stage, UniTask[] taskUnits, CancellationTokenSource stageCts) { if (taskUnits.Length == 0) return; int left = taskUnits.Length; bool succeeded = false; Exception firstError = null; var done = new UniTaskCompletionSource(); foreach (var task in taskUnits) Watch(task).Forget(); await done.Task; // The others are cut off as the stage ends stageCts.Cancel(); if (!succeeded && firstError != null) throw firstError; async UniTaskVoid Watch(UniTask task) { try { await task; succeeded = true; done.TrySetResult(); return; } catch (OperationCanceledException) { } catch (Exception error) { firstError ??= error; } if (--left == 0) done.TrySetResult(); } } } } The Task Sequence Examples sample has another, a lead task the stage lasts as long as. Traps A synced runner can't run a policy of a game's own. It warns, and its stage waits for all its tasks. An ability's stages take All or Any alone (Ability tasks). A policy that returns ends the stage. One that waits on fewer than all its tasks cancels its source, so the rest stop with it.

guides/extending/sequence-tasks-injectio.title: Tasks | PlayForge
guides/extending/sequence-tasks-injectio.summary: Tasks A sequence task is one step of a sequence's stage, run in an async sequence or a synced one. Implement ISequenceTask, or derive from one of two bases that fill in what a task doesn't need: Base What it fills in SequenceTaskBase Execute is required, and its Step ends at once, so it does nothing in a synced sequence. SyncSequenceTaskBase Step is required. Its Execute steps it once a frame with the run's clock, holding while the run is paused, so one task serves both kinds. Hooks ISequenceTask has four members: Hook When PlayForge calls it Prepare(SequenceDataPacket data) Before its first step or its run. UniTask Execute(SequenceDataPacket data, CancellationToken token) Its run, in an async sequence. bool Step(SequenceDataPacket data, float deltaTime) Each frame in a synced sequence, with the run's time. True ends it. Clean(SequenceDataPacket data) After it ends, however it ended. In the picker No picker offers a sequence task: code builds it into a stage with TaskSequenceBuilder, as the example below does. Example This task fades a canvas group to an alpha over a time, in an async sequence or a synced one: using FarEmerald.PlayForge; using UnityEngine; namespace MyGame { // Fades a canvas group to an alpha over a time, in an async sequence or a synced one public sealed class FadeTask : SyncSequenceTaskBase { private readonly CanvasGroup group; private readonly float to; private readonly float seconds; private float from; private float elapsed; public FadeTask(CanvasGroup group, float to, float seconds) { this.group = group; this.to = to; this.seconds = seconds; } public override void Prepare(SequenceDataPacket data) { from = group != null ? group.alpha : to; elapsed = 0f; } public override bool Step(SequenceDataPacket data, float deltaTime) { if (group == null) return true; elapsed += deltaTime; float t = seconds > 0f ? Mathf.Clamp01(elapsed / seconds) : 1f; group.alpha = Mathf.Lerp(from, to, t); return t >= 1f; } } public static class MenuSequences { public static TaskSequence FadeOut(CanvasGroup group) => TaskSequenceBuilder.Create("Fade Out") .Stage(stage => stage.Task(new FadeTask(group, 0f, 0.4f))) .BuildSequence(); } } MenuSequences.FadeOut(group).RegisterAndRun(SequenceDataPacket.Default()) runs it under ProcessControl. Traps A task that keeps its state in its own fields serves one run at a time, as this one does. A sequence that runs several at once builds a task for each, or keeps a run's state in its data packet.

guides/extending/smaller-kinds.html.title: Smaller kinds | PlayForge
guides/extending/smaller-kinds.html.summary: Smaller kinds This section covers the smaller kinds a game picks in one field each: where an entity respawns, how charges come back, what a purge takes, how a modifier changes an effect, a Local Data value's type, and the clock a run takes. In this section Respawn places: A respawn place says where an entity revives. Charge recharges: A charge recharge says how an ability's spent charges come back. Purge filters: A purge filter says which effects an effect's purge takes. Effect changes: An effect change is one of the changes a modifier's rule makes to an effect it reaches. Local Data values: A Local Data value is the type of a Local Data entry's value. Clock choices: A clock choice says which clock a run takes. Stack behaviours: An effect's Stack Behaviours are AbstractStackingConfigs.

guides/extending/smaller-kinds/charge-re.title: Charge recharges | PlayForge
guides/extending/smaller-kinds/charge-re.summary: Charge recharges A charge recharge says how an ability's spent charges come back. Derive from AbstractChargeRecharge. Each hook has a default, so a recharge overrides only what it changes. Hooks Hook When PlayForge calls it InHand(AbilityCharges charges) The charges in hand. By default, its most less those cooling down. Spend(AbilityCharges charges, ProcessDataPacket data) As a charge is spent. By default, it starts one's cooldown. CountsASingleCharge Whether a single charge is still counted, rather than the ability being an ordinary cooldown. True unless it says; PlayForge's own recharges say false. In the picker A Charges component's Recharge offers every class derived from AbstractChargeRecharge.

guides/extending/smaller-kinds/clock-cho.title: Clock choices | PlayForge
guides/extending/smaller-kinds/clock-cho.summary: Clock choices A clock choice says which clock a run takes. Derive from AbstractClockChoice. Hooks Its one hook is IForgeClock ClockFor(ProcessDataPacket data), the clock a run on the packet takes, or null for the run's own. OwnersClock(data), protected, gives the clock of the entity the packet is for (Time, Input and Logging). In the picker A Run Sequence task's or a Sequence cue's Clock offers every class derived from AbstractClockChoice.

guides/extending/smaller-kinds/effect-ch.title: Effect changes | PlayForge
guides/extending/smaller-kinds/effect-ch.summary: Effect changes An effect change is one of the changes a modifier's rule makes to an effect it reaches. Derive from AbstractEffectChange. Hooks Hook When PlayForge calls it Apply(EffectChanges changes, GameplayEffectSpec spec, EffectModifierRule rule) As the rule reaches an effect. It writes what it changes into changes. Describe() Its line. In the picker A modifier's rule offers it in its Changes (Effects: Workers: Modifiers).

guides/extending/smaller-kinds/local-dat.title: Local Data values | PlayForge
guides/extending/smaller-kinds/local-dat.summary: Local Data values A Local Data value is the type of a Local Data entry's value. Derive from LocalDataValue, or for one that holds a single value, from LocalDataValue<T>, whose Value it holds. Hooks Hook When PlayForge calls it Read(in NumberContext) As a packet takes it: its value. TryReadNumber(in NumberContext, out float) As a number reads it, where it's one. In the picker The Local Data list offers a kind with a constructor that takes nothing, named without "Local". Example using System; using FarEmerald.PlayForge; namespace MyGame { public enum EElement { None, Fire, Frost, Storm } [Serializable] [ForgeMenu(Name = "Element", Description = "One of the game's elements.")] public class LocalElement : LocalDataValue<EElement> { } } asset.TryGetLocalData(key, out DataWrapper entry) && entry.TryGet(out EElement element) reads it. Traps An entry is the asset's own. A value changed at run time changes the asset, so Local Data is read, not written, as the game runs.

guides/extending/smaller-kinds/purge-fil.title: Purge filters | PlayForge
guides/extending/smaller-kinds/purge-fil.summary: Purge filters A purge filter says which effects an effect's purge takes. Derive from AbstractPurgeFilter. An effect's purge takes the effects its Filters let it (Effects: Purging). Hooks Its one hook is bool Takes(in PurgeContext ctx), with ctx.Container, the effect it might take; ctx.Purged, the entity it's on; and ctx.Purger, who purges, where an effect or code names one. It says whether the purge takes the effect. In the picker An effect's purge Filters offer every class derived from AbstractPurgeFilter.

guides/extending/smaller-kinds/respawn-p.title: Respawn places | PlayForge
guides/extending/smaller-kinds/respawn-p.summary: Respawn places A respawn place says where an entity revives. Derive from AbstractRespawnPlace. Hooks Hook When PlayForge calls it Vector3? Where(EntityComponentContext context, Vector3? home) As the entity revives, handed where it stood as it registered: where it revives. Null revives it where it died. Describe() The component's line, as "at home". In the picker A Respawn component's At offers every class derived from AbstractRespawnPlace. The picker shows NearHomeRespawnPlace as Near Home. Example using System; using FarEmerald.PlayForge; using UnityEngine; namespace MyGame { [Serializable] [ForgeMenu(Description = "A random point within a radius of where it registered.")] public class NearHomeRespawnPlace : AbstractRespawnPlace { [Tooltip("How far from home it may come back")] [Min(0f)] public float Radius = 3f; public override Vector3? Where(EntityComponentContext context, Vector3? home) { if (home == null) return null; var offset = ForgeRandom.InsideUnitCircle * Radius; return home.Value + new Vector3(offset.x, 0f, offset.y); } public override string Describe() => $"within {Radius:0.#} of home"; } }

guides/extending/smaller-kinds/stack-beh.title: Stack behaviours | PlayForge
guides/extending/smaller-kinds/stack-beh.summary: Stack behaviours An effect's Stack Behaviours are AbstractStackingConfigs. A game can derive one, but its members work on the effect system's stacking containers, which this guide doesn't cover. Effects: Duration: Stacking (Stack Existing only) covers the built-in ones.

guides/extending/tags-in-code.html.title: Tags in code | PlayForge
guides/extending/tags-in-code.html.summary: Tags in code A game's code names tags for its kinds to read: a data key, an event, a state its components grant. This section covers what a kind of a game's own does with tags; Tags covers tags in full. A tag field's picker offers the tags of the contexts its [ForgeTagContext(...)] names. They're PlayForge's (ForgeContext.Granted, ForgeContext.Event, ForgeContext.DataKey, ForgeContext.ImpactType, ForgeContext.ContextTag, ForgeContext.AssetTag and the rest), or a project's own, by name. A tag written in code is Tag.GenerateAsUnique("State.Stunned"), the tag the editor's New Tag makes of the path. [ForgeTagExposed(context)] on a static Tag field or property offers it to the pickers of that context. An event goes to an entity with entity.SendGameplayEvent(eventTag, data), which its abilities' triggers and Wait For Event tasks hear. A game's own events are tags of the Event context. A tag's weight is entity.GetTagWeight(tag). An absent tag's weight is -1, so a test for one is > 0. A tag is shown by its ToString(), its display name.

guides/extending/targeting-tasks.html.title: Targeting tasks | PlayForge
guides/extending/targeting-tasks.html.summary: Targeting tasks A targeting task picks what an activation acts on before its stages run. It's the ability's Targeting, one task, run as the activation starts. This section covers writing one, and what a task must do while its ability waits on it. Traps, last in this section, lists a targeting task's traps. In this section Writing a targeting task: A targeting task of a game's own picks an activation's target its own way, as a click near an enemy. While it waits: A task that waits for the player holds its ability in targeting, and the game shows it. Traps: These traps apply to every targeting task.

guides/extending/targeting-tasks/traps.h.title: Traps | PlayForge
guides/extending/targeting-tasks/traps.h.summary: Traps These traps apply to every targeting task. An override of Prepare calls the base's last, which connects the input handler. No task state. data.GetTaskState<T> takes an ability task. A targeting task keeps what it needs in its Activate's locals. Take a handed target first. An AI's or a replay's activation hands its target in its data. A task that waits for a click whatever the data holds can't be cast by an AI. An exception other than a cancellation fails the activation, written to the Console. The pick is a packet. SetTargetingPacket files a place: an entity's packet points at its entity, and a StaticTargetingPacket(point) at none. An activation whose pick is a point has no target, so its Target Checks don't run.

guides/extending/targeting-tasks/while-i.title: While it waits | PlayForge
guides/extending/targeting-tasks/while-i.summary: While it waits A task that waits for the player holds its ability in targeting, and the game shows it. The slot says it's choosing. AbilitySpecContainer.IsTargeting is true while a run of the ability waits on its targeting. A game shows the ability's targeting's Prompt beside its name while it is. A task that doesn't wait for the player returns a null Prompt. Another ability can take its place. Another of the entity's abilities may activate on a request that cancels targeting, as a player's press. An ability still choosing then gives way where its While Targeting says it yields. Yields gives way. Entity's Rule follows the entity's Targeting Yields. Holds keeps it. A trigger's request and an activation at start don't cancel targeting: AbilityActivationRequest.CancelsTargeting is off for them. Code that makes a request chooses. Giving way cancels the task's token. Its claim lets go at once, so the other activation starts while the cancelled task winds down. Nothing of the activation is paid, it ends as cancelled, and the task's Clean runs. So a task awaits with its token, as WaitForPointerPress does. Once its token is cancelled, it files nothing and applies nothing: a pick filed after the token was cancelled lands in an activation that's gone.

guides/extending/targeting-tasks/writing.title: Writing a targeting task | PlayForge
guides/extending/targeting-tasks/writing.summary: Writing a targeting task A targeting task of a game's own picks an activation's target its own way, as a click near an enemy. Derive from AbstractTargetingAbilityTask (from AbstractAbilityRelatedTask). It isn't marked [Serializable], so mark a task of your own. AbstractGasTargetingAbilityTask adds Requirements (AvoidRequireTagGroup), which an entity's applied tags must meet. Its helpers: TryGetDataTarget(data, out target) and TryGetDataPoint(data, out point): a target or a point the activation's data holds already, as an AI's request does. WaitForPointerPress(button, token): waits for a press of the game's input, ForgeInput.Current. It gives the ray it aims along, or null with nothing to aim through. PressWords(button): "Click", "Right-click" or "Middle-click", for a Prompt. Hooks Hook When PlayForge calls it Activate(data, token) Required: it picks, and files the pick's targeting packet with data.SetTargetingPacket(Tags.TARGET, packet), or several with data.SetTargetingPackets(Tags.TARGET, targets), the first the primary. Or it calls WhenTargetingInvalid(data). Prompt While the task waits for the player: the words a game shows, as "Click a point on the ground". Null for a task that doesn't wait for the player. TargetIsValid(...) Which targets it takes: an ITarget, a GameObject, a Transform or a point. WhenTargetingInvalid(data) Marks the targeting failed. With Break Runtime On Invalid on (BreakRuntimeOnInvalid), it throws OperationCanceledException, which ends the activation as cancelled. ConnectInputHandler(data), DisconnectInputHandler(data) As it's prepared, to hook an input handler of its own, and as it's cleaned, to unhook it. A false from ConnectInputHandler fails the targeting. IsCriticalSection True: targeting holds the activation's claim. What follows a task's pick: The ability's components hear it in CanTakeTarget, and may refuse it (Components). The pick resolves. The entity each packet under Tags.TARGET, or the ability's implicit tag, points at is filed under Tags.TARGET_REAL, where tasks and checks find it. Where the pick is an entity, the caster's checks and the components' CanStart are asked again, then the Target Checks on the target. Then come the wind-ups, the cost and the first stage. In the picker An ability's Targeting offers every class derived from AbstractTargetingAbilityTask (How a kind is found). The picker shows ClickNearestEnemyTargetTask as Click Nearest Enemy. Example The player clicks the ground, and the enemy nearest the click is the target: using System; using System.Collections.Generic; using System.Threading; using Cysharp.Threading.Tasks; using FarEmerald.PlayForge; using UnityEngine; namespace MyGame { [Serializable] [ForgeMenu("Picked", Description = "The player clicks the ground, and the enemy nearest the click is the target.")] public class ClickNearestEnemyTargetTask : AbstractTargetingAbilityTask { [Tooltip("How far from the click an enemy may stand, read at the ability's level")] [NumberMin(0f)] public ScalableFloat Radius = 2f; [Tooltip("The layers the click's ray hits")] public LayerMask Ground = ~0; [Tooltip("The pointer button that picks: 0 the primary, 1 the secondary, 2 the middle")] public int Button; public override string Prompt => $"{PressWords(Button)} near an enemy"; public override async UniTask Activate(AbilityDataPacket data, CancellationToken token) { // An AI's activation hands its target: take it rather than wait for a click if (TryGetDataTarget(data, out var handed)) { if (TargetIsValid(handed)) data.SetTargetingPacket(Tags.TARGET, handed.GetTargetingPacket()); else WhenTargetingInvalid(data); return; } var ray = await WaitForPointerPress(Button, token); if (ray == null || !Physics.Raycast(ray.Value, out var hit, Mathf.Infinity, Ground)) { WhenTargetingInvalid(data); return; } var caster = data.EffectOrigin.GetSource(); var sides = data.EffectOrigin.GetAffiliation(); var near = new List<ITarget>(); ForgeEntities.Within(hit.point, Read(Radius, data), true, near, caster, false); ITarget best = null; float bestDistance = float.MaxValue; foreach (var each in near) { if (each.IsDead || !ForgeEntities.Takes(EAffiliationFilter.Enemies, caster, sides, each) || !TargetIsValid(each)) continue; float distance = ForgeEntities.Distance(each, hit.point, true); if (distance >= bestDistance) continue; best = each; bestDistance = distance; } if (best == null) WhenTargetingInvalid(data); else data.SetTargetingPacket(Tags.TARGET, best.GetTargetingPacket()); } } }

guides/extending/testing-your-extensions.title: Testing your extensions | PlayForge
guides/extending/testing-your-extensions.summary: Testing your extensions PlayForge's test kit runs a game's own kinds in a world of entities stepped frame by frame, in Unity's Test Runner. This section covers what it offers a kind of a game's own; Testing Your Content covers setting it up and writing tests. To test What the kit offers A component, a worker or a scaler An asset the kit makes. Make.Effect(name, new EffectConfig { ... }) takes Workers, effect workers of the game's own, and a MagnitudeScaler, a scaler of its own. An ability task Make.Stage(new PulseTask { ... }), and the stage goes into Make.Ability(name, stage). World.Cast(caster, ability, target) casts it. A hit World.Hit(source, target, effect). Its rolls are World.Rolls(...), a scripted source put in for the test, and its time is World.Clock(step). A number kind or a condition No world: number.Evaluate(NumberContext.For(caster, target, level)) and condition.Holds(context). The kit's assembly, FarEmerald.PlayForge.Testing, is referenced by the game's test assembly. It's compiled only where Unity's Test Framework package is in the project.

guides/extending/the-creator-lab.html.title: The Creator Lab | PlayForge
guides/extending/the-creator-lab.html.summary: The Creator Lab The Creator Lab plays a project's assets on units of its own (The Creator Lab). This section covers driving its units the game's own way, through a driver. Writing a driver A driver of a game's own moves, attacks with, casts with and stops the lab's units its own way, as through a NavMesh. A driver is an ILabUnitDriver. Derive from LabDriver, a ScriptableObject that implements each member as the lab does unless overridden. Hooks Hook When PlayForge calls it MoveTo(LabUnit unit, Vector3 point) As the lab moves a unit to a point. Attack(LabUnit unit, LabUnit target) As a unit attacks another. bool Cast(LabUnit unit, Ability ability, ProcessDataPacket data) As a unit casts an ability. Stop(LabUnit unit) As a unit stops. In the picker LabDriver is made with Create → PlayForge → Lab Driver. A class of the game's own derives from it, and its asset is named on the lab's rules' Driver (The Creator Lab: Your unit). Example This driver moves and stops its units through a NavMesh agent, where a unit has one on a NavMesh: using FarEmerald.PlayForge.Lab; using UnityEngine; using UnityEngine.AI; namespace MyGame.Lab { [CreateAssetMenu(menuName = "MyGame/NavMesh Lab Driver")] public class NavMeshLabDriver : LabDriver { public override void MoveTo(LabUnit unit, Vector3 point) { if (unit != null && unit.TryGetComponent(out NavMeshAgent agent) && agent.isOnNavMesh) agent.SetDestination(point); else base.MoveTo(unit, point); } public override void Stop(LabUnit unit) { if (unit != null && unit.TryGetComponent(out NavMeshAgent agent) && agent.isOnNavMesh) agent.ResetPath(); base.Stop(unit); } } } Traps The lab is its own assembly, FarEmerald.PlayForge.Lab, left out where the project defines PLAYFORGE_NO_LAB. A driver's assembly references it and carries the same constraint, !PLAYFORGE_NO_LAB among its Define Constraints, so it's left out with it.

guides/extending/the-editor.html.title: The editor | PlayForge
guides/extending/the-editor.html.summary: The editor A game's editor code can check PlayForge's assets, draw a base type of its own as PlayForge draws its kinds, and start new assets from its own templates. This section covers each. The code lives in an editor-only assembly that references FarEmerald.PlayForge.Editor. In this section Validation rules: An editor validation rule checks PlayForge's assets, and the Problems view and each asset's inspector list what it finds (The Editor Tools). Drawing a base type of a game's own: A drawer of a game's own draws a field whose type is a base of the game's own, as PlayForge draws its kinds. Inspectors, presets and templates: PlayForge's inspectors share a base, and a game's own effect fields can start from the project's templates.

guides/extending/the-editor/drawing-a-ba.title: Drawing a base type of a game's own | PlayForge
guides/extending/the-editor/drawing-a-ba.summary: Drawing a base type of a game's own A drawer of a game's own draws a field whose type is a base of the game's own, as PlayForge draws its kinds. PlayForge draws its kinds' fields through drawers registered for their bases, so a kind of a game's own is drawn with no drawer of its own. A field whose type is a base of the game's own, as a [SerializeReference] AbstractWeatherRule on a component of its own, takes a drawer made from one of PlayForge's: Base Draws AbstractTypeRefDrawer<T> The kind picker and the kind's fields. AbstractGenericDrawer<T> The same, folding to a line of its values, and naming kinds without the words in TypeNameSuffixes. AbstractWorkerDrawer<T> A generic drawer that offers no None. AbstractComponentDrawer<T> For a base made from AbstractForgeComponent: a worker drawer that offers a kind that allows one only while its list holds none. Hooks AbstractTypeRefDrawer<T>'s virtual members say how it offers and names kinds: Hook When PlayForge calls it FilterType, Offers Which kinds it offers. CleanTypeName, GetStringValue How it names them. AcceptClear Whether it offers None. OnTypeChanged What follows a pick. Example In the game's runtime assembly, a base of its own and a field of it: using System; using UnityEngine; namespace MyGame { [Serializable] public abstract class AbstractWeatherRule { public abstract float SpeedFactor { get; } } [Serializable] public class RainWeatherRule : AbstractWeatherRule { [Range(0f, 1f)] public float Slow = 0.2f; public override float SpeedFactor => 1f - Slow; } public class Weather : MonoBehaviour { [SerializeReference] public AbstractWeatherRule Rule = new RainWeatherRule(); } } In its editor assembly, the drawer, whose picker shows the kind as Rain Weather, "Rule" taken off its name: using FarEmerald.PlayForge.Editor; using UnityEditor; namespace MyGame.EditorRules { [CustomPropertyDrawer(typeof(AbstractWeatherRule), true)] public class WeatherRuleDrawer : AbstractGenericDrawer<AbstractWeatherRule> { protected override bool AcceptClear(SerializedProperty prop) => false; } }

guides/extending/the-editor/inspectors-p.title: Inspectors, presets and templates | PlayForge
guides/extending/the-editor/inspectors-p.summary: Inspectors, presets and templates PlayForge's inspectors share a base, and a game's own effect fields can start from the project's templates. BasePlayForgeEditor is the base of PlayForge's asset inspectors. The Forge's presets and a project's templates are where new assets start (The Editor Tools). A GameplayEffect field of a game's own marked [ForgeEffectTemplate("Cost")] or [ForgeEffectTemplate("Cooldown")] offers, in its right-click menu, to copy or use the project's Cost or Cooldown template. Those are the two keys it knows.

guides/extending/the-editor/validation-r.title: Validation rules | PlayForge
guides/extending/the-editor/validation-r.summary: Validation rules An editor validation rule checks PlayForge's assets, and the Problems view and each asset's inspector list what it finds (The Editor Tools). Derive from ForgeValidationRule, with a public constructor that takes nothing. For a rule about one kind of component, derive from ForgeComponentRule<T> instead. Hooks Hook When PlayForge calls it Check(Object asset, List<ForgeProblem> problems) Each time the validator runs, for each PlayForge asset. It adds what it finds in the asset. Reads(Object asset) True for an asset the rule reads to check others, so an edit to it has the others checked again. Name What the Problems view groups its problems under. By default, its class's name spaced out, without "Rule". ForgeComponentRule<T> hears each component of its kind an asset holds, whichever kind of asset holds it, through Check(Object asset, T component, int nth, string path, List<ForgeProblem> problems), with nth the component's count among its kind and path its place, as "Components.Array.data[1]". A problem is a ForgeProblem(asset, severity, message, propertyPath): its severity is ForgeProblemSeverity.Note, Warning or Error; its Fix is a ForgeQuickFix(name, apply), the button that fixes it. In the picker No picker offers a rule: the validator finds it. Example This rule warns of a Minimum Range component whose range of 0 refuses no target, and offers to fix it: using System.Collections.Generic; using FarEmerald.PlayForge.Editor; using MyGame; using UnityEditor; using Object = UnityEngine.Object; namespace MyGame.EditorRules { public sealed class MinimumRangeRule : ForgeComponentRule<MinimumRangeAbilityComponent> { public override string Name => "Minimum ranges that refuse nothing"; protected override void Check(Object asset, MinimumRangeAbilityComponent component, int nth, string path, List<ForgeProblem> problems) { if (component.Least == null || !component.Least.IsConstant || component.Least.Constant > 0f) return; problems.Add(new ForgeProblem(asset, ForgeProblemSeverity.Warning, "Its Minimum Range of 0 refuses no target. Give it a range, or take the component off.", path) { Fix = new ForgeQuickFix("Set its range to 1", () => { Undo.RecordObject(asset, "Set Minimum Range"); component.Least = 1f; EditorUtility.SetDirty(asset); }), }); } } } Traps A rule is asked of every asset each time the validator runs. Return at once for an asset it doesn't check.

guides/extending/time-randomness-and-inp.title: Time, randomness and input | PlayForge
guides/extending/time-randomness-and-inp.summary: Time, randomness and input PlayForge reads its time, its random numbers and its pointer through sources a game can replace, so a game can run it on a fixed step, repeat its rolls, or aim with a gamepad. This section covers the interfaces; Time, Input and Logging covers clocks, rolls and input in full. In this section Clocks: A clock is where PlayForge reads its time, so a game can run it on a step of its own. Random sources: A random source is where PlayForge draws its random numbers, so a test or a replay can repeat its rolls. Input: An input source is where PlayForge reads the pointer, so a game can aim with a gamepad's cursor.

guides/extending/time-randomness-and-inp.title: Clocks | PlayForge
guides/extending/time-randomness-and-inp.summary: Clocks A clock is where PlayForge reads its time, so a game can run it on a step of its own. Implement IForgeClock. Hooks Hook When PlayForge calls it DeltaTime, UnscaledDeltaTime, FixedDeltaTime, Time, UnscaledTime, FrameCount As PlayForge reads its time from the clock. FollowsTicks True unless it runs while the game's time stands. In the picker No picker offers a clock: code puts one in. ForgeTime.Use(clock) puts one in for the game, and returns the one it replaced. Null puts Unity's back. A run takes one of its own through its packet's Clock. A sequence takes one through TaskSequenceBuilder.WithClock(clock).

guides/extending/time-randomness-and-inp.title: Input | PlayForge
guides/extending/time-randomness-and-inp.summary: Input An input source is where PlayForge reads the pointer, so a game can aim with a gamepad's cursor. Implement IForgeInput. Hooks Hook When PlayForge calls it PointerPressed(int button), TryGetPointerRay(out Ray ray) Required. As the click-targeting tasks and the sequence library's waits read ForgeInput.Current. PointerHeld, TryGetPointerPosition, ScrollDelta, KeyPressed, KeyHeld Optional. In the picker No picker offers an input source: ForgeInput.Use(input) puts one in. Example This input is a pointer the game moves itself, as a gamepad's cursor: using FarEmerald.PlayForge; using UnityEngine; namespace MyGame { // A pointer the game moves itself, as a gamepad's cursor public sealed class CursorInput : IForgeInput { public Camera Camera; public Vector2 Position; public bool PressedThisFrame; public bool PointerPressed(int button) => button == 0 && PressedThisFrame; public bool TryGetPointerRay(out Ray ray) => ForgeInput.TryAimThrough(Camera, Position, out ray); public bool TryGetPointerPosition(out Vector2 position) { position = Position; return true; } } } ForgeInput.Use(new CursorInput { Camera = Camera.main }) puts it in. The game sets Position as its cursor moves, and PressedThisFrame for the one frame of a press.

guides/extending/time-randomness-and-inp.title: Random sources | PlayForge
guides/extending/time-randomness-and-inp.summary: Random sources A random source is where PlayForge draws its random numbers, so a test or a replay can repeat its rolls. Implement IForgeRandom. Hooks Hook When PlayForge calls it Value A number from 0 to 1. InsideUnitCircle, InsideUnitSphere A point in a circle of radius 1, or in a sphere of radius 1. In the picker No picker offers a random source. ForgeRandom.Use(source) puts one in and returns the one it replaced. SeededRandom(seed) is one of PlayForge's. The cues draw from their own, ForgeCues.Random.

guides/extending/validation-rules.html.title: Validation rules | PlayForge
guides/extending/validation-rules.html.summary: Validation rules A validation rule refuses an ability's activation, as one of the ability's Caster Checks, asked of the caster, or its Target Checks, asked of the target once its targeting has picked one. This section covers writing one; Abilities: Requirements covers the checks. Writing a rule A rule of a game's own refuses an activation by a test of its own, as whether the caster faces its target. Implement IAbilityValidationRule. AbstractAttributeValidationRule and AbstractTagValidationRule are bases for a rule about an attribute or a tag. Hooks Hook When PlayForge calls it bool Validate(AbilityDataPacket data, Func<ITarget> getSource, out string error) As its list of checks is asked: whether it passes. error says why it refused, in words a player could read. string GetName() Its name, which a refusal names. RefusedAs The refusal kind it's told as among the Caster Checks: Rule unless it says, as the Cost check says Cost. A Target Check's refusal is always told as Target. getSource() gives the entity a rule checks: the caster among the Caster Checks, the target among the Target Checks. In the picker Both lists of checks offer a rule. [ValidationSide(EValidationSide.Caster)] or EValidationSide.Target offers it in one list alone; without it, both lists offer it. Example This rule activates only where the caster faces the target within an angle: using System; using FarEmerald.PlayForge; using UnityEngine; namespace MyGame { [Serializable] [ValidationSide(EValidationSide.Target)] [ForgeMenu(Name = "Facing Target", Description = "Activates only where the caster faces the target within an angle.")] public class FacingTargetValidation : IAbilityValidationRule { [Tooltip("How far either side of straight ahead the target may be, in degrees")] [Range(0f, 180f)] public float HalfAngle = 45f; public bool Validate(AbilityDataPacket data, Func<ITarget> getSource, out string error) { var caster = data?.EffectOrigin?.GetSource()?.GetTargetingPacket(); var target = getSource?.Invoke()?.GetTargetingPacket(); if (caster == null || target == null) { error = "There's no one to face"; return false; } var toTarget = target.position - caster.position; toTarget.y = 0f; var forward = caster.rotation * Vector3.forward; forward.y = 0f; if (toTarget.sqrMagnitude < 0.0001f || Vector3.Angle(forward, toTarget) <= HalfAngle) { error = null; return true; } error = $"Its target is more than {HalfAngle:0}° from where its caster faces"; return false; } public string GetName() => "Facing Target"; } } Traps A Caster Check is asked of every request, an AI's among them, before anything is paid. Keep it quick, free of allocation where it passes, and free of side effects. A condition of a game's own does as much through PlayForge's Condition check, and serves effects' requirements and Conditionals as well (Scalers, number kinds and conditions). A rule a component enforces is an AbstractComponentValidationRule<T>, which the component returns as its TargetCheck or CasterCheck. No picker offers one (Components).

guides/extending/value-stages.html.title: Value stages | PlayForge
guides/extending/value-stages.html.summary: Value stages A value stage reshapes a hit's value on its way to its attribute, as one of a Value Pipeline's Stages, which an effect's impact names as its Pipeline (Value Pipelines: Stages). This section covers writing one. In this section Writing a value stage: A value stage of a game's own reshapes each hit through its pipeline, as armor shrinking a loss. Stop stages: A stop stage stops an effect outright, as a block or a dodge.

guides/extending/value-stages/stop-stage.title: Stop stages | PlayForge
guides/extending/value-stages/stop-stage.summary: Stop stages A stop stage stops an effect outright, as a block or a dodge. Derive from AbstractStopStage, whose Chance, Roll and Stops every stop has. Hooks A stop names three members: Hook When PlayForge calls it StoppedEvent As it stops an effect: the event the one hit hears. DealerEvent The event its dealer hears. Verb Its verb, as "blocked". The effect system honours every enabled stop in a pipeline, wherever it sits in the list. As the effect lands, the first stop that reaches it and rolls stops it. In the picker A Value Pipeline's Stages offer it, as they offer every stage.

guides/extending/value-stages/writing-a-.title: Writing a value stage | PlayForge
guides/extending/value-stages/writing-a-.summary: Writing a value stage A value stage of a game's own reshapes each hit through its pipeline, as armor shrinking a loss. Derive from AbstractValueStage. Label and Enabled are every stage's: off, the value passes it by. Its hook is handed a ValueRun: Member Holds Carrier The hit's effect spec. Context The hit's NumberContext: its caster, its target and its level. Breakdown What the run keeps of each stage, or null. Note(text) Notes what the stage did on its step in the breakdown, as "critical". Hooks Hook When PlayForge calls it float Apply(float value, in ValueRun run) For every hit through its pipeline: the value it passes on. A loss is negative. Describe() What it does, as "× 1.5", which the pipeline's line and a breakdown show. Its Label replaces it. In the picker A Value Pipeline's Stages offer every class derived from AbstractValueStage (How a kind is found). Example This stage shrinks a loss by the armor of the one hit: as much armor as its Halves halves the loss. using System; using FarEmerald.PlayForge; using UnityEngine; using ForgeAttribute = FarEmerald.PlayForge.Attribute; namespace MyGame { [Serializable] [ForgeMenu(Description = "Shrinks a loss by the armor of the one hit: as much armor as its Halves halves it.")] public class ArmorStage : AbstractValueStage { [Tooltip("The attribute that is the armor of the one hit")] public ForgeAttribute Armor; [Tooltip("The armor that halves a loss, read for the hit")] [NumberMin(1f)] public ScalableFloat Halves = 100f; public override float Apply(float value, in ValueRun run) { if (value >= 0f || Armor == null || !run.Context.TryGetAttribute(NumberSide.Target, Armor, out var armor)) return value; float halves = Mathf.Max(1f, Halves?.Evaluate(in run.Context, this) ?? 100f); float factor = halves / (halves + Mathf.Max(0f, armor.CurrentValue)); if (factor < 1f) run.Note($"{armor.CurrentValue:0} armor"); return value * factor; } public override string Describe() => $"armor, {NumberText.Of(Halves)} halving a loss"; } } Traps Apply runs for every hit through the pipeline: no allocation. run.Note with a constant string is free. One built with $"...", as above, allocates only where it notes. A stage is shared by every hit through its pipeline: it keeps nothing of one hit.

guides/extending/workers.html.title: Workers | PlayForge
guides/extending/workers.html.summary: Workers A worker is a small rule that reacts to what happens: an attribute's change, a hit it deals, its tags, its frame's events, an effect's life. An entity holds workers in a worker group, and an effect holds them in its Workers. This section covers writing each kind. Workers: The map maps when each runs and on whose system, and Workers: The action queue covers the queue its actions wait in. Base Picked in Hooks AbstractAttributeWorker, AbstractFocusedAttributeWorker a worker group's attribute workers Intercept, DeferredIntercept AbstractImpactWorker, AbstractContextImpactWorker a worker group's impact workers ActivateInline, CreateDeferredActions AbstractTagWorker a worker group's tag workers Activate, Tick, Resolve AbstractAnalysisWorker a worker group's analysis workers Analyze AbstractEffectWorker an effect's Workers OnEffectApplication, OnEffectTick, OnEffectRemoval, OnEffectImpact A worker group (StandardWorkerGroup) sits on an attribute set, an Entity asset, a Forge Project's settings, an item, an ability and an effect (Workers: Where workers come from). Code gives an entity one with group.ProvideWorkersTo(entity), and takes it back with group.RemoveWorkersFrom(entity). A deferred worker returns actions, IEnumerable<IRootAction>, which wait in its entity's action queue for its end of frame (Deferred actions). Return Array.Empty<IRootAction>() for none. Each kind lists its own traps, and Traps, last in this section, lists those every worker shares. In this section Attribute workers: An attribute worker runs inside a change to one of its entity's attributes, where it can edit the change or queue actions. Impact workers: An impact worker runs as a change its holder dealt lands on another's attribute, for the attribute it subscribes to. Tag workers: A tag worker acts while its entity's tags meet its Tag Requirements. Analysis workers: An analysis worker reads its entity's frame as it ends, after the tag workers. Effect workers: An effect worker hears its effect's life: as it lands, as it lasts, as it comes off, and as a change it made lands. A worker that answers a number: A worker of any kind can answer number fields of the Worker kind, under a key. Traps: These traps apply to every kind of worker.

guides/extending/workers/a-worker-that-a.title: A worker that answers a number | PlayForge
guides/extending/workers/a-worker-that-a.summary: A worker that answers a number A worker of any kind can answer number fields of the Worker kind, under a key. Implement INumberWorker on the worker, beside its base. Hook When PlayForge calls it bool TryGetNumber(Tag key, in NumberContext context, out float value) As a number field of the Worker kind asks it for its key (Scalers: Asking a worker).

guides/extending/workers/analysis-worker.title: Analysis workers | PlayForge
guides/extending/workers/analysis-worker.summary: Analysis workers An analysis worker reads its entity's frame as it ends, after the tag workers. Derive from AbstractAnalysisWorker. Its hook is handed the entity and the frame's summary. The summary holds the frame's impacts, dealt and received (ImpactsDealt, ImpactsReceived, and by attribute, target and source). It also holds the effects applied and removed, the deaths, and the actions dropped and failed. For a worker that fires once, the base keeps a mark in the entity's Local Data, under its own key, MyKey. HasTriggered(system) reads the mark, SetTriggered(system) sets it, and ResetTriggered(system) clears it. Hooks Hook When PlayForge calls it Analyze(IGameplayAbilitySystem system, FrameSummary frameSummary) At every end of frame of every entity that holds the worker, after the tag workers. It returns the actions it queues. Rearm(system) As the entity revives. It resets the mark. In the picker A worker group's analysis workers offer every class derived from AbstractAnalysisWorker (How a kind is found). Example This worker applies an effect to its entity in a frame it deals enough hits to others: using System; using System.Collections.Generic; using FarEmerald.PlayForge; using UnityEngine; namespace MyGame { [Serializable] [ForgeMenu(Description = "Applies an effect to its entity in a frame it deals enough hits to others.")] public class FlurryWorker : AbstractAnalysisWorker { [Tooltip("The losses it deals others in one frame that fire it")] [Min(1)] public int Hits = 3; [Tooltip("The effect its entity takes as it fires")] public GameplayEffect Effect; public override IEnumerable<IRootAction> Analyze(IGameplayAbilitySystem system, FrameSummary frameSummary) { if (Effect == null || system == null || frameSummary == null) return Array.Empty<IRootAction>(); int dealt = 0; var impacts = frameSummary.ImpactsDealt; for (int i = 0; i < impacts.Count; i++) { var impact = impacts[i]; // A workable loss to another: an entity's own changes are recorded as dealt to itself too if (impact.SourcedModifier.ImpactIsWorkable && impact.RealImpact.CurrentValue < 0f && !ReferenceEquals(impact.Target, system)) dealt++; } if (dealt < Hits) return Array.Empty<IRootAction>(); return new IRootAction[] { new ApplyEffectAction(system, Effect, IEffectOrigin.GenerateSourceDerivation(system)) }; } } } Traps Analyze runs at every end of frame of every entity that holds the worker. A method that yield returns makes an object each call. So one that usually returns nothing returns Array.Empty<IRootAction>() instead, as above.

guides/extending/workers/attribute-worke.title: Attribute workers | PlayForge
guides/extending/workers/attribute-worke.summary: Attribute workers An attribute worker runs inside a change to one of its entity's attributes, where it can edit the change or queue actions. Derive from AbstractFocusedAttributeWorker. It watches one attribute, its Target Attribute, and registers itself. It filters the changes it takes by its Timing (TimingConfig: Pre Change, Post Change or both), its Sign Policy, Allow Self Modification, impact types and context tags. AbstractRelativeAttributeWorker adds GetRelative(ctx), the value of the attribute it's relative to. Its hooks are handed a WorkerContext: Member Holds System The entity whose attribute changes. AttributeCache Its attributes' values as they stand. Change The change. FrameSummary The frame's summary, which records its impacts. ActionQueue The entity's action queue. Hooks A worker of AbstractFocusedAttributeWorker overrides Execution and its hook: Hook When PlayForge calls it Execution Says which hook runs: EWorkerExecution.Inline, EWorkerExecution.Deferred, or EWorkerExecution.InlineAndDeferred for both. Intercept(WorkerContext ctx) Inside the change, for an inline worker. In Pre Change it edits ctx.Change.Value, and what it leaves is what commits. DeferredIntercept(WorkerContext ctx) During the change, for a deferred worker. It returns actions, which run at the end of frame. AbstractAttributeWorker itself, the base under it, leaves everything to the worker. A worker derived from it directly also implements these: Hook When PlayForge calls it Timing Says when in the change it runs. PreValidateWorkFor(ChangeValue) First, as a quick test of the change. ValidateWorkFor(WorkerContext) Then, with the whole context: whether it works on the change. RegisterWithHandler, DeRegisterFromHandler They add it to the pre- and post-change handlers with handler.AddWorker(attribute, this), and take it off with RemoveWorker. In the picker A worker group's attribute workers offer every class derived from AbstractAttributeWorker (How a kind is found). Its constructor can set defaults over its base's, as the example's sets its timing and its sign. Example This worker keeps any one loss of its attribute to a share of the attribute's base, so no hit takes it all: using System; using FarEmerald.PlayForge; using UnityEngine; namespace MyGame { [Serializable] [ForgeMenu(Description = "Keeps any one loss of its attribute to a share of the attribute's base, so no hit takes it all.")] public class CapLossWorker : AbstractFocusedAttributeWorker { [Tooltip("The most one loss takes, as a share of the attribute's base: 0.25 for a quarter")] [NumberRange(0f, 1f)] public ScalableFloat MostShare = 0.25f; public CapLossWorker() { TimingConfig = EChangeEventTiming.PreChange; SignPolicy = ESignPolicyExtended.Negative; } public override EWorkerExecution Execution => EWorkerExecution.Inline; public override void Intercept(WorkerContext ctx) { if (TargetAttribute == null || !ctx.AttributeCache.TryGetValue(TargetAttribute, out var cached)) return; var change = ctx.Change.Value; float most = cached.ActiveValue.BaseValue * (MostShare?.Evaluate(NumberContext.Of(in ctx)) ?? 1f); if (most <= 0f || change.CurrentValue >= -most) return; // The same change, its carrier and its workable mark kept, taking no more than the most ctx.Change.Value = new SourcedModifiedAttributeValue(change, -most, change.BaseValue, change.ImpactIsWorkable); } } } Traps Edit a change by building it again from itself, as above. ChangeValue.Add, Multiply and Override mark the change workable whatever it was. So a system change they touch starts reaching impact workers and lifesteal (Workers: Workable and unworkable). An inline worker never changes an attribute itself, which would run workers inside workers. It edits the change, or it's deferred.

guides/extending/workers/effect-workers..title: Effect workers | PlayForge
guides/extending/workers/effect-workers..summary: Effect workers An effect worker hears its effect's life: as it lands, as it lasts, as it comes off, and as a change it made lands. Derive from AbstractEffectWorker. An effect holds it in its Workers. Each hook is handed an EffectWorkerContext and returns actions: Member Holds System The one it's on, or for OnEffectImpact the dealer. Carrier The effect's application, with Spec the same as a GameplayEffectSpec. ExecuteTicks For a tick, the ticks that frame executes. ImpactData For an impact, the change that landed. Impacts For an instant effect's removal, every impact it made, one for each attribute. Empty otherwise. FrameSummary The frame's summary. ActionQueue The action queue. GetState<T>(this) What the worker keeps for this application. Two bases under it add more: AbstractAccumulatingEffectWorker adds a running total of the effect's impacts, through GetAccumulationData(ctx), which a worker of it implements to keep that total. TargetAttributeThresholdEffectWorker queues the actions its OnThresholdMet(ctx) returns as its target's attribute meets a threshold. Hooks Hook When PlayForge calls it OnEffectApplication(ctx) As the effect lands. System is the one it's on. OnEffectTick(ctx) Every frame a periodic effect lasts, with ExecuteTicks, the ticks that frame executes: most frames none. System is the one it's on. OnEffectRemoval(ctx) As it comes off. System is the one it's on. OnEffectImpact(ctx) As a change it made lands, with ImpactData. System is the dealer, its caster. In the picker An effect's Workers list offers every class derived from AbstractEffectWorker (How a kind is found). Example This worker applies an effect from the caster as its effect comes off, once it has ticked enough: using System; using System.Collections.Generic; using FarEmerald.PlayForge; using UnityEngine; namespace MyGame { [Serializable] [ForgeMenu(Description = "Applies an effect from the caster as its effect comes off, once it has ticked enough.")] public class PayoffWorker : AbstractEffectWorker { [Tooltip("The effect the one it's on takes as it comes off, from its caster")] public GameplayEffect Payoff; [Tooltip("The ticks its effect must have executed")] [Min(1)] public int Ticks = 3; // What it counts for one application of its effect private sealed class Count { public int Ticks; } public override IEnumerable<IRootAction> OnEffectTick(EffectWorkerContext ctx) { if (ctx.ExecuteTicks > 0 && ctx.GetState<Count>(this) is { } count) count.Ticks += ctx.ExecuteTicks; return Array.Empty<IRootAction>(); } public override IEnumerable<IRootAction> OnEffectRemoval(EffectWorkerContext ctx) { var target = ctx.Carrier?.GetTarget(); var caster = ctx.Carrier?.GetOrigin()?.GetSource(); if (Payoff == null || target == null || caster == null || target.IsDead || ctx.GetState<Count>(this) is not { } count || count.Ticks < Ticks) return Array.Empty<IRootAction>(); return new IRootAction[] { new ApplyEffectAction(target, Payoff, IEffectOrigin.GenerateSourceDerivation(caster)) }; } } } Traps OnEffectTick runs every frame of a periodic effect, not on each tick. Act where ExecuteTicks is above 0. OnEffectImpact runs on the dealer's side, as an impact worker does.

guides/extending/workers/impact-workers..title: Impact workers | PlayForge
guides/extending/workers/impact-workers..summary: Impact workers An impact worker runs as a change its holder dealt lands on another's attribute, for the attribute it subscribes to. It runs for the dealer: its context's System is its holder, the one who dealt the change, and the one hit is ImpactData.Target. Derive from AbstractContextImpactWorker, which does the validation and the subscription from its fields, or from AbstractImpactWorker for a worker that does them itself. Its hooks are handed an ImpactWorkerContext: Member Holds System Its holder, the dealer. ImpactData The hit: Target, Attribute, SourcedModifier, RealImpact, OldValue. FrameSummary The frame's summary. ActionQueue The action queue. AbstractContextImpactWorker's fields are Impacted Attribute, impact types, Impact Target, Impact Sign, Allow Self Impact, context tags, and a Work Attribute for its work. It starts narrow, Any Context Tag off and Impact Sign Positive, so it takes only gains carrying the context tags it names. A worker of it that means losses from anything says so in its constructor, as the example does. Hooks AbstractImpactWorker's members: Hook When PlayForge calls it PreValidateWorkFor(ImpactData) First, as a quick test. ValidateWorkFor(ImpactData) Then, as the whole test. Execution Deferred unless it says. CreateDeferredActions(ctx) For a deferred worker: it returns its actions. ActivateInline(ImpactData) For an inline worker: it acts here. SubscribeToCache(ImpactWorkerCache), UnsubscribeFromCache They give it to the cache under an attribute with cache.ProvideWorker(attribute, this), and take it back with RemoveWorker.
