OncePerHit True runs it once for a hit, however many of it its holder has, its project's and its own. Accept Unworkable Impact (AcceptUnworkableImpact) Off, it hears only workable changes. In the picker A worker group's impact workers offer every class derived from AbstractImpactWorker (How a kind is found). The picker shows GainOnHitWorker as Gain On Hit. Example This worker gives its holder some of its Work Attribute for each point of loss it deals another, as rage: using System; using System.Collections.Generic; using FarEmerald.PlayForge; using UnityEngine; namespace MyGame { [Serializable] [ForgeMenu(Description = "Gives its holder some of its Work Attribute for each point of loss it deals another, as rage.")] public class GainOnHitWorker : AbstractContextImpactWorker { [Tooltip("What its holder gains for each point of loss it deals")] public ScalableFloat PerPoint = 0.5f; public GainOnHitWorker() { AnyContextTag = true; ImpactSign = ESignPolicy.Negative; } public override IEnumerable<IRootAction> CreateDeferredActions(ImpactWorkerContext ctx) { // Its holder dealt the hit: the context's System var holder = ctx.System; if (WorkAttribute == null || holder == null || holder.IsDead) return Array.Empty<IRootAction>(); float gain = -ctx.ImpactData.RealImpact.CurrentValue * (PerPoint?.Evaluate(NumberContext.Of(in ctx)) ?? 0f); if (gain <= 0f) return Array.Empty<IRootAction>(); return new IRootAction[] { new ModifyAttributeAction(holder, WorkAttribute, SourcedModifiedAttributeValue.GenerateSimple(holder, WorkAttribute, gain, 0f)), }; } } } SourcedModifiedAttributeValue.GenerateSimple(source, attribute, current, base) makes a change of the source's own, a workable one. Traps An impact worker's System is the dealer (Workers: Traps). A change made for a worker is never built over the hit's carrier, ctx.ImpactData.SourcedModifier: that would count as the hit's effect again.

guides/extending/workers/tag-workers.htm.title: Tag workers | PlayForge
guides/extending/workers/tag-workers.htm.summary: Tag workers A tag worker acts while its entity's tags meet its Tag Requirements. Derive from AbstractTagWorker. Its hooks are handed the entity. Hooks Hook When PlayForge calls it Activate(system) As its requirements come to be met. It runs as an action at the entity's end of frame, at ActionPriority.TagWorker. Resolve(system) As they no longer are. It runs as an action the same way. Tick(system) At each end of frame while they hold, after the activations, as its Tick Pause says. ValidateWorkFor(ITagHandler) Whether its requirements are met: by default, its packets' weights. EvaluateEveryFrame True has it asked in every end of frame, for a worker whose ValidateWorkFor reads more than tags. Otherwise it's asked only in a frame the entity's tags changed. Tick Pause (TickPause) is the frames between ticks, read at the entity's level. 0 ticks every frame, and -1, the value it starts at, never ticks. It counts frames, not seconds. In the picker A worker group's tag workers offer every class derived from AbstractTagWorker (How a kind is found). Example This worker sends its entity an event as its tag requirements come to be met, and another as they stop: using System; using FarEmerald.PlayForge; using UnityEngine; namespace MyGame { [Serializable] [ForgeMenu(Description = "Sends its entity an event as its tag requirements come to be met, and another as they stop.")] public class TagEventsWorker : AbstractTagWorker { [Tooltip("The event its entity is sent as its requirements come to be met")] [ForgeTagContext(ForgeContext.Event)] public Tag OnMet; [Tooltip("The event its entity is sent as they stop being met")] [ForgeTagContext(ForgeContext.Event)] public Tag OnLost; public override void Activate(IGameplayAbilitySystem system) { if (OnMet.IsValid) system?.SendGameplayEvent(OnMet); } public override void Resolve(IGameplayAbilitySystem system) { if (OnLost.IsValid) system?.SendGameplayEvent(OnLost); } } } The events feed the entity's abilities' triggers and their Wait For Event tasks. Traps A tag worker is handed only its entity, and it's one object for every entity that holds it. What it keeps for one entity goes in an entity service or the entity's Local Data.

guides/extending/workers/traps.html.title: Traps | PlayForge
guides/extending/workers/traps.html.summary: Traps These traps apply to every kind of worker. A deferred worker's actions wait for the end of frame, so what it reads as it builds them may have changed as they run. An action reads the state it acts on as it executes. A worker is shared: a tag or analysis worker keeps nothing for one entity in its fields. Allocation. Workers run in the frame's hot path, an attribute worker for every change. Hold back from new lists, closures and iterators in a hook that runs for every change, and return Array.Empty<IRootAction>() for nothing.

guides/getting-started/index.html.title: Getting Started | PlayForge
guides/getting-started/index.html.summary: Getting Started PlayForge is a Gameplay Ability System (GAS) framework for Unity 6+. In it: The Demo sample in play: pick heroes, give them items and fight. entities own attributes; gameplay effects modify them; abilities orchestrate effects through staged task pipelines; tags glue everything together for requirements, filtering and UI. In this guide Requirements: PlayForge needs Unity 6 and UniTask, and installs a little differently from the Asset Store and from git. The pieces in one paragraph: This section shows how PlayForge's pieces fit together. Quickstart: a damage ability in ~10 minutes: This quickstart builds a damage ability, Fireball, from its attribute up to a scene that runs it. Tooling tour: This tour says what each of PlayForge's editor tools is for, and how to open it. Logging: All the runtime says goes through ForgeLog, whose level you control. Profiling: PlayForge's work shows in Unity's Profiler: markers time it, counters say how much of it there is, and two modules chart the counters.

guides/getting-started/logging.html.title: Logging | PlayForge
guides/getting-started/logging.html.summary: Logging All the runtime says goes through ForgeLog, whose level you control. In the editor, set the level in Preferences → PlayForge → Logging: Verbose, Info, Warning, Error or None. In builds, set ForgeLog.MinimumLevel from code. Some output is said only when asked, and it's information: ProcessControl's lifecycle logs, while its inspector's toggles are on; a sequence's or a chain's logging; a debug tool's output. For such output, the toggle makes it, and the level shows it. ForgeLog.Exception logs an exception as Unity's own LogException does, its stack in the console. A double-click on a message ForgeLog wrote opens the code that logged it, not ForgeLog. ForgeLog's methods are marked [HideInCallstack], so the Console's Strip Logging Callstack leaves them out of the stack. A logging wrapper of your own marked so is skipped too. Each message is of a system (ForgeLog.ESystem): effects, abilities, numbers, processes, sequences, saves, input and the rest. A system can take a level of its own, as ForgeLog.SetLevel(ForgeLog.ESystem.Effects, ForgeLog.ELevel.Verbose), or give it back with null. ForgeLog.Logged hears each message let through, with its system, and the entity it's about where it names one. The Creator Lab's Log page hears messages this way.

guides/getting-started/profiling.html.title: Profiling | PlayForge
guides/getting-started/profiling.html.summary: Profiling PlayForge's work shows in Unity's Profiler: markers time it, counters say how much of it there is, and two modules chart the counters. The markers are in the Profiler's Scripts category (ForgeProfiler): Marker What it times PlayForge.Update, PlayForge.LateUpdate, PlayForge.FixedUpdate The step loop at each timing. PlayForge.ProcessStep One process's step. Inside it, PlayForge.Step. and the process's type's name, with the process's ID as the marker's metadata. PlayForge.GASStep A GAS's step, where its effects tick. PlayForge.EndOfFrame A GAS's end of frame, where its queued actions and its tag and analysis workers run. PlayForge.ApplyEffect An effect's application, with its contained effects' inside it. PlayForge.ActivateAbility An ability's activation, up to the first of its tasks that waits. PlayForge.TagCompile A GAS's tag compile. PlayForge.Recompute An attribute's recompute. PlayForge.Stage A sequence stage's start, an ability's among them: its tasks, up to the first that waits. The counters are in the Profiler's PlayForge category (ForgeCounters): Counters What they count ProcessControl's The processes running, waiting and created, and each frame's registrations, terminations, steps, state changes and step time. The GAS's The entities by hub and the effects active, and each frame's effects applied and removed, impacts, activations, refused activations, tag compiles and recomputes. TaskSequence's The sequences running, and each frame's stages started. Two Profiler modules chart the counters. Turn them on in the Profiler window's list of modules: Module What it charts PlayForge Processes ProcessControl's and TaskSequence's counters. Its details list the selected frame's costliest processes, by their steps' time. PlayForge GAS The GAS's counters. PlayForge puts the costliest processes into the capture while the Profiler records, so a saved capture shows them too. A ProfilerRecorder reads a marker or a counter by its name, in the editor or in a development build. Unity compiles the markers and counters out of release builds.

guides/getting-started/quickstart-a-dama.title: Quickstart: a damage ability in ~10 minutes | PlayForge
guides/getting-started/quickstart-a-dama.summary: Quickstart: a damage ability in ~10 minutes This quickstart builds a damage ability, Fireball, from its attribute up to a scene that runs it. You can make each asset below from Window → PlayForge → The Forge, with its Create menu. You can also use the Create → PlayForge asset menu, which lists the Forge Project, then the assets The Forge lists, in its order, then the numbers, rules and the Tag Library. Attribute: create an Attribute asset named "Health". AttributeSet: create a set, and add an element for Health: Base/Current 100; Overflow policy ZeroToBase, so Current can never exceed Base (pool-style). EntityIdentity: create one. Assign the AttributeSet, and set its level range. GameplayEffect "Fireball Damage": set its Duration policy to Instant, and give it an impact: Attribute = Health, Operation = Add, Magnitude = -30; or attach a scaler for per-level values, like −20/−30/−40/−50. Ability "Fireball": Add a targeting task, for example SelectGasTargetTask. Add one stage, with an ApplyEffectsAbilityTask referencing the damage effect. Assign Cost and Cooldown effects, if you want them. Set the level range, and link the damage effect's scaler with LockToLevelProvider. Scene: Add a GameplayAbilitySystem to a GameObject, and assign the EntityIdentity. Bring PlayForge up with a Bootstrapper: the prefab PlayForge makes in Assets/PlayForge/Bootstrap as your first Forge Project is made, or a GameObject with the component, naming the Forge Project the scene plays. The Bootstrapper makes ProcessControl and the GameRoot, which runs as the project's Game Root entity. Grant and activate the ability through the AbilitySystemComponent. Instead of a GameObject, you can drive everything from code with RuntimeGameplayAbilitySystem, which needs none. ProcessControl.Register(gas).Run() starts it. In this section Code-driven abilities (sequences): For behaviour beyond declarative tasks, an ability runs a code-driven sequence. Running a process or a sequence: You run a process or a sequence from code through ProcessControl.Register. Time and random numbers: This section covers where PlayForge's time and random numbers come from, and the clocks an entity or a sequence runs by. Tooltips: what does this ability do?: AbilityInspector.Build(ability) describes what an ability does, for a tooltip.

guides/getting-started/quickstart-a-dama.title: Code-driven abilities (sequences) | PlayForge
guides/getting-started/quickstart-a-dama.summary: Code-driven abilities (sequences) For behaviour beyond declarative tasks, an ability runs a code-driven sequence. Add a RunSequenceTask pointing at a static [TaskSequenceMethod] builder. Load the effects the sequence applies with a SetEffectsTask asset loader. In the builder, annotate the sequence, so tooltips and analysis can decipher it: [TaskSequenceMethod("Ability: Chain Lightning")] public static TaskSequence ChainLightning() => TaskSequenceBuilder.Create("Chain Lightning") .WithAppliedEffects(Tags.EFFECTS, maxApplications: 4, "per enemy struck") .WithAnnotation("Chains to up to 4 nearby enemies") .Task(async (d, t) => { /* ... d.TryApplyEffects(target, Tags.EFFECTS) ... */ }) .BuildSequence();

guides/getting-started/quickstart-a-dama.title: Running a process or a sequence | PlayForge
guides/getting-started/quickstart-a-dama.summary: Running a process or a sequence You run a process or a sequence from code through ProcessControl.Register. It starts a registration, and Run makes it. Call What it does ProcessControl.Register Starts a registration of a process: a MonoBehaviour or runtime process, a TaskSequence, or a chain of them. HandledBy Names what the process belongs to, which ends it as it ends. With Names the packet the process carries. Run Registers the process, and starts it. Left out, HandledBy follows the packet: an ability's packet hands the process to the packet's source, and anything else hands it to GameRoot. A refused registration says why: var result = ProcessControl.Register(projectile).HandledBy(gas).With(data).Run(); if (!result) ForgeLog.Warning($"Not registered: {result.Refusal}"); A process that requires control waits after it registers. relay.Run() starts it. Processes an ability spawns A process an ability's Create Mono Process task spawns takes the ability as its origin. So the effects it applies are the caster's, at the ability's level. The task's Spawn At says where the process appears: Spawn At Where the process appears At the Caster At the caster, as a projectile does. At the Target At the ability's target, as a fire on the ground does. As Its Data Says Where the data's Position says. A gameplay mono process, as ProjectileMonoProcess, carries attributes of its own in Attributes. Each entry has: an attribute; the role it's read by, as a projectile reads its speed as ProjectileSpeed; where it starts: its own value, the caster's attribute, or the caster's where the caster has it. Its own value is a number, or a scaler read at the spawning ability's level. The data that spawns the process can set an attribute under its role. The process's code reads and sets its attributes with TryGetRole, SetRole, TryGetAttribute and SetAttribute. To go further: Processes covers processes, their lifecycles, pausing and groups. Task Sequences covers task sequences: their stages, tasks, repeats, injections, chains, synced runners and libraries.

guides/getting-started/quickstart-a-dama.title: Time and random numbers | PlayForge
guides/getting-started/quickstart-a-dama.summary: Time and random numbers This section covers where PlayForge's time and random numbers come from, and the clocks an entity or a sequence runs by. PlayForge reads time through ForgeTime, and draws random numbers through ForgeRandom. They read Unity's Time and Random unless you put in your own: Call What you put in ForgeTime.Use(clock) A clock of your own, an IForgeClock. ForgeRandom.Use(new SeededRandom(seed)) Seeded rolls, which repeat from their seed whatever else draws from Unity's Random. Each Use returns what it replaced, so you can put it back. Each entity numbers its effects' applications (GameplayEffectSpec.ApplicationId) and its abilities' activations. An entity's clock Each entity also has a clock of its own, gas.GetClock(): the game's time, scaled by the entity's TimeScale. The entity's effects run by it, its cooldowns among them. Its abilities' waits and sequences run by it too. So TimeScale = 0.5f slows one entity and no other. A scale of 0 holds the entity's time still, but it isn't a pause. A sequence's clock A sequence can run by a clock of its own: WithClock(UnscaledClock.Instance) runs a pause menu's sequence while the game's time stands still. A ScaledClock runs a sequence at a pace of its own. A packet's Clock, an entity's among them, comes before either. An ability's Run Sequence task picks a clock in its inspector, with its Clock. Task Sequences has the order a run takes them in. Fixed ticks For a run that comes out the same at any frame rate, set ProcessControl's Fixed Tick Rate, as 60. The game then steps in ticks, each a fixed step of its time, as many a frame as the frame's time holds: Every process steps once a tick, its end of frame with it. Each sequence's wait goes on by the tick. Code of your own that waits for a sequence's next frame awaits ForgeTick.Next(token). 0, the default, steps once a frame. The ticks stand still with the game's time, so a sequence on the unscaled clock waits for Unity's frames instead.

guides/getting-started/quickstart-a-dama.title: Tooltips: what does this ability do? | PlayForge
guides/getting-started/quickstart-a-dama.summary: Tooltips: what does this ability do? AbilityInspector.Build(ability) describes what an ability does, for a tooltip. It returns a full static breakdown: every effect, with its role, its target scope, and its per-level numbers, evaluated through the real scaler pipeline; the ability's components; what sets it off on its own, and its chance to activate; its Attribute Costs. var breakdown = AbilityInspector.Build(fireball); foreach (var line in breakdown.Describe(level)) // "Deals 30 Health to target", "Cooldown: 8s" tooltip.AppendLine(line); var impact = breakdown.GameplayUsages.First().Series.Impacts[0]; string perLevel = impact.FormatTotal(); // "20/30/40/50"

guides/getting-started/requirements.html.title: Requirements | PlayForge
guides/getting-started/requirements.html.summary: Requirements PlayForge needs Unity 6 and UniTask, and installs a little differently from the Asset Store and from git. Unity 6.0+, built and tested on 6000.0. UniTask 2.5.11 (Cysharp, MIT). How you get it depends on how you install PlayForge, as below. From the Asset Store: PlayForge installs in Assets/Plugins/PlayForge, and your Forge Projects go in Assets/PlayForge, so the two never share a folder. PlayForge includes UniTask, in PlayForge/ThirdParty/UniTask. A project that already has UniTask from Package Manager deletes that folder. The samples are in PlayForge/Samples. Installed as a package from git: PlayForge needs UniTask added in Package Manager by git URL, pinned to that release: https://github.com/Cysharp/UniTask.git?path=src/UniTask/Assets/Plugins/UniTask#2.5.11. A package can't declare a git dependency, so the project's manifest has to name UniTask. The samples import from Package Manager's Samples tab. The samples need nothing more: Battle: a battle that plays itself. Demo: a hero arena to pick heroes, give items and fight. It reads the Input System where the project has it, and the Input Manager otherwise. Survivors: a horde shooter with hundreds of enemies at once, to see what PlayForge carries. Task Sequence Examples and Process Group Examples. The samples render in the Built-in Render Pipeline or URP. HDRP isn't supported.

guides/getting-started/the-pieces-in-one.title: The pieces in one paragraph | PlayForge
guides/getting-started/the-pieces-in-one.summary: The pieces in one paragraph This section shows how PlayForge's pieces fit together. classDiagram class BaseForgeAsset:::ext { <<abstract ScriptableObject>> +LocalData : List~DataWrapper~ +TryGetLocalData(Tag, out DataWrapper) bool +Template +SetTemplate(asset) GetGrantedTags() } class BaseForgeLevelProvider:::ext { <<abstract>> GetMaxLevel() GetStartingLevel() LinkToProvider(provider) } class EntityIdentity:::asset { +AttributeSet +StartingAbilities +StartingItems, with EquipOnInit +TimeScaleAttribute +Modifiers +CrowdControl +Death: OnDeath and OnRevive effects, Body +Components: Bounty and Aura effects } class AttributeSet:::asset { +Attributes +SubSets +WorkerGroup } class Attribute:::asset { +AbsorbsFor +GainsScaledBy } class Ability:::asset { +Behaviour: tasks name effects, items, processes, sequences +Cost +Cooldown +AttributeCosts +OnHit +Modifiers } class GameplayEffect:::asset { Every asset derives from BaseForgeAsset, the levelled ones from BaseForgeLevelProvider. An Ability, effect, Item, AttributeSet or entity can LinkToProvider and follow another's level. An EntityIdentity asset configures an entity: its AttributeSet: attributes with starting Current/Base values, clamping and regulation; its starting Abilities and starting Items; its tags and its level range. At runtime, a GameplayAbilitySystem (a MonoBehaviour) or a RuntimeGameplayAbilitySystem (a plain class) instantiates that identity. GameplayEffect assets change attributes. Each effect's impact entry has a delivery, which decides everything about its lifecycle: Delivery Meaning Reversal Continuous modifier while the effect is active ("+20% speed") automatic, exact OnApply one permanent commit ("take 30 damage") never Periodic one permanent commit per tick ("5 HP/s") never Abilities run staged task lists (targeting → apply effects → run code-driven sequences). guides/getting-started/tooling-tour.html.title: Tooling tour | PlayForge
guides/getting-started/tooling-tour.html.summary: Tooling tour This tour says what each of PlayForge's editor tools is for, and how to open it. The Editor Tools covers each tool in depth. In this section The Creator Lab: The Creator Lab is a space to try the project's own assets in. The Forge: The Forge is PlayForge's main window: every PlayForge asset of the active Forge Project, in one list beside a detail pane. Forge Projects: A Forge Project holds one game's PlayForge assets, and its settings. The Tags view: The Forge's Tags view lists the project's tags, and what uses each. Spreadsheets: The Spreadsheets commands write the project's numbers by level, or its items' stats, to CSV, and read a sheet back. The Debugger: The Debugger shows the game as it plays, in four views the toolbar switches between. The Problems view: The Problems view lists every problem the validator finds in the project's PlayForge assets, with its severity and its asset. The settings pages: PlayForge's Settings are on two pages: the project's, and your own. Asset fields: Asset fields are Unity's object fields: every reference to a PlayForge asset is one. Import and Clear: Import and Clear sit on each inspector section's header, beside Help. Templates: Templates let an asset take its fields from another asset of its type, its template. Golden tests: The Golden tests are the framework's behavioural contract. The test kit: The test kit (FarEmerald.PlayForge.Testing) plays your own abilities, effects and items in your own tests.

guides/getting-started/tooling-tour/asse.title: Asset fields | PlayForge
guides/getting-started/tooling-tour/asse.summary: Asset fields Asset fields are Unity's object fields: every reference to a PlayForge asset is one. Open, beside a field, shows the asset in a window of its own. New, beside an empty field, asks for the new asset's name, then makes it where Project Settings → PlayForge puts its type. An effect field's right-click menu has the field's template, where it has one, a pick of the effects nothing links, and New Linked Effect. The Editor Tools: Fields and drawers covers asset fields and PlayForge's other fields.

guides/getting-started/tooling-tour/forg.title: Forge Projects | PlayForge
guides/getting-started/tooling-tour/forg.summary: Forge Projects A Forge Project holds one game's PlayForge assets, and its settings. The Forge's toolbar, its project menu first. It's a folder with a project asset at its root (Create → PlayForge → Forge Project). It holds the assets under it that no project inside it does. The Forge's project menu switches projects, and makes a new one. With no project, The Forge asks for the first. The active project is the one The Forge shows. Every asset picker, an object field's among them, offers the active project's assets alone, and the tag picker the tags they use. The Demo's assets are a project of their own. The Editor Tools: Forge Projects covers projects, the active project, and moving assets between projects.

guides/getting-started/tooling-tour/gold.title: Golden tests | PlayForge
guides/getting-started/tooling-tour/gold.summary: Golden tests The Golden tests are the framework's behavioural contract. Find them in the Test Runner's EditMode tab, under FarEmerald.PlayForge.Tests.Golden. Run them after upgrading.

guides/getting-started/tooling-tour/impo.title: Import and Clear | PlayForge
guides/getting-started/tooling-tour/impo.summary: Import and Clear Import and Clear sit on each inspector section's header, beside Help. Import opens the Import window. Choose a source on the left: the type's defaults first, then the assets of the type. The right lists the fields that differ, each checked, beside their values now and the source's. Uncheck a field to leave it. Import N Changes imports the checked fields, as one Undo step. The asset menu's Import from Another Asset... does the same for the whole asset. Clear resets the section's fields at once, and Undo takes it back. The Editor Tools: Import and Clear covers both in depth.

guides/getting-started/tooling-tour/spre.title: Spreadsheets | PlayForge
guides/getting-started/tooling-tour/spre.summary: Spreadsheets The Spreadsheets commands write the project's numbers by level, or its items' stats, to CSV, and read a sheet back. Open them from The Forge's window menu, under Spreadsheets. Reading a sheet back lists its changes before it makes them. Spreadsheets covers spreadsheets in full, and The Editor Tools: Spreadsheets names their editor parts.

guides/getting-started/tooling-tour/temp.title: Templates | PlayForge
guides/getting-started/tooling-tour/temp.summary: Templates Templates let an asset take its fields from another asset of its type, its template. An asset's menu Set Template... picks, from a searchable list of the other assets of its type, the template it becomes a child of. A child takes the template's fields when the template is pushed, with the template's asset menu Push to Its Children, as one Undo step. Saving a template changes no child. A child keeps each field it overrides. An edit to a child's field makes it the child's own, and its inspector marks it as Unity marks a prefab instance's override. The Editor Tools: Templates covers templates in depth.

guides/getting-started/tooling-tour/the-.title: The Creator Lab | PlayForge
guides/getting-started/tooling-tour/the-.summary: The Creator Lab The Creator Lab is a space to try the project's own assets in. The Creator Lab: a quick battle with the Demo's heroes. Open it from Window → PlayForge → Creator Lab. It opens in a new scene, and plays. Put units and test dummies down, and drop effects, abilities and items on them. Read any asset's numbers, level by level. Its time pauses, steps and speeds up on its own. The Creator Lab covers the lab, and The Editor Tools: The Creator Lab its editor parts.

guides/getting-started/tooling-tour/the-.title: The Debugger | PlayForge
guides/getting-started/tooling-tour/the-.summary: The Debugger The Debugger shows the game as it plays, in four views the toolbar switches between. The Debugger beside the Demo in play. Open it from Window → PlayForge → Debugger. Entities lists every entity, of either kind, with its attributes, effects, abilities, tags and combat log. A foot row under each table acts on the entity: set values, apply or remove effects, grant and activate abilities, add tags. Processes lists every process with its state and how long its steps take. It pauses, resumes or terminates the one selected. Tags shows every tag the entities hold, as a tree, and who holds the one selected. Timeline records each run of an ability, stage by stage, each effect's time on the shelf, and the refusals, and draws them over the last seconds. The Editor Tools: The Debugger covers each view in depth.

guides/getting-started/tooling-tour/the-.title: The Forge | PlayForge
guides/getting-started/tooling-tour/the-.summary: The Forge The Forge is PlayForge's main window: every PlayForge asset of the active Forge Project, in one list beside a detail pane. The Forge: the active project's assets beside the one selected. Open it from Window → PlayForge → The Forge, or with Alt+Shift+F, which focuses its search. Its toolbar holds Back and Forward, the project menu, Create, a filter for each asset type, Tags, the search and the problem count. A click on an asset shows its summary and its inspector in the detail pane. A double click shows it in the Project window. Create makes an asset, blank or from a preset: a Damage, Damage over Time, Buff, Debuff, Stun or Aura effect, an On-Hit or Active item, a Passive ability, or a Hero entity. The project's own Templates follow the presets in Create, each a new asset's copy. The asset menu renames an asset, as F2 on the list does, and moves or copies the selected assets into another project. The Editor Tools: The Forge covers The Forge in depth, and The Editor Tools: New assets and presets its presets.

guides/getting-started/tooling-tour/the-.title: The Problems view | PlayForge
guides/getting-started/tooling-tour/the-.summary: The Problems view The Problems view lists every problem the validator finds in the project's PlayForge assets, with its severity and its asset. The Problems view, by asset. Open it from Window → PlayForge → Problems, or from a problem count in The Forge's toolbar or an inspector's header. A problem is, for example, a link with no provider, an impact that never applies, or a field that reads a scaler it hasn't got. A click selects the asset. By Rule, in its toolbar, groups the problems under the rule each breaks. Where one step fixes a problem, its row has a Quick Fix, as Store the Tag. In batch mode, ForgeValidator.LogAll writes the problems to the Console. Add a check of your own by deriving from ForgeValidationRule: override Name to name its group, and give a problem a step that fixes it with its Fix. The Editor Tools: The Problems view and validation covers the view, PlayForge's rules and the validator.

guides/getting-started/tooling-tour/the-.title: The settings pages | PlayForge
guides/getting-started/tooling-tour/the-.summary: The settings pages PlayForge's Settings are on two pages: the project's, and your own. Project Settings → PlayForge. Project Settings → PlayForge shows the active Forge Project's settings, kept in its asset under version control, each game its own. They say where new assets go and what they start as, and what the game reads through its GameRoot as it runs, as the roles its attributes play (Attributes: Roles). The page's PlayForge Folder is where a new Forge Project goes. Preferences → PlayForge holds your own view toggles, the most PlayForge's dropdowns grow to (Menu Width and Menu Height), and the log level. The Forge's window menu opens both. The Editor Tools: Preferences and Project Settings covers both pages in depth.

guides/getting-started/tooling-tour/the-.title: The Tags view | PlayForge
guides/getting-started/tooling-tour/the-.summary: The Tags view The Forge's Tags view lists the project's tags, and what uses each. The Forge's Tags view. Open it with Tags, in The Forge's toolbar. A context is a kind of tag, as Granted, Event, Impact Type or Local Data Key. A tag field's picker offers the kinds it takes. A tag's Declared For declares it for contexts, so their fields' pickers offer it. A Tag Library asset (Create → PlayForge → Tag Library) keeps the declarations. The view renames a tag, as F2 or a row's Rename… does, and the tags under its path with it, everywhere they're stored. An asset's own tag follows its asset's name instead. The Editor Tools: The Tags view covers the view, and Tags covers tags, their contexts and the Tag Library.

guides/getting-started/tooling-tour/the-.title: The test kit | PlayForge
guides/getting-started/tooling-tour/the-.summary: The test kit The test kit (FarEmerald.PlayForge.Testing) plays your own abilities, effects and items in your own tests. Each test gets a live world, stepped a frame at a time, with entities on either hub. A test plays them with Cast, Use, Hold and Hit, with scripted time and rolls. After each test, the kit checks that nothing leaked. Testing Your Content sets it up.

guides/items/abilities.html.title: Abilities | PlayForge
guides/items/abilities.html.summary: Abilities The Abilities section names the ability the item lends its holder. Property Description Active Ability An ability the entity learns while the item is equipped. It's granted at the item's level when the item is equipped, and removed when the item is unequipped. If the entity can't take the ability, because of its Max Abilities or Allow Duplicate Abilities settings, the item is still equipped, without the ability. To make the ability's levels follow the item's, use Link Ability & Effects in Leveling.

guides/items/built-in-kinds.html.title: Built-in kinds | PlayForge
guides/items/built-in-kinds.html.summary: Built-in kinds The kinds PlayForge ships for this guide's pickers, each with its menu and what it does, as its picker says. A project's own kinds join them in the same pickers. Components Kind Menu What it does AuraItemComponent — Gives those near the holder an aura's effects while the item is equipped. CuesItemComponent — Shows and sounds the item's moments on its holder: as it's equipped, while it's equipped, and as it's used. SetBonusItemComponent — An effect its holder has while enough of a set's pieces are equipped. UsesItemComponent — How many times the item's ability can be used before one of the item goes.

guides/items/components.html.title: Components | PlayForge
guides/items/components.html.summary: Components An item's components are features it carries, each a class with hooks into the item's life. Add one with the list's +. A kind that makes no sense twice is offered only while the item holds none of it. A component hears these moments: Hook When it runs Given As the item is given to an entity. Equipped As the item is equipped. Unequipped As the item is unequipped. Removed As the item is removed. Used As its holder's use of the item's Active Ability ends, having paid what it costs. Its context's Restoring says a moment comes from a load. A load puts back what the component's earlier moments did, such as the effects it applied. In this section Auras: An Aura component holds an effect on those near its holder while the item is equipped, such as a banner that inspires the allies round its bearer. Uses: A Uses component counts the uses of the item's Active Ability, such as a potion's sips or a wand's charges. Set Bonus: A Set Bonus component gives its holder a bonus effect while it has enough of a set's pieces equipped. Cues: A Cues component plays what the item shows and sounds on its holder. Writing your own component: A component of your own derives from AbstractItemComponent and overrides the hooks it needs.

guides/items/components/auras.html.title: Auras | PlayForge
guides/items/components/auras.html.summary: Auras An Aura component holds an effect on those near its holder while the item is equipped, such as a banner that inspires the allies round its bearer. Property Description Effect The effect it holds on each one it takes while they're near. Radius How far it reaches from its holder, read at each check. Flat Measures along the ground, leaving height out. Off, it measures a sphere. Takes Whom it takes, by how each stands to its holder, its holder too or not: Allies (the default, itself among them), Other Allies, Enemies, Self, All But Self or Everyone. Interval How often it checks who's near, by its holder's own time: 0.25 s by default. Effects: Components: Auras describes how an aura holds its effect.

guides/items/components/cues.html.title: Cues | PlayForge
guides/items/components/cues.html.summary: Cues A Cues component plays what the item shows and sounds on its holder. Property Description On Equip Plays as the item is equipped. While Equipped Plays for as long as it's equipped. On Use Plays as it's used, as the ability it lends is. A load that puts an equipped item back begins its While Equipped cues and plays no burst. Each list holds cues as an effect's does (Effects: Cues). An item holds one at most.

guides/items/components/set-bonus.html.title: Set Bonus | PlayForge
guides/items/components/set-bonus.html.summary: Set Bonus A Set Bonus component gives its holder a bonus effect while it has enough of a set's pieces equipped. For example, two pieces of a set give fire resistance, and four a flame aura. Property Description Set The set the item is a piece of, named by a tag. Pieces How many of the set's pieces the holder needs equipped: a number field read at its holder's level. Bonus The effect the holder has while it has that many equipped. Each piece names its Set and carries the set's bonuses, each a Set Bonus component with the Pieces it needs. The holder's equipped pieces count each item once. A bonus holds while they're as many as it needs: once for the holder, however many pieces carry it. A bonus comes from one of the pieces, and moves to another as that one leaves while enough stay. A load puts the bonus back with the other effects, and weighs each set once.

guides/items/components/uses.html.title: Uses | PlayForge
guides/items/components/uses.html.summary: Uses A Uses component counts the uses of the item's Active Ability, such as a potion's sips or a wand's charges. Each use is one that paid what it costs. Property Description Uses How many uses the item has, read at the item's level. With none left, one of the item goes, at the frame's end: a stack of it, its uses whole again for the next; or the item with its last, and its ability with it. A load gives its uses whole. An item with no Active Ability never counts any, which the Problems view says. An item holds one at most.

guides/items/components/writing-your-own.title: Writing your own component | PlayForge
guides/items/components/writing-your-own.summary: Writing your own component A component of your own derives from AbstractItemComponent and overrides the hooks it needs. Each hook is a no-op otherwise. A component is the item's, shared by every entity that holds the item. So what it keeps for one entity's item, it keeps through its context: ctx.GetState<T>(this).

guides/items/effects.html.title: Effects | PlayForge
guides/items/effects.html.summary: Effects The Effects section lists the effects the item applies to the entity while it's equipped. Property Description Granted Effects Effects applied to the entity while the item is equipped. Each is applied with the item as its origin, so it takes the item's level. Unequipping removes the effects this item applied. It leaves the same effect alone where something else applied it. An effect's duration decides how it behaves on an equipped item: Duration What it does Infinite Lasts while the item is equipped. Use it for bonuses that last while the item is equipped. Instant Commits once, when the item is equipped. Unequipping doesn't undo it. Durational Ends when its time runs out, even while the item is still equipped. A line under each effect says how it takes its levels, and Link makes it take this item's. New, beside an empty field, makes an effect linked to this item.

guides/items/identity.html.title: Identity | PlayForge
guides/items/identity.html.summary: Identity The Identity section names the item, shows its asset tag, and sets how many of it one inventory slot holds. Property Description Name The item's display name, which also gives the asset tag. Renaming the item changes its tag, so update anything that names the old tag. Description Free text for your UI. Asset Tag Read-only, made from the Name: punctuation is dropped, and each word is capitalised and joined. Visibility A tag your UI can read for filtering, such as Always Visible or Not Visible. The Forge lists it, and the runtime doesn't act on it. Max Stack Size How many of the item one inventory slot holds: a number field read at the item's level, as StackSizeOf(spec) reads it. At 1 or less, each is a slot of its own. Textures Icons, each paired with a tag. The texture tagged Primary is the item's icon; without one, the first texture is used. The asset tag is stored when you edit the Name, and the inspector header shows it after the item's type. If the stored tag differs from the one the Name gives, it shows in warning text with an Update button that stores the new one. Whether an inventory may hold an item more than once is the entity's choice, through its Allow Duplicate Items setting (see Entities). Stacking An item stacks in one inventory slot, up to its Max Stack Size. A give fills the item's stack first, up to its Max Stack Size, and takes no new slot. A full stack opens another only with Allow Duplicate Items on. Without it, what doesn't fit isn't taken. A slot's count is its container's ItemStacks. Code gives and takes stacks through the entity's item system: Method What it does ItemSystemComponent.GiveItem(item, count) Takes what fits, and returns how many it took. GiveItem(item, out index) Gives one, into the stack if there's room. RemoveItem(item, count) Takes stacks off, from the last slot first. A slot whose last stack comes off goes. RemoveItem(item) Still takes the whole slot. A stack applies its effects and its ability once. An Item Stacks scaler reads the count of the item that applied the effect. So a magnitude of 5 with Multiply With Scaler grants +5 a stack. As the count changes, an equipped item's effects read it again. An effect that reads an item's stacks where no item in the project applies it reads 1, and the Problems view says so.

Uses and Consume are two independent routes to spending an item. Giving an item puts it in the entity's inventory. Equipping it applies what it grants: its Granted Effects, its Active Ability, its Granted Tags and its workers. Unequipping the item, or removing it from the inventory, takes them away again. An entity gets items from its Entity asset's Starting Items, or from code through its ItemSystemComponent, with GiveItem, EquipItem, UnequipItem and RemoveItem. The entity's limits on items are set on its Entity asset. Tags are names, such as State.Stunned, that an entity carries and that requirements check. Each asset stores a tag made from its Name: Iron Sword gives Item.IronSword. The entity carries this tag while the item is in its inventory, equipped or not, and keeps the item's level under it. Each section below matches the inspector section of the same name. A collapsed section shows one line about what it holds, such as the level range or how many effects the item grants. The inspector's header shows the item's one-line summary, as The Forge's Summary column does. The line gives what each effect it gives changes while it's equipped, by its first impact across its levels, then the ability it grants: "+20 Armor; Blink". In this guide Identity: The Identity section names the item, shows its asset tag, and sets how many of it one inventory slot holds. Leveling: The Leveling section sets the item's level range. Tags: The Tags section sets the tags that describe the item and the tags it grants. Effects: The Effects section lists the effects the item applies to the entity while it's equipped. Abilities: The Abilities section names the ability the item lends its holder. Components: An item's components are features it carries, each a class with hooks into the item's life. Workers: Workers are reusable behaviours, picked from a list, that react to what happens to an entity. Local Data: Local Data is a list of named values stored on the asset. Used By: The Used By section lists the PlayForge assets that refer to this item, each with its type icon, such as an entity that starts with it or an effect linked to it. Built-in kinds: The kinds PlayForge ships for this guide's pickers, each with its menu and what it does, as its picker says. guides/items/leveling.html.title: Leveling | PlayForge
guides/items/leveling.html.summary: Leveling The Leveling section sets the item's level range. An item has its own level on each entity that holds it, kept under the item's asset tag. Its Granted Effects take this level, and its Active Ability is granted at it. A level provider is an asset whose level range another asset follows. Property Description Link Mode Standalone (default): keeps the item's own range. Linked To Provider: takes the range from a level provider instead. Starting Level The start of the item's own range, 1 by default. It's kept within the range. Max Level The end of the item's own range, 4 by default. Level Provider Shown while linked: the asset the range comes from, an Entity, Ability, Effect, Item or Attribute Set. Both levels are at least 1. While linked, Starting Level and Max Level show the range in use, read-only. Right-click the Level Provider field to pick from one type. A link that would make a loop is refused, with an error in the Console. While no provider is set, a warning says the item uses its own range. Two buttons link the item's Granted Effects and Active Ability to it, or unlink them. Each asks first, and one Undo takes it back. Link Ability & Effects links the Granted Effects and the Active Ability to this item, so their per-level values follow its range. Unlink Ability & Effects removes the links that point at this item. A given item starts at its Starting Level, unless code gives it at another level. Its level then stays between that level and the Max Level. Code changes it through the entity's GAS, with SetLevel or ModifyLevel and the item's asset tag. The link serves the inspector: the Leveling section, and the scalers of effects linked to this item, read the provider's range. Note At runtime, the item's level comes from its own Starting Level and Max Level, even while it is linked.

guides/items/local-data.html.title: Local Data | PlayForge
guides/items/local-data.html.summary: Local Data Local Data is a list of named values stored on the asset. Each row has a Key (a tag) and a value of a kind. Column Description Key A tag that names the row. Kind The kind of value: Float, Int, String, Bool, Tag, Attribute, Effect, Ability, Entity, Object, MonoBehaviour or ScriptableObject, or a kind of your own. Value The row's value. A row saves its own value alone. A kind of your own is a [Serializable] class made from LocalDataValue<T>, such as a point or a colour. The row's kinds offer it beside PlayForge's. Object fields take project assets, not scene objects. Code reads a value by its type, with data.TryGet(out float range) or data.TryGet(out MyPoint point). A number, a Float or an Int, can scale. Code reads it with data.Value.TryReadNumber(context, out float number). PlayForge doesn't read an item's Local Data itself. Your code and workers can, with item.TryGetLocalData(key, out var data). The first row with that key wins.

guides/items/tags.html.title: Tags | PlayForge
guides/items/tags.html.summary: Tags The Tags section sets the tags that describe the item and the tags it grants. Property Description Context Tags Tags that describe the item, such as Weapon. The changes made by effects this item applies carry them as context, and workers can filter by them. Granted Tags Tags applied to the entity while the item is equipped. Context Tags are not applied to the entity.

guides/items/used-by.html.title: Used By | PlayForge
guides/items/used-by.html.summary: Used By The Used By section lists the PlayForge assets that refer to this item, each with its type icon, such as an entity that starts with it or an effect linked to it. Click a row to select the asset. The list follows the project as it changes.

guides/items/workers.html.title: Workers | PlayForge
guides/items/workers.html.summary: Workers Workers are reusable behaviours, picked from a list, that react to what happens to an entity. This group is subscribed to the entity when the item is equipped, and removed when it is unequipped. Property Description Name Labels the group. Attribute Workers that run before or after an attribute changes, for example to reduce incoming damage. Impact Workers that inspect the changes the entity deals. Tag Workers that react when the entity's tags change. Analysis Workers that examine the frame at its end, for example to detect death. Each list's + adds an empty worker to pick a kind for. The section's import button copies a worker group from another asset. Above the worker group, the section holds the item's On Hit and Modifiers. In this section On Hit: On Hit, above the workers, holds the effects the item applies as its holder's hits land, while it's equipped. Modifiers: Modifiers, under On Hit, change other effects as they're made, while the item is equipped. Lifesteal: An item gives its holder lifesteal through an effect, one of its Granted Effects while it's equipped.

guides/items/workers/lifesteal.html.title: Lifesteal | PlayForge
guides/items/workers/lifesteal.html.summary: Lifesteal An item gives its holder lifesteal through an effect, one of its Granted Effects while it's equipped. The effect raises the holder's Lifesteal: the attribute the project's Lifesteal worker names as its Share, which the Lifesteal worker heals by (Workers: Lifesteal). For example, a vampiric mask's Infinite effect of +0.15 Lifesteal heals its wearer 15% of each blow it deals. Note The item's Lifesteal list is gone.

guides/items/workers/modifiers.html.title: Modifiers | PlayForge
guides/items/workers/modifiers.html.summary: Modifiers Modifiers, under On Hit, change other effects as they're made, while the item is equipped. They change its holder's own effects, such as a boon that adds a burst to its holder's every Chill. They change those landing on it, such as a cloak that halves the stuns its wearer takes. Each entry is a rule of its own, or names a shared Effect Modifier asset (Effects: Workers: Modifiers).

guides/items/workers/on-hit.html.title: On Hit | PlayForge
guides/items/workers/on-hit.html.summary: On Hit On Hit, above the workers, holds the effects the item applies as its holder's hits land, while it's equipped. Examples include a dagger's bleed, a hammer's armor break and a barrier on a kill. Property Description Attribute What a hit lowers, such as Health: a hit is a loss to it that the holder deals another entity. None counts the attribute playing the project's Health role (Attributes: Roles), where it has one. Effects What it applies. Each effect's own Chance to Apply rolls as it lands, and its hits set the entry off no more, so a shock it applies doesn't shock again. To Whom they land on: the one hit (Target), or the Holder, as a barrier on a kill does. Only On Kill Only the hit that takes the attribute from above 0 to 0 or below. Impact Types Only hits of one of these types, such as attacks, so a bleed's ticks, typed apart, set off nothing. None takes any hit. When A condition read at the hit, the holder its caster and the one hit its target. A hit's proc coefficient scales the effects' chance and duration, and 0 sets nothing off (Effects: Workers: On Hit). The Problems view warns of an impact type no effect in the project deals, which never matches.

guides/processes/groups.html.title: Groups | PlayForge
guides/processes/groups.html.summary: Groups A group is a process that holds other processes, found by a tag. Each member still runs as a process of its own. The group adds what the members have in common: A cap on its members. A data packet they share. What's done to all of them at once. How long the group lasts, and events as its members come and go. Only runtime processes join a group. The Process Group Examples sample runs each of these from a key in a scene. In this section Making and joining a group: A group is made first, to configure it, or else made by its first member, with no cap. Capping a group: A group's cap, MaxMembers, limits how many members it holds. Acting on every member: A group acts on all its members at once, and finds them for you. Group lifetime and events: A group lasts until its last member leaves, and ending it ends its members.

guides/processes/groups/acting-on-every-.title: Acting on every member | PlayForge
guides/processes/groups/acting-on-every-.summary: Acting on every member A group acts on all its members at once, and finds them for you. Member What it does PauseAll Pauses every member. UnpauseAll Unpauses every member. TerminateAllMembers Ends every member. ForEach Visits each member, in the order they joined. ForEach<T> Visits the members of a kind. GetOldest, GetNewest, TryGetFirst<T>, HasMember, MemberCount, IsFull Find, check and count its members. DetachMember Takes one member out without ending it.

guides/processes/groups/capping-a-group..title: Capping a group | PlayForge
guides/processes/groups/capping-a-group..summary: Capping a group A group's cap, MaxMembers, limits how many members it holds. Its overflow policy says what happens to one member more: Overflow policy What it does EGroupOverflowPolicy.Reject Refuses the new member, so RegisterWithGroup returns false. EvictOldest Ends the oldest member to make room.

guides/processes/groups/group-lifetime-a.title: Group lifetime and events | PlayForge
guides/processes/groups/group-lifetime-a.summary: Group lifetime and events A group lasts until its last member leaves, and ending it ends its members. Two properties set this, and both are on by default: Property While it's on TerminateWhenEmpty The group lasts until its last member leaves. TerminateMembersOnGroupTerminate Ending the group ends its members. Its events, OnMemberJoined, OnMemberLeft and OnGroupEmpty, hear its members come and go.

guides/processes/groups/making-and-joini.title: Making and joining a group | PlayForge
guides/processes/groups/making-and-joini.summary: Making and joining a group A group is made first, to configure it, or else made by its first member, with no cap. // Made first, to configure it; or made by its first member, with no cap var buffs = new GroupProcess("Buffs", 3, EGroupOverflowPolicy.EvictOldest) { TerminateWhenEmpty = false }; ProcessControl.RegisterGroup(buffsTag, buffs, out _); ProcessControl.RegisterWithGroup(buffsTag, new TimedBuff("Haste", 6f), out var relay); if (ProcessControl.TryGetGroup(buffsTag, out var group)) group.PauseAll(); A member joins with the group's data packet, so what one member writes, the others read. A member uses a packet of its own instead when it asks for its own (useSharedData: false) or brings one.

guides/processes/lifecycles.html.summary: Lifecycles A process's lifecycle says how it starts and what happens when its run is done. flowchart LR classDef general fill:#FFE86D,stroke:#CBB333,color:#574900 classDef terminator fill:#DDDDD8,stroke:#A8A8A0,color:#434339 c(["Created"]):::terminator r["Running"]:::general w["Waiting"]:::general t(["Terminated"]):::terminator c -->|SelfTerminating, RunThenWait or Synchronous| r c -->|RequiresControl| w w -->|relay.Run or Unpause| r r -->|RunThenWait or RequiresControl, RunProcess returns| w r -->|SelfTerminating, RunProcess returns| t r -->|Terminate| t w -->|Terminate| t The default transitions of each EProcessLifecycle. Lifecycle Starts When its run is done Runs async For SelfTerminating Running Terminated Yes One-shot work: a projectile, a hit, a spawn RunThenWait Running Waiting Yes Work run again and again: an ability, a dialogue RequiresControl Waiting Waiting Yes Work started from outside: an ability on a key, a gated event Synchronous Running Waiting No Work every frame for good: a health bar, steering, a buff's tick An async process's RunProcess is awaited. A Synchronous process isn't: ProcessControl steps it each frame at its timing instead, through WhenUpdate, WhenFixedUpdate or WhenLateUpdate.

guides/processes/logging.html.title: Logging | PlayForge
guides/processes/logging.html.summary: Logging What processes log is set in two places. ProcessControl's own logs are its inspector's toggles. What processes say through ForgeLog is of the Processes system, and what a sequence says is of Sequences (Task Sequences: Logging).

guides/processes/pausing.html.title: Pausing | PlayForge
guides/processes/pausing.html.summary: Pausing A pause holds a process in place, at once. What happens to the process's run depends on whether the process can hold it: Process On a pause On Unpause One that can hold its run, and says so by returning true from TryHandlePause Its run stays alive, and watches relay.IsWaiting. Its run carries on after TryHandleResume. Any other process Its run is cancelled. A new run starts. ProcessControl can pause every process at once. Setting it to Waiting or ClosedWaiting pauses everything running, in the same way. Leaving those states sends back exactly what they stopped. A process paused on its own stays paused. Unpause is refused until ProcessControl is back. A Terminate asked for outranks a pause. A paused task sequence holds its run: No stage starts or ends. Its time limits stop counting. Its conditions aren't checked. The task library's waits hold, given the token their task was handed.

guides/processes/registering-one.html.title: Registering one | PlayForge
guides/processes/registering-one.html.summary: Registering one You register a process with ProcessControl, which gives you a relay to control it with. sequenceDiagram participant U as Unity participant PC as ProcessControl participant W as ProcessWorld participant H as GAS hub participant C as GASCore participant T as TaskSequenceProcess Note over U,T: FixedUpdate U->>PC: FixedUpdate() PC->>W: StepProcesses(FixedUpdate) Note over U,T: Update U->>PC: Update() PC->>W: SweepDestroyed() alt ticks off PC->>W: StepProcesses(Update) else FixedTickRate above 0 PC->>W: RunTicks(), up to maxTicksPerFrame W->>W: each tick ForgeTime.Use(tickClock), Tick.Advance() W->>W: StepProcesses(Update), then StepProcesses(LateUpdate) end W->>H: pcb.Step, Wrapper.WhenUpdate(relay) H->>C: Tick() C->>C: FollowTimeScale, Clock.Step() C->>C: EffectSystem.Tick(), TickEffectShelf, ClearFinishedEffects C->>C: AbilitySystem.CheckWhileActive(), StepBuffer(dt) C->>C: Services.Step(dt), the auras and a Respawn's wait, Turn.Step(dt), StepBarriers(dt) W->>T: StepAt(Update) when it has conditions, CheckConditions(), or SyncedTaskSequence.Step(data, dt) Note over U,T: LateUpdate U->>PC: LateUpdate() PC->>W: StepProcesses(LateUpdate), with ticks off W->>H: pcb.Step, Wrapper.WhenLateUpdate(relay) H->>C: EndOfFrame() C->>C: ActionQueue.ProcessAll C->>C: EvaluateTagWorkers, ProcessAll, TickTagWorkers, ProcessAll C->>C: AnalysisCache.Analyze, WatchProjectHealth, EffectSystem.CheckConditions(), ProcessAll C->>C: FrameComplete(snapshot) if anyone listens, FrameSummary.Clear() C->>C: a pending death runs Die(), FollowBody() C-->>H: a pending destruction, SystemDisabled, HandleDestruction() PC->>PC: ForgeFrameCosts.EndFrame() Note over H,C: A GAS that does not step in LateUpdate never runs its end of frame Note over PC,T: Async work resumes at UniTask's Update slot, before ProcessControl.Update, or inside RunTicks when ticks are on Which phase each system steps in. A GAS hub steps at UpdateAndLate: GASCore.Tick() in Update, its end of frame in LateUpdate. ProcessControl.Register(process).HandledBy(gas).With(data).Run(out ProcessRelay relay); relay.Pause(); // Waiting at once, out of the steps relay.Unpause(); // Running again relay.Terminate(); // ended, and cleaned up await relay.WhenTerminated(); The relay is the handle on a registered process. It holds the process's state and how long it has lived, and it's how you act on the process. A mono process's relay reaches its children too. Processes on child GameObjects pause and end with it, unless told not to. Instantiators A mono process's object comes from an instantiator, an AbstractMonoProcessInstantiator. An instantiator works as a pool does: it hands out an idle object, and takes it back as the process ends. A registration can give an instantiator of its own with .InstantiatedBy(pool). It goes ahead of the handler's instantiator and the object's own. With no instantiator, the object is cloned, and destroyed as its process ends. An object whose process has ended is no longer IsInitialized, so a pool's object can run again.

guides/recipes/a-counter.html.title: A counter | PlayForge
guides/recipes/a-counter.html.summary: A counter A counter answers each loss another entity deals to its holder: it strikes back at that entity for 10. Retaliate (an ability): One stage, with Apply Effects applying Retaliation. Under Activation's Triggers, one trigger: Gameplay Event, the core's Impact Taken, with Attribute Health, Sign Loss and Target Instigator. Retaliation (an effect): Instant, -10 Health. The counter's own hit is a loss to the attacker, not to its holder, so it doesn't set itself off. For a chance, as Counter Helix's 20%, set the trigger's Chance. To strike everyone near, give the ability Auto Target, and leave the trigger's Target at Own.

guides/recipes/a-crit.html.title: A crit | PlayForge
guides/recipes/a-crit.html.summary: A crit A crit doubles a hit on a 25% chance. Critical Strike (a Value Pipeline): one Chance stage, with Chance 0.25, Multiplier 2 and Note "critical". Crit Blow (an effect): Instant, -20 Health, with its impact's Pipeline set to Critical Strike. The hit's breakdown notes the crit, as the combat log shows it. The stage's Roll sets pseudo-random and luck.

guides/recipes/a-curse-that-bursts.html.title: A curse that bursts | PlayForge
guides/recipes/a-curse-that-bursts.html.summary: A curse that bursts This curse deals 5 each second for 3 seconds, then 30 as it ends, whether it runs out or comes off. Curse (an effect): Durational, with Duration 3. Periodic Ticks on, with Ticks 3. Its impact: -5 Health, which lands each tick. Under its impact's contained effects: Curse Burst, On Remove, landing on its Target. Curse Burst (an effect): Instant, -30 Health.

guides/recipes/a-phase.html.title: A phase | PlayForge
guides/recipes/a-phase.html.summary: A phase As the boss's Health falls to half, it enrages, once. Boss (an attribute set): Health 1000. In its Worker Group, one analysis worker, Threshold, with Target Health, What Share, Threshold 0.5, Crossing Falling, Trigger Once on and Effects Enrage. Enrage (an effect): Infinite, granting Recipe.Enraged. The phase's own moves start from the tag: an ability with a Tag Added trigger on Recipe.Enraged; or a stage condition that reads the tag. The worker's Event sends a gameplay event as well, for a trigger of its own.

guides/recipes/a-starter-set.html.title: A starter set | PlayForge
guides/recipes/a-starter-set.html.summary: A starter set The sample holds plain assets named for what they are, under Starter Set. The recipes above hold the rest of a starter set: a damage over time, an on hit, an on kill and a boss's phase. Each hit reads the recipes' Health. Melee Attack (an ability): Apply Effects with Melee Hit, on what it's cast at, and Cooldown Melee Cooldown. Melee Hit (an effect): Instant, -10 Health. Melee Cooldown (an effect): Durational, 1 s. Bolt (an ability): the same as Melee Attack, with its Bolt Hit of -25 Health and its Bolt Cooldown of 3 s. Slow (an effect): Durational, 3 s: a Multiply of Movement Speed by 0.7, undone as it ends. Shield (an effect): Durational, 5 s. +50 to Shield's current and base while it lasts. Its Modifiers hold one Incoming rule, whose Change Impact on Health adds an Absorb stage into Shield. Each hit on its holder's Health then comes off its Shield first. Give Shield's element a base of 0, between 0 and its base, so Shield is 0 without the effect. The starter set reads the Movement Speed and Shield attributes in Starter Set/Attributes.

guides/recipes/an-execute.html.title: An execute | PlayForge
guides/recipes/an-execute.html.summary: An execute With an execute, a hit that would leave its target under a fifth of its Health takes the rest. Execute (a Value Pipeline): one Execute stage, with Share 0.2 and Attribute Health. Culling Blow (an effect): Instant, -15 Health, with its impact's Pipeline set to Execute.

guides/recipes/cant-die.html.title: Can't die | PlayForge
guides/recipes/cant-die.html.summary: Can't die While Undying lasts, no blow takes its target below 1, as Shallow Grave does. Undying (an effect): Durational, Duration 5. Its Worker Group holds one attribute worker, Can't Fall Below, with Target Attribute Health and Floor 1.

guides/recipes/damage-return.html.title: Damage return | PlayForge
guides/recipes/damage-return.html.summary: Damage return While Thorns lasts, half of each loss its holder takes goes back to the one who dealt it. Thorns (an effect): Infinite. Its Worker Group holds one attribute worker, Return Damage, with Target Attribute Health and Share 0.5. What it returns is typed Returned, so nothing returns it again, and no lifesteal heals from it.

guides/recipes/formulas.html.title: Formulas | PlayForge
guides/recipes/formulas.html.summary: Formulas The sample holds Scaler assets for a genre's formulas, under Formulas, each named for what it computes. A field reads one with its Shared kind (Scalers). Each is a Stacking Curve of a count, with an a. Scaler asset Curve What it gives 1 ÷ (1 + 0.06 × Armor) Reciprocal, a 0.06, of the hit's target's Armor In a Value Pipeline's Multiply stage, a hit leaves all of itself at 0 Armor, a half at about 17, and never none. 100 ÷ (100 + Armor) Reciprocal, a 0.01 A half at 100 Armor, a third at 200. −Armor Linear, a −1 In an Add stage, a blow of 100 against 20 Armor lands as 80. 0.15 × Stacks Linear, a 0.15, of an item's stacks A bonus that grows by as much with each stack. 1 − 1 ÷ (1 + 0.15 × Stacks) Hyperbolic A chance that nears 1 and never reaches it: 13% with one stack, 60% with ten. 0.9 ^ Stacks Exponential A share that falls by a tenth with each stack. The Armor ones read the Armor attribute in Formulas/Attributes, as the hit lands. Point them at your own.

guides/recipes/index.html.title: Recipes | PlayForge
guides/recipes/index.html.summary: Recipes These ten recipes build common rules from PlayForge's own assets and fields, with no code. Each is in the Additional Content sample (Package Manager → PlayForge → Samples), in a folder of its own under Recipes. Each reads the sample's Health attribute, in Recipes/Attributes. Point its fields at your own. Workers maps the workers some of them use. In this guide A curse that bursts: This curse deals 5 each second for 3 seconds, then 30 as it ends, whether it runs out or comes off. A counter: A counter answers each loss another entity deals to its holder: it strikes back at that entity for 10. A crit: A crit doubles a hit on a 25% chance. An execute: With an execute, a hit that would leave its target under a fifth of its Health takes the rest. Lifesteal: While Vampirism lasts, its holder heals half of each loss it deals another. Damage return: While Thorns lasts, half of each loss its holder takes goes back to the one who dealt it. Can't die: While Undying lasts, no blow takes its target below 1, as Shallow Grave does. On hit: While Frost Blade is equipped, each hit its holder deals bites for 5 more. On kill: While Reaper's Mark is equipped, the hit that takes a target's Health to 0 feeds its holder 20. A phase: As the boss's Health falls to half, it enrages, once. Formulas: The sample holds Scaler assets for a genre's formulas, under Formulas, each named for what it computes. A starter set: The sample holds plain assets named for what they are, under Starter Set.

guides/recipes/lifesteal.html.title: Lifesteal | PlayForge
guides/recipes/lifesteal.html.summary: Lifesteal While Vampirism lasts, its holder heals half of each loss it deals another. Lifesteal (an attribute): the Share of the Lifesteal worker in your Forge Project's Workers. Your Forge Project has Health in its Health role. Vampirism (an effect): Infinite, +0.5 Lifesteal. The Lifesteal worker heals by Lifesteal. It's the one your Forge Project's Workers give every entity as a project starts, and it heals the Health role's attribute (Workers: Lifesteal). An effect has no lifesteal of its own: For a blow that steals more than others, an effect raises its caster's Lifesteal while it should. An item gives Lifesteal with such an effect, as one of its Granted Effects (Items: Workers: Lifesteal).

guides/recipes/on-hit.html.title: On hit | PlayForge
guides/recipes/on-hit.html.summary: On hit While Frost Blade is equipped, each hit its holder deals bites for 5 more. Frost Blade (an item): its On Hit has one entry, with Attribute Health, Effects Frost Bite and To Target. Frost Bite (an effect): Instant, -5 Health. Frost Bite's own hit sets nothing off again.

guides/recipes/on-kill.html.title: On kill | PlayForge
guides/recipes/on-kill.html.summary: On kill While Reaper's Mark is equipped, the hit that takes a target's Health to 0 feeds its holder 20. Reaper's Mark (an item): its On Hit has one entry, with Attribute Health, Effects Feast, To Holder and Only On Kill on. Feast (an effect): Instant, +20 Health.

guides/saving/copying-an-entity.html.title: Copying an entity | PlayForge
guides/saving/copying-an-entity.html.summary: Copying an entity ForgeSave.Copy(from, onto) copies what lasts on one entity onto another, as a mirror clone takes its original's state. It's a capture and a restore with no catalog and no IDs, since both entities are in the same session. So it copies assets made as the game runs too. An effect another entity applied stays that entity's. The entity's own level goes onto the other's own. var clone = new RuntimeGameplayAbilitySystem(identity); ProcessControl.Register(clone).Run(); ForgeSave.Copy(original, clone);

guides/saving/effects-from-other-entitie.title: Effects from other entities | PlayForge
guides/saving/effects-from-other-entitie.summary: Effects from other entities An effect knows what applied it: an entity, or one of its abilities or items. When that is another entity, the save needs a name for it that lasts. Give Capture and Restore an IForgeEntityIds, which maps the game's own IDs to its entities: class Roster : IForgeEntityIds { public string IdOf(IGameplayAbilitySystem entity) => /* the game's ID for it, or null */; public IGameplayAbilitySystem Find(string id) => /* the entity, or null if it's gone */; } var save = ForgeSave.Capture(hero, catalog, roster); ForgeSave.Restore(hero, save, catalog, roster); Without IDs, or when the other entity is gone, the effect comes back as the entity's own. An entity whose abilities are in their saved slots keeps them through its load. So several entities can load in any order, and their effects on each other still name the abilities that applied them. Items aren't kept that way. When several entities load together, restore those whose items applied effects first, so the others find them.

guides/saving/index.html.title: Saving and Loading | PlayForge
guides/saving/index.html.summary: Saving and Loading ForgeSave saves an entity at rest and loads it back. ForgeSave.Capture takes what lasts on an entity into a ForgeSnapshot. ForgeSave.Restore puts it back, on the entity it came from or on a fresh one of the same kind. A snapshot is plain serializable types, so a game writes it where it likes, through JsonUtility or its own serializer. // Save ForgeSnapshot save = ForgeSave.Capture(gas, catalog); string json = JsonUtility.ToJson(save); // Load ForgeSnapshot loaded = JsonUtility.FromJson<ForgeSnapshot>(json); ForgeSave.Restore(gas, loaded, catalog); Only a hub built from an entity can be saved or loaded: a GameplayAbilitySystem with its Entity asset; a RuntimeGameplayAbilitySystem made from an identity. In this guide The Asset Catalog: An Asset Catalog names the assets a save refers to, and finds them again. What a save holds: A save holds what lasts on the entity. What a load does: A load puts the save back in four steps. Effects from other entities: An effect knows what applied it: an entity, or one of its abilities or items. Rolling back: A rollback saves each step, and on a late input loads a step back and runs again. Copying an entity: ForgeSave.Copy(from, onto) copies what lasts on one entity onto another, as a mirror clone takes its original's state. Versions: Each save names the format it was written in. In the API The types of this guide's area: AbilitySave, AttributeRole, AttributeSave, CommitSave, EffectSave, ESavedOrigin, ForgeAssetCatalog, ForgeAssetCatalog.Entry, ForgeAuthoringSettings, ForgeProject, ForgeProjectSettings, ForgeRoles, ForgeSave, ForgeSnapshot, IForgeEntityIds, ItemSave, LevelSave, MagnitudeSave, NewAssetSettings, OriginSave, TypeDefaults.

guides/saving/rolling-back.html.title: Rolling back | PlayForge
guides/saving/rolling-back.html.summary: Rolling back A rollback saves each step, and on a late input loads a step back and runs again. The run again lands where the first did, to the last digit of every save, given both of these: a fixed tick: ProcessControl's Fixed Tick Rate, or a world of its own stepped by a fixed time; the random source seeded for each step (ForgeRandom.Use). Tip Keep the saves in memory, as ForgeSnapshots. JsonUtility can move the last digit of a double as it reads one back. A load ends the abilities running. So an ability that runs over several steps isn't replayed by a load into its middle, but one that ends as it activates is.

guides/saving/the-asset-catalog.html.title: The Asset Catalog | PlayForge
guides/saving/the-asset-catalog.html.summary: The Asset Catalog An Asset Catalog names the assets a save refers to, and finds them again. A save can't hold references to assets, because a reference doesn't last from one session to the next. Instead, it names each asset by an ID, and the catalog finds the asset by that ID. The catalog lists attributes, effects, abilities and items. A Forge Project is the catalog of its own assets, those in its folder. To give your saves a catalog: Use your Forge Project, or create one with Create → PlayForge → Forge Project. Its catalog keeps itself current: Each PlayForge asset made, copied or moved into the project's folder is named as it lands, by its GUID. The GUID stays the same when the asset is renamed or moved. A deleted asset's entry goes. An asset moved out stays named, so a save made before still finds it. The project catches up on assets it doesn't name yet, as it's imported and once each editor session. So a project made before PlayForge kept catalogs catches up too. Pass the project to every capture and restore. Note A capture leaves out an asset the catalog doesn't name, and logs a warning. A restore does the same for an ID the catalog can't find. Adding assets by hand You can stop the catalog keeping itself current, and name its assets yourself. Keep Catalog Current, on the project, turns the catalog's own upkeep off. Then name the assets from the project's inspector: Open the menu in the inspector's header. Choose Add Its Assets, which names each PlayForge asset in the project's folder by its GUID. Add Every PlayForge Asset, in the same menu, names every one in the Unity project. Run either again after you add assets. Code can add entries while the game runs, with catalog.Add(id, asset). An ID or an asset can be listed only once.

guides/saving/versions.html.title: Versions | PlayForge
guides/saving/versions.html.summary: Versions Each save names the format it was written in. Member What it names ForgeSnapshot.Version The save's format. ForgeSave.Version The format this PlayForge writes. A restore refuses a save with a newer format.

guides/saving/what-a-load-does.html.title: What a load does | PlayForge
guides/saving/what-a-load-does.html.summary: What a load does A load puts the save back in four steps. Running abilities are interrupted, and the input buffer empties. The entity lets go of its effects, items and abilities, and the actions queued this frame are dropped. An ability it holds in the slot the save gives it stays as it is. So another entity's effect that it applied still names it. The save's abilities, items, effects, levels and commits come back. The tags compile once, and OnRestored fires. A load tells nothing as it goes: No effect is told as applied or removed, and no attribute as changed. Nothing of an effect's application runs again: not its workers, its commits on application, or its contained effects. A worn item's effects come back from the save, so wearing it again applies none. The one tag compile tells what the load changed, as any compile does. Then gas.GetCallbacks().OnRestored fires once. Listen to it to refresh what shows the entity, such as a health bar or a hotbar. Before you load A load needs the right attributes, and a moment between the entity's steps. The entity's attribute set has to define the attributes the save names. An attribute the catalog names but the save doesn't list loses its commits, since the entity had none when it was saved. Load between the entity's steps. A restore called from inside the entity's step or its end of frame, as from one of its callbacks, is refused with a warning. It would empty the lists the step is going through, so load on the next frame instead.

guides/saving/what-a-save-holds.html.title: What a save holds | PlayForge
guides/saving/what-a-save-holds.html.summary: What a save holds A save holds what lasts on the entity. Part What the save holds Attributes Each attribute's permanent commits, as a total per retention group. Modifiers aren't saved: they come back with the effects that carry them. Levels The levels the entity keeps: its own, and its abilities' and items'. Its own is saved as the entity's own, so a save of one kind loads onto another kind as that one's level. Abilities The abilities it knows of its own, in their slots, at their levels. Items Its items in order, each with its level and stacks, worn or not. Effects Each effect, with what applied it, its stacks, its time left and the time to its next tick, and the magnitudes its caller set. Tags and time scale Its loose tags, and the time scale its code set. Its Time Scale attribute's is read again from the attribute. An effect's times are saved exactly: Stacks with durations of their own keep their own times. The times are kept in full, as the effect's timers keep them. So a restored effect keeps time with one that never went through a save, to the last digit. An ability that an effect or a worn item lends isn't saved on its own. It comes back with the effect or the item. What a save leaves out A save leaves out three things: the entity's Local Data; its sides, which come from its asset and its registration; what an effect captured as it landed, such as a source's attribute or a roll made once. The effect captures it again as it comes back.

guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field.html.title: A magnitude field | PlayForge
guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field.html.summary:
A magnitude field A magnitude field, such as an effect's Magnitude or Duration, is a number field. It's a ScalableFloat, or a ScalableInt for a whole number. flowchart TD classDef general fill:#FFE86D,stroke:#CBB333,color:#574900 classDef decision fill:#A0C4FB,stroke:#6A8BBF,color:#14315E classDef terminator fill:#DDDDD8,stroke:#A8A8A0,color:#434339 s(["number.Evaluate(NumberContext.Of(x)), where x is a spec,
