The field's row shows its name, then its kind, then what it reads, then its field menu. The field menu opens as wide as its items. The sections below cover where number fields appear, how a field picks its kind, each kind in turn, and the field's tools. In this section Where number fields appear: Every number an asset authors is a number field, read at the level of what holds it. The kind menu: The kind menu says where a field's number comes from. Combine and Rounding: A kind other than Constant shows a one-line summary of what the field reads under its row, as "0.3 × Target's Health (base)". Constant: A Constant field reads its number, with its unit beside it, as Tick Every's "1 s". Table: A Table reads one value for each level, exactly. By Level: A By Level field reads its values spread over a level range, as points on a curve. Shared: A Shared field reads a Scaler asset, one scaler that many fields can use. × Attribute: × Attribute reads an attribute of the caster or the target. Set By Caller: Set By Caller reads a value the code passes in. Asset Part: Asset Part finds effects, abilities or items on the caster or the target by a tag, and reads a part of them. Group: A Group joins several numbers as one. Group Impact: Group Impact reads one retention group's part of an attribute on the caster or the target. Local Data: Local Data reads the number under a Key in Local Data. Relative to a Field: Relative to a Field reads another number field of the same object, picked from a menu of them. Worker: Worker asks workers for a number under a Key. Clamped: A Clamped keeps a number within bounds. Conditional: A Conditional reads one number where a condition holds, and another where it doesn't. Fixed Value: A Fixed Value is one number, whatever the level. Randomized: A Randomized scaler rolls a random value. Stacking Curve: Stacking Curve turns a Count, as an item's stacks or an attribute, into its number by a Curve and its Coefficient, a. Threshold: A Threshold steps at thresholds: it reads one value for each tier of levels. Effect Stacks: Effect Stacks reads the stack count of the effect's own container. Tracked Impact: Tracked Impact reads what an effect has dealt. Item Stacks: Item Stacks reads the stack count of the item that applied the effect (Items). Retention groups: An attribute's value is the sum of its retention groups' parts: the base its set gives, what items add in their group, and what a buff adds in its. The field menu: The field menu holds a number field's tools. Editing several assets: With more than one asset selected, the field edits each asset's own field.

guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/asset-p.title: Asset Part | PlayForge
guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/asset-p.summary: Asset Part Asset Part finds effects, abilities or items on the caster or the target by a tag, and reads a part of them. Property Description What What it looks for: effects on the entity, abilities it knows, or items it holds. Tagged The tag they carry. A tag under the one given matches too. On Whose: the caster's or the target's. Effect Part, Ability Part, Item Part What it reads of each one it finds (below). Each shows only for its kind of asset. Worker Key For an effect's Worker Value, the key it asks that effect's workers for. Among How several that match read as one: their Sum, the First, the Highest or the Lowest. Default What a part other than a count reads where none matches. An effect matches by its asset tag, a context tag or a tag it grants. An ability or an item matches by its asset tag or a context tag. Of an The parts it reads Effect Count, Stacks, Level, Last Impact, Total Impact, Impact Count, Duration Remaining, Duration, Time Until Tick, or a Worker Value: what that effect's workers answer under a key Ability Count, Level, Is Active, Is on Cooldown, or Cooldown Remaining Item Count, Stacks, Level, or Is Equipped A true-or-false part reads 1 or 0, so its sum is how many are so. Where none matches, a count reads 0, and any other part the Default.

guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/attribu.title: × Attribute | PlayForge
guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/attribu.summary: × Attribute × Attribute reads an attribute of the caster or the target. Property Description Capture Attribute The attribute it reads. Capture From Whose attribute: Source, the caster's, or Target, the target's. Capture When On Creation captures the value once, as the effect's spec is made, and reads that snapshot after. On Application reads the live value each time. Capture What Its current, its base, what's missing of it (base − current), or its share of its base (current ÷ base). Groups All of it, or only some of its retention groups (Retention groups). Read As How it reads the value: as its attribute's role says, as it is, as a multiplier (1 + x), or as what's left (1 − x). The menu starts it as the field's number times it. By its attribute's role, it reads a Bonus Share as 1 + x and a Resistance as 1 − x. Its Read As can say otherwise.

guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/by-leve.title: By Level | PlayForge
guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/by-leve.summary: By Level A By Level field reads its values spread over a level range, as points on a curve. Property Description Over Levels The level range its values spread over (Spread Over Levels). Points How many values. Between Points How a level between two points reads: Steps, Straight Line or Smooth Curve. Behaviours Rules that adjust the value the scaler works out, in order. A level between two points reads between them (Values per level). It's the same number by level as a Table, read another way. So choosing one for the other keeps its values. One saved reading exactly shows as a Table, and nothing saved changes. Spreadsheets writes a project's Tables and By Levels to a spreadsheet and reads them back.

guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/clamped.title: Clamped | PlayForge
guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/clamped.summary: Clamped A Clamped keeps a number within bounds. Property Description Value What it clamps. Min Value The least it reads. Max Value The most it reads. It keeps its Value between its Min Value and Max Value, three numbers of any kind. One made in the inspector clamps a value by level. Its numbers read the Clamped as their object, so its Max Value can be Relative to a Field, 2 × its Min Value.

guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/combine.title: Combine and Rounding | PlayForge
guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/combine.summary: Combine and Rounding A kind other than Constant shows a one-line summary of what the field reads under its row, as "0.3 × Target's Health (base)". Under the summary sit the field's Combine and, on a whole-number field, its Rounding. Property Description Combine How the field joins its number with the scaler: Scaler reads the scaler's value. Scaler + Number adds the field's number. Scaler × Number multiplies by the field's number. Number Only reads the number. Rounding On a whole-number field, such as Ticks: Floor, Ceil, or Round, to the nearest, a half away from zero. A field whose unit is "%" stores 0.3, and shows and takes it as 30%. A kind its field can't work out says so under the field, as one copied from a field that has a target into one that hasn't. The Problems window lists it, and the field reads its number.

guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/conditi.title: Conditional | PlayForge
guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/conditi.summary: Conditional A Conditional reads one number where a condition holds, and another where it doesn't. Property Description When Its condition (below). True Value What it reads where the condition holds. False Value What it reads where the condition doesn't hold, or where it has none. Its summary says all three, as "−0.1 × Target's Health (base) if Target's Health < 0.3 × Target's Health (base), else 0". Conditions A condition picks its kind from a menu, as a number does, and says itself in a line. Condition What it checks Tag Whether the caster or the target holds a tag, counted by its weight, so a tag granted twice counts twice. Attribute An attribute of the caster or the target compared with a number, as 0.3 × the target's base Health. It reads its current, its base, what's missing of it or its share of its base. Level The level, or how far up its range it is, from 0 to 1, compared with a number. Compare Numbers One number compared with another. Always and Never Nothing: Always holds wherever it's read, and Never holds nowhere. All Of, Any Of and Not Under Logic, these join others. All Of none holds; Any Of none doesn't. An Attribute condition says "above 90%" as a share above 0.9. Where what the number is read in lacks what a condition reads, the condition doesn't hold, and neither does a Not around it. A target's tag where there's no target is one example.

guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/constan.title: Constant | PlayForge
guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/constan.summary: Constant A Constant field reads its number, with its unit beside it, as Tick Every's "1 s". A field that used to read its scaler, and has none, reads 0, and a warning says so.

guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/editing.title: Editing several assets | PlayForge
guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/editing.summary: Editing several assets With more than one asset selected, the field edits each asset's own field. Kinds that differ show as mixed. Choosing a kind gives it to each field, from that field's own value. A field of that kind keeps its scaler. Levels and Make Constant work on each field's own values. A count, range or curve the fields disagree on shows as mixed. Save as Scaler Asset waits for one asset.

guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/effect-.title: Effect Stacks | PlayForge
guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/effect-.summary: Effect Stacks Effect Stacks reads the stack count of the effect's own container. It reads 1 where there's nothing stacked. It has no settings of its own. The kind menu files it under Effect.

guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/fixed-v.title: Fixed Value | PlayForge
guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/fixed-v.summary: Fixed Value A Fixed Value is one number, whatever the level. Property Description Value The number it reads. Its settings show its value alone (Values per level). Make Constant turns a scaler field of its own, with no number, into a Fixed Value (The field menu).

guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/group-i.title: Group Impact | PlayForge
guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/group-i.summary: Group Impact Group Impact reads one retention group's part of an attribute on the caster or the target. Property Description Attribute The attribute whose part it reads. Of Whose attribute: the caster's or the target's. Group The retention group whose part it reads, as the group items add to. Part The part's current value, or its base. "Caster's Strength (Bonus)", for example, reads the Strength items add, and none of the hero's own. See Retention groups.

guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/group.h.title: Group | PlayForge
guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/group.h.summary: Group A Group joins several numbers as one. Property Description Calculations Its members. Each is an Operation, then its Scaler, which can be any kind. Operation How the member joins the others: Add, Multiply, Divide, Flat Bonus or Override. Override Member Collision Policy Where several members override, which one gives the group's value (below). Its members join in this order, whatever order they're listed in: The members that Add are added up. That sum is multiplied by each member that Multiplies, and divided by each that Divides. One that reads 0 divides nothing. Then each Flat Bonus is added on. So (5 + Caster's Strength) × 2 + 3 is one number, and 1.7 ÷ Caster's Attack Speed another. A first member needn't add. Members that multiply or divide with none that adds work on 0, and the Group says so. A member that Overrides gives the group's value alone. Where several do, the group's policy picks the highest, the lowest, their average, the first or the last. Ignore sets them aside. A Group has no values per level. With no members, or none that holds a kind, it's no kind at all. Its field then reads its number, as a Constant does.

guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/item-st.title: Item Stacks | PlayForge
guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/item-st.summary: Item Stacks Item Stacks reads the stack count of the item that applied the effect (Items). It reads 1 where there's nothing stacked. The kind menu files it under Item.

guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/local-d.title: Local Data | PlayForge
guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/local-d.summary: Local Data Local Data reads the number under a Key in Local Data. Property Description Key The key the number is under. From Whose Local Data: Its Own, what the number belongs to, as its ability's or its item's asset. Or the Caster's or the Target's, as the entity holds it. Default What it reads where there's no number under the key. A hero's attack range kept in its Local Data is one field read by every ability. The entry's number can scale too, read where the kind reads it. Its Own reads it in the number's context. The Caster's or the Target's reads it at that entity's own level. One that reads its own key stops at the Default.

guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/randomi.title: Randomized | PlayForge
guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/randomi.summary: Randomized A Randomized scaler rolls a random value. Property Description Variance How its roll varies its value (below). With none, it doesn't vary. Roll Once Per Spec On, it rolls once per effect spec and keeps the roll, so every tick of one application deals the same. Off, it rolls on every evaluation. Its Variance is a kind of its own: Variance How it varies the value Percentage Up or down by a Share of its value. Flat Up or down by an Amount. Multiplier Times one between its Min and its Max. One of your own As two dice: a [Serializable] class made from AbstractVariance that overrides Vary, Lowest and Highest. A variance's numbers read the variance as their object. So a Share can widen by level, and a Max can be 3 × its Min. Its settings show its variance, then the values its base value comes from.

guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/relativ.title: Relative to a Field | PlayForge
guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/relativ.summary: Relative to a Field Relative to a Field reads another number field of the same object, picked from a menu of them. Property Description Field The other number field of the same object it reads. The field's number joins the other field's as Combine says. A Clamped scaler's Max can be 2 × its Min, and a stack bound's Max its Min + 3. The other field is read in the same context, so a relative Max follows a Min that scales by level. A field offers this kind where its code hands its object over as it reads (A number field in your own code). A scaler's own numbers read the scaler as their object. So a Clamped's Max Value can be Relative to a Field, 2 × its Min Value, whatever field the Clamped is in.

guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/retenti.title: Retention groups | PlayForge
guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/retenti.summary: Retention groups An attribute's value is the sum of its retention groups' parts: the base its set gives, what items add in their group, and what a buff adds in its. Retention groups in any attribute read work alike. × Attribute, the Attribute condition, a relative attribute worker's Relative To and the Threshold worker each have Groups, which say which parts the read takes: Groups What the read takes All The whole value, as before. Only These Only the groups named, as a bonus of the items' Strength reads their group. All But These Every group but those named, as a bonus of a hero's own damage leaves its items' out. A group names the groups under it too, so Items takes Items.Ring. The read says which: "Caster's Strength (Items)", "Caster's Attack Damage (all but Items)". Group Impact reads one group's part alone.

guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/set-by-.title: Set By Caller | PlayForge
guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/set-by-.summary: Set By Caller Set By Caller reads a value the code passes in. Property Description Key The tag the value is set under. Only the key itself matches, not a tag above or below it in the tag tree. Default What the field reads where no value is set under the key. It's a number of any kind, so it can read a value by level. It checks one thing: whether what the number is read in holds a value under exactly its Key. Code sets a value in one of three places: on an effect's spec before applying it (spec.SetByCaller(tag, value)), on an ability activation's data (data.SetByCaller(tag, value)), or on the data that spawns a process (Effects). Each effect the ability makes takes the activation's values, and the ability's tasks read them. A value set to 0 is a value. Its summary says both the key and the default, as "the caller's Damage, else 0".

guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/shared..title: Shared | PlayForge
guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/shared..summary: Shared A Shared field reads a Scaler asset, one scaler that many fields can use. Property Description Asset The Scaler asset the field reads. An edit to the asset changes every field that shares it. See Scaler assets.

guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/stackin.title: Stacking Curve | PlayForge
guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/stackin.summary: Stacking Curve Stacking Curve turns a Count, as an item's stacks or an attribute, into its number by a Curve and its Coefficient, a. Property Description Count What it counts, n. Curve How the count turns into the number (below). Coefficient The curve's a. Plus Added after the curve. 1 makes a share a multiplier. Curve Formula For example Linear a × n 15% a stack Hyperbolic 1 − 1 / (1 + a × n) A chance that nears 1 and never reaches it: 13% with one stack and 60% with ten, at 0.15 Reciprocal 1 / (1 + a × n) What Dota's armor leaves of a hit, at 0.06 Inverse a / n A wind-up an attack speed shortens Exponential a to the n A chance that falls by a share each stack, as 0.9 to the n

guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/table.h.title: Table | PlayForge
guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/table.h.summary: Table A Table reads one value for each level, exactly. Property Description Levels Whose levels it has a value for: its asset's level provider's, or Own levels (Per Level). Behaviours Rules that adjust the value the scaler works out, in order. Level 1 reads the first value, level 4 the 4th, and a level past the last reads the last, as Laguna Blade's 450, 600 and 750. The range it gives shows beside the kind, as "6–8 s", or "-25 to -10" where it goes below 0. Its values sit in a row under it, with no curve.

guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/the-fie.title: The field menu | PlayForge
guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/the-fie.summary: The field menu The field menu holds a number field's tools. A scaler field of its own, as a Group member's, has the same menu, and its kind menu files its kinds by category, as a number field's does. Item What it does Save as Scaler Asset… Asks for a name and a folder. Save and Use then saves the field's scaler as a Scaler asset and makes the field share it. Scaler Assets A submenu of the project's Scaler assets, the one the field shares checked. The field shares the one you pick. Import Values… Copies another asset's values per level (below). Quick Fill… Fills the table from a pattern (below). Make Constant The field reads a number again: the value its first level read. A scaler field of its own, with no number, becomes a Fixed Value of that value. Import Values Import Values… opens a window that lists the Scaler assets, and the other assets' fields with values per level. Pick one to compare its values with the field's, level by level, with both curves. Click Copy Values. A shorter table's last value holds for the levels past its end, and the window says which levels those are. One Undo takes it back. Quick Fill Quick Fill… fills the table from a pattern, from one value to another. Its patterns are Same Value, Straight Line, Slow Then Fast and Fast Then Slow with a Strength, Steps, Add Each Level, Multiply Each Level, Ease In and Out, or a Custom Curve you draw. Rounding makes the values whole numbers, or rounds them to a Step. A preview shows the values as the table will, with their curve. One Undo takes them back. On a scaler spread over levels, it fills the points, as many as Points says. The preview then shows what each level reads between them.

guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/the-kin.title: The kind menu | PlayForge
guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/the-kin.summary: The kind menu The kind menu says where a field's number comes from. It lists its kinds in three groups: At its top: Constant, Table, By Level, Shared, × Attribute and Set By Caller. Then the kinds that read the game: Asset Part, Group, Group Impact, Local Data, Relative to a Field and Worker. Then the rest, filed by category. Category Its kinds Scaler The scalers of every kind: Clamped, Conditional, Fixed Value, Randomized, Stacking Curve and Threshold Effect Effect Stacks and Tracked Impact Item Item Stacks A project's own A kind of a project's own goes under the category it names A field whose code declares what its context provides, with [NumberContext], offers only the kinds that can be worked out there. A targeting task's range, which has no target yet, offers no kind that reads one. Choosing a kind is one Undo step. A constant made a Table or By Level keeps its number as its first level's value.

guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/thresho.title: Threshold | PlayForge
guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/thresho.summary: Threshold A Threshold steps at thresholds: it reads one value for each tier of levels. Property Description Thresholds Its thresholds. Each has a Level and an optional Tier name, with the Value it reads from that level up under them, a number of any kind. Default Value What it reads below every threshold. Of the thresholds at or below a level, the highest gives the value.

guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/tracked.title: Tracked Impact | PlayForge
guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/tracked.summary: Tracked Impact Tracked Impact reads what an effect has dealt. Property Description What Its Last impact, its Total, or its impact Count. Of Whose impacts: This Effect; An Effect on the caster or the target, by its asset; or Effects Tagged there, added up. Effect For An Effect, the effect whose impacts it reads. Tagged For Effects Tagged, the tag the effects carry. Part The impact's current part, or its base. By Size Reads the impact positive, as a heal of half a blow wants. This Effect suits a burn that grows by its own tick count. An impact is as it landed, after the target's workers, and signed, so damage is negative. Before an effect's first impact, and after a load, it reads 0. The kind menu files it under Effect.

guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/where-n.title: Where number fields appear | PlayForge
guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/where-n.summary: Where number fields appear Every number an asset authors is a number field, read at the level of what holds it. What holds it Its number fields Read at An ability Its Buffer Window, and its tasks' numbers The ability's level An effect Its Stack Bounds' Min and Max, its Starting Stacks, and a Stacks change's number The effect's level A cue Its Strength, Duration, Lifetime and Volume For its effect, as it lands An item Its Max Stack Size The item's own level A set bonus Its Pieces Its holder's level An entity A barrier's Decay Per Second, an attribute set's Snap Interval, an aura's Interval, and a worker's Threshold, Floor, Share, Every Ticks, Tick Pause or Required Weight The entity's level, or the change's A level, a pointer's button, an order, a priority among configs and a log's size stay whole numbers. So do a kind's and a scaler's own numbers. A folded field's line shows a number field by what it reads, as "Uses 3". An attribute set's values use the cached kinds, which read other attributes as the entity's values change.

guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/worker..title: Worker | PlayForge
guides/scalers/a-magnitude-field/worker..summary: Worker Worker asks workers for a number under a Key. Property Description Key The key it asks for. From Whose workers: This Effect's own, or the Caster's or the Target's. Default What it reads where no worker answers. See Asking a worker.

guides/scalers/a-number-field-in-your-ow.title: A number field in your own code | PlayForge
guides/scalers/a-number-field-in-your-ow.summary: A number field in your own code A field of your own is one line, and a float converts to it: [Tooltip("How far it reaches")] [NumberContext(NumberReads.Level | NumberReads.Caster, Unit = "m")] [NumberMin(0)] public ScalableFloat Range = 20f; Read it with Range.Evaluate(context), with a NumberContext built Of what the code has: an effect's spec, an activation's data, a worker's context, an entity, a cue or a process. Range.Evaluate(context, this) also hands the field's object over, which is what Relative to a Field reads. A field read that way declares NumberReads.Owner, or NumberReads.All, and its kind menu then offers that kind. Attribute What it does [Tooltip] Shows on the field's name. [NumberMin(0)], [NumberMax(10)] and [NumberRange(0, 1)] Limit the constant typed in the inspector. A range sets it on a slider. [ShownWhen(nameof(UsePhysics))] Shows a field only while a toggle of the same object is on. [ShownWhen(nameof(Mode), (int)EMode.Area)] Shows a field only while an enum is one of the values. [ForgeMenu("Path/Sub", Name = "...", Description = "...")] Files a kind of your own in its picker. In this section Limits: The limits apply to the constant alone. In a kind of your own: [ShownWhen] works in a kind of your own, as an ability task, a targeting task or a scaler.

guides/scalers/a-number-field-in-your-ow.title: In a kind of your own | PlayForge
guides/scalers/a-number-field-in-your-ow.summary: In a kind of your own [ShownWhen] works in a kind of your own, as an ability task, a targeting task or a scaler. A targeting task's Detection Layers, for example, show under Use Physics. A task reads its numbers with Read(number, data), at its ability's level. Every kind of your own takes [ForgeMenu(...)]: a task, a worker, a component, a cue, a kind of number or a condition. Its path files it under the submenus the path names, a slash nesting them. Name replaces its class's name in the picker and in its field. Description is what the picker's Context says while it's highlighted. A path holds for the classes made from the one that names it. [ForgeMenu("")] puts a kind at the top, whatever its base names.

guides/scalers/a-number-field-in-your-ow.title: Limits | PlayForge
guides/scalers/a-number-field-in-your-ow.summary: Limits The limits apply to the constant alone. On a field whose unit is "%", the limit is in what the field stores, so [NumberRange(0, 1)] is 0% to 100%. A whole-number field takes the whole numbers inside the limits. A number of another kind is worked out as the game runs. Where what it reads must stay inside limits, give it the Clamped kind, or clamp what the code reads. Note Unity's own [Min] and [Range] don't work on a number field. Unity gives the field to that attribute's drawer, which draws "Use Range with float or int" where the number was. As scripts load, the console names each number field that has one, with the attribute to use in its place.

guides/scalers/asking-a-worker.html.title: Asking a worker | PlayForge
guides/scalers/asking-a-worker.html.summary: Asking a worker A number can't count or remember, but a worker can. So a number of the Worker kind asks workers for a value under a key, and any worker answers by implementing INumberWorker: public class OverkillWorker : AbstractEffectWorker, INumberWorker { public Tag Key; public bool TryGetNumber(Tag key, in NumberContext context, out float value) { value = 0f; if (key != Key) return false; // not a key it knows: the next worker is asked var state = (context.Carrier as GameplayEffectSpec)?.GetWorkerState<State>(this); value = state?.Overkill ?? 0f; return true; } } An effect's workers answer about one application of their effect. A worker is one object on its effect's asset, shared by every application. So what it counts for each is kept on the spec. It reads that with ctx.GetState<State>(this) in its events, and spec.GetWorkerState<State>(this) as it answers. An entity's workers, those its worker groups give it, answer about the entity. A worker group installs the ones that answer as it's given. Code that adds a worker itself calls NumberWorkers.Provide(entity, worker). The first worker that answers the key gives the value. Where none does, the number reads its Default. Any number field can ask: an effect's magnitude, a task's range, a threshold. Code can ask too, with NumberWorkers.TryAsk. An Asset Part's Worker Value asks the workers of each effect it finds. The Attribute Change worker The Attribute Change effect worker is one that answers. It notes an attribute as each application of its effect begins. It answers how much the attribute has Lost, Gained or Changed since, or what it was At Start. With Every Ticks above 0, it answers only on each Nth tick, and 0 on the others. Property Description Key The key it answers under. Attribute The attribute it watches. Of Whose attribute: the target's, the entity the effect is on, or the caster's. What What it answers: Lost, Gained, Change or At Start. Part The attribute's current value, or its base. Every Ticks At 0, it answers at every read. Above 0, only on each Nth tick of its effect. A curse that deals 5 a second, and every fourth second a quarter of the health its target has lost since it landed, from every source, is one periodic effect: Its first impact is −5. Its second is a Worker number, −0.25 × the worker's answer. The worker watches the target's Health, Lost, Every Ticks 4.

guides/scalers/built-in-kinds.html.title: Built-in kinds | PlayForge
guides/scalers/built-in-kinds.html.summary: Built-in kinds The kinds PlayForge ships for this guide's pickers, each with its menu and what it does, as its picker says. A project's own kinds join them in the same pickers. In this section Scalers Number kinds Variances Scaler behaviours Conditions

guides/scalers/built-in-kinds/conditions.title: Conditions | PlayForge
guides/scalers/built-in-kinds/conditions.summary: Conditions Kind Menu What it does AllCondition Logic Holds where every one of its conditions holds. AlwaysCondition — Always holds. AnyCondition Logic Holds where any one of its conditions holds. AttributeCondition — Compares an attribute of the caster or the target with a number. ChanceCondition — Holds on a roll of its chance. CompareCondition — Compares one number with another. LevelCondition — Compares the level with a number. NeverCondition — Never holds. NotCondition Logic Holds where its condition doesn't. TagCondition — Holds where the caster or the target has a tag.

guides/scalers/built-in-kinds/number-kin.title: Number kinds | PlayForge
guides/scalers/built-in-kinds/number-kin.summary: Number kinds Kind Menu What it does AssetPartKind — A part of an effect, an ability or an item on the caster or the target, found by a tag, as its stacks. ClampedScaler Scaler A number kept between a floor and a ceiling. ConditionalScaler Scaler One number where a condition holds, and another where it doesn't. GroupImpactKind — One retention group's part of an attribute. LocalDataKind — A value kept in Local Data, under a key. RelativeToFieldKind — Another number field of the same object, times or plus a number. SetByCallerScaler — A value code passes in under a tag as it applies the effect or activates the ability. StackingCurveKind Scaler A count, as stacks, through a stacking curve, then a number added. ThresholdScaler Scaler A number for each tier of levels. TrackedImpactKind Effect What an effect has dealt: its last impact, its total, or how many. WorkerNumberKind — A value a worker answers under a key.

guides/scalers/built-in-kinds/scaler-beh.title: Scaler behaviours | PlayForge
guides/scalers/built-in-kinds/scaler-beh.summary: Scaler behaviours Kind Menu What it does AttenuateScalerBehaviour — Turns the number into a factor: as it is, one plus it, or one minus it.

guides/scalers/built-in-kinds/scalers.ht.title: Scalers | PlayForge
guides/scalers/built-in-kinds/scalers.ht.summary: Scalers Kind Menu What it does AttributeBackedScaler — An attribute of the caster or the target, times a number for each level. CachedAttributeBackedScaler Scaler An attribute's value through a curve by level, kept as the attribute changes. CachedAttributeScaler Scaler Another attribute's value, kept as it changes. CachedScalerGroup Scaler Several kept numbers joined as one. CachedSimpleScaler — A number for each level, for an attribute set's start. ConstantScaler Scaler One number, whatever the level. EffectStacksScaler Effect The effect's stack count. ItemStacksScaler Item The stack count of the item that applied the effect. RandomizedScaler Scaler A number for each level, with random variance. ScalerGroup — Several numbers joined as one. SharedCachedScaler — A shared Scaler asset's number, for an attribute set. SharedScaler — A shared Scaler asset's number, so one edit reaches every field that uses it. SimpleScaler — A number for each level.

guides/scalers/built-in-kinds/variances..title: Variances | PlayForge
guides/scalers/built-in-kinds/variances..summary: Variances Kind Menu What it does FlatVariance (Flat) — Up or down by an amount, as 5 for a hit of 20 landing from 15 to 25. MultiplierVariance (Multiplier) — The value times a multiplier between its Min and its Max, as 0.9 to 1.1. PercentageVariance (Percentage) — Up or down by a share of the value, as 0.1 for 10% either way.

guides/scalers/scaler-assets.html.title: Scaler assets | PlayForge
guides/scalers/scaler-assets.html.summary: Scaler assets A Scaler asset (Create → PlayForge → Scaler) holds one scaler that many fields can use. A field of the Shared kind reads its Asset's scaler. An edit to the asset changes every field that uses it, with nothing to copy or propagate. Open shows the asset in a window of its own. Under the field, the asset's curve shows beside its range, as "6–8, levels 1–5", and how many fields share it. A field adjusts the shared values only through its own number and Combine. Scaler × Number with a number of 1.5 reads the asset's values times 1.5, as in Fire Duration × 1.5. Note The Scaler asset was the Scaler Template, whose link and sync settings nothing read, so those settings are gone. So are the old scaler window's curve editor and import window: a scaler's values are its table, and Import Values compares them before it copies. In this section The asset's inspector: The asset's own inspector shows its name, its kind and how many fields use it. Trying a scaler: The asset's Try section reads it at each level of a range, Levels 1 to 5 to start, as an effect's Levels does. What can share one: Any magnitude field can share a Scaler asset, within a few rules.

guides/scalers/scaler-assets/the-assets-.title: The asset's inspector | PlayForge
guides/scalers/scaler-assets/the-assets-.summary: The asset's inspector The asset's own inspector shows its name, its kind and how many fields use it. Property Description Name Renames it, as The Forge and the field menus list it. Description What the scaler is for. Values Its scaler's values (Values per level). Used By Each field that shares it, by its asset and field. Click a row to select the asset. In The Forge, its summary says its description, its kind, what it reads and how many fields use it.

guides/scalers/scaler-assets/trying-a-sc.title: Trying a scaler | PlayForge
guides/scalers/scaler-assets/trying-a-sc.summary: Trying a scaler The asset's Try section reads it at each level of a range, Levels 1 to 5 to start, as an effect's Levels does. It shows a row of what it gives at each level, and under it the parts behind the level picked. It reads against a stand-in Caster and Target, and a Caller. Each has a row for what the scaler asks of it, found as it reads. Stand-in Its rows Caster and Target An attribute on its side: whether the side Has it, its current and its base. Caller A key the caller sets: whether it's Set, and its value. Unset reads the scaler's default. A side's Entity fills its attributes from what that entity's attribute set starts each at, at its starting level. One the set doesn't give, it lacks. A stand-in holds attributes alone. So a number that reads an effect, an item, a tag, a retention group's part or Local Data reads as on an entity with none of them. What's typed is kept for the session, never in the asset. ScalerTry does the same in code: new ScalerTry { From = 1, To = 5 }.Read(scaler).

guides/scalers/scaler-assets/what-can-sh.title: What can share one | PlayForge
guides/scalers/scaler-assets/what-can-sh.summary: What can share one Any magnitude field can share a Scaler asset, within a few rules. An attribute set's element shares one whose scaler is a cached kind, and its Scaler Assets lists only those. A Scaler asset can't hold a Shared scaler of its own. A field whose asset is missing reads as a field with no scaler. An element whose asset is missing reads its root value. A chain of shared scalers that comes back to its own asset stops after eight steps, rather than run forever.

guides/scalers/values-per-level.html.title: Values per level | PlayForge
guides/scalers/values-per-level.html.summary: Values per level A scaler's settings sit on a shaded block under its field, so they read as the scaler's among the fields around them. A kind shows only what it reads. A Fixed Value shows its value, and a Randomized scaler its variance, then the values its base value comes from. A kind's field that applies only to some of its settings shows only for them, as an Asset Part's worker key for an effect's Worker Value. Property Description Values Per Level or Spread Over Levels. A Table reads Per Level and By Level spreads, as their kinds say, so they have no choice here. A scaler of another kind with values for each level chooses. Behaviours Rules that adjust the value the scaler works out, in order. A read-only curve beside the table shows the values, and spread, the curve they make. Its tooltip reads them, as "6 at level 1, rising to 8 at level 5". Quick Fill fills the levels the table shows. Nothing changes a scaler's values while it's drawn: its table keeps its length until you change it. In this section Per Level: With Per Level, the scaler has one value per level, ten levels to a row. Spread Over Levels: With Spread Over Levels, the values are points on a curve over a level range, and a level between two points reads between them.

guides/scalers/values-per-level/per-leve.title: Per Level | PlayForge
guides/scalers/values-per-level/per-leve.summary: Per Level With Per Level, the scaler has one value per level, ten levels to a row. Property Description Levels Whose levels it has a value for: its asset's level provider's, or its Own levels. Level 1 reads the first value, level 4 the 4th, and a level past the end reads the last. An asset with a level provider, as an ability, or an effect linked to one, follows the provider's levels, as Fireball's levels (1–4), with a value for each. A level past the scaler's values shows the last in secondary text. Type there to give it a value of its own. Own levels gives the scaler a count of its own. An asset whose levels come from whatever uses it shows the count alone. An unlinked effect, an attribute set and a Scaler asset do. A new level takes the last value. A scaler you make in the inspector starts Per Level.

guides/scalers/values-per-level/spread-o.title: Spread Over Levels | PlayForge
guides/scalers/values-per-level/spread-o.summary: Spread Over Levels With Spread Over Levels, the values are points on a curve over a level range, and a level between two points reads between them. Property Description Over Levels The level range the values spread over (below). Points How many values. Between Points Steps, Straight Line or Smooth Curve. Over Levels takes one of three ranges: Over Levels The range The provider's levels The levels of its asset's level provider. Own levels Levels up to the scaler's own Max Level. The provider's up to a level The provider's levels, up to the Max Level. The values reach the last at the lower of the Max Level and the provider's last level, and a level past it reads the last value. Three values, 10, 20 and 30, spread over levels 1 to 5 read 10, 15, 20, 25 and 30. The points are numbered, and under them each level shows what it reads. The scalers saved before the choice existed spread, so they read as they did.

guides/scalers/writing-your-own-scaler.h.title: Writing your own scaler | PlayForge
guides/scalers/writing-your-own-scaler.h.summary: Writing your own scaler You can add three kinds of your own: a scaler, a kind of number, and a condition for a Conditional. In this section A scaler of your own: A scaler of your own derives from AbstractScaler, or from AbstractCachedScaler for an attribute set's values. A kind of number of your own: A kind of number of your own is simpler than a scaler. A condition of your own: A condition of your own, for a Conditional, is made the same way.

guides/scalers/writing-your-own-scaler/a.title: A condition of your own | PlayForge
guides/scalers/writing-your-own-scaler/a.summary: A condition of your own A condition of your own, for a Conditional, is made the same way. Derive from GameplayCondition. Override Evaluate(in NumberContext context) to say whether it holds, and Describe() for its line. Name it with [GameplayCondition("Target Is Caster", Reads = NumberReads.Caster | NumberReads.Target)]. The condition menu offers it, and condition.Holds(context) reads it. A kind or a condition that holds numbers reads them with itself as their owner, MaxValue.Evaluate(context, this). It passes Initialize(carrier) on to them, so a number in it captures what it captures as an effect's spec is made. PlayForge's conditions are in Runtime/PlayForge/Numbers/Conditions.

guides/scalers/writing-your-own-scaler/a.title: A kind of number of your own | PlayForge
guides/scalers/writing-your-own-scaler/a.summary: A kind of number of your own A kind of number of your own is simpler than a scaler. Derive from NumberKind. Override its one method, Evaluate(in NumberContext context). Name it, and say what it reads, with [NumberKind("Distance to Target", Reads = NumberReads.Caster | NumberReads.Target)]. Evaluate reads what the field's site has: context.Caster, context.Target, context.Level, the caller's magnitudes, Local Data, an attribute on either side, and more. context.Has(...) says which. Describe() gives the field's summary, as "the distance to the target". A field offers the kind only where what it reads can be worked out. Where it can't, the field reads its number. [ForgeMenu("Space")] files it in the kind menu. A kind is a scaler, so it also works in an effect's magnitude, and inside a Group or a Conditional. Its fields draw as a scaler's do. Test one without an effect: number.Evaluate(NumberContext.For(caster, target, level)). A kind is saved by its class's name, so renaming the class needs Unity's [MovedFrom]. PlayForge's own kinds, Local Data, Tracked Impact, Asset Part and the rest, are written this way, in Runtime/PlayForge/Numbers/Kinds.

guides/scalers/writing-your-own-scaler/a.title: A scaler of your own | PlayForge
guides/scalers/writing-your-own-scaler/a.summary: A scaler of your own A scaler of your own derives from AbstractScaler, or from AbstractCachedScaler for an attribute set's values. It has a public constructor with no parameters. The Kind menu lists it by its name without "Scaler", as Damage Curve for DamageCurveScaler. Its inspector draws: Each field it adds, public or [SerializeField], as Unity draws the field's type, through any property drawer you write for that type. The fields of an abstract base of your own too. A field marked [ForgeShowWhen(nameof(Mode), EMode.Curved)] only while another field, an enum or a bool, holds one of the values given. The parts every scaler has, as its Parts say (below). [HideInInspector] keeps a field out. Parts A scaler's Parts say which of the parts every scaler has it reads. Part What it is EScalerParts.LevelValues Its values per level EScalerParts.LevelRange The level range they spread over EScalerParts.Behaviours Its behaviours Unless you override it, a scaler reads all three, or its behaviours alone where its UseScalingOptions() returns false. Override Parts to say what yours reads. A scaler that reads only an attribute returns EScalerParts.Behaviours. Parts can follow the scaler's own fields, as one that reads its values per level in one mode alone.

guides/services/chance.html.title: Chance | PlayForge
guides/services/chance.html.summary: Chance ForgeChance rolls every chance PlayForge has. Each rolls by its ChanceRoll, which says whether it's pseudo-random and whose luck it reads. PlayForge's chances are: an effect's Chance to Apply; an ability's Chance to Activate; a trigger's Chance; a Value Pipeline's Chance, Block and Evade stages; the Chance condition. Each has a ChanceRoll beside it, its Chance Roll, Activation Roll or Roll, which says how it rolls (Effects: Requirements): Property Description Pseudo Random Each miss raises the next roll's odds, and a hit starts them again (Pseudo-random rolls). Own Luck The roll reads the chance's own Luck, in place of the caster's attribute in the project's Luck role (Luck). Luck The chance's own luck, a number read for the roll. In this section Rolling a chance: ForgeChance.Roll(chance, in context, roll, key) says whether a chance, from 0 to 1, comes up for the caster its NumberContext gives. Pseudo-random rolls: A pseudo-random roll evens out streaks: each miss raises the next roll's odds, and a hit starts them again. Luck: A roll's luck, ForgeChance.LuckOf(in context, roll), is the first of these that applies The Chance condition: The Chance condition, ChanceCondition, holds on a roll of its Chance, rolled by its Roll.

guides/services/chance/luck.html.title: Luck | PlayForge
guides/services/chance/luck.html.summary: Luck A roll's luck, ForgeChance.LuckOf(in context, roll), is the first of these that applies: With Own Luck, the chance's own Luck, a number read for the roll. Else, the current value of the caster's attribute playing the project's Luck role, ForgeChance.ProjectLuck (Attributes: Roles). Else, 0. Either is rounded to a whole number. Above 0, the roll draws that many more times and keeps the best. Below 0, it keeps the worst. A draw below the odds comes up.

guides/services/chance/pseudo-random-rol.title: Pseudo-random rolls | PlayForge
guides/services/chance/pseudo-random-rol.summary: Pseudo-random rolls A pseudo-random roll evens out streaks: each miss raises the next roll's odds, and a hit starts them again. The chance over many rolls stays the same. The odds are ForgeChance.Constant(chance) times one more than the misses in a row, at most 1. That constant is the one whose distribution's mean is the chance, as Dota's pseudo-random distribution is. Each caster keeps its own streak for each chance, by the chance's key. PlayForge's own chances key by what holds them: the effect, the ability, the trigger, the stage or the condition. A pseudo-random roll with no key or no caster rolls its chance as it is. A caster's streaks go with it. ForgeChance.ForgetStreaks(caster) forgets them, as a test does to start clean.

guides/services/chance/rolling-a-chance..title: Rolling a chance | PlayForge
guides/services/chance/rolling-a-chance..summary: Rolling a chance ForgeChance.Roll(chance, in context, roll, key) says whether a chance, from 0 to 1, comes up for the caster its NumberContext gives. A chance of 1 or more always comes up, and one of 0 or less never does. Neither draws, so a chance that can't miss leaves the numbers others draw as they were. A chance of the game's own rolls the same way: using FarEmerald.PlayForge; public static class Lockpicking { // The key the thief's pseudo-random streak for this chance is kept under private static readonly object Key = new object(); // Pseudo-random, and lucky by the thief's attribute in the project's Luck role private static readonly ChanceRoll Roll = new ChanceRoll { PseudoRandom = true }; public static bool Picks(IGameplayAbilitySystem thief, float chance) { var context = NumberContext.Of(thief); return ForgeChance.Roll(chance, in context, Roll, Key); } }

guides/services/chance/the-chance-condit.title: The Chance condition | PlayForge
guides/services/chance/the-chance-condit.summary: The Chance condition The Chance condition, ChanceCondition, holds on a roll of its Chance, rolled by its Roll. Its Chance is a number of any kind, as a critical strike chance read from an attribute. Read in a hit, it rolls once and keeps the roll, so the hit's preview and its commit read the same. Read with no hit, it rolls each time it's read.

guides/services/clocks.html.title: Clocks | PlayForge
guides/services/clocks.html.summary: Clocks A clock is an IForgeClock, a source of time. PlayForge has one for Unity's time, one for the game's, an unscaled one, a scaled one and each entity's own, and a game can write its own. Clock Its time UnityClock Unity's Time, through UnityClock.Instance. It's the clock in force until code puts another in. GameClock The game's, through GameClock.Instance: the clock in force, read each time it's asked. So it can be kept and handed on, and still follows a clock put in later. A sequence on it runs by the game's time, whatever its packet's owner's is. UnscaledClock The game's without its time scale, through UnscaledClock.Instance. Its step is the clock in force's unscaled step, and its Time the unscaled time. So a sequence on it runs while the game's time is slowed or stopped, as a pause menu's does. ScaledClock A scale of its own, ScaledClock.Scale, over another clock, its ScaledClock.Source (Scaled clocks). EntityClock An entity's own, gas.GetClock(): the game's, at the entity's TimeScale (Entity clocks). Each has what ForgeTime reads: DeltaTime, UnscaledDeltaTime, FixedDeltaTime, Time, UnscaledTime and FrameCount. Each also has FollowsTicks: whether a sequence on it waits for ProcessControl's ticks, where its tick rate is set. FollowsTicks is true for a clock of the game's time. The ticks run on the game's time, and stand with it. So UnscaledClock, which runs while that time stands, says false, and its sequences wait for Unity's frames instead. GameClock and a ScaledClock say as the clock they read does. In this section Scaled clocks: A ScaledClock runs at a scale of its own against another clock. Entity clocks: An entity's clock, gas.GetClock(), runs at the entity's TimeScale: OwnScale times AttributeScale. A clock of your own: A class of your own that implements IForgeClock is read as any clock is.

guides/services/clocks/a-clock-of-your-o.title: A clock of your own | PlayForge
guides/services/clocks/a-clock-of-your-o.summary: A clock of your own A class of your own that implements IForgeClock is read as any clock is. You can: put it in with ForgeTime.Use; name it by a packet's Clock, or a sequence's WithClock; give it by a clock pick of your own (Picking a clock in an inspector). Its FollowsTicks is true unless it says otherwise. GameClock, UnscaledClock, ScaledClock and EntityClock read the clock in force. So a world of its own's steps and the fixed tick drive them. A clock that reads Unity's Time itself doesn't follow them.

guides/services/clocks/entity-clocks.htm.title: Entity clocks | PlayForge
guides/services/clocks/entity-clocks.htm.summary: Entity clocks An entity's clock, gas.GetClock(), runs at the entity's TimeScale: OwnScale times AttributeScale. Property Description OwnScale The scale code sets, as a hit-stop's 0. AttributeScale The scale the entity's Time Scale attribute gives, read as each of the entity's steps begins. It's 1 where its identity names none (Entities: Attributes). Setting TimeScale sets OwnScale. So a hit-stop holds under a slow, and the slow is still there after. Its DeltaTime and FixedDeltaTime are the game's times its scale. Its Time is its steps added up since it started. Its unscaled times and its frame are the game's. A scale of 0 holds the entity's time still: its effects, its cooldowns among them, and its abilities' waits and sequences stand. It isn't a pause, which ProcessControl's is (Processes: Pausing). // A hit-stop on the entity struck: its own time held, its slows and hastes kept for after var clock = gas.GetClock(); clock.OwnScale = 0f; // ... a moment later clock.OwnScale = 1f;

guides/services/clocks/scaled-clocks.htm.title: Scaled clocks | PlayForge
guides/services/clocks/scaled-clocks.htm.summary: Scaled clocks A ScaledClock runs at a scale of its own against another clock. new ScaledClock(scale, source) makes one. Property Description ScaledClock.Scale How fast it runs against its source: 1 as that one, 0.5 at half, 2 at double, 0 stopped. A scale below 0 is taken as 0. ScaledClock.Source The clock it's given, or, with none, the clock in force. Its DeltaTime and FixedDeltaTime are its source's times its scale. Its unscaled times and its frame are its source's. Its Time counts from the first time it's read: its source's time, at each scale it had. So a change of its scale or its source carries on from where it was. Making one reads no clock, so a component's field can make one where it's declared. With no source, it counts whichever clock is in force as it's read. Give it a source to count by where a world of its own steps. The sequences that share one slow, speed up or stop together as it's set.

guides/services/entity-services.html.title: Entity services | PlayForge
guides/services/entity-services.html.summary: Entity services An entity service is a per-entity object that an entity's components share. It's made the first time it's asked for, and stepped by the entity's own time. The auras an entity runs, AuraSet, and the wait a Respawn counts down, RespawnTimer, are two of them. Method What it does gas.GetService<T>() Gives the entity's service of a kind, made the first time it's asked for. gas.FindService<T>() Gives it without making one, or null. A service derives from AbstractEntityService, with a parameterless constructor. It overrides the hooks it needs, each a no-op otherwise. Its System is the entity it's of. Method When it runs Step(deltaTime) Each frame, by the entity's own time, after its effects tick and before its turn. Revive() As an entity that stays revives, before anything else of the revive. End() As the entity ends. The entity keeps none of its services after. Entities: Components: Services has the rest. This service keeps a heat meter that cools by its entity's own time: using FarEmerald.PlayForge; using UnityEngine; // A heat meter each entity keeps, which cools by the entity's own time: a slowed entity cools slower public class Heat : AbstractEntityService { public float Value { get; private set; } public float CoolingPerSecond = 10f; public void Add(float heat) => Value += heat; public override void Step(float deltaTime) => Value = Mathf.Max(0f, Value - CoolingPerSecond * deltaTime); // Back from the dead, cold public override void Revive() => Value = 0f; } public static class Overheat { public static void Fire(IGameplayAbilitySystem gunner) => gunner.GetService<Heat>().Add(25f); public static float HeatOf(IGameplayAbilitySystem gunner) => gunner.FindService<Heat>()?.Value ?? 0f; }

guides/services/fixed-ticks.html.title: Fixed ticks | PlayForge
guides/services/fixed-ticks.html.summary: Fixed ticks ProcessControl's fixed tick steps the game in fixed steps of its time. A frame runs as many as its time holds, so a run comes out the same at any frame rate. Set it under Fixed Tick in ProcessControl's inspector: Property Description Fixed Tick Rate The ticks in a second of game time, as 60. 0, the default, steps once a frame. In code, it's ProcessControl.FixedTickRate. Max Ticks Per Frame The most ticks a frame runs, 8 by default. A frame too long for them drops the rest of its time, so the game doesn't fall further behind. In this section Inside a tick: A tick steps the game in this order Waiting on ticks: Code waits on the ticks through ForgeTick

guides/services/fixed-ticks/inside-a-tic.title: Inside a tick | PlayForge
guides/services/fixed-ticks/inside-a-tic.summary: Inside a tick A tick steps the game in this order: What waits for a tick goes on. Every process steps at Update. Every process steps at LateUpdate, its end of frame with it. While a tick runs, the clock in force is the tick's. ForgeTime.DeltaTime is its step, and ForgeTime.FrameCount the ticks so far. A process that steps at FixedUpdate steps with Unity's physics, as ever. The ticks run on the game's time, so they stand while it does.

guides/services/fixed-ticks/waiting-on-t.title: Waiting on ticks | PlayForge
guides/services/fixed-ticks/waiting-on-t.summary: Waiting on ticks Code waits on the ticks through ForgeTick: ForgeTick Waits for Next(token) The next tick, or, with ticks off, Unity's next frame, as a sequence's waits do Next(timing, token) The same at a frame's timing: the Update family waits for a tick, and FixedUpdate, the physics step's, for Unity's NextFrame(token) The next tick, or, with ticks off, Unity's next frame as UniTask.NextFrame waits for it WaitUntil(condition, token) and WaitWhile(condition, token) A condition, asked once a tick, or once a frame with ticks off Next(clock, token) The next step of a clock's time. For a clock whose FollowsTicks is false, as UnscaledClock's is, that's Unity's next frame, where the scene ticks. For any other clock, it waits as Next(token) does Member What it says ForgeTick.Ticking Whether the tick in force ticks. ForgeTick.Ticks How many ticks it has run. ForgeTick.Scene The scene's tick, a ForgeTickSource, which ProcessControl's rate turns on. ForgeTick.Current The tick in force: a world of its own's while it steps or one of its processes changes state, the scene's otherwise. A ProcessWorld its owner steps ticks once for each Step(deltaTime). So its sequences wait on its steps.

guides/services/forgehelper.html.title: ForgeHelper | PlayForge
guides/services/forgehelper.html.summary: ForgeHelper ForgeHelper is a static class of the checks and small sums PlayForge's own systems share. A game's workers, conditions and tools can call it too. Group Members What they do Tags HasTag, HasAnyTag, HasAllTags, HasNoneOfTags, CountMatchingTags, GetMatchingTags, MatchesTag Look for tags in a list by an ETagMatchMode: Exact; IncludeChildren, the tag or one under it; IncludeParents, the tag or one above it; or SameRoot Requirements ValidateAvoidRequire, ValidateAvoidRequireQueries, ValidateTagQuery, ValidateAllQueries, ValidateAnyQuery Whether tags, a list or a TagCache, hold every required tag and none to avoid, or pass lists of TagQuery. A null query passes, and so does an empty list Tag paths IsValidTagPath, BuildTagPath, GetUniqueRoots, GroupByRoot, GetCommonAncestor Whether a path is well formed; a path from its parts, joined by dots; tags' roots; and the deepest tag two tags both are or are under, or null Effects ValidateEffectApplicationRequirements, ValidateEffectOngoingRequirements, ValidateEffectRemovalRequirements, ValidateAffiliationPolicy An effect spec's requirements as it applies, while it lasts and to remove it, and its affiliation policy against its target's sides Worker filters ValidateImpactTypes, ValidateContextTags, ValidateSelfModification, ValidateImpactTargets, ValidateSignPolicy The filters a worker puts a change through: its impact types, its context tags, whether its source is its target, which part of the attribute it changed, and its sign Signs SignPolicy, SignPolicyExtended, SignInt, SignFloat, AlignedSignInt, AlignedSignFloat, AlignToSign A change's sign as an ESignPolicy (Sign and math policies); a sign as −1, 0 or 1, alone or several multiplied; and a value's size given a sign, negative for Negative and positive for the rest Sums PerformCalculationOperation, MagnitudeAndScalerOperation, PerformScalerRelativeOperation, AttributeMathEvent An ECalculationOperation on two values; a magnitude with its scaler's value by an EMagnitudeOperation, with an ERoundingOperation for a whole number, whose Round takes a half away from zero; and an operation on attribute values whose operand an EMathApplicationPolicy turns first Enums Translate One enum read as another: an EAbilityActivationPolicyExtended as an EAbilityActivationPolicy, an EMagnitudeOperation as an ECalculationOperation, an EAttributeTargetLimited as an EAttributeTarget Collections RandomChoice, Shuffle, WeightedSample, SafeAdd, SafeAddRange, SafeRemove, ContainsAll, TrueForAny A list's item at random; the list shuffled in place; N items picked by their weights, an item as often as it's drawn; a dictionary's entries added, or added to a key's list or set, and removed; and whether a sequence holds every item of another, or has an item a condition holds for. The random ones draw from ForgeRandom Points RandomPointWithinCircle, RandomPointWithinSphere A point at random within a radius of the origin, drawn from ForgeRandom. The circle's lies in the XY plane, a Vector3 with a z of 0, and one nearer than its minRadius is moved out to it Icons GetTextureItem, TextureUnder An icon from an asset's Textures: GetTextureItem the texture under a tag, else the first that has one, and TextureUnder the one under exactly that tag, or null

guides/services/index.html.title: Time, Randomness, Input and Logging | PlayForge
guides/services/index.html.summary: Time, Randomness, Input and Logging PlayForge works through four services of its own: Service What it does ForgeTime Reads the game's time. ForgeRandom Draws its random numbers. ForgeInput Reads the player's pointer. ForgeLog Says what PlayForge does. The first three read Unity's own until code puts another in, with ForgeTime.Use, ForgeRandom.Use or ForgeInput.Use. A test, a replay, a server or a game with input of its own does this. Each returns the one it replaced, to put back. This guide is the reference behind the short sections of Getting Started: Quickstart: a damage ability in ~10 minutes: Time and random numbers on time, logging and profiling. It covers: the clocks, and which one a run takes; the fixed tick; chances and luck; pointer input; log levels; the Profiler's markers and counters; an entity's own services; the small utilities a game's code uses. In this guide Time: ForgeTime is the clock PlayForge's runtime reads in place of Unity's Time. Clocks: A clock is an IForgeClock, a source of time. Which clock a run takes: Everything PlayForge times goes by a clock, most by their owner's. Picking a clock in an inspector: An inspector picks a clock with an AbstractClockChoice field, as an ability's Run Sequence task's Clock does. Fixed ticks: ProcessControl's fixed tick steps the game in fixed steps of its time. Random numbers: ForgeRandom is where PlayForge draws its random numbers. Chance: ForgeChance rolls every chance PlayForge has. Repeatable runs: A run that must come out the same twice needs the same time and the same rolls each time it runs. Time and rolls in tests: The test kit makes time and chance a test's own, through the same two services (Testing Your Content: The world). Pointer input: ForgeInput is what PlayForge reads of the player's input Logging: ForgeLog is where everything PlayForge says goes. Log levels: A message is let through where its level is at least its system's level. Process and sequence logs: ProcessControl and task sequences have switches of their own, which decide whether they say what they do. Profiling: PlayForge's work shows in Unity's Profiler (Getting Started: Profiling) Entity services: An entity service is a per-entity object that an entity's components share. ForgeHelper: ForgeHelper is a static class of the checks and small sums PlayForge's own systems share. Packet helpers: ProcessTaskUtil holds extension methods for a data packet's targets and the effects it carries. The attribute registry: AttributeRegistry finds an attribute by its name, among those the game's entities have been given. Lists: ReadOnlyListView<T> and ForgeUtils are two small list helpers Sign and math policies: Three enums say how PlayForge reads the sign of a change and turns a number into a factor: ESignPolicy, ESignPolicyExtended and EMathApplicationPolicy. In the API The types of this guide's area: AbstractClockChoice, AttributeRegistry, CasterClockChoice, EMathApplicationPolicy, ESignPolicy, ESignPolicyExtended, ForgeCounters, ForgeFrameCosts, ForgeHelper, ForgeInput, ForgeProcessCost, ForgeProfiler, ForgeRandom, ForgeTime, GameClock, GameClockChoice, IForgeClock, IForgeInput, IForgeRandom, InputSystemPointerInput, LegacyPointerInput, ProcessTaskUtil, ReadOnlyListView<T>, ScaledClock, ScaledClockChoice, SeededRandom, UnityClock, UnityRandom, UnscaledClock, UnscaledClockChoice.

guides/services/lists.html.title: Lists | PlayForge
guides/services/lists.html.summary: Lists ReadOnlyListView<T> and ForgeUtils are two small list helpers: ReadOnlyListView<T> is a view of a list that foreach walks without allocating. ForgeUtils gives the index of a list's least or greatest item. ReadOnlyListView<T> is a read-only struct over a List<T>. It has a Count, an indexer, and a GetEnumerator that hands foreach the list's own struct enumerator, so walking it allocates nothing. Walked as an IEnumerable<T>, as LINQ walks it, its enumerator is boxed, as any list's is. A view of no list reads as empty. An effect spec's GetImpactedAttributes(delivery) returns one. Method What it gives ForgeUtils.IndexMin(list, selector) The index of the item whose selected value is least. ForgeUtils.IndexMax(list, selector) The index of the item whose selected value is greatest. Each gives the first of equals, and 0 for an empty list.

guides/services/log-levels.html.title: Log levels | PlayForge
guides/services/log-levels.html.summary: Log levels A message is let through where its level is at least its system's level. That's the system's own, where it has one, or else ForgeLog.MinimumLevel, Info by default. Method What it does ForgeLog.SetLevel(system, level) Gives a system a level of its own. ForgeLog.SetLevel(system, null) Gives the system back to ForgeLog.MinimumLevel. ForgeLog.LevelOf(system) Gives the system's level now. ForgeLog.HasOwnLevel(system) Says whether the system has a level of its own. ForgeLog.ClearLevels() Gives every system back. Note What's said only when asked is information, of level Info: its switch makes it, and the level shows it (Process and sequence logs). A level above Info hides it, however it's switched on. In this section In the editor: In the editor, you set the level in PlayForge's preferences. In a build: A build reads no preference.

guides/services/log-levels/in-a-build.ht.title: In a build | PlayForge
guides/services/log-levels/in-a-build.ht.summary: In a build A build reads no preference. It logs Info and above, unless its code sets the level. using FarEmerald.PlayForge; using UnityEngine; public static class BuildLogging { // A build reads no preference: problems only, but every message about effects [RuntimeInitializeOnLoadMethod(RuntimeInitializeLoadType.BeforeSceneLoad)] private static void Configure() { if (Application.isEditor) return; ForgeLog.MinimumLevel = ForgeLog.ELevel.Warning; ForgeLog.SetLevel(ForgeLog.ESystem.Effects, ForgeLog.ELevel.Verbose); } }

guides/services/log-levels/in-the-editor.title: In the editor | PlayForge
guides/services/log-levels/in-the-editor.summary: In the editor In the editor, you set the level in PlayForge's preferences. Edit → Preferences → PlayForge sets ForgeLog.MinimumLevel with Minimum Log Level, under Logging. The level is yours, not the project's. It's kept in the editor's preferences, and put back on each domain reload. Use Defaults puts every preference on the page back, the level to Info. Editor code sets the level with ForgeLogSettingsBridge.SetLevel(level). The Creator Lab's Log page gives a system a level of its own, with System and Level. As all gives it back to the preference's (The Creator Lab: Showing its working).

guides/services/logging.html.title: Logging | PlayForge
guides/services/logging.html.summary: Logging ForgeLog is where everything PlayForge says goes. Each message has a level and a system, and a gate on the two decides what reaches Unity's Console. Levels, ForgeLog.ELevel, from the most said to the least: Verbose, Info, Warning, Error, and None. None lets nothing through, errors neither (Log levels). Systems, ForgeLog.ESystem: General, Effects, Abilities, Attributes, Workers, Numbers, Processes, Tags, Items, Saves, Input, Lab and Sequences. Each can take a level of its own. Its messages reach the Console with [PlayForge] before them: a warning as a warning, and an error as an error. Its methods are marked [HideInCallstack]. So the Console's Strip Logging Callstack leaves them out of the stack, and a double-click on a message opens the code that logged it. In this section Logging from code: Your code logs through ForgeLog as PlayForge does. Hearing the log: ForgeLog.Logged hears each message let through, as a ForgeLogEntry

guides/services/logging/hearing-the-log..title: Hearing the log | PlayForge
guides/services/logging/hearing-the-log..summary: Hearing the log ForgeLog.Logged hears each message let through, as a ForgeLogEntry: Field Description Level, System The message's level and system. Message The message, without the prefix. Context, Subject The object the Console points at, and the entity the message is about. Time, Frame The game's time and frame as it was logged. An exception is heard as its type and its message. An entry's ToString() writes it in a line, as "Effects, warning: …". The Creator Lab's Log page hears the messages so. This component keeps an in-game console of the warnings and errors PlayForge lets through: using System.Collections.Generic; using FarEmerald.PlayForge; using UnityEngine; // An in-game console: the last 50 warnings and errors PlayForge let through, newest last public class ForgeConsole : MonoBehaviour { private readonly Queue<string> lines = new Queue<string>(); private void OnEnable() => ForgeLog.Logged += Heard; private void OnDisable() => ForgeLog.Logged -= Heard; private void Heard(ForgeLogEntry entry) { if (entry.Level < ForgeLog.ELevel.Warning) return; lines.Enqueue($"[{entry.Frame}] {entry}"); while (lines.Count > 50) lines.Dequeue(); } private void OnGUI() { foreach (var line in lines) GUILayout.Label(line); } }

guides/services/logging/logging-from-cod.title: Logging from code | PlayForge
guides/services/logging/logging-from-cod.summary: Logging from code Your code logs through ForgeLog as PlayForge does. Method What it does ForgeLog.Verbose, ForgeLog.Info, ForgeLog.Warning, ForgeLog.Error Take a message and the Unity object the Console points at, its context, as a message of General. Given a system first, they take the entity the message is about too, its subject. ForgeLog.Exception(system, exception, context, subject) Logs an exception as Unity's Debug.LogException does, its stack in the Console, where an error is let through. ForgeLog.Allows(system, level) Says whether a message would be let through, so a costly one is built only when it will be shown. A message of a system names the system first, as ForgeLog.Warning(ForgeLog.ESystem.Abilities, "No target", this, gas).

guides/services/packet-helpers.html.title: Packet helpers | PlayForge
guides/services/packet-helpers.html.summary: Packet helpers ProcessTaskUtil holds extension methods for a data packet's targets and the effects it carries. It also holds three loops for async code, which wait through ForgeTick. In this section Targets and effects: These extension methods read and file a data packet's targets, and apply the effects it carries. Async loops: ProcessTaskUtil has three loops for async code, which wait a tick at a time through ForgeTick.

guides/services/packet-helpers/async-loo.title: Async loops | PlayForge
guides/services/packet-helpers/async-loo.summary: Async loops ProcessTaskUtil has three loops for async code, which wait a tick at a time through ForgeTick. Method What it does ProcessTaskUtil.WhileAsync(condition, token) Waits while a condition holds, a tick at a time. ProcessTaskUtil.DoWhileAsync(body, condition, token) Awaits the body, then a tick, while the condition holds, the body at least once. ProcessTaskUtil.DoWhile(body, duration, token) Does so until the duration has passed, by ForgeTime.Time, or by its unscaled time where its useUnscaledTime says. Each takes a PlayerLoopTiming, Update by default, and waits as ForgeTick.Next does (Fixed ticks).

guides/services/packet-helpers/targets-a.title: Targets and effects | PlayForge
guides/services/packet-helpers/targets-a.summary: Targets and effects These extension methods read and file a data packet's targets, and apply the effects it carries. Method What it does data.GetTargetingPacket(tag, out packet) Gives the primary AbstractTargetingPacket under a tag. Where there's none, it's false, and it interrupts the packet's sequence, where it's a SequenceDataPacket, unless it's called with autoInterrupt: false. data.SetTargetingPacket(tag, packet) Files a packet as the primary. data.SetTargetingPackets(tag, targets) Files the targeting packet of each target, in their order and in place of what was there, so the first is the primary. data.TryApplyEffects(target, tag) Applies each effect loaded under the tag to a target, an ITarget or a GameObject that has one. Each is made from the ability's origin, with the magnitudes its caller set. data.TryGetLoadedAssets<T>(tag, out assets), data.GetLoadedAssets<T>(tag) Give every value of a kind under a tag, as a DataValue<T>, empty where there's none. data.TryApplyEffects(target, tag) is false where: the packet isn't an ability's, an AbilityDataPacket; it holds no effects under the tag; there's no target.

guides/services/picking-a-clock-in-an-in.title: Picking a clock in an inspector | PlayForge
guides/services/picking-a-clock-in-an-in.summary: Picking a clock in an inspector An inspector picks a clock with an AbstractClockChoice field, as an ability's Run Sequence task's Clock does. Each kind of pick gives the clock for a run on a packet, as the run starts. Pick Kind The clock a run gets None The field left empty The clock it would have had Caster's CasterClockChoice An ability's caster's own time, its time scale times the game's; the game's for any other packet Game's GameClockChoice The game's, whatever an ability's caster's is: a slowed caster's sequence on it isn't slowed Unscaled UnscaledClockChoice The game's without its time scale, which runs while the game's time is slowed or stopped Scaled ScaledClockChoice A ScaledClock made for each run, at its Scale (1 as the clock it scales, 0.5 at half, 2 at double), over the clock its Of picks, or the caster's where it picks none A pick's ClockFor(data) gives its clock for a run on the packet. The base gives null, which leaves the run the clock it would have had. Caster's reads the packet's owner, not a clock the packet names, since a pick is what names one. In this section Where the picks are offered: Three things offer the clock picks A pick of your own: You can offer a clock pick of your own.

guides/services/picking-a-clock-in-an-in.title: A pick of your own | PlayForge
guides/services/picking-a-clock-in-an-in.summary: A pick of your own You can offer a clock pick of your own. A [Serializable] class of your own made from AbstractClockChoice is offered beside PlayForge's picks. It's offered by its [ForgeMenu] name, or else by its class's name without "ClockChoice". The picker makes it with its parameterless constructor. using System; using FarEmerald.PlayForge; using UnityEngine; // One slow-motion clock the game sets, shared by every run that picks it [Serializable] [ForgeMenu(Name = "Bullet Time", Description = "The game's shared slow-motion clock.")] public class BulletTimeClockChoice : AbstractClockChoice { public static ScaledClock Shared { get; private set; } = new ScaledClock(1f); // A fresh one each time the game starts, as statics outlive play mode where domain reload is off [RuntimeInitializeOnLoadMethod(RuntimeInitializeLoadType.SubsystemRegistration)] private static void Fresh() => Shared = new ScaledClock(1f); public override IForgeClock ClockFor(ProcessDataPacket data) => Shared; } // The game slows every run that picked it: BulletTimeClockChoice.Shared.Scale = 0.2f

guides/services/picking-a-clock-in-an-in.title: Where the picks are offered | PlayForge
guides/services/picking-a-clock-in-an-in.summary: Where the picks are offered Three things offer the clock picks: An ability's Run Sequence task. Its pick is its run's alone, so the ability's other tasks keep the caster's (Abilities: Stages). A Sequence cue. Its run goes by its pick, else the sequence's own clock, else its packet's: the clock of the cue's owner (Cues: Data packets). A component of your own, through a [SerializeReference] field. Its pick sets its packet's clock. This component runs its sequence on the clock its inspector picks: using FarEmerald.PlayForge; using UnityEngine; // Runs its sequence on the clock its inspector picks, or on the one it would have had public class IntroSequence : MonoBehaviour { [SerializeReference] public AbstractClockChoice Clock; private void Start() { var data = SequenceDataPacket.SceneRoot(); data.Clock = Clock?.ClockFor(data); TaskSequenceBuilder.Create("Intro") .Delay(2f) .Do(_ => ForgeLog.Info("The intro's two seconds are up")) .BuildSequence() .RegisterAndRun(data); } }

guides/services/pointer-input.html.title: Pointer input | PlayForge
guides/services/pointer-input.html.summary: Pointer input ForgeInput is what PlayForge reads of the player's input: the press and aim of click targeting; the task libraries' waits for a key or a press; the Creator Lab's controls. ForgeInput.Current is the input read now, an IForgeInput. It's the project's own, ForgeInput.Default(), until code puts another in. Method What it does ForgeInput.Use(input) Puts an input in, and returns the one it replaced. ForgeInput.Use(null) Puts the project's own back. The project's own input is the first of these that applies: InputSystemPointerInput, where the Input System package is installed and the Player settings' Active Input Handling takes it, as it does where it takes both. Else LegacyPointerInput, where it takes the Input Manager. Else an input that never presses and aims nowhere. An IForgeInput has seven members: IForgeInput What it says PointerPressed(button) Whether a button went down this frame: 0 the primary, the left button or a touch; 1 the secondary, the right; 2 the middle TryGetPointerRay(out ray) The ray the pointer aims along, or false with nothing to aim through, as with no camera PointerHeld(button) Whether a button is down now TryGetPointerPosition(out position) Where the pointer is on the screen, in pixels from its bottom left, or false where there's none ScrollDelta How far the scroll wheel turned this frame, in notches, away from the player positive KeyPressed(key) Whether a key went down this frame KeyHeld(key) Whether a key is down now, pressed this frame or held from an earlier one Only the first two must be written. The rest read as nothing held, no position, no scroll and no key, unless an input gives its own.
