In this section What reads it: Three parts of PlayForge read ForgeInput The defaults: The project's own inputs are LegacyPointerInput and InputSystemPointerInput. Input of your own: A game with a crosshair, a gamepad's reticle or a controller's ray writes an IForgeInput, and puts it in.

guides/services/pointer-input/input-of-y.title: Input of your own | PlayForge
guides/services/pointer-input/input-of-y.summary: Input of your own A game with a crosshair, a gamepad's reticle or a controller's ray writes an IForgeInput, and puts it in. Give it all seven members, passing those it doesn't change on to the project's own. An input that writes only the two click targeting reads has no key, no pointer position and no scroll. Through such an input, WaitForKey, WaitForAnyKey and the Creator Lab's keys, clicks and camera hear nothing. Note An input put in stays until code puts another in, past the end of play mode where domain reload is off. So code that puts one in puts back the one it replaced. This input aims from the crosshair in the middle of the screen, and passes the rest on to the project's own: using FarEmerald.PlayForge; using UnityEngine; // A third-person game's targeting: it presses as the project's own input does, but aims from the crosshair in the // middle of the screen, through the player's camera public sealed class CrosshairInput : IForgeInput { private readonly IForgeInput device = ForgeInput.Default(); public Camera Camera { get; set; } public bool PointerPressed(int button) => device.PointerPressed(button); public bool TryGetPointerRay(out Ray ray) => ForgeInput.TryAimThrough(Camera, new Vector2(Screen.width * 0.5f, Screen.height * 0.5f), out ray); // The rest as the device reads them, so the task libraries' waits and the Creator Lab still hear it public bool PointerHeld(int button) => device.PointerHeld(button); public bool TryGetPointerPosition(out Vector2 position) => device.TryGetPointerPosition(out position); public float ScrollDelta => device.ScrollDelta; public bool KeyPressed(KeyCode key) => device.KeyPressed(key); public bool KeyHeld(KeyCode key) => device.KeyHeld(key); } // Puts it in while the player's camera is on, and gives back the input it replaced public class CrosshairTargeting : MonoBehaviour { public Camera PlayerCamera; private IForgeInput previous; private void OnEnable() => previous = ForgeInput.Use(new CrosshairInput { Camera = PlayerCamera }); private void OnDisable() => ForgeInput.Use(previous); }

guides/services/pointer-input/the-defaul.title: The defaults | PlayForge
guides/services/pointer-input/the-defaul.summary: The defaults The project's own inputs are LegacyPointerInput and InputSystemPointerInput. Each aims through its Camera, or Camera.main where that's null. Input What it reads LegacyPointerInput The Input Manager's mouse and keys. It has no pointer position where no mouse is present. InputSystemPointerInput The Input System's. A mouse presses each of its three buttons, and a pen or a touch the primary. Its ScrollDelta is the mouse's scroll over 120, a notch on most mice. InputSystemPointerInput reads these keys: the letters; the top row's digits; F1 to F12; Escape, Space, Return, Tab, Backspace and Delete; the arrows; left and right Shift, Control and Alt. Any other KeyCode reads as never pressed. Each is compiled only where its input handling is on. So code that names one sits under the same condition: Input Condition LegacyPointerInput #if ENABLE_LEGACY_INPUT_MANAGER InputSystemPointerInput #if ENABLE_INPUT_SYSTEM, with the Input System package installed Aiming through a camera ForgeInput.TryAimThrough(camera, screenPoint, out ray) gives the ray from a camera through a point on the screen: the camera given, or else Camera.main. With neither, it logs a warning of the Input system, and returns false. ForgeInput.CameraOr(camera) is the camera given, or else Camera.main, as a floating text faces.

guides/services/pointer-input/what-reads.title: What reads it | PlayForge
guides/services/pointer-input/what-reads.summary: What reads it Three parts of PlayForge read ForgeInput: Click targeting, the Select tasks (Position, Direction, GAS Target, GAS Or Position and GAS Target In Range), waits for PointerPressed of its Mouse Button. Then it aims along TryGetPointerRay (Abilities: Activation). The task libraries' waits: WaitForKey and WaitForAnyKey read KeyPressed, and WaitForPointer reads PointerPressed, in SequenceTaskLibrary and SyncSequenceTaskLibrary alike (Task Sequences: Waiting). The Creator Lab: its presses and keys, the pointer's place, the middle button held to pan, and the wheel to zoom (The Creator Lab).

guides/services/process-and-sequence-log.title: Process and sequence logs | PlayForge
guides/services/process-and-sequence-log.summary: Process and sequence logs ProcessControl and task sequences have switches of their own, which decide whether they say what they do. Most of what they say is information, which the level must let through to show. In this section ProcessControl's logs: ProcessControl logs as the Processes system, by two switches (Processes: Logging) Sequence logs: Sequences log as the Sequences system (Task Sequences: Logging). Debug tool logs: Debug tools say what they find as information too

guides/services/process-and-sequence-log.title: Debug tool logs | PlayForge
guides/services/process-and-sequence-log.summary: Debug tool logs Debug tools say what they find as information too: Tool System TagCache.LogWeights() Tags The Threshold Debugger effect worker, ThresholdDebuggerEffectWorker Workers A queued LogAction General

guides/services/process-and-sequence-log.title: ProcessControl's logs | PlayForge
guides/services/process-and-sequence-log.summary: ProcessControl's logs ProcessControl logs as the Processes system, by two switches (Processes: Logging): Property Description Output Logs Off by default. Logs each process registered and unregistered, the scene's processes it collects as it starts, and the hierarchy it makes of them. Logs, as a warning, a change of state its rules don't cover. Detailed Logs On by default. Adds to those while Output Logs is on: each process's handler, each process collected, and each process's state as it's queued, set and forced. A world of its own has the same switches, ProcessWorld.OutputLogs and ProcessWorld.DetailedLogs. A scene's world's are its ProcessControl's.

guides/services/process-and-sequence-log.title: Sequence logs | PlayForge
guides/services/process-and-sequence-log.summary: Sequence logs Sequences log as the Sequences system (Task Sequences: Logging). They log their errors unless told otherwise: A run that fails is logged as an error, with what it threw, unless its sequence's WithErrorLogging(false) says otherwise. A stage whose OnException hears a throw and lets it on logs it too, unless the stage's WithErrorLogging(false) says otherwise. A handler that throws, as an OnComplete, is logged as an error. Two switches log more: WithInjectionLogging(true), on a sequence or a stage, logs each injection as it's applied: its kind, where it came from and the stage. A chain's WithLogging(true) logs its progress: each sequence it starts, finishes or skips, the conditions that fire, its repeats and its interruptions.

guides/services/profiling.html.title: Profiling | PlayForge
guides/services/profiling.html.summary: Profiling PlayForge's work shows in Unity's Profiler (Getting Started: Profiling): markers that time it; counters that say how much of it there is; each recorded frame's costliest processes. In this section Markers: ForgeProfiler holds PlayForge's markers, each a sample in the Profiler's Scripts category Counters: ForgeCounters holds PlayForge's counters, in the Profiler's PlayForge category. The costliest processes: While the Profiler records, each frame's costliest processes go into its capture as the frame's metadata, so a saved capture keeps them. Reading them in code: A ProfilerRecorder reads a marker or a counter by its name, in the editor or in a development build.

guides/services/profiling/counters.html.title: Counters | PlayForge
guides/services/profiling/counters.html.summary: Counters ForgeCounters holds PlayForge's counters, in the Profiler's PlayForge category. The category's name is ForgeCounters.CategoryName, and the category itself is ForgeCounters.Category. Each counter is of one of two kinds: Kind How it counts Level It holds until it changes. Per frame Its count starts from 0 each frame, and counts every world's work in the frame. Counter ForgeCounters Kind What it counts Processes Running ProcessesRunning Level The scene's processes running, as its ProcessControl's LateUpdate loop last ended Processes Waiting ProcessesWaiting Level The scene's processes waiting Processes Created ProcessesCreated Level The processes the scene's ProcessControl has taken Registrations Registrations Per frame Processes registered Terminations Terminations Per frame Processes unregistered as they ended Steps Steps Per frame Process steps, one for each process at each timing it steps in State Changes StateChanges Per frame Processes' changes of state Step Time StepTime Per frame The time in the step loops, every timing's, in nanoseconds Mono Entities MonoEntities Level The MonoBehaviour entities running, GameRoot left out Runtime Entities RuntimeEntities Level The runtime entities running, in every world Effects Active EffectsActive Level The effects on the entities' shelves, as each last stepped Effects Applied EffectsApplied Per frame Effect applications, a contained effect's among them Effects Removed EffectsRemoved Per frame Effects taken off a shelf Impacts Impacts Per frame Impacts, as each entity received them Activations Activations Per frame Ability activations Refused Activations RefusedActivations Per frame Refused activations, as each was told Tag Compiles TagCompiles Per frame Tag compiles Recomputes Recomputes Per frame Attribute recomputes Sequences Running SequencesRunning Level The sequences running, an ability's among them Stages Started StagesStarted Per frame Sequence stages started Two Profiler modules chart the counters. Turn them on in the Profiler window's list of modules: PlayForge Processes charts the process and sequence counters. PlayForge GAS charts the rest.

guides/services/profiling/markers.html.title: Markers | PlayForge
guides/services/profiling/markers.html.summary: Markers ForgeProfiler holds PlayForge's markers, each a sample in the Profiler's Scripts category: Marker ForgeProfiler What it times PlayForge.Update, PlayForge.LateUpdate, PlayForge.FixedUpdate StepUpdate, StepLateUpdate, StepFixedUpdate The step loop at each timing: each process that steps then, in step order PlayForge.ProcessStep ProcessStep One process's step PlayForge.Step. and the process's type's name StepOf(type) The same step under its type's own marker, inside PlayForge.ProcessStep, with the process's ID as its metadata; made the first time a process of the type steps PlayForge.GASStep GASStep A GAS's step: its clock, its effects' ticks, its abilities' While Active checks, its input buffer, its services, its turn and its barriers PlayForge.EndOfFrame EndOfFrame A GAS's end of frame: its queued actions, its tag and analysis workers, and its frame's summary PlayForge.ApplyEffect ApplyEffect An effect's application, its contained effects' inside it PlayForge.ActivateAbility ActivateAbility An ability's activation, up to the first of its tasks that waits PlayForge.TagCompile TagCompile A GAS's tag compile: its tags rebuilt from their sources PlayForge.Recompute Recompute An attribute's recompute, from its root through its modifiers to its bounds PlayForge.Stage Stage A sequence stage's start, an ability's among them: its tasks, up to the first that waits

guides/services/profiling/reading-them-i.title: Reading them in code | PlayForge
guides/services/profiling/reading-them-i.summary: Reading them in code A ProfilerRecorder reads a marker or a counter by its name, in the editor or in a development build. Unity compiles them out of a release build. using FarEmerald.PlayForge; using Unity.Profiling; using UnityEngine; // The effects applied each frame, and the time PlayForge's Update loop took, on screen in a development build public class ForgeStats : MonoBehaviour { private ProfilerRecorder applied, update; private void OnEnable() { applied = ProfilerRecorder.StartNew(ForgeCounters.Category, "Effects Applied"); update = ProfilerRecorder.StartNew(ProfilerCategory.Scripts, "PlayForge.Update"); } private void OnDisable() { applied.Dispose(); update.Dispose(); } private void OnGUI() { GUILayout.Label($"Effects applied: {applied.LastValue}"); GUILayout.Label($"PlayForge.Update: {update.LastValue / 1e6:0.00} ms"); } }

guides/services/profiling/the-costliest-.title: The costliest processes | PlayForge
guides/services/profiling/the-costliest-.summary: The costliest processes While the Profiler records, each frame's costliest processes go into its capture as the frame's metadata, so a saved capture keeps them. The scene's ProcessControl puts them in as its frame ends. The PlayForge Processes module's details list the selected frame's: each process's ID, its type and the time its steps took. Member Description ForgeFrameCosts.Most How many a frame keeps: 10. ForgeFrameCosts.LastFrame The last recorded frame's, the costliest first, each a ForgeProcessCost. ForgeFrameCosts.Recording Whether this frame's steps are timed: whether the Profiler recorded as the last frame ended. While it doesn't, nothing is timed for them. A ForgeProcessCost holds: its Process, the process's ID; the Nanoseconds its steps took in the frame, every timing's. Reading the costs in a tool A tool of your own reads the costs from a frame's data, as the module does: the costs, under the ID ForgeFrameCosts.MetaDataId and the tag ForgeFrameCosts.Tag; the type's name of the cost at i, in UTF-8, under the tag ForgeFrameCosts.Tag + 1 + i.

guides/services/random-numbers.html.title: Random numbers | PlayForge
guides/services/random-numbers.html.summary: Random numbers ForgeRandom is where PlayForge draws its random numbers. The game's rolls and random picks all draw from its source, an IForgeRandom. Member What it draws ForgeRandom.Value A number from 0 to 1, as Random.value. InsideUnitCircle, InsideUnitSphere A point within a radius of 1. Range(min, max) A float from the first to the second. Range(min, maxExclusive) A whole number, up to but not including the second. Where the range is empty, the first itself. In this section The source: ForgeRandom draws from Unity's source, UnityRandom, through UnityRandom.Instance, until code puts another in. What draws from it: These draw from ForgeRandom

guides/services/random-numbers/the-sourc.title: The source | PlayForge
guides/services/random-numbers/the-sourc.summary: The source ForgeRandom draws from Unity's source, UnityRandom, through UnityRandom.Instance, until code puts another in. It reads UnityEngine.Random, so Random.InitState(seed) seeds it, and anything else that draws from Unity's moves it. A SeededRandom, made with a seed, draws numbers of its own that nothing else draws from. Two runs from one seed draw the same numbers. Method What it does ForgeRandom.Use(source) Puts a source in, and returns the one it replaced. ForgeRandom.Use(null) Puts Unity's back. ForgeRandom.Source The source drawn from now. using FarEmerald.PlayForge; // A match's rolls from its seed: its replay, from the same seed, rolls the same int seed = 20261118; IForgeRandom previous = ForgeRandom.Use(new SeededRandom(seed)); int die = ForgeRandom.Range(1, 7); // 1 to 6 float spread = ForgeRandom.Range(-5f, 5f); // ... and, as the match ends ForgeRandom.Use(previous); An IForgeRandom of your own gives Value, from 0 to 1, and InsideUnitCircle and InsideUnitSphere, a point in a circle and in a sphere of radius 1. Note A source put in stays until code puts another in, past the end of play mode where domain reload is off. So code that puts one in puts back the one it replaced.

guides/services/random-numbers/what-draw.title: What draws from it | PlayForge
guides/services/random-numbers/what-draw.summary: What draws from it These draw from ForgeRandom: every chance PlayForge rolls (Chance); auto targeting whose Mode is Random; a Randomized scaler's roll (Scalers: A magnitude field); ForgeHelper's random picks and points (ForgeHelper); the Creator Lab. Cues don't. A placement's scatter and a floating text's random velocity draw from ForgeCues.Random, a SeededRandom of their own, so a cue never moves the game's rolls (Cues: Placement).

guides/services/repeatable-runs.html.title: Repeatable runs | PlayForge
guides/services/repeatable-runs.html.summary: Repeatable runs A run that must come out the same twice needs the same time and the same rolls each time it runs. A replay, a rollback and a lockstep match are such runs. Time: step the game in fixed steps, with ProcessControl's Fixed Tick Rate (Fixed ticks). Or step a world of its own by a fixed time, world.Step(deltaTime). A clock of the game's time follows either. Rolls: put in a SeededRandom, ForgeRandom.Use(new SeededRandom(seed)), seeded for the run, or for each step as a rollback does (Saving and Loading: Rolling back). Unity's random numbers, the default, move whenever anything else in the game draws from them. Cues draw from ForgeCues.Random, numbers of their own. So a run that plays its cues rolls as one that doesn't, with ForgeCues.Enabled off, as on a server or while a simulation runs ahead. Your own code reads time through ForgeTime and draws through ForgeRandom, as PlayForge does. Code that reads Unity's Time or Random itself follows neither a clock nor a source put in.

guides/services/sign-and-math-policies.h.title: Sign and math policies | PlayForge
guides/services/sign-and-math-policies.h.summary: Sign and math policies Three enums say how PlayForge reads the sign of a change and turns a number into a factor: ESignPolicy, ESignPolicyExtended and EMathApplicationPolicy. ESignPolicy is a change's sign: Option What it means Positive The change is positive. Negative The change is negative. ZeroBiased Its parts sum to 0 but aren't all 0, as +5 to an attribute's current value and −5 to its base. ZeroNeutral Every part is 0. ForgeHelper.SignPolicy reads it from one number, which is never ZeroBiased, or from a change's current and base parts. A change's own SignPolicy, as a SourcedModifiedAttributeValue's, is its parts read so. An impact worker made from AbstractContextImpactWorker takes the hits of one sign, its Impact Sign. ESignPolicyExtended adds Any, which takes every sign. A focused attribute worker's Sign Policy takes every sign by default (Workers: The map). EMathApplicationPolicy turns a number into a factor: Option What it does AsIs The number as it is. OnePlus One plus it: a bonus of 0.2 multiplies by 1.2. OneMinus One minus it: a resistance of 0.2 leaves 0.8. AttenuateScalerBehaviour's Policy and MathAttributeWorker's Operation Policy read it.

guides/services/the-attribute-registry.h.title: The attribute registry | PlayForge
guides/services/the-attribute-registry.h.summary: The attribute registry AttributeRegistry finds an attribute by its name, among those the game's entities have been given. An attribute is registered under its name: as an entity's attribute system takes it; as a Bootstrapper brings PlayForge up, for each attribute of the sets its Register Sets lists. The first of a name keeps it: AttributeRegistry.Add(attribute) is false where the name is taken. Names compare by AttributeRegistry.RefactorByNamingConvention(name): in capitals, with each space an underscore. So "Attack Speed", "attack speed" and "ATTACK_SPEED" are one name. Method What it does AttributeRegistry.TryGetByName(name, out attribute) Finds an attribute by its name. AttributeRegistry.GetByName(name) Gives the attribute, or null. With createIfFalse: true, a name none has gives a new RuntimeAttribute of that name, which isn't registered. AttributeRegistry.Contains Asks by a name, or by an attribute's name. AttributeRegistry.GetAll() Lists the attributes registered. AttributeRegistry.Reset() Empties the registry, as the test kit's world does as it ends. The registry starts empty each time the game starts, play mode with domain reload off among them.

guides/services/time-and-rolls-in-tests..title: Time and rolls in tests | PlayForge
guides/services/time-and-rolls-in-tests..summary: Time and rolls in tests The test kit makes time and chance a test's own, through the same two services (Testing Your Content: The world). Method What it does World.Clock(step) Puts in a SteppingClock, and returns it. World.Rolls(0.1f, 0.9f) Puts in a ScriptedRandom. ForgeChance.ForgetStreaks(caster) Starts a caster's pseudo-random streaks clean. A SteppingClock gives step seconds of PlayForge's time each frame: its DeltaTime, UnscaledDeltaTime and FixedDeltaTime. Its Time, UnscaledTime and FrameCount stay Unity's. Its Step can change. A ScriptedRandom gives each draw the next of its rolls, in turn and round again, and its Drawn counts them. Its points in a circle and in a sphere are zero. A chance comes up where it's above the roll. So a roll of 0 always lands, and one of 0.99 almost never does. A roll with luck draws more than one. The world gives back the clock and the source it replaced as it ends. Outside it, ForgeTime.Use(new SteppingClock(step)) and ForgeRandom.Use(new ScriptedRandom(0f)) do the same, put back by hand.

guides/services/time.html.title: Time | PlayForge
guides/services/time.html.summary: Time ForgeTime is the clock PlayForge's runtime reads in place of Unity's Time. It's also where a game puts in a time of its own. ForgeTime reads the clock in force, ForgeTime.Clock, an IForgeClock. That's Unity's, UnityClock.Instance, until code puts another in. Nothing else in the runtime reads Unity's Time. Its properties read the clock in force as Unity's own do: ForgeTime As Unity's DeltaTime Time.deltaTime: the frame's step, scaled UnscaledDeltaTime Time.unscaledDeltaTime FixedDeltaTime Time.fixedDeltaTime: the fixed step Time Time.time: the time since the game started, scaled UnscaledTime Time.unscaledTime FrameCount Time.frameCount In this section Putting a clock in: You replace the clock in force with ForgeTime.Use An owner's clock: An owner's time is its own, where it has one.

guides/services/time/an-owners-clock.htm.title: An owner's clock | PlayForge
guides/services/time/an-owners-clock.htm.summary: An owner's clock An owner's time is its own, where it has one. Method What it gives ForgeTime.ClockOf(owner) An entity's own clock, for an entity, an IGameplayAbilitySystem. The game's, GameClock.Instance, for anything else. ForgeTime.DeltaTimeFor(owner) The owner's step this frame. ForgeTime.ClockFor(data) The clock a data packet names, data.Clock, or else its owner's: an ability's caster's, or the game's. ForgeTime.DeltaTimeFor(data) The step of the packet's clock.

guides/services/time/putting-a-clock-in..title: Putting a clock in | PlayForge
guides/services/time/putting-a-clock-in..summary: Putting a clock in You replace the clock in force with ForgeTime.Use: Method What it does ForgeTime.Use(clock) Puts a clock in, and returns the one it replaced. ForgeTime.Use(null) Puts Unity's back. Two things put a clock of their own in while they step, and put the one before back after: each of ProcessControl's fixed ticks (Fixed ticks); a world of its own: a ProcessWorld its owner steps with Step(deltaTime), whose clock reads that step. This class puts in a scaled clock over Unity's before the first scene loads: using FarEmerald.PlayForge; using UnityEngine; // PlayForge's time apart from Unity's: at a Scale of 0 every effect, cooldown and sequence on the game's time stands // still, while Unity's own time, and all that reads it, runs on, and so does a sequence on the unscaled clock public static class GameplayTime { public static ScaledClock Clock { get; private set; } // Put in before the first scene loads, so all that keeps a time keeps it by this clock from the start [RuntimeInitializeOnLoadMethod(RuntimeInitializeLoadType.BeforeSceneLoad)] private static void PutIn() { Clock = new ScaledClock(1f, UnityClock.Instance); ForgeTime.Use(Clock); } } // A menu that stops the game's time sets GameplayTime.Clock.Scale to 0 as it opens, and back to 1 as it closes A clock put in reads its time from somewhere else. GameClock, UnscaledClock, an EntityClock and a ScaledClock with no source each read the clock in force, so each, put in as it, would read itself. ForgeTime.Use refuses the GameClock. A ScaledClock over UnityClock.Instance, as above, scales Unity's. What waits until a time keeps ForgeTime.Time, as a pooled cue's burst does. So a clock put in while the game runs should carry its Time on from the one it replaces. Note A clock put in stays until code puts another in, past the end of play mode where domain reload is off. So code that puts one in puts back the one it replaced.

guides/services/which-clock-a-run-takes..title: Which clock a run takes | PlayForge
guides/services/which-clock-a-run-takes..summary: Which clock a run takes Everything PlayForge times goes by a clock, most by their owner's. An effect goes by the entity it's on, and a sequence's run by the first clock it finds. An effect counts its time by the clock of the entity it's on, its duration and its period both. So a slowed entity's effects, its cooldowns among them, last longer. Its Delta Time Scaler changes it further (Effects: Duration). An entity's own step goes by its clock: its input buffer's windows, its services, its turn and its barriers' decay. A sequence's run, an ability's among them, takes the first clock it finds, in the order below. A synced runner steps by its packet's clock, else its sequence's, else its packet's owner's (runner.ClockFor(data)). A cue's packet carries its owner's clock: the activation's for an ability's cue, else that of the one it plays on. A Sequence cue's run goes by its Clock pick, else the sequence's own, else that one (Cues: Data packets). Code of your own reads its owner's step with ForgeTime.DeltaTimeFor(owner), as ProjectileMonoProcess moves by its handler's. A task reads its run's with SequenceTaskLibrary.DeltaTime(token), 0 while the run is paused. TaskSequenceRuntime.ClockOfRun(token) is the run's clock. Anything else goes by the game's time, the clock in force. The clock a sequence's run takes A sequence's run, an ability's among them, takes the first clock it finds, in this order: its own, runtime.Clock, which what runs it sets: a TaskSequenceProcess's Clock, a chain's Clock or an ability's Run Sequence task's pick; its packet's, data.Clock; its sequence's, WithClock on the builder; its packet's owner's: an ability's caster's own clock; else the game's, GameClock.Instance. Its waits, delays, timeouts, longest runs and ElapsedTime go by it, and so do its tasks' tweens and its synced tasks (Task Sequences: Clocks). An ability runs on its activation's packet. So its waits go by its caster's clock, unless the packet names another.

guides/spreadsheets/index.html.title: Spreadsheets | PlayForge
guides/spreadsheets/index.html.summary: Spreadsheets Games are balanced in spreadsheets: a column of damage by level, a row of stats for each item. PlayForge writes its numbers by level and its items' stats to CSV, which any spreadsheet opens. It also reads a sheet back, and lists each change before it makes it. The Forge's window menu (its tab's ⋮) holds these commands under Spreadsheets: Command What it does Export Numbers… Writes a sheet of every number by level in the active Forge Project. Export Selected Numbers… Writes a sheet of the selected assets' numbers alone. Export Item Stats… Writes a sheet of every item's stats in the active Forge Project. Export Selected Item Stats… Writes a sheet of the selected items' stats. Import… Reads a sheet of either kind back, and opens the import window. A sheet is UTF-8, marked as such with a byte order mark, so Excel and Google Sheets open it as UTF-8. In code, ForgeSpreadsheets.NumbersOf(assets) and StatsOf(items) give a sheet's text. ForgeSpreadsheets.Read(csv) gives what a sheet would change. In this guide Numbers by level: A sheet of numbers by level has a row for each number whose kind is a Table or By Level (Scalers). Item stats: A sheet of item stats has a row for each item, and a column for each attribute its granted effects add to Reading a sheet back: Reading a sheet back finds the asset each row names, and lists the changes the sheet makes before it makes them. In the API The types of this guide's area: ForgeSpreadsheets, ForgeSpreadsheetWindow, SpreadsheetChange, SpreadsheetImport.

guides/spreadsheets/item-stats.html.title: Item stats | PlayForge
guides/spreadsheets/item-stats.html.summary: Item stats A sheet of item stats has a row for each item, and a column for each attribute its granted effects add to: Asset Tag Name Armor Health Item.Ring Ring 5 10/15/20 Item.Band Band A cell is the number the item's effect adds to the attribute, or one for each level, as 10/15/20. An item whose effects add to an attribute twice leaves that cell empty. Set each of those numbers in a sheet of numbers instead. When you read a sheet back: A cell sets the effect's number: a constant's value, or a Table's values. A cell with one number for each level makes a constant a Table. An empty cell changes nothing.

guides/spreadsheets/numbers-by-level.htm.title: Numbers by level | PlayForge
guides/spreadsheets/numbers-by-level.htm.summary: Numbers by level A sheet of numbers by level has a row for each number whose kind is a Table or By Level (Scalers). It holds the numbers of every asset, and of each Scaler asset, whose table its fields share: Asset Tag Name Field Kind Level 1 Level 2 Level 3 Effect.LagunaBlade Laguna Blade Impact Specification › Magnitude Table -450 -600 -750 AttributeSet.Hero Hero Attributes › Health › Base Table 500 560 620 Column What it holds Asset Tag, Name The asset the number is in. A row read back finds its asset by them (Reading a sheet back). Field The number's place in the asset, its parts named as the inspector names them. Kind The number's kind, Table or By Level. Level 1, Level 2 and on What the number reads at each level. In Field, a list's element is named by the attribute it names, as an attribute set's Health. An element that names no attribute is named by its place from 1, as Additional Impacts 2. The levels hold what the number reads at each level: its values combined with its number, as its field says. So a table of 450, 600 and 750, read times -1, is -450, -600 and -750. Reading a row back sets the values so the number reads what the row says. A number that reads its number alone has no row. Neither has a number of another kind, as × Attribute.

guides/spreadsheets/reading-a-sheet-back.title: Reading a sheet back | PlayForge
guides/spreadsheets/reading-a-sheet-back.summary: Reading a sheet back Reading a sheet back finds the asset each row names, and lists the changes the sheet makes before it makes them. A row names its asset in two ways: by its asset tag, which stays the same as files move and are renamed; by its name, which reads well in a spreadsheet. A row with a tag finds the asset with that tag. A row with no tag finds the one asset of that name. The import reports these problems, and leaves their rows out: a tag no asset has, a name no asset has, or a name two assets share (give that row its tag); a field the asset hasn't got, or a kind a sheet can't set; an item with no effect adding to a column's attribute; a cell that isn't a number; two rows setting one shared effect's number to different values. To import a sheet: In The Forge's window menu, choose Spreadsheets > Import…, and pick the CSV file. The import window lists each change: the asset, the field, what it reads now and what it will read. The rows that can't be read sit under a fold. Each change is ticked. Untick one to leave it. Click Import to make the ticked changes, as one Undo step. A sheet read back just as it was written changes nothing.

guides/tags/conditions-and-checks.html.title: Conditions and checks | PlayForge
guides/tags/conditions-and-checks.html.summary: Conditions and checks Besides requirements, conditions, ability checks, tasks and triggers read tags: an entity's, or an asset's. In this section The Tag condition: The Tag condition, TagCondition, holds where an entity answers its tag query. The Tag Weight check: The Tag Weight check, TagWeightValidation, compares a tag's weight on the checked entity with a number. Triggers, tasks and stages: An ability's triggers, tasks and stages can act on a tag (Abilities: Stages) Matching effects and abilities: Some fields match effects by their tags, not entities

guides/tags/conditions-and-checks/matchi.title: Matching effects and abilities | PlayForge
guides/tags/conditions-and-checks/matchi.summary: Matching effects and abilities Some fields match effects by their tags, not entities: an effect's Removes Effects Tagged and Blocks Effects Tagged; the Has Effect check's Tagged; the Asset Part number's Effects Tagged. An effect answers for a tag by its asset tag, a context tag or a tag it grants, each the tag or under it (Effects: Tags). GameplayEffectTags.Names(tags, effect) asks this in code. AbilityTags.Names(tags, ability) asks the same of an ability: whether its asset tag or a context tag is one of the tags, or under one. Cancelled By and Blocks match abilities this way.

guides/tags/conditions-and-checks/the-ta.title: The Tag condition | PlayForge
guides/tags/conditions-and-checks/the-ta.summary: The Tag condition The Tag condition, TagCondition, holds where an entity answers its tag query. Property Description On The entity it reads: the caster or the target. Query A tag query, counted by weight. A tag granted twice counts twice. Where the number's context lacks that entity, the condition doesn't hold, as with a target's tag and no target. These read conditions (Scalers: A magnitude field): a Conditional number; an effect's Apply, Ongoing and Removal Conditions; an On Hit; an ability's Condition check.

guides/tags/conditions-and-checks/the-ta.title: The Tag Weight check | PlayForge
guides/tags/conditions-and-checks/the-ta.summary: The Tag Weight check The Tag Weight check, TagWeightValidation, compares a tag's weight on the checked entity with a number. It's one of an ability's Caster or Target Checks. Property Description Tag The tag whose weight it reads. An entity without the tag holds it at 0. Weight The number it compares the weight with. Comparison How it compares the two. A check of your own that reads a tag derives from AbstractTagValidationRule (Abilities: Requirements). Its GetValue gives its tag's weight on the checked entity. Where that entity holds none of the tag, it gives the ability's Local Data under the tag.

guides/tags/conditions-and-checks/trigge.title: Triggers, tasks and stages | PlayForge
guides/tags/conditions-and-checks/trigge.summary: Triggers, tasks and stages An ability's triggers, tasks and stages can act on a tag (Abilities: Stages): A Tag Added trigger activates its ability as the entity gains a tag, or one under it, that it didn't have. A Wait For Tag task waits for its caster or its target to gain a tag, that very tag, or to lose it. A stage's Condition runs the stage by a tag, in the activation's data or on the caster or the target.

guides/tags/contexts.html.title: Contexts | PlayForge
guides/tags/contexts.html.summary: Contexts A context is a kind of tag, such as Granted, Event or Local Data Key. A tag field takes the kinds its ForgeTagContext attribute names, and its picker offers the tags of those kinds and the Universal ones. A tag is of a context where: a field of that context uses it in one of the project's PlayForge assets; a Tag Library declares it for the context (The Tag Library); the code that writes it exposes it for the context (Tags written in code). A field of several contexts makes the tag it holds of each of them alone, so each one's fields offer it. A field that names no context offers every tag, and the tags it holds are of no context. In this section PlayForge's contexts: ForgeContext names PlayForge's contexts. The project's own contexts: A project can make contexts of its own, through any contexts field.

guides/tags/contexts/playforges-contexts.title: PlayForge's contexts | PlayForge
guides/tags/contexts/playforges-contexts.summary: PlayForge's contexts ForgeContext names PlayForge's contexts. Each is a constant whose value is its name: ForgeContext.LocalDataKey is "Local Data Key". Context Its tags Fields that take them Asset Tag an asset's own tag an asset's Asset Tag; with Context Tag, what names abilities or effects by their tags, as Cancelled By, Blocks, a crowd control rule's Ability Tags and a purge's Kinds Context Tag an asset's context tags, as Spell or Fire Context Tags, an item's Set Granted a tag an entity carries while something grants it, as Stunned Granted Tags, Passive Tags, Active Tags, a requirement's tag, a crowd control rule's Tag, the Grant Tags and Wait For Tag tasks, a tag worker's requirements Affiliation a side, as Team.Red an entity's Affiliation, an effect's Affiliations, a Side Change's Sides Visibility whether an effect or an item shows Visibility Impact Type a change's kind, as Damage.Fire Impact Types, and the workers' type filters Retention Group a group an attribute keeps its changes under Retention Group Event a gameplay event, as Died a trigger's tag, the Send Event and Wait For Event tasks, a Threshold's Event, the combat log's Events Attribute Role a part an attribute plays, as Health the Forge Project's Roles, an attribute cost's Role Texture Slot an icon's slot, as Primary Textures, Origin Texture Cue a cue tag, as Cue.Hit.Fire a Cue Tag cue, the Cue Library's routes, a Cue Receiver's Variant Data Key a key in an activation's or a process's data the Set loaders' keys, Implicit Tag Local Data Key a key in an asset's Local Data a Local Data row's Key, the Local Data number's Key Worker Key a key a worker answers a number under the Worker number's Key Set By Caller Key a key a caller sets a value under the Set By Caller number's Key, a process attribute's Stage Flag a flag a stage records in the activation's data Record As, Record Landed As, a stage's Condition Requirement Category a Requirement Template's category a template's Category Code a tag code exposes for no context fields that name no context Universal a tag a Tag Library declares for no context every field but one that leaves them out

guides/tags/contexts/the-projects-own-co.title: The project's own contexts | PlayForge
guides/tags/contexts/the-projects-own-co.summary: The project's own contexts A project can make contexts of its own, through any contexts field. A contexts field, such as New Tag's Contexts or the Tags view's Declared For, shows the contexts chosen, or None. Pressing the field opens every context: PlayForge's, those the project's fields name, and the project's own. Universal comes first and the rest by name, with those chosen checked. Choosing one adds it, or takes it away. To make a context of the project's own: Press a contexts field. Choose New Context…, last in the list. Name the context. The field chooses the new context, and the first Tag Library keeps it. Every contexts field offers it from then on. New Context… refuses an empty name, and a name a context has already, whatever its case. A field of the project's own takes the context's tags with [ForgeTagContext("Weather")], the context's name as written.

guides/tags/crowd-control.html.title: Crowd control | PlayForge
guides/tags/crowd-control.html.summary: Crowd control Crowd control stops abilities by the tags their caster carries. So no ability has to list Stunned among the tags it must not have. A Crowd Control Rules asset, CrowdControlRules, holds its Rules. Make one with Create → PlayForge → Crowd Control Rules. Each rule is a CrowdControlRule: Property Description Tag The tag its holder carries, as Stunned. Stops What it stops, an ECrowdControlStops: Every Ability, as a stun does. Abilities Tagged: those whose asset tag or a context tag is one of its Ability Tags, or under one, as Silenced stops spells. Ability Tags The tags Abilities Tagged looks for. While the caster carries a rule's tag, or one under it: an ability the rule stops is refused, as Crowd Control, the refusal's Rule naming the tag; an ability the rule stops that's running is interrupted. An ability's Ignores Crowd Control names the rules it ignores, by their tags. Each tag there also ignores the rules whose tags are under it. An entity follows its own rules, its Crowd Control, or else its Forge Project's. Method What it does gas.GetCrowdControl() Gives the rules an entity follows. rules.Stopping(ability, tags) Gives the first rule that stops an ability, or null. Abilities: Requirements: Crowd Control has the rest.

guides/tags/hearing-tags-change.html.title: Hearing tags change | PlayForge
guides/tags/hearing-tags-change.html.summary: Hearing tags change An entity's TagCache tells each change to a tag's weight. It tells the listeners on that tag, and on the tags above it. A change is a TagChange: Member Description Tag The tag whose weight changed. Before, After Its weight before and after. Each is 0 where the entity doesn't hold the tag, never −1. Added Says the tag came. Removed Says the tag went. There are two ways to listen: Member What it hears tags.Listen(tag, onChange, kind) The tag, and every tag under its path: a listener on Status hears Status.Burning. It gives a TagListener, whose Dispose() stops it. tags.TagChanged Every change to every tag. A listener's ETagChangeKind says what it hears: Option What it hears AddedOrRemoved The default: a tag coming and going. AnyCount Every change to a weight. A listener's Tag, Kind and Listening say what it hears, and whether it still does. These listeners show an icon while an entity is stunned, and log each change to a combo's weight: using FarEmerald.PlayForge; using UnityEngine; public static class StatusDisplay { // The tags New Tag makes of these paths static readonly Tag Stunned = Tag.GenerateAsUnique("State.Stunned"); static readonly Tag Combo = Tag.GenerateAsUnique("Combo.Points"); // Shows the icon while the entity holds State.Stunned or a tag under it; dispose the listener to stop public static TagListener ShowWhileStunned(IGameplayAbilitySystem gas, GameObject icon) { var tags = gas.GetTagCache(); icon.SetActive(tags.HasTag(Stunned, ETagMatchMode.IncludeChildren)); return tags.Listen(Stunned, _ => icon.SetActive(tags.HasTag(Stunned, ETagMatchMode.IncludeChildren))); } // Logs each change to the weight of Combo.Points, and of each tag under it public static TagListener LogCombo(IGameplayAbilitySystem gas) => gas.GetTagCache().Listen(Combo, change => ForgeLog.Info($"{change.Tag}: {change.Before} -> {change.After}"), ETagChangeKind.AnyCount); } The entities' guide listens for a stun too (Entities: Tags). When a change is told When a change to a tag's weight is told depends on how it was made: A change made straight to the weights is told as it happens. A compile is told as it ends, with only what it changed. So a tag held throughout is told nothing. A load's one compile tells what the load changed (Saving and Loading: What a load does). A listener that throws is logged, and stops neither the change nor the other listeners. A listener disposed while a change is told hears no more of it. One added then hears the next change.

guides/tags/how-an-entity-holds-tags.htm.title: How an entity holds tags | PlayForge
guides/tags/how-an-entity-holds-tags.htm.summary: How an entity holds tags An entity carries the tags its sources grant it, each with a weight. A tag's weight is the number of grants of it that the entity holds now. In this section Where its tags come from: An entity's tags come from its sources, which it reads as its tags are compiled Weights and compiles: A tag's weight counts its grants, and a compile rebuilds the weights from the entity's sources. Loose tags: A loose tag is one granted to the entity directly, with nothing behind it, as Unreal's loose gameplay tags are. Reading them: An entity's TagCache holds its tags and their weights, and gas.GetTagCache() gives it. What holds and what grants: Two interfaces describe what carries tags and what grants them: ITagHandler and ITagSource.

guides/tags/how-an-entity-holds-tags/loo.title: Loose tags | PlayForge
guides/tags/how-an-entity-holds-tags/loo.summary: Loose tags A loose tag is one granted to the entity directly, with nothing behind it, as Unreal's loose gameplay tags are. Method What it does gas.AddLooseTag(tag) Grants a loose tag. Each grant is counted. gas.RemoveLooseTag(tag) Takes one grant back, or returns false where the entity has none. gas.GetLooseTags() Lists the loose tags, a tag once for each grant. A save keeps an entity's loose tags (Saving and Loading: What a save holds). An ability's Grant Tags task grants loose tags while its stage runs (Abilities: Stages). The Debugger's Entities view adds them, and takes them back, by hand.

guides/tags/how-an-entity-holds-tags/rea.title: Reading them | PlayForge
guides/tags/how-an-entity-holds-tags/rea.summary: Reading them An entity's TagCache holds its tags and their weights, and gas.GetTagCache() gives it. A GameplayAbilitySystem component's cache is null until the component initializes. Method What it does GetWeight(tag) Gives the weight of that very tag: −1 where the entity hasn't it, not 0. gas.GetTagWeight(tag) is GetWeight. TryGetWeight(tag, out weight) Says whether the entity has the tag, and gives its weight. HasTagExact(tag) Says whether the entity has that very tag. HasTag(tag, mode) Says whether it has the tag, by a match mode (Querying tags). HasAnyTag, HasAllTags, HasNoneOfTags Ask the same of several tags, Exact unless told. GetMatchingWeight(tag, mode) Adds up the weights of the tags that match, 0 where none does. In Exact mode it is GetWeight: −1 for an absent tag. GetMatchingTags(tag, mode) Gives the tags held that match. GetAppliedTags() Gives each tag held, once. gas.GetAppliedTags() is the same list. Note The list GetAppliedTags() gives is the cache's own, reused until a tag comes or goes. Read it, and copy it to keep it. Changing the weights directly AddTag, AddTags, RemoveTag, RemoveTags, RemoveTagCompletely and RemoveMatchingTags change the weights directly. An Instant effect's tags are granted this way, for the moment it applies. Each change is told as it happens. The next compile rebuilds the weights from their sources, and drops these changes. So a tag meant to last is a loose tag (Loose tags). Method What it does ResetWeights() Empties the weights, telling each tag's going. ResetCache() Empties the weights, and resolves the active tag workers as well. BeginRebuild(), EndRebuild() Frame a compile. LogWeights(), LogActiveWorkers(), GetHierarchyDebugString() Write the cache out, for debugging.

guides/tags/how-an-entity-holds-tags/wei.title: Weights and compiles | PlayForge
guides/tags/how-an-entity-holds-tags/wei.summary: Weights and compiles A tag's weight counts its grants, and a compile rebuilds the weights from the entity's sources. A tag two sources grant weighs 2, as with two burns that each grant Status.Burning. It stays until both are gone. An effect grants its tags once for each container on its shelf, not once a stack. A burn stacked five times in one container grants Status.Burning once. The entity compiles its tags as a source comes, goes or changes: an ability is learned, starts or ends; an item is given, equipped or taken; a loose tag comes or goes; its sides change; an effect lands or comes off. A compile rebuilds the weights from the sources. As it ends, it tells only what it changed (Hearing tags change).

guides/tags/how-an-entity-holds-tags/wha.title: What holds and what grants | PlayForge
guides/tags/how-an-entity-holds-tags/wha.summary: What holds and what grants Two interfaces describe what carries tags and what grants them: ITagHandler and ITagSource. ITagHandler is what carries tags, which every entity is. A tag worker reads its entity through it. Method What it does GetAppliedTags() Gives the tags it carries. GetTagWeight(tag) Gives a tag's weight. QueryTags(query) Asks a tag query, against its weights. CompileGrantedTags() Compiles its tags now. ITagSource is what grants tags, through GetGrantedTags(): An asset gives what it grants of itself, as an ability its asset tag and its Passive Tags. What holds the asset on an entity gives what it grants there. A known ability gives its Active Tags while it runs, and an effect on the shelf its asset tag with the rest. The Debugger shows tags as the game runs (Getting Started: Tooling tour): its Entities view shows an entity's tags, with what grants each; its Tags view shows every tag the entities hold, as a tree, with who holds the one selected.

guides/tags/how-an-entity-holds-tags/whe.title: Where its tags come from | PlayForge
guides/tags/how-an-entity-holds-tags/whe.summary: Where its tags come from An entity's tags come from its sources, which it reads as its tags are compiled: Source The tags it grants Its identity Its asset tag, its sides and its Granted Tags (Entities: Tags). Its attribute set The set's asset tag, and each sub-set's. Each effect on its shelf The effect's asset tag, its Granted Tags, and those its modifiers add (Effects: Tags). An Instant effect grants its Granted Tags only as it applies. Each ability it knows The ability's asset tag and its Passive Tags, and its Active Tags while an activation of it runs (Abilities: Tags). Each item it holds The item's asset tag, and its Granted Tags while it's equipped (Items: Tags). Its loose tags Each loose tag (Loose tags). An entity's sides are its Affiliation, or those its registration or SetAffiliation gave it, or a Side Change's while one lasts. An asset keeps its tags in its Tags section: an ability's is an AbilityTags; an effect's is a GameplayEffectTags; an item's is an ItemTags; an entity's are fields of its EntityIdentity. Context Tags describe an asset, and are granted to no one.

guides/tags/index.html.title: Tags | PlayForge
guides/tags/index.html.summary: Tags A tag is a name in a tree, such as State.Stunned under State. PlayForge uses tags to name whatever it matches by name. classDiagram class Tag:::rt { <<Serializable struct>> +Name : string, the identity +DisplayName : string +static Generate(name, displayName) Tag +Child(name) Tag +ToString() the display name, for UI +IsValid : bool +GetParent() Tag +IsChildOf(Tag) bool +MatchesOrIsChildOf(Tag) bool } class ETagMatchMode:::rt { <<enumeration>> Exact IncludeChildren IncludeParents SameRoot } class TagCache:::rt { one per entity +GetAppliedTags() +GetWeight(Tag) int, -1 when absent +HasTag(Tag, ETagMatchMode) bool +HasAnyTag() +TagChanged : event +Listen(Tag, handler, ETagChangeKind) TagListener +BeginRebuild() +EndRebuild() +ProvideWorker(AbstractTagWorker) } class TagChange:::rt { <<readonly struct>> +Tag +Before +After +Added : bool +Removed : bool } class TagListener:::rt { IDisposable hears its tag and the tags under it } class TagQuery:::asset { <<Serializable>> +Tag +Operator : EComparisonOperator +Magnitude +MatchMode : ETagMatchMode +Validate(tags or TagCache) bool +CountMatches() } class AvoidRequireTagGroup:::asset { +AvoidTags : List~TagQuery~ +RequireTags : List~TagQuery~ +SourceTemplate : RequirementTemplate +Validate(tags or TagCache) bool } class ITagHandler:::ext { <<interface>> +GetAppliedTags() +GetTagWeight(Tag) +QueryTags(TagQuery) +CompileGrantedTags() } class ITagSource:::ext { <<interface>> +GetGrantedTags() } class TagRegistry:::rt { <<static>> +Initialize() +Register() +Resolve(name) Tag +GetAllTags() +GetDirectChildren() } class Tags:::rt { <<static partial>> built-in tags marked ForgeTagExposed SYSTEM, GAME_ROOT, NONE IMPACT_DEALT, IMPACT_TAKEN, KILL, DIED, REVIVED TARGET, TARGET_REAL, SOURCE, DERIVATION, EFFECTS } class GrantedTagCompiler:::rt { <<internal static>> +Compile(TagCache, AttributeSet, effects, abilities, items) +AddEffect(TagCache, spec) } class ForgeEvents:::rt { <<static>> +Send(to, Tag, source, subject) queued on the receiver, only if it listens } TagCache ..> TagChange : TagChanged TagCache ..> TagListener : Listen TagCache ..> ETagMatchMode TagQuery --> ETagMatchMode AvoidRequireTagGroup o-- TagQuery ITagHandler ..> TagQuery : QueryTags GrantedTagCompiler ..> TagCache : compiles into TagRegistry ..> Tag : Resolve Tags ..> Tag classDef rt fill:#FFE86D,stroke:#CBB333,color:#574900 classDef ext fill:#A0C4FB,stroke:#6A8BBF,color:#14315E classDef asset fill:#B8ACFB,stroke:#7D6DD4,color:#231266 Each entity's TagCache holds weights, listeners and tag workers. Show a tag with ToString(), its DisplayName, never its raw Name. PlayForge names these with tags: what an entity carries, such as Stunned while a stun lasts; what an ability, an effect or an item is, by its asset tag and its context tags; an entity's sides; a gameplay event, a kind of impact, a cue and an attribute's role; the keys of an activation's data, and of an asset's Local Data. Requirements, crowd control, conditions and workers read the tags an entity carries. This page covers what a tag is, and how a project makes, declares and finds its tags in the editor. It also covers how an entity holds its tags and tells their changes, and what reads them. In this guide What a tag is: A tag, a Tag, is a path of names joined by dots, parents first. PlayForge's own tags: Tags holds PlayForge's own tags, each a unique tag in a static property. Contexts: A context is a kind of tag, such as Granted, Event or Local Data Key. The Tag Library: A Tag Library asset, ForgeTagLibrary, declares tags for contexts, so those contexts' pickers offer them before any asset uses them. Tags written in code: Code makes a tag of a path with Tag.GenerateAsUnique, and offers it to the editor's pickers with [ForgeTagExposed]. Tag field attributes: Attributes on a Tag field, or on a list of tags, say what its tag field offers and does. The tag field: Each Tag field, alone or in a list, draws as a tag field, TagDrawer. The Tags view: The Forge's Tags view lists the active Forge Project's tags and what uses each. How an entity holds tags: An entity carries the tags its sources grant it, each with a weight. Hearing tags change: An entity's TagCache tells each change to a tag's weight. Querying tags: A match mode, ETagMatchMode, says which of an entity's tags answer for the tag it's asked about. Requirements: Tag requirements are the tags an entity must have, and must not have, for an ability to activate and run, or for an effect to land, go on and come off. Crowd control: Crowd control stops abilities by the tags their caster carries. Conditions and checks: Besides requirements, conditions, ability checks, tasks and triggers read tags: an entity's, or an asset's. Tag workers: A tag worker, AbstractTagWorker, acts while its entity's tags meet its requirements, as flames shown while Status.Burning weighs 3 or more. The editor's tag registry: ForgeTagRegistry, in the editor, is what the tag pickers, the Tags view and New Tag know of the project's tags. Traps: Tags invite a few mistakes. In the API The types of this guide's area: AbilityTagRequirementsDrawer, AvoidRequireTagGroupDrawer, EffectTagRequirementsDrawer, ETagChangeKind, ETagMatchMode, ForgeTagLibrary, ForgeTagLibrary.Entry, ForgeTagRegistry, ForgeTagRegistry.ContextUsage, ForgeTagRegistry.FieldUsageInfo, ForgeTagRegistry.TagContext, ForgeTagRegistry.TagUsageRecord, ITagHandler, ITagSource, Tag, TagCache, TagChange, TagDrawer, TagListener, TagQuery, TagQueryDrawer, TagRegistry, TagRegistry.TagUtil, TagRegistryAssetPostprocessor, Tags.

guides/tags/playforges-own-tags.html.title: PlayForge's own tags | PlayForge
guides/tags/playforges-own-tags.html.summary: PlayForge's own tags Tags holds PlayForge's own tags, each a unique tag in a static property. The editor's pickers offer each for its kind. Each reads as its text: Tags.DIED reads Died, and Tags.ROLE_HEALTH reads Health. What they are Tags Context The gameplay events the core sends IMPACT_DEALT, IMPACT_TAKEN, KILL, DIED, REVIVED, BLOCKED, EVADED, HIT_BLOCKED, HIT_EVADED Event The roles PlayForge's features read ROLE_HEALTH, ROLE_LUCK, ROLE_MOVEMENT_SPEED Attribute Role Impact types ALWAYS_ALLOW, NEVER_ALLOW, RETURNED Impact Type Retention groups IGNORE, DEFAULT, BONUS Retention Group An icon's slot PRIMARY Texture Slot Whether an effect or an item shows ALWAYS_VISIBLE, NOT_VISIBLE Visibility The role a projectile reads its speed by PROJECTILE_SPEED Set By Caller Key The keys the core reads and writes an activation's or a process's data under SOURCE, TARGET, TARGET_REAL, TARGET_POS, POSITION, ROTATION, TRANSFORM, EFFECTS, EVENT_SUBJECT, EVENT_IMPACT, CUE, ASSET, SPEC and more Data Key Keys for a project's own coded behaviours, of which PlayForge's code reads none INDEX, RADIUS, DURATION, DISTANCE, CENTER and more Data Key A side SYSTEM Affiliation The rest GAME_ROOT, NONE, DEBUG, FAILED_TO_INITIALIZE, FAILED_WHILE_ACTIVE Code Four of them have other names: Other name Same tag as Tags.IgnoreRetention IGNORE DefaultRetention DEFAULT AllowImpact ALWAYS_ALLOW DisallowImpact NEVER_ALLOW Three of the kinds come up in other guides: The events are what an ability's triggers hear (Abilities: Activation). The roles are what a Forge Project fills with its attributes (Attributes: Roles). The keys are what a cue's data packet holds (Cues: Data packets). A path given to New Tag that is one of these tags' text, as Died or Health, would make that very tag. So New Tag says so, and offers PlayForge's own with Use It. The Tags view renames none of them.

guides/tags/querying-tags.html.title: Querying tags | PlayForge
guides/tags/querying-tags.html.summary: Querying tags A match mode, ETagMatchMode, says which of an entity's tags answer for the tag it's asked about. Option Which tags answer Exact The tag itself. Include Children The tag, or one under its path: Status.Debuff.Burn answers for Status.Debuff. Include Parents The tag, or one above its path: Status.Debuff answers for Status.Debuff.Burn. Same Root Any tag of its root: Status.Buff answers for Status.Debuff.Burn. In this section Tag queries: A TagQuery asks one thing of an entity's tags, as a requirement's entry and a Tag condition do. What a query counts: What a query counts depends on what it's asked of

guides/tags/querying-tags/tag-queries.ht.title: Tag queries | PlayForge
guides/tags/querying-tags/tag-queries.ht.summary: Tag queries A TagQuery asks one thing of an entity's tags, as a requirement's entry and a Tag condition do. Field Description Tag The tag it asks about. MatchMode Which tags answer for it, Exact unless set. Operator How the count of matches compares with Magnitude, an EComparisonOperator. Magnitude The number the count is compared with. Greater Than 0, as a query starts, asks for the tag. Equal 0 asks for its absence. Its inspector, TagQueryDrawer, shows its Tag, its Match and its Count. Count is the comparison and the number. These make the common queries: Method What it asks TagQuery.HasTag(tag, mode) Whether the tag is there. DoesNotHaveTag(tag, mode) Whether the tag is absent. HasExactCount(tag, count, mode) Whether the count is exactly a number. HasTagOrChildren(tag) Whether the tag, or one under it, is there.

guides/tags/querying-tags/what-a-query-c.title: What a query counts | PlayForge
guides/tags/querying-tags/what-a-query-c.summary: What a query counts What a query counts depends on what it's asked of: Method What it counts Validate(cache) Weights, as gas.QueryTags(query) asks. Exact reads the tag's weight, and the other modes add up the weights of the tags that match. Validate(list) The tags that match in a list of tags, as GetAppliedTags() gives, each once. CountMatches gives the count either way. These checks ask for a debuff by a match mode, and for a bleed by its weight: using FarEmerald.PlayForge; public static class StatusChecks { static readonly Tag Debuff = Tag.GenerateAsUnique("Status.Debuff"); static readonly Tag Bleed = Tag.GenerateAsUnique("Status.Debuff.Bleed"); // Status.Debuff, or any tag under it public static bool IsDebuffed(IGameplayAbilitySystem gas) => gas.GetTagCache().HasTag(Debuff, ETagMatchMode.IncludeChildren); // Bleed granted three times or more, by its weight static readonly TagQuery Bleeding = new TagQuery { Tag = Bleed, Operator = EComparisonOperator.GreaterOrEqual, Magnitude = 3, }; public static bool BleedsHard(IGameplayAbilitySystem gas) => gas.QueryTags(Bleeding); }

guides/tags/requirements.html.title: Requirements | PlayForge
guides/tags/requirements.html.summary: Requirements Tag requirements are the tags an entity must have, and must not have, for an ability to activate and run, or for an effect to land, go on and come off. Each is a group, an AvoidRequireTagGroup, of two lists of tag queries: Property Description Requires (RequireTags) Each query must pass. Must not have (AvoidTags) No query may pass. Name Optional. Tells the group apart where it's imported. A group passes when each query it requires passes and none it must not have does. So an empty group passes. In this section Requirement sets: Groups come in sets, each an AbstractTagRequirements, which says What a row counts: A requirement row reads its entity's tags as a list: each tag once, whatever its weight. Templates: A Requirement Template, RequirementTemplate, is a group of requirements that other groups can follow. In code: You can build and check an AvoidRequireTagGroup in code.

guides/tags/requirements/in-code.html.title: In code | PlayForge
guides/tags/requirements/in-code.html.summary: In code You can build and check an AvoidRequireTagGroup in code. Method What it does AddRequirement(tag, mode) Adds a query of the tag's presence to Requires. AddAvoidance(tag, mode) Adds a query of the tag's presence to Must not have. AddRequirementWithChildren(tag), AddAvoidanceWithChildren(tag) Add the same queries, under Include Children. RemoveTag(tag) Takes a tag's queries out. Clear() Takes every query out. Validate Passes or fails the group against a cache or a list, as a query does. ValidateDetailed Says why, as an AvoidRequireTagGroup.ValidationResult. GetAllReferencedTags() Lists the tags the group names. Clone() Copies the group. CopyFrom(group) Takes another group's name and queries. A ValidationResult holds: FailedRequirements, the queries the group requires that failed; TriggeredAvoidances, the queries it must not have that passed; GetSummary(), which gives the result as a line of text. This group asks for Grounded and nothing under State.Disabled, and says why it fails: using FarEmerald.PlayForge; public static class Landing { static readonly Tag Grounded = Tag.GenerateAsUnique("State.Grounded"); static readonly Tag Disabled = Tag.GenerateAsUnique("State.Disabled"); // Grounded, and nothing under State.Disabled static readonly AvoidRequireTagGroup CanLand = Make(); static AvoidRequireTagGroup Make() { var group = new AvoidRequireTagGroup { Name = "Can Land" }; group.AddRequirement(Grounded); group.AddAvoidanceWithChildren(Disabled); return group; } public static bool Allows(IGameplayAbilitySystem gas, out string why) { var result = CanLand.ValidateDetailed(gas.GetTagCache()); why = result.IsValid ? null : result.GetSummary(); return result.IsValid; } }

guides/tags/requirements/requirement-set.title: Requirement sets | PlayForge
guides/tags/requirements/requirement-set.summary: Requirement sets Groups come in sets, each an AbstractTagRequirements, which says: whether any of its groups asks anything (HasAnyRequirements); how many queries they hold (TotalRequirementCount); whether one names a template (HasLinkedTemplates). An effect has two EffectTagRequirements, one on its target and one on its source. Each has three groups (Effects: Requirements): Property Description Applying (ApplicationRequirements) Must pass for the effect to land. While on (OngoingRequirements) Without it, the effect's ticks don't execute. Removed by (RemovalRequirements) Takes the effect off once met. It asks nothing while empty. An ability has an AbilityTagRequirements (Abilities: Requirements): Property Description Caster (SourceRequirements) Checked as the ability is asked to activate, and again after targeting. While active (WhileActiveRequirements) The caster's, for as long as the ability runs. Checked as it's asked to activate, and as the caster's tags change. It interrupts the ability as it fails. Target (TargetRequirements) Checked after targeting, where there's a target. A targeting task has a lone group, its Requirements, which the target it takes must pass. How a set draws A set draws as a table, EffectTagRequirementsDrawer or AbilityTagRequirementsDrawer. Each group is a row, with a cell for what it requires and a cell for what it must not have. Each cell lists its tags, or says None. A lone group draws as a table of one row, AvoidRequireTagGroupDrawer. Pressing a cell opens its list under the table, with the group's Name, Template and Sync With Template. Pressing it again closes the list.

guides/tags/requirements/templates.html.title: Templates | PlayForge
guides/tags/requirements/templates.html.summary: Templates A Requirement Template, RequirementTemplate, is a group of requirements that other groups can follow. Make one with Create → PlayForge → Requirement Template. Property Description Requirements The template's own group. Description The template's description. Category A tag of the Requirement Category context, which groups templates. Its inspector, RequirementTemplateEditor, is the shared header over those fields. A group's Template names a template. Sync With Template marks the group as following it (ShouldSyncFromTemplate). Method What it does TrySyncFromTemplate() Copies the template's tags into a group that follows it. LinkToTemplate(template) Links a template, and copies it. UnlinkFromTemplate() Lets the template go, keeping its tags. A group checks its own tags.

guides/tags/requirements/what-a-row-coun.title: What a row counts | PlayForge
guides/tags/requirements/what-a-row-coun.summary: What a row counts A requirement row reads its entity's tags as a list: each tag once, whatever its weight. So a row's numbers count tags: Greater Than 0 asks for the tag. Greater Than 1 under Include Children asks for two different tags under it. The ability's While active row alone is read against the weights. A Tag condition, the Tag Weight check and a tag worker read weights too (Conditions and checks). Tip To ask for stacks of one tag, as three grants of Combo.Points, use a Tag condition, the Tag Weight check or a tag worker.

guides/tags/tag-field-attributes.html.title: Tag field attributes | PlayForge
guides/tags/tag-field-attributes.html.summary: Tag field attributes Attributes on a Tag field, or on a list of tags, say what its tag field offers and does. Attribute What it does ForgeTagContext Names the contexts the field takes, PlayForge's or the project's own, as [ForgeTagContext(ForgeContext.Granted)] or [ForgeTagContext("Weather")]. It makes the tags the field holds of each. A field without one offers every tag. ForgeTagNoCreate Offers neither New Tag… nor Make It a Child Of…, as AllowCreate = false does. ForgeTagExcludeUniversal Leaves the Universal tags out, as IncludeUniversal = false does. ForgeTagReadOnly Shows the tag greyed, with no picker and no menu. Code still sets it. ForgeTagTooltip Gives the field its tooltip, as [ForgeTagTooltip("...")], in place of Unity's [Tooltip]. The field reads [Tooltip] where it has none. ForgeTagExposed Goes on a static tag of code, not on an asset's field (Tags written in code). ForgeTagContext has two settings, each true unless set: Setting What it does IncludeUniversal Offers the Universal tags too. AllowCreate Offers New Tag… and Make It a Child Of…. This ability component takes a tag of the project's Weather context. Its field can't make tags, and leaves the Universal tags out: using System; using FarEmerald.PlayForge; using UnityEngine; // Refuses its ability while its caster is out of the weather it names [Serializable] public class NeedsWeatherAbilityComponent : AbstractAbilityComponent { [Tooltip("The weather its caster must be under, or one beneath it")] [ForgeTagContext("Weather", AllowCreate = false)] [ForgeTagExcludeUniversal] public Tag Weather; public override string CanStart(AbilityComponentContext ctx) { var tags = ctx.Source?.GetTagCache(); if (!Weather.IsValid || tags == null || tags.HasTag(Weather, ETagMatchMode.IncludeChildren)) return null; return $"Needs {Weather}"; } } Attributes no drawer reads Six more attributes are declared for a tag field, but no drawer reads them. So they change nothing in the inspector: Attribute Declared for ForgeTagDefault A default tag ForgeTagRequired A tag the field must have ForgeTagPrefix The prefixes the field takes ForgeTagGroup A group of fields ForgeTagLockedCountAttribute, ForgeTagLockedIndicesAttribute A list's locked entries ForgeTagDefault can't be written on a field at all, since a Tag can't be an attribute's argument. AvoidRequireTagGroupColor, on the requirement groups' fields, gives each a colour that no drawer reads.

guides/tags/tag-workers.html.title: Tag workers | PlayForge
guides/tags/tag-workers.html.summary: Tag workers A tag worker, AbstractTagWorker, acts while its entity's tags meet its requirements, as flames shown while Status.Burning weighs 3 or more. A worker is one of a Worker Group's Tag workers, its kind picked from the list. Its entity holds it as it holds the group (Workers: Where workers come from). In this section A worker's requirements: A tag worker's Tag Requirements (TagWorkerRequirements) say when it acts. A worker's hooks: A tag worker's hooks run at its entity's end of frame. When requirements are read: The entity reads its workers' requirements at the end of a frame in which One worker for many entities: One tag worker serves every entity whose group holds it.

guides/tags/tag-workers/a-workers-hooks..title: A worker's hooks | PlayForge
guides/tags/tag-workers/a-workers-hooks..summary: A worker's hooks A tag worker's hooks run at its entity's end of frame. Each is a virtual no-op. Method When it runs Activate(system) Once, as its requirements come to be met. Tick(system) While they hold, after the activations, as its Tick Pause says. Resolve(system) Once, as they no longer hold. Or at once where the worker is taken away while active, as when its item is unequipped. Tick Pause is a number read at the entity's level: At 0, the worker ticks every frame. At n, it ticks every n + 1 frames. Below 0, as at −1, the default, it never ticks. This worker shows a child of its entity's object while its requirements are met: using System; using FarEmerald.PlayForge; using UnityEngine; // Shows a child of its entity's object while the worker's Tag Requirements are met, as flames while // Status.Burning weighs 3 or more [Serializable] public sealed class ShowWhileTagged : AbstractTagWorker { [Tooltip("The child shown, by name, at any depth")] public string Child = "Flames"; public override void Activate(IGameplayAbilitySystem system) => Show(system, true); public override void Resolve(IGameplayAbilitySystem system) => Show(system, false); private void Show(IGameplayAbilitySystem system, bool shown) { var body = system?.ToGASObject(); if (body == null) return; foreach (var each in body.GetComponentsInChildren<Transform>(true)) if (each.name == Child) each.gameObject.SetActive(shown); } }

guides/tags/tag-workers/a-workers-requir.title: A worker's requirements | PlayForge
guides/tags/tag-workers/a-workers-requir.summary: A worker's requirements A tag worker's Tag Requirements (TagWorkerRequirements) say when it acts. They list entries, each a TagWorkerRequirementPacket: Part Description A tag That very tag. A policy An ERequireAvoidPolicy: Require passes while the tag's weight is the entry's number or more. Avoid passes while it's below it. A number The weight that decides, read at the entity's level. The requirements are met where every entry passes, and always where there are none. Note An absent tag weighs −1 here, as GetWeight gives it. So Require 1, and Require 0 too, ask for the tag, and Avoid 1 asks for its absence.

guides/tags/tag-workers/one-worker-for-m.title: One worker for many entities | PlayForge
guides/tags/tag-workers/one-worker-for-m.summary: One worker for many entities One tag worker serves every entity whose group holds it. Each entity tracks it apart, so the worker keeps nothing of one entity in its fields. Given by two sources, as two copies of an item, a worker runs once. It stays until the last source takes it back. A tag worker draws as TagWorkerDrawer draws a worker of any kind. Its Tag Requirements draw as a list (TagWorkerRequirementsDrawer) of rows, each the tag, the policy and the number (TagWorkerRequirementPacketDrawer).

guides/tags/tag-workers/when-requirement.title: When requirements are read | PlayForge
guides/tags/tag-workers/when-requirement.summary: When requirements are read The entity reads its workers' requirements at the end of a frame in which: its tags changed; a worker came or went; its last reading started or stopped one. It queues each activation and resolution on its action queue, ahead of the ticks (Workers: The action queue). A worker whose ValidateWorkFor(handler) reads more than the tags, as an attribute, overrides EvaluateEveryFrame too. It's then read every frame. Member What it is TagWorkerActivateAction, TagWorkerResolveAction The actions queued, at ActionPriority.TagWorker. OnTagWorkerActivated, OnTagWorkerResolved The callbacks that hear each. FrameSummary The frame's summary, which keeps them. tags.IsWorkerActive(worker), ActiveWorkers, RegisteredWorkers Say which workers run on an entity.

guides/tags/tags-written-in-code.html.title: Tags written in code | PlayForge
guides/tags/tags-written-in-code.html.summary: Tags written in code Code makes a tag of a path with Tag.GenerateAsUnique, and offers it to the editor's pickers with [ForgeTagExposed]. These make tags in code: Method What it gives Tag.GenerateAsUnique("State.Stunned") The unique tag of the path: the very tag New Tag makes of it. PlayForge's own are among them: Tag.GenerateAsUnique("Died") is Tags.DIED. TagRegistry.FromSegments("State", "Stunned") The same unique tag, made of its parts. Tag.Generate("State.Stunned") The plain tag of the path, which no unique tag equals. A string where a tag is asked for, as Tag tag = "State.Stunned"; The plain tag of the path, as Tag.Generate gives. Tag.Generate(name, displayName) A tag of a name, with a display name of its own. tag.Child("Burn"), TagRegistry.CreateChild(tag, "Burn") The plain tag of the child's path. GetParent(), GetAncestors() The plain tags of their paths. GetRoot() The plain tag of the root's path. Of a root, it gives the tag itself. Use plain tags for tags that code alone makes and reads. TagRegistry.TagUtil makes the names: GenerateDeterministicTag(text, prefix, length) makes a unique tag's name. It pads the prefix and the text to the length, 32 to 64, by a SHA-256 hash of them, or cuts them short there. GenerateUniqueRandomTag() makes a random tag that no registered tag has. TagUtil.rngGenerationBufferSize, 64, is the length New Tag pads to. Exposing them to the pickers Mark a static Tag field or property of the project's code with ForgeTagExposed to offer it in the editor's tag pickers. The field or property can be public or not. Where the tag is offered depends on the contexts the mark names: Naming contexts, as [ForgeTagExposed(ForgeContext.Granted)], it's offered by the pickers of those contexts. Naming none, it's offered under Code, which the fields that name no context offer. A code tag that isn't marked stays out of the pickers. So a project chooses which of its tags its designers see. The Tags view shows the contexts a tag is exposed for in Declared For, checked and locked. It can declare the tag for other contexts besides. The editor finds the marks once each domain reload, in the player assemblies that reference PlayForge. It leaves test assemblies out. A tag written in an editor assembly reaches the pickers once its type is registered as the editor loads. Register it from an [InitializeOnLoad] class, for example, with ForgeTagRegistry.RegisterContextDefaultSource(typeof(EditorTags)). Only the type's marked members are read. This class exposes two tags for contexts and one under Code, and keeps one out of the pickers: using FarEmerald.PlayForge; public static class GameTags { // The tag New Tag makes of State.Stunned, offered by the fields that take granted tags [ForgeTagExposed(ForgeContext.Granted)] public static readonly Tag Stunned = Tag.GenerateAsUnique("State.Stunned"); // Offered by the project's own fields of its Weather context [ForgeTagExposed("Weather")] public static readonly Tag Rain = Tag.GenerateAsUnique("Weather.Rain"); // Exposed for no context: under Code [ForgeTagExposed] public static Tag Cheats { get; } = Tag.GenerateAsUnique("Game.Cheats"); // Not exposed: a key the game's code alone writes and reads public static readonly Tag Combo = Tag.Generate("Game.Combo"); }

guides/tags/the-editors-tag-registry.htm.title: The editor's tag registry | PlayForge
guides/tags/the-editors-tag-registry.htm.summary: The editor's tag registry ForgeTagRegistry, in the editor, is what the tag pickers, the Tags view and New Tag know of the project's tags. It knows each tag, and each use of it, by context. In this section What the registry reads: The editor's tag registry reads the project's tags as the editor loads. Reading the registry in code: Tools of the project's own can read the editor's tag registry.

guides/tags/the-editors-tag-registry/rea.title: Reading the registry in code | PlayForge
guides/tags/the-editors-tag-registry/rea.summary: Reading the registry in code Tools of the project's own can read the editor's tag registry. Method What it does GetAllTags() Gives every tag in the project. GetTagsForContext(contexts, includeUniversal) Gives the tags of the contexts, and the Universal ones where asked. GetTagUsage(tag) Gives a tag's uses. GetAllTagRecords() Gives every tag's uses. GetAllContexts() Gives every context in use. GetSystemDefaultTags() Gives the code tags. MarkDirty() Has the registry read again as it's next asked. RefreshCache() Has the registry read again at once. A tag's uses are its ForgeTagRegistry.TagUsageRecord, by context: each context's uses are a ForgeTagRegistry.ContextUsage; each use is a ForgeTagRegistry.FieldUsageInfo: its Asset, its FieldPath, and whether it's code's (IsSystemDefault). A context is a ForgeTagRegistry.TagContext. Its ContextKey is Uncontextualized for a field that names none. The tag field tells the registry each pick, with RegisterTagUsage and UnregisterTagUsage. So a picker knows of it at once.

guides/tags/the-editors-tag-registry/wha.title: What the registry reads | PlayForge
guides/tags/the-editors-tag-registry/wha.summary: What the registry reads The editor's tag registry reads the project's tags as the editor loads. It reads them again after any .asset file is imported, moved or deleted (TagRegistryAssetPostprocessor). It reads: the code tags marked [ForgeTagExposed]: in Tags, in the player assemblies that reference PlayForge, and in each type given to RegisterContextDefaultSource; every Tag Library; every Tag field, list and array of the project's PlayForge assets, each use under its field's contexts.
