The assets it reads are the project's abilities, effects, items, entities, attributes, attribute sets, Scaler assets, Requirement Templates, Value Pipelines, Effect Modifiers, Crowd Control Rules, Forge Projects and Creator Lab rules. It reads through their nested classes and [SerializeReference] fields, as their components and workers. Note A tag that only a Cue Library, a scene, a prefab or an asset of the project's own type holds is offered nowhere. It's offered once a PlayForge asset uses it, or a Tag Library declares it.

guides/tags/the-tag-field.html.title: The tag field | PlayForge
guides/tags/the-tag-field.html.summary: The tag field Each Tag field, alone or in a list, draws as a tag field, TagDrawer. It shows its tag by its display name, and picks another from the tags its contexts offer. The field shows its label, or none in a list. Then it shows the tag's parents in secondary text and its leaf in strong text, or its whole path while Show Full Tag Paths is on. An empty field shows None, and a dash shows where the selected assets' tags differ. In this section The picker: Pressing a tag field opens its picker, which lists, in order Its menu: A tag field's right-click menu holds four items New Tag: New Tag makes a unique tag, and gives it to the field. Preferences: Preferences → PlayForge holds each user's own tag preferences, under Tags.

guides/tags/the-tag-field/its-menu.html.title: Its menu | PlayForge
guides/tags/the-tag-field/its-menu.html.summary: Its menu A tag field's right-click menu holds four items: Item What it does None Empties the field. New Tag… Makes a new tag for the field (New Tag). Make It a Child Of… Picks another tag, and puts the field's leaf under it: Burn under Status.Debuff makes Status.Debuff.Burn. Copy Path Copies the tag as the field reads it. New Tag… and Make It a Child Of… show only where the field may make tags.

guides/tags/the-tag-field/new-tag.html.title: New Tag | PlayForge
guides/tags/the-tag-field/new-tag.html.summary: New Tag New Tag makes a unique tag, and gives it to the field. It asks for two things: Property Description Path The new tag's path. It starts as the field's tag's parents. Contexts The contexts the tag is for. They start as the field's. Create, or Enter, makes the tag and gives it to the field. A context chosen beyond the field's declares the tag for that context in the Tag Library, so that context's fields offer it too. New Tag refuses a path that is: empty; of anything but letters, digits, underscores and spaces, in names joined by single dots; 64 characters or more, which the padding would cut short, so it could be another tag's. A path that is one of PlayForge's own tags' text, as Died or Health, would make that very tag. New Tag says so, and Use It gives the field PlayForge's own.

guides/tags/the-tag-field/preferences.ht.title: Preferences | PlayForge
guides/tags/the-tag-field/preferences.ht.summary: Preferences Preferences → PlayForge holds each user's own tag preferences, under Tags. Property Description Show Full Tag Paths Off by default. Shows a tag's whole path in strong text, in place of its parents before its leaf. It applies in the tag fields and The Forge's Tags view. Group Tags by Root On by default. Shows the picker's tags under their roots. The page's Menu Width and Menu Height are the most the picker grows to.

guides/tags/the-tag-field/the-picker.htm.title: The picker | PlayForge
guides/tags/the-tag-field/the-picker.htm.summary: The picker Pressing a tag field opens its picker, which lists, in order: None; New Tag…, where the field may make tags; the tags the field offers, by their paths, in natural order. While Group Tags by Root is on, each tag sits under a folder of its root, where the root has more than one tag. The field's tag is checked. The search finds a tag by any part of its path. While a tag is highlighted, the picker's Context says the contexts it's for, or that it's for none yet. A pick writes the tag, its name and its display name, into each selected asset, as one Undo step. What a field offers A field offers the tags of its contexts (Contexts), and the Universal ones, of the active Forge Project: PlayForge's own, and those code exposes; those the project's assets use; those a Tag Library in its folder declares. It leaves out a tag that only another project uses.

guides/tags/the-tag-library.html.title: The Tag Library | PlayForge
guides/tags/the-tag-library.html.summary: The Tag Library A Tag Library asset, ForgeTagLibrary, declares tags for contexts, so those contexts' pickers offer them before any asset uses them. It also keeps the project's own contexts. Create → PlayForge → Tag Library makes one. PlayForge also makes one in the active Forge Project's folder while there's none, as a tag is first declared or a context first made. Its inspector, ForgeTagLibraryEditor, is the shared header over two lists: Property Description Entries The library's declarations, each a ForgeTagLibrary.Entry. Contexts The project's own contexts. Each entry declares one tag: Property Description Name The tag's name, padded where the tag is unique. Display Name How the tag reads, where that differs from its name. Contexts The contexts the tag is declared for. An empty list declares it Universal. Note What the tag is for. You seldom edit a library by hand. The Tags view's Declared For and New Tag's Contexts write its entries, each change one Undo step. A library edited by hand is read again as it's saved. A declaration goes into the library that declares the tag already, or else into the first, by its path. Every Tag Library in the Unity project is read, wherever it sits, and the contexts each keeps are every Forge Project's. The tags a library declares are offered by the pickers of the Forge Project whose folder holds it. Another project's pickers offer them only where that project's own assets use them.

guides/tags/the-tags-view.html.title: The Tags view | PlayForge
guides/tags/the-tags-view.html.summary: The Tags view The Forge's Tags view lists the active Forge Project's tags and what uses each. In it you declare a tag for contexts, and rename it. Open The Forge with Window → PlayForge → The Forge, and choose Tags in its toolbar. Each row of the list shows a tag the pickers offer: the tag, by its leaf, or by its whole path while Show Full Tag Paths is on; For, the contexts it's for; Uses, how many of the project's assets use it, a Tag Library among them. Each column sorts, and the search finds a tag by any part of its path. In this section The detail pane: Selecting a tag in the Tags view shows it in the detail pane, which holds Renaming a tag: The Tags view renames a tag, and every tag under its path, in the assets that store them. Asset tags follow their names: An asset's own tag follows its name.

guides/tags/the-tags-view/asset-tags-fol.title: Asset tags follow their names | PlayForge
guides/tags/the-tags-view/asset-tags-fol.summary: Asset tags follow their names An asset's own tag follows its name. You rename an ability, an effect, an item, an entity or an attribute set in any of three ways: by its Name; with F2 in The Forge; with its asset menu's Rename…. The rename stores the tag the new name gives. It carries the new tag into each asset a tag's rename reaches that stored the old one (Renaming a tag). It carries nothing if another asset still has the old tag as its own, as the asset it was duplicated from does. An asset's stored tag can differ from the one its name gives. Then: its Identity section shows the stored tag in warning text, with Update; the Problems view warns of it under "Asset tags their names don't give", with the quick fix Store the Tag. Update and Store the Tag each store the tag, and carry it the same way.

guides/tags/the-tags-view/renaming-a-tag.title: Renaming a tag | PlayForge
guides/tags/the-tags-view/renaming-a-tag.summary: Renaming a tag The Tags view renames a tag, and every tag under its path, in the assets that store them. To rename a tag: Choose Rename… in its row's right-click menu, or press F2. Enter the tag's new Path. The rename is one Undo step. It reaches every ability, effect, item, entity, attribute set, attribute, Scaler asset, Value Pipeline and Requirement Template that stores one of the tags, and the Tag Library entries that declare them. A unique tag stays unique, and a plain one stays plain. Nothing else follows. These keep the old name: code; scenes and prefabs; a Forge Project's settings; Crowd Control Rules and Effect Modifiers; a Cue Library; the Creator Lab's rules. A rename refuses a path a tag has already, and one of PlayForge's own tags' text. It renames no tag that is, or has under it, one of PlayForge's own or an asset's own tag.

guides/tags/the-tags-view/the-detail-pan.title: The detail pane | PlayForge
guides/tags/the-tags-view/the-detail-pan.summary: The detail pane Selecting a tag in the Tags view shows it in the detail pane, which holds: its leaf, with its whole path under it, and, where it's unique, its padded name on hover; its For and its Uses; Declared For, the contexts its Tag Library entry declares it for, with those its code exposes it for checked and locked; a row for each of the project's assets that uses it, with the fields that do. The row shows that asset in The Forge. Choosing a context in Declared For declares the tag for it at once, as one Undo step. Taking every context away takes the declaration away, so the tag is for the contexts its uses are in alone.

guides/tags/traps.html.title: Traps | PlayForge
guides/tags/traps.html.summary: Traps Tags invite a few mistakes. Each is below, with its way out. Text makes a plain tag. "State.Stunned" where a tag is asked for, and Tag.Generate, give the plain tag of the path. New Tag made a unique one, and the two are different tags: Neither equals the other. Neither answers a query for the other, in any mode but Same Root. Neither is heard by the other's listener. Write Tag.GenerateAsUnique("State.Stunned"), or expose the tag from code so that designers pick that very one. An absent tag weighs −1. GetWeight, GetTagWeight, and GetMatchingWeight in Exact mode give −1 for a tag the entity hasn't got, not 0. Ask for more than 0, or use TryGetWeight. A tag added to the cache doesn't last. TagCache.AddTag is dropped at the next compile, as an ability starts or an item changes. Grant a lasting tag with AddLooseTag. A requirement row counts tags, not weights. An Exact entry's Greater Than 1 never passes in a row but While active. Ask for stacks with the Tag Weight check, a Tag condition or a tag worker. A tag shows by ToString(). Its Name is padded where it's unique. It's the Name a tag converts to where a string is asked for. A tag's relatives are plain. Child, GetParent, GetAncestors and GetRoot make plain tags, which no unique tag equals. Compare families by path, with IsChildOf or a match mode. A rename reaches assets, not code. The Tags view renames what assets store, so a tag the project's code writes keeps its old text there. Rename it in the code too. The applied list is the cache's. GetAppliedTags() changes as tags come and go. Copy it to keep it.

guides/tags/what-a-tag-is.html.title: What a tag is | PlayForge
guides/tags/what-a-tag-is.html.summary: What a tag is A tag, a Tag, is a path of names joined by dots, parents first. Status.Debuff.Burn is under Status.Debuff, which is under Status, its root. A Tag is a struct that an asset saves as two strings: Field Description Name What tells the tag apart. Two tags are equal, by == or Equals, exactly when their names are. DisplayName How the tag reads. ToString() gives it, or the name where it has none, and PlayForge's windows show a tag this way. A tag is of one of three makes: Make Where it comes from Its name Its display name Unique New Tag makes one (New Tag). PlayForge's own tags are unique (PlayForge's own tags). Its path, padded to 64 characters by a hash of it, as Status.Debuff.BurnQx3… Its path An asset's own tag The asset's Name gives it, as Ability.FireBall for an ability named Fire Ball (Abilities: Identity). Its whole path Its leaf, FireBall Plain Code makes one of a text, as Tag.Generate("Status.Debuff.Burn"). Its path Its path One path always gives one unique name. So the padding only keeps a unique tag apart from the plain tag of its path. IsValid says whether a tag has a name. An empty tag field holds default(Tag), which has none. In this section Its place in the tree: A tag's place in the tree comes from its Path, the text its family goes by. Showing a tag: Show a tag by its display name, with ToString(), GetName() or an interpolated string, $"{tag}". The registry: TagRegistry keeps the tags made as the game runs, by name.

guides/tags/what-a-tag-is/its-place-in-t.title: Its place in the tree | PlayForge
guides/tags/what-a-tag-is/its-place-in-t.summary: Its place in the tree A tag's place in the tree comes from its Path, the text its family goes by. A unique tag's path is its display name, and any other tag's path is its name. These members read the path, here of Status.Debuff.Burn: Member What it gives Depth Its depth in the tree, 1 for a root. IsRoot Whether it's a root. GetLeafName() Its leaf: Burn. GetParentPath() Its parent's path: Status.Debuff. GetAncestorPaths() Its ancestors' paths, from its parent to its root. GetSegments() The names in its path. These methods compare two tags by their paths: Method What it asks IsChildOf(tag) Whether its path is under another tag's, at any depth. IsDirectChildOf(tag) Whether its path is one level under another tag's. IsParentOf(tag) The reverse of IsChildOf: whether another tag's path is under its own. MatchesOrIsChildOf As IsChildOf, but the tag itself matches too. MatchesOrIsParentOf As IsParentOf, but the tag itself matches too. SharesAncestorWith Whether the two tags have one root. A family goes by paths, but equality goes by names. So Status.Debuff.Burn is under Status.Debuff, whichever makes the two are. Note The plain Status.Debuff and the unique one are two tags, and neither is under the other.

guides/tags/what-a-tag-is/showing-a-tag..title: Showing a tag | PlayForge
guides/tags/what-a-tag-is/showing-a-tag..summary: Showing a tag Show a tag by its display name, with ToString(), GetName() or an interpolated string, $"{tag}". Don't show its Name, which is padded where the tag is unique. A tag converts to its Name where a string is asked for, as in string text = tag; or "Stunned by " + tag.

guides/tags/what-a-tag-is/the-registry.h.title: The registry | PlayForge
guides/tags/what-a-tag-is/the-registry.h.summary: The registry TagRegistry keeps the tags made as the game runs, by name. Making a tag registers it, and a Bootstrapper registers PlayForge's own tags as it starts, with TagRegistry.Initialize(). Method What it does TagRegistry.Resolve(name) Gives the registered tag of a name, with its display name, or else the plain tag of the name. A saved name is read back this way. TagRegistry.IsValidPath(path) Says whether a text can be a tag's path: names of letters, digits, underscores and spaces, joined by single dots, with no dot at either end. GetDirectChildren, GetAllDescendants, GetParent, GetAncestors The registry's lookups of a tag's family, by the registered names. Note The registry's family lookups go by the registered names, so they miss a unique tag's family. Read that from the tag's own Path, with IsChildOf.

guides/task-sequences/building-one.html.title: Building one | PlayForge
guides/task-sequences/building-one.html.summary: Building one You build a sequence in code, stage by stage, with TaskSequenceBuilder. var cast = TaskSequenceBuilder.Create("Fireball") .WithMaxDuration(5f) .Stage(stage => stage .WithName("Wind Up") .Task((data, token) => SequenceTaskLibrary.PlayAnimationState(animator, "Cast", token))) .Stage(stage => stage .WithName("Flight") .Task((data, token) => SequenceTaskLibrary.ArcTowards(fireball, target, 20f, 2f, token))) .Stage(stage => stage .WithName("Impact") .Do(data => ForgeLog.Info("Fireball lands"))) .BuildSequence(); cast.RegisterAndRun(SequenceDataPacket.SceneRoot()); The builder ends with one of three methods: Method Gives Build The definition, which a TaskSequence runs and a synced runner is built from. BuildSequence The sequence itself. BuildSyncRunner A synced runner (Synced sequences). A static method marked [TaskSequenceMethod] that returns a sequence, a chain or a definition appears in two places: an ability's sequence dropdown; a TaskSequenceReference field. An ability runs a chain as a process too, which asks its conditions each frame. The data packet A task reads and writes the run's data packet, a SequenceDataPacket. What started the run put its caster, targets and values there. A task can leave values for the stages after it (SetPrimary, GetPrimary).

guides/task-sequences/built-in-kinds.htm.title: Built-in kinds | PlayForge
guides/task-sequences/built-in-kinds.htm.summary: Built-in kinds The kinds PlayForge ships for this guide's pickers, each with its menu and what it does, as its picker says. A project's own kinds join them in the same pickers. In this section Injections Stage policies Clock choices

guides/task-sequences/built-in-kinds/clo.title: Clock choices | PlayForge
guides/task-sequences/built-in-kinds/clo.summary: Clock choices Kind Menu What it does CasterClockChoice (Caster's) — An ability's caster's own time, its time scale times the game's; the game's for anything else. GameClockChoice (Game's) — The game's time, whatever an ability's caster's is. ScaledClockChoice (Scaled) — A pace of its own over another clock, as half speed or double; over the caster's unless it picks another. UnscaledClockChoice (Unscaled) — The game's time without its time scale: it runs while the game is paused or slowed.

guides/task-sequences/built-in-kinds/inj.title: Injections | PlayForge
guides/task-sequences/built-in-kinds/inj.summary: Injections Kind Menu What it does BreakStageRepeatInjection — Breaks out of a stage's repeat loop (for WithRepeat or RepeatUntilSkippedPolicy). ChainInterruptInjection — Marker injection for chain-level interrupts. DelegateSequenceInjection — An injection that does what a function of your own says: applyFunc is handed the run's runtime and returns whether it applied, as one that adds to a count on a key press or jumps to a stage by name. InterruptSequenceInjection — Interrupts the entire sequence. JumpToStageInjection — Jumps to a specific stage by index. SkipAndMaintainInjection — Skips the current stage but maintains it running in background. SkipStageInjection — Skips the current stage and moves to the next. StopMaintainedAllInjection — Stops all maintained stages. StopMaintainedAtIndexInjection — Stops the maintained stage at a stage index. StopMaintainedLastInjection — Stops the oldest maintained stage.

guides/task-sequences/built-in-kinds/sta.title: Stage policies | PlayForge
guides/task-sequences/built-in-kinds/sta.summary: Stage policies Kind Menu What it does RepeatUntilSkippedPolicy — Stage repeats infinitely until explicitly skipped, interrupted, or broken. WhenAllStagePolicy — Stage completes when ALL tasks complete. WhenAnyStagePolicy — Stage completes when ANY task completes. WhenNStagePolicy — Stage completes when N tasks complete.

guides/task-sequences/chains.html.title: Chains | PlayForge
guides/task-sequences/chains.html.summary: Chains A chain runs its sequences in order, with one data packet. // countdown and fight are TaskSequences; the last is built in place var round = countdown.Then(fight).Then(builder => builder.WithName("Results").Stage(stage => stage.Do(ShowResults))); await round.Run(SequenceDataPacket.SceneRoot()); A chain can: repeat; pause and resume; skip its current sequence; be interrupted. It takes conditions of its own (InterruptWhen, SkipSequenceWhen). From inside, data.Chain is the chain, and data.InterruptChain() ends it.

guides/task-sequences/changing-the-run.h.title: Changing the run | PlayForge
guides/task-sequences/changing-the-run.h.summary: Changing the run You can change a run from one of its tasks, from outside, or by a condition, as far as the sequence allows. In this section From a task: A task changes its run through its data packet. From outside: Code outside the run changes it through the sequence or its runtime. By a condition: A condition injects when its predicate holds, and is checked each frame. What may change a run: What may change a run is the sequence's to say, on the sequence or on a stage.

guides/task-sequences/changing-the-run/b.title: By a condition | PlayForge
guides/task-sequences/changing-the-run/b.summary: By a condition A condition injects when its predicate holds, and is checked each frame. Condition Set on What it injects InterruptWhen The sequence An interrupt. SkipStageWhen The sequence A skip of the current stage. SkipWhen A stage A skip of that stage. StopRepeatWhen A stage A break of its repeat. InjectWhen The sequence or a stage Any injection. A condition fires once or every time it holds. A stage's condition is asked each frame by the process. So where a repeating stage's round ends, the next may have begun before StopRepeatWhen hears its predicate hold. A break from a task, or from OnRepeat, stops at the round exactly.

guides/task-sequences/changing-the-run/f.title: From a task | PlayForge
guides/task-sequences/changing-the-run/f.summary: From a task A task changes its run through its data packet. data.SkipStage(); // end this stage, on to the next data.SkipAndMaintain(); // on to the next, leaving this one's tasks running data.JumpToStage("Impact"); // or by index data.RestartSequence(); data.BreakStageRepeat(); data.Interrupt(); // end the run data.SetStageTimeout(2f); // this stage gets two seconds, then it's skipped SkipAndMaintain keeps the stage that is current as it's called running on. Called again later, it keeps that later stage running on as well.

guides/task-sequences/changing-the-run/f.title: From outside | PlayForge
guides/task-sequences/changing-the-run/f.summary: From outside Code outside the run changes it through the sequence or its runtime. Call What it does Inject(injection) Injects an injection. Interrupt() Interrupts the run. SkipCurrentStage() Skips the current stage.

guides/task-sequences/changing-the-run/w.title: What may change a run | PlayForge
guides/task-sequences/changing-the-run/w.summary: What may change a run What may change a run is the sequence's to say, on the sequence or on a stage. Call Allows AllowInjections(types) Only the injection types given. AllowOnlyInterrupt() Only an interrupt. DisallowInjections() No injection. A critical stage (WithCriticalFlag(true)) refuses every injection but those it names (WithCriticalAllowedInjections). OnCriticalSectionExited hears the last critical stage end. InjectStageLocal(injection, stage) asks the given stage's permissions, and the injection acts on the current stage.

guides/task-sequences/clocks.html.title: Clocks | PlayForge
guides/task-sequences/clocks.html.summary: Clocks A run's time is its clock's. These all go by it: its waits and delays; its timeouts and longest runs; its ElapsedTime; the library's tweens; its synced tasks. A run takes the first clock it finds: Its own, runtime.Clock, which whatever runs it sets: a chain's Clock, a TaskSequenceProcess's, or an ability's Run Sequence task's pick. So a packet others share keeps its own. Its packet's, data.Clock, which whatever starts the run sets. Its sequence's own, WithClock(clock) on the builder. Its packet's owner's: an ability's caster's own clock, its time scale times the game's. The game's, GameClock.Instance, which reads the clock in force, ForgeTime.Clock, as it's asked. In this section Clocks you can use: Besides the game's clock, a run can go by an unscaled clock, a scaled clock, an entity's clock or a clock of your own. Reading a run's clock: Code reads a run's clock from its runtime, from a task's token, or from a synced runner. Picking a clock in an inspector: An inspector picks a clock with an AbstractClockChoice field, marked [SerializeReference]. Clocks and fixed ticks: Under ProcessControl's fixed tick, a sequence waits for the next tick.

guides/task-sequences/clocks/clocks-and-.title: Clocks and fixed ticks | PlayForge
guides/task-sequences/clocks/clocks-and-.summary: Clocks and fixed ticks Under ProcessControl's fixed tick, a sequence waits for the next tick. The ticks run on the game's time, so they stand with it. A clock that runs while the game's time stands says so: its FollowsTicks is false, as the unscaled clock's is. Its sequences wait for Unity's frames instead. Code outside a sequence awaits ForgeTick.Next(clock) for the next step of a clock's time. A synced sequence run as a process steps with ProcessControl, by its ticks, whatever its clock.

guides/task-sequences/clocks/clocks-you-.title: Clocks you can use | PlayForge
guides/task-sequences/clocks/clocks-you-.summary: Clocks you can use Besides the game's clock, a run can go by an unscaled clock, a scaled clock, an entity's clock or a clock of your own. // A pause menu's runs while the game's time stands var menu = TaskSequenceBuilder.Create("Menu").WithClock(UnscaledClock.Instance) /* … */; // A finisher's slow motion: every sequence on the clock slows, speeds up or stops with it var slowMotion = new ScaledClock(0.25f); var finisher = TaskSequenceBuilder.Create("Finisher").WithClock(slowMotion) /* … */; // One run on an entity's time, from its packet var data = SequenceDataPacket.Default(); data.Clock = gas.GetClock(); UnscaledClock.Instance reads the game's time without its time scale. A ScaledClock runs at a Scale of its own over its Source, the clock in force unless it's given one. It counts its own Time through each change of scale. An entity's EntityClock is a clock as any other is. A clock of your own implements IForgeClock, and is read as it is. The clocks above read the clock in force, so a world of its own's steps and the fixed tick still drive them. A clock that reads Unity's time itself doesn't follow them.

guides/task-sequences/clocks/picking-a-c.title: Picking a clock in an inspector | PlayForge
guides/task-sequences/clocks/picking-a-c.summary: Picking a clock in an inspector An inspector picks a clock with an AbstractClockChoice field, marked [SerializeReference]. Choice The clock a run goes by None The clock it would have had. Caster's The caster's own. Game's The game's. Unscaled The game's time without its time scale. Scaled A pace of its own over the clock it picks: the caster's, unless it picks another. A [Serializable] class of your own made from it is offered beside them. Its ClockFor(data) gives the clock for a run on a packet. These have a clock choice: An ability's Run Sequence task. It gives the sequence it runs a clock of its own, and leaves the ability's other tasks the caster's. The Task Sequence Examples' components. A Sequence cue. Its run goes by its pick, else the sequence's own clock, else that of the one the cue plays on.

guides/task-sequences/clocks/reading-a-r.title: Reading a run's clock | PlayForge
guides/task-sequences/clocks/reading-a-r.summary: Reading a run's clock Code reads a run's clock from its runtime, from a task's token, or from a synced runner. runtime.Clock is a run's clock. TaskSequenceRuntime.ClockOfRun(token) is the clock of the run a task's token belongs to. A synced runner takes its sequence's clock (runner.Clock), and a packet's before it (runner.ClockFor(data)). runner.Step(data) steps by it.

guides/task-sequences/index.html.title: Task Sequences | PlayForge
guides/task-sequences/index.html.summary: Task Sequences A task sequence is a workflow over time, built in code. Its stages run one after another, and each stage is a set of tasks run together. An ability runs as a task sequence. So can anything with steps: a projectile's flight, a channel, a cutscene, a tutorial, a boss's phases. A sequence runs as a process (Processes), so ProcessControl starts, pauses and ends it like any other. Tip The Task Sequence Examples sample shows every part of this guide in code. It also has a component that runs any example from a scene. In this guide The parts: A task sequence is built from five parts: sequences, stages, tasks, injections and chains. Building one: You build a sequence in code, stage by stage, with TaskSequenceBuilder. Waiting: A sequence can wait as a stage, inside a task, or on the player's input. Repeating: A sequence, or one of its stages, can repeat. Changing the run: You can change a run from one of its tasks, from outside, or by a condition, as far as the sequence allows. Time limits and endings: A run can have time limits, and handlers that hear how it ends. Clocks: A run's time is its clock's. Running one: You can run a sequence as a process, in place, or through a runtime of your own. Chains: A chain runs its sequences in order, with one data packet. Synced sequences: A synced runner is the same sequence stepped a frame at a time, with no async. The libraries: Two libraries hold ready-made tasks, one for async stages and one for synced ones. Logging: What a sequence says goes through ForgeLog, under its own system, Sequences. Built-in kinds: The kinds PlayForge ships for this guide's pickers, each with its menu and what it does, as its picker says. In the API The types of this guide's area: BranchBuilder, BranchCase, BranchStage, BreakStageRepeatInjection, ChainInterruptInjection, DelegateSequenceInjection, DelegateSequenceTask, DelegateSyncTask, ESyncStagePolicy, IActiveSequence, InterruptSequenceInjection, ISequenceInjection, ISequenceStagePolicy, ISequenceTask, JumpToStageInjection, MainThreadSequenceTask, RepeatUntilSkippedPolicy, SequenceAnnotation, SequenceCondition, SequenceDataPacket, SequenceEventContext, SequenceMetadata, SequenceStage, SequenceStageMetadata, SequenceTaskBase, SequenceTaskLibrary, SequenceTimeout, SkipAndMaintainInjection, SkipStageInjection, StageBuilder, StopMaintainedAllInjection, StopMaintainedAtIndexInjection, StopMaintainedLastInjection, SyncedTaskSequence, SyncedTaskSequence.ERunnerState, SyncSequenceStage, SyncSequenceTaskBase, SyncSequenceTaskLibrary, TaskSequence, TaskSequenceBuilder, TaskSequenceChain, TaskSequenceDefinition, TaskSequenceMethodAttribute, TaskSequenceProcess, TaskSequenceReference, TaskSequenceRuntime, WhenAllStagePolicy, WhenAnyStagePolicy, WhenNStagePolicy.

guides/task-sequences/logging.html.title: Logging | PlayForge
guides/task-sequences/logging.html.summary: Logging What a sequence says goes through ForgeLog, under its own system, Sequences. A handler's throw is logged as an error. Where a sequence's or a chain's logging is on (WithInjectionLogging, a chain's WithLogging), what it does is logged as information. Preferences > PlayForge > Logging sets the quietest message every system logs. ForgeLog.SetLevel(ForgeLog.ESystem.Sequences, …) gives the sequences a level of their own, to hear more or less of them than the rest.

guides/task-sequences/repeating.html.title: Repeating | PlayForge
guides/task-sequences/repeating.html.summary: Repeating A sequence, or one of its stages, can repeat. Call On What it does WithRepeat(true) The builder Repeats the whole sequence until it's interrupted. WithRepeat(true) A stage Repeats the stage until it's broken (data.BreakStageRepeat(), StopRepeatWhen), skipped or interrupted. WithRepeatAndDelay(seconds) A stage Repeats the stage in the same way, and waits between repeats. WithRepeat(3) A stage Runs the stage three times in all, then the sequence moves on. A break, a skip or an interrupt still ends it sooner. A stage's OnRepeat hears each repeat, and runtime.GetRepeatCount(stage) says how many runs are done.

guides/task-sequences/running-one.html.title: Running one | PlayForge
guides/task-sequences/running-one.html.summary: Running one You can run a sequence as a process, in place, or through a runtime of your own. Way What it does RegisterAndRun(data), or ProcessControl.Register(sequence).With(data).Run() Runs it as a process: it shows in the Debugger, pauses with ProcessControl, and ends with its scene. await sequence.Run(data, token) Runs it in place, from code that's async already. TryRun says whether it finished. CreateRuntime Gives the runtime that runs it, to pause, resume, inject and read: its stage, its time, whether it finished, what it threw. TaskSequenceProcess Wraps a sequence, a chain or a synced runner as a process of a lifecycle and timing given.

guides/task-sequences/synced-sequences.h.title: Synced sequences | PlayForge
guides/task-sequences/synced-sequences.h.summary: Synced sequences A synced runner is the same sequence stepped a frame at a time, with no async. A process with the Synchronous lifecycle calls its Step each frame. A synced runner suits what runs for good, as a patrol, a regeneration or a bob. It costs nothing but the calls. using SyncSeq = FarEmerald.PlayForge.SyncSequenceTaskLibrary; runner = TaskSequenceBuilder.Create("Regenerate") .WithRepeat(true) .Stage(stage => stage.Task(SyncSeq.Delay(1f))) .Stage(stage => stage.Do(_ => Heal(5))) .BuildSyncRunner(); // In the process's WhenUpdate: a step of its clock, or Step(data, deltaTime) for a time of your own runner.Step(data); A synced task works in an async sequence too: it's stepped once a frame, and held while the sequence is paused. Its first step comes in the frame its stage starts, so SyncSequenceTaskLibrary.Yield waits no frame there. The async Yield does. What a synced runner runs A synced runner runs only part of what an async sequence can. Part of a sequence Synced runner Stages and their tasks Runs it The three policies Runs it Repeats, with or without a count Runs it Critical stages Runs it A stage's longest run Runs it A sub-stage Can't A branch Can't A condition Can't The sequence's own timeout or longest run Can't An async task Can't Building a runner from a sequence that holds any it can't says so. A synced runner is changed by hand: Interrupt, SkipStage, JumpToStage, BreakStageRepeat and Reset.

guides/task-sequences/the-libraries.html.title: The libraries | PlayForge
guides/task-sequences/the-libraries.html.summary: The libraries Two libraries hold ready-made tasks, one for async stages and one for synced ones. SequenceTaskLibrary has tasks to await inside a stage's Task, each taking the task's token. SyncSequenceTaskLibrary has the same tasks as ISequenceTasks, for a synced runner or for any stage. Kind Tasks Position MoveTo, MoveBy, MoveLocalTo, MoveAlongPath, ArcTo, Dash; following a transform, MoveTowards, ArcTowards, Orbit, MoveAlongPathToTarget Rotation RotateTo, RotateBy, LookAt, and LookAtTracking, which follows Scale ScaleTo, PunchScale, and TransformTo, position, rotation and scale at once Looks FadeAlpha, ColorTo, MaterialColorTo, MaterialFloatTo Sound and animation PlayAndWait, FadeVolume, PlayAnimationState, LerpAnimFloat UI Toolkit SlideElement, FadeElement, ScaleElement, ColorElement, each with a …To from where the element is; PunchScaleElement, WidthTo, HeightTo, TypeText, TypeTextSkippable Any value Lerp, LerpFloat, LerpVector3, LerpColor Waiting Delay, WaitFrames, Yield, WaitUntil, WaitWhile, WaitForKey, WaitForAnyKey, WaitForPointer The two libraries differ in a few ways: Only the async library has ArcForce, which flies a Rigidbody by physics between FixedUpdates, whatever a runner's timing. ArcTo moves a transform along the same arc, in either library. IsPaused(token) and DeltaTime(token) read the run that holds the token. A synced task has no token. A timed task takes an AnimationCurve for its easing. It ends exactly on its value, and ends at once for a time of 0 or less.

Part What it is Sequence Its stages, in order, with what holds for all of them: its name, its conditions, a timeout or a longest run, whether it repeats, and the handlers that hear it end. guides/task-sequences/time-limits-and-en.title: Time limits and endings | PlayForge
guides/task-sequences/time-limits-and-en.summary: Time limits and endings A run can have time limits, and handlers that hear how it ends. Limit What it does WithTimeout(seconds, injection) Injects when the time is up, a skip by default. WithMaxDuration(seconds) Ends the run, or the stage, at its longest. Handler What it hears OnTimeout The timeout. OnMaxDuration The longest run. OnException A task's throw. It says whether the run goes on. OnComplete The run end, and whether it finished. OnTerminate The run end, however it ends. A stage has its own OnInit, OnRepeat and OnTerminate.

guides/task-sequences/waiting.html.title: Waiting | PlayForge
guides/task-sequences/waiting.html.summary: Waiting A sequence can wait as a stage, inside a task, or on the player's input. Delays wait as a stage, or inside one: Delay What it does Delay(seconds) A stage of its own that waits. DelayUntil, DelayWhile Wait on a predicate. WaitUntil A stage that waits on a predicate. SyncDelay Waits inside a stage, as one of its tasks. The library's waits go inside a task: Wait Waits for SequenceTaskLibrary.Delay A number of seconds. WaitFrames A number of frames. Yield One frame. WaitUntil A predicate to hold. WaitWhile A predicate to stop holding. The player's input is read through ForgeInput, so a game's own input or a test's stands in: Wait Waits for WaitForKey A key to go down. WaitForAnyKey Any of the keys given, and returns the key pressed. WaitForPointer A pointer's button to go down. Each of the library's waits holds while its sequence is paused. A press while it's paused isn't heard. A task that keeps time itself should read SequenceTaskLibrary.DeltaTime(token). It's a step of its run's clock (Clocks), and it's 0 while the sequence is paused. Linking a token A task can link its token, to cancel a wait of its own without its stage. Link it through TaskSequenceRuntime.CreateLinkedTokenSource(token). Its token belongs to the task's run, so a wait on it keeps the run's clock, and holds while the run is paused. A token that CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource links belongs to no run. Its waits go by the game's clock, and don't hold. Dispose of the source once you're done, as with any: .Task(async (data, token) => { // Cancelled with the stage, or on its own through charge.Cancel(), and by the run's clock either way using var charge = TaskSequenceRuntime.CreateLinkedTokenSource(token); await SequenceTaskLibrary.Delay(1.5f, charge.Token); })

guides/testing/a-test.html.title: A test | PlayForge
guides/testing/a-test.html.summary: A test A test class derives from ForgeTest. ForgeTest makes a ForgeTestWorld before each test, and audits and ends it after the test. A test is a [UnityTest] whose body runs through Live, from a frame's end: using System.Collections; using FarEmerald.PlayForge; using FarEmerald.PlayForge.Testing; using NUnit.Framework; using UnityEngine.TestTools; public class BurnTests : ForgeTest { [UnityTest] public IEnumerator A_burn_ticks_twice_in_its_second([Values] Hub hub) => Live(async () => { var health = Make.Attribute("Health"); var target = World.Entity(hub, Make.Set(Make.Pool(health, 100f, 100f)), "Target"); var burn = Make.Effect("Burn", new EffectConfig { Policy = EEffectDurationPolicy.Durational, Target = health, Magnitude = -10f, Duration = 1f, PeriodicTicks = true, Ticks = 2, }); Assert.IsTrue(World.Hit(World.Entity(hub, name: "Source"), target, burn)); await Frames.Until(() => World.Value(target, health) <= 80f, 90, "its two ticks land"); Assert.AreEqual(80f, World.Value(target, health), 0.001f); }); } A test class whose tests need a base class of their own makes a world instead, and ends it, with await using: [UnityTest] public IEnumerator My_test() => UniTask.ToCoroutine(async () => { await using var world = await ForgeTestWorld.Start(); // ... the test, through world; then, if it wants the checks, await world.Audit() });

guides/testing/allocation.html.title: Allocation | PlayForge
guides/testing/allocation.html.summary: Allocation AllocationProbe measures what's allocated, with the profiler's counter, as the GC's own reads 0 under Mono. Member What it measures Measure(action) What one run allocates. MeasureEach(action, runs, warmup) The mean of many runs, after a warm-up. await MeasureFrames(Frames, count) What whole frames allocate: the cleanest of up to three tries, as stray noise doesn't repeat and a leak does. Dispose the probe as the test ends.

guides/testing/index.html.title: Testing Your Content | PlayForge
guides/testing/index.html.summary: Testing Your Content A game's abilities, effects and items are easiest to trust when a test plays them as the game does: a burn's ticks landing over its second, a ring's armor while it's held, a cast paying its cost. PlayForge's test kit is the assembly FarEmerald.PlayForge.Testing, in the package's TestKit folder, which a project's own tests reference. For each test, the kit: brings up a live PlayForge, and steps it a frame at a time; makes entities on either hub, and plays them; checks afterwards what must always hold, and takes it all down again, so tests run in any order. In this guide Setting up: The kit is compiled wherever the Test Framework package (com.unity.test-framework) is installed, as the Test Framework's own test runner is. A test: A test class derives from ForgeTest. The world: The world makes a test's entities and assets, plays them, reads them, and controls its time, its chance and its processes. What must hold: After each test that passed, the world's audit checks what must always hold Allocation: AllocationProbe measures what's allocated, with the profiler's counter, as the GC's own reads 0 under Mono. Traps: These are the mistakes a test most easily makes with the kit. In the API The types of this guide's area: AllocationMarker, AllocationProbe, EffectConfig, ForgeTest, ForgeTestWorld, FrameAllocation, FramePulse, FrameStepper, Hub, Invariants, ScriptedRandom, SteppingClock, TestAssets.

guides/testing/setting-up.html.title: Setting up | PlayForge
guides/testing/setting-up.html.summary: Setting up The kit is compiled wherever the Test Framework package (com.unity.test-framework) is installed, as the Test Framework's own test runner is. To use it from your project's tests: Use a test assembly of the project's: an assembly definition whose Define Constraints hold UNITY_INCLUDE_TESTS, referencing nunit.framework.dll. Add these to its Assembly Definition References: FarEmerald.PlayForge and FarEmerald.PlayForge.Testing UniTask UnityEngine.TestRunner and UnityEditor.TestRunner Give the assembly every platform, not the Editor alone. The assembly needs every platform because the kit's tests are PlayMode tests, which step the real player loop.

guides/testing/the-world.html.title: The world | PlayForge
guides/testing/the-world.html.summary: The world The world makes a test's entities and assets, plays them, reads them, and controls its time, its chance and its processes. Entities: the world makes entities on either hub. Member What it does World.Entity(hub, set, name) Makes an entity of an attribute set on either hub: Hub.Runtime, a RuntimeGameplayAbilitySystem, or Hub.Mono, a GameplayAbilitySystem on a GameObject of its own. World.FromIdentity(hub, identity) Makes an entity from an identity asset, the game's own or one Make built, with its set, its starting abilities and items, and its sides. RuntimeEntity, MonoEntity Make an entity on one hub. NewMonoEntity Makes a Mono hub's entity, not yet registered. Playing: each of these says whether it worked. Member What it does World.Hit(source, target, effect) Applies an effect, as a hit. World.Cast(caster, ability, target, level) Gives an ability and asks it to start, as a player does. Cast(caster, slot, target) Starts the ability in a slot. World.Use(caster, ability, target) Starts an ability the entity has already, as an item's. World.Hold(holder, item, stacks) Gives and equips an item. Reading: each reads an entity, passed as gas. Member What it reads World.Value(gas, attribute) An attribute's current value, or NaN where the entity hasn't the attribute. World.Base(gas, attribute) An attribute's base value, or NaN where the entity hasn't the attribute. World.Has(gas, effect) Whether an effect is on the entity. World.Stacks(gas, effect) An effect's stacks on the entity. World.HasTag(gas, tag) Whether the entity has a tag, or one under it. Time: a test steps whole frames, each Frames.DeltaTime long, with one FixedUpdate. Frames.DeltaTime is 1/60 of a second, or a class's DeltaTime. Member What it does Frames.Step(n) Runs whole frames. Frames.Seconds(s) Runs as many frames as that time takes. Frames.Until(condition, within, what) Steps until the condition holds, failing past within frames. ExactlyIn Fails unless the condition holds exactly so many frames on. Holds Fails if the condition stops holding. World.Clock(step) Makes each frame take step seconds of PlayForge's own time (ForgeTime) instead. Chance: World.Rolls(0.1f, 0.9f) makes each roll come out as written, in turn and round again. It returns the rolls, counting what's drawn (Drawn). A chance lands where it's above the roll, so a roll of 0 always lands. Processes: the world ends each process it owns, if the test doesn't. Member What it does World.Register(process) Registers a process, which the world ends if the test doesn't. World.Own(relay) Makes the world end a process registered some other way. World.Template<T>(name) Stands in for a prefab. World.Spawn(template) Registers a template, and returns the clone. Assets: Make builds them in code, and they're destroyed with the world. Its tag names are unique in the world. The game's own assets are the test's to load. Make member What it builds Attribute An attribute. Element, Pool, Stat An attribute set's element. A Pool stays between 0 and its base. Set, UnusedSet An attribute set. UnusedSet is a set of one attribute nothing reads. Identity, RuntimeIdentity An entity's identity: an asset, or a runtime GAS's. Effect An effect, as an EffectConfig says: one impact, its duration and ticks, how another application stacks, its impact types, granted tags and workers. Item, Ability, Stage An item, an ability, and an ability's stage.

guides/testing/traps.html.title: Traps | PlayForge
guides/testing/traps.html.summary: Traps These are the mistakes a test most easily makes with the kit. Step frames; never call a process's update by hand. The world's ProcessControl steps what runs, as the game's does. Calling an update yourself runs it out of order, and hides what the frame does. A tag converts to text. NUnit's Does.Contain(tag) compares a list of tags as text, and fails. Check with World.HasTag, or with Contains on the list itself. Unscaled time isn't stepped. Anything timed on Unity's unscaled time stays on the wall clock. One world at a time. ForgeTestWorld.Current is the one a test is in. PlayForge's static state is the world's while it lives, and the world gives back the clock and the rolls as it ends.

guides/testing/what-must-hold.html.title: What must hold | PlayForge
guides/testing/what-must-hold.html.summary: What must hold After each test that passed, the world's audit checks what must always hold: It lets three frames settle. It ends what the test left running of what the world began. It fails the test where any of these broke: an entity's attribute parts don't sum to its value; what an entity dealt, read from its frame summaries, isn't what its targets received from it; a process is still running that the world didn't begin. The audit checks the entities the world makes. World.Observe(gas) adds an entity made elsewhere, as from a scene. An entity made with observed: false is left out, as a test that measures allocation wants. A class whose tests leave processes running on purpose overrides Audits to false.

guides/value-pipelines/a-typical-damage-.title: A typical damage pipeline | PlayForge
guides/value-pipelines/a-typical-damage-.summary: A typical damage pipeline A typical damage pipeline has five stages: Amplification: Multiply by the caster's Damage Amplification (a Bonus Share, read as 1 + x). Critical: Chance, the caster's Crit Chance, × 2. Armor: Multiply by a curve of the target's Armor. Resistance: Multiply by the target's Damage Resistance (a Resistance, read as 1 − x). Barrier: Absorb into the target's Barrier. Every damage effect names it. So a blow of 100 from a caster with 50% amplification, on a target with 20% resistance, lands as 120. The Demo's blows go through two such pipelines, Physical Damage and Magic Damage, in its Effects/Pipelines. Each multiplies a blow by its dealer's Attack or Magic Amplification, a Stacking Curve of it read as 1 + it. Then it multiplies by what its target's defence leaves: Pipeline Then multiplies by Physical Damage What its target's Armor leaves, 100 ÷ (100 + Armor) Magic Damage Its target's Magic Resistance, 1 − it, kept between 0 and 1 Its Physical and Magic Strike templates name them, and so does each blow that takes one. So a new attack takes its kind's pipeline from its template.

guides/value-pipelines/built-in-kinds.ht.title: Built-in kinds | PlayForge
guides/value-pipelines/built-in-kinds.ht.summary: Built-in kinds The kinds PlayForge ships for this guide's pickers, each with its menu and what it does, as its picker says. A project's own kinds join them in the same pickers. Stages Kind Menu What it does AbsorbStage — Takes a loss from another attribute first, as a shield takes a blow before health. AddStage — Adds a number to the value's size. BlockStage — On a chance, nothing of the effect lands, as a block. ChanceStage — On a chance, multiplies the value, as a critical hit. ClampStage — Keeps the value's size between two numbers. EvadeStage — On a chance, nothing of the effect lands, as a dodge. ExecuteStage — Takes the rest where a hit would leave less than a share of the attribute's base. MultiplyStage — Multiplies the value by a number, as a bonus or a resistance.

guides/value-pipelines/index.html.title: Value Pipelines | PlayForge
guides/value-pipelines/index.html.summary: Value Pipelines A Value Pipeline is an asset that takes a value as it lands, sends it through ordered stages, and gives what comes out. An effect's impact names one as its calculation, as an Unreal effect names its execution calculation. Each hit of that impact goes through the pipeline's stages. So a project writes once how a hit's damage is worked out, and a new item that changes every hit is a stage, not an edit to each attack. It's generic: the value is any number an impact lands with, a blow, a heal, a drain. You create one in either of two ways: From Create > PlayForge > Value Pipeline. With New beside an impact's Pipeline field, which makes one named for the effect and uses it. Once the field names one, Open shows it. A Crowd Control Rules or Effect Modifier field has the same two buttons. In this guide Not a Scaler asset: A Value Pipeline and a Scaler asset both give numbers, but they work differently. When it runs: A pipeline runs for what an impact commits: an instant impact's hit, and each tick of a periodic one. Stages: A pipeline's stages take the value in order, each giving what goes on to the next. A typical damage pipeline: A typical damage pipeline has five stages The breakdown: An effect's spec keeps its last run as a Breakdown: the value in, each stage's before and after with its note, and the value out. Trying a pipeline: A Value Pipeline's inspector has a Try section under its stages. Built-in kinds: The kinds PlayForge ships for this guide's pickers, each with its menu and what it does, as its picker says. In the API The types of this guide's area: AbsorbStage, AbstractStopStage, AbstractValueStage, AddStage, BlockStage, ChanceStage, ClampStage, EStopImpacts, EvadeStage, ExecuteStage, MultiplyStage, ValueBreakdown, ValuePipeline, ValueRun, ValueStep.

guides/value-pipelines/not-a-scaler-asse.title: Not a Scaler asset | PlayForge
guides/value-pipelines/not-a-scaler-asse.summary: Not a Scaler asset A Value Pipeline and a Scaler asset both give numbers, but they work differently. A Scaler asset is a number worked out from its context: a level table, × an attribute, a condition. A number field reads it wherever a number is read. A Value Pipeline transforms a value it's given. It runs once for each hit, as the hit lands, with the caster and the target both known. Its stages can do what a number can't: roll a chance once for the hit, and keep it; route part of the value into a barrier; say what each stage did. A stage's own numbers are number fields, so a stage reads × Attribute, conditions, curves and Scaler assets as any field does.

guides/value-pipelines/stages.html.title: Stages | PlayForge
guides/value-pipelines/stages.html.summary: Stages A pipeline's stages take the value in order, each giving what goes on to the next. Every stage has these fields: Property Description Label The name a breakdown gives it, as Amplification, Armor or Critical. Left empty, the breakdown says what the stage does. Enabled Off, the value passes it by. The stages PlayForge ships are below, and a project can write its own. In this section Multiply: A Multiply stage multiplies the value by a number read for the hit. Add: An Add stage adds a number to the value's size. Chance: A Chance stage multiplies the value by a number on a chance: a critical hit. Clamp: A Clamp stage keeps the value's size between two numbers, its sign as it was. Absorb: An Absorb stage takes a loss first from another attribute of the one hit, as a barrier or a shield takes a blow before health. Block and Evade: A Block or Evade stage is a Chance, read as the effect lands, that stops it. Execute: An Execute stage finishes off a hit's target, as Culling Blade. Writing your own stage: A project writes its own stage by deriving from AbstractValueStage and overriding Apply(value, in run).

guides/value-pipelines/stages/absorb.htm.title: Absorb | PlayForge
guides/value-pipelines/stages/absorb.htm.summary: Absorb An Absorb stage takes a loss first from another attribute of the one hit, as a barrier or a shield takes a blow before health. Property Description Into The attribute that takes the loss first: a barrier, a shield. On Whose attribute: the one hit's, or the caster's. What it soaks comes off that attribute at the frame's end, and the rest goes on. A gain passes it by. An attribute with the Barrier role soaks the losses to the one it absorbs for with no stage at all (Attributes).

guides/value-pipelines/stages/add.html.title: Add | PlayForge
guides/value-pipelines/stages/add.html.summary: Add An Add stage adds a number to the value's size. Property Description Amount What's added to the value's size, read for the hit. A flat bonus of 10 makes a blow of −100 one of −110, and a heal of 50 one of 60.

guides/value-pipelines/stages/block-and-.title: Block and Evade | PlayForge
guides/value-pipelines/stages/block-and-.summary: Block and Evade A Block or Evade stage is a Chance, read as the effect lands, that stops it. Property Description Chance The chance it stops the effect, from 0 to 1. It's a number of any kind, as the one hit's Block Chance. Roll How it rolls: pseudo-random, and its luck. Stops What it can stop: Losses, the default, or Any Impact (below). Each rolls once, before anything of the effect lands. Where it comes up, nothing of the effect lands: its damage, tags, contained effects and on-hits. Its ticks aren't rolled again. The one hit hears Blocked or Evaded, and the dealer Hit Blocked or Hit Evaded. As the hit commits, it passes the value on. Its Stops has two options: Stops What it can stop Losses An effect that lowers its attribute: an add below 0, a multiplier below 1, or an override below where it stands. So a heal lands past it, unrolled. Any Impact Any effect, heals and buffs too. A defender brings one through an incoming modifier's Change Impact (Effects: Workers: Modifiers). Tougher Times, for example, blocks the hits landing on its holder by a stacking curve of its stacks.

guides/value-pipelines/stages/chance.htm.title: Chance | PlayForge
guides/value-pipelines/stages/chance.htm.summary: Chance A Chance stage multiplies the value by a number on a chance: a critical hit. Property Description Chance The chance, from 0 to 1, read for the hit, as the caster's Crit Chance. Multiplier What the value is multiplied by when the roll comes up: 2 for a double. Note What the breakdown notes when it comes up: critical. Roll How it rolls: pseudo-random, or lucky (Effects: Requirements). It rolls once for the hit, and the breakdown notes it.

guides/value-pipelines/stages/clamp.html.title: Clamp | PlayForge
guides/value-pipelines/stages/clamp.html.summary: Clamp A Clamp stage keeps the value's size between two numbers, its sign as it was. Property Description Least The least its size can be, read for the hit. Most The most its size can be, read for the hit.

guides/value-pipelines/stages/execute.ht.title: Execute | PlayForge
guides/value-pipelines/stages/execute.ht.summary: Execute An Execute stage finishes off a hit's target, as Culling Blade. A hit that would leave the one hit with less than its Share of its Attribute's base takes the rest. Property Description Share The share of its base below which a hit takes the rest, as 0.13. Attribute The attribute it reads, the one hit's. With none, the one in the project's Health role. The breakdown notes it.

guides/value-pipelines/stages/multiply.h.title: Multiply | PlayForge
guides/value-pipelines/stages/multiply.h.summary: Multiply A Multiply stage multiplies the value by a number read for the hit. Property Description By What the value is multiplied by, read for the hit. It suits any factor: A bonus: × the caster's Damage Amplification, read as 1 + x. A reduction: × the target's Damage Resistance, read as what's left. An armor curve. A bonus that reads the target, as 75% more while the target is above 90% of its health.

guides/value-pipelines/stages/writing-yo.title: Writing your own stage | PlayForge
guides/value-pipelines/stages/writing-yo.summary: Writing your own stage A project writes its own stage by deriving from AbstractValueStage and overriding Apply(value, in run). run.Context reads the hit's caster, target and level, as any number does. run.Note notes what the stage did.

guides/value-pipelines/the-breakdown.htm.title: The breakdown | PlayForge
guides/value-pipelines/the-breakdown.htm.summary: The breakdown An effect's spec keeps its last run as a Breakdown: the value in, each stage's before and after with its note, and the value out. spec.Breakdown.ToString() says it in a line: -100 → Amplification -150 → Resistance -120. A combat log, a debugger or a test reads it.

guides/value-pipelines/trying-a-pipeline.title: Trying a pipeline | PlayForge
guides/value-pipelines/trying-a-pipeline.summary: Trying a pipeline A Value Pipeline's inspector has a Try section under its stages. It puts a value through them at each level of a range, as a Scaler asset's Try reads a scaler. Property Description Value In The value a hit lands with, going in: a loss below 0, as a blow of 100 is −100, and a gain above. Chances Come Up Settles each roll, so a try gives the same each time (below). Levels The hit's levels, 1 to 5 to start, for a stage whose number scales by level. Caster, Target and Caller The same stand-ins as a Scaler asset's Try (below). Chances Come Up settles each chance a stage rolls: On, each comes up where it can: a critical strike doubles the hit, and a block stops it. Off, each misses where it can. A chance of 1 always comes up, and one of 0 never does. The Caster and Target have a row for each attribute a stage reads on that side, as a Multiply stage's Damage Amplification or an Absorb stage's Barrier. You type its values, or fill them from an Entity. The Caller has a row for each key a caller sets. Its Out row says what lands at each level. Click one to see its steps under the table: the value in, each stage's value in and out with its note, as "critical", and what comes out. A Block or Evade stage rolls first, as it does as an effect lands. One that comes up stops the hit: nothing of it lands, and its level shows "—". No effect is behind a try. So what an Absorb stage soaks comes off no one, and a stage of your own that reads run.Carrier reads none. What's typed is kept for the session, never in the asset. ValuePipelineTry does the same in code: new ValuePipelineTry { Value = -100f }.Read(pipeline). pipeline.Run(value, in context) puts a value through a pipeline against a number context of your own, with no effect behind it.

guides/value-pipelines/when-it-runs.html.title: When it runs | PlayForge
guides/value-pipelines/when-it-runs.html.summary: When it runs A pipeline runs for what an impact commits: an instant impact's hit, and each tick of a periodic one. A lasting impact, as +10 Strength while a buff holds, is read again whenever its attribute changes. So a pipeline doesn't run it. A modifier's Change Impact brings a stage of its own (Effects: Workers: Modifiers): A hit runs it after its pipeline, or alone where it has none. The breakdown keeps it with the pipeline's steps. A lasting impact takes it on its magnitude.

guides/workers/built-in-kinds.html.title: Built-in kinds | PlayForge
guides/workers/built-in-kinds.html.summary: Built-in kinds The kinds PlayForge ships for this guide's pickers, each with its menu and what it does, as its picker says. A project's own kinds join them in the same pickers. In this section Attribute workers Impact workers Effect workers Analysis workers Actions

guides/workers/built-in-kinds/actions.ht.title: Actions | PlayForge
guides/workers/built-in-kinds/actions.ht.summary: Actions Kind Menu What it does ApplyEffectAction — Deferred action to apply an effect. DeathAction — The deferred action that kills its entity as its turn comes, at Critical priority: the entity is marked dead, which its callbacks, its components, its effects and its killer hear, and it ends, or stays dead, at its frame's end, as its Death says. LambdaAction — Simple action that executes a lambda. LogAction — A deferred action that writes its text through ForgeLog, at Info, as its turn comes: at Cleanup priority unless it's given another, and only where its validity check, if it's given one, holds. ModifyAttributeAction — Deferred action to modify an attribute. RemoveEffectAction — Deferred action to remove an effect. TagWorkerActivateAction — Deferred action to activate a tag worker. TagWorkerResolveAction — Deferred action to resolve (deactivate) a tag worker.

guides/workers/built-in-kinds/analysis-w.title: Analysis workers | PlayForge
guides/workers/built-in-kinds/analysis-w.summary: Analysis workers Kind Menu What it does DeathWatcherAnalysisWorker — Kills its entity as an attribute reaches its threshold, as Health reaching 0. ThresholdAnalysisWorker — Applies effects and sends an event as an attribute crosses a threshold.

guides/workers/built-in-kinds/attribute-.title: Attribute workers | PlayForge
guides/workers/built-in-kinds/attribute-.summary: Attribute workers Kind Menu What it does CantFallBelowAttributeWorker — Keeps its attribute from falling below a floor. MathAttributeWorker — Changes each change to its attribute by another attribute. ReturnDamageAttributeWorker — Sends a share of each loss back to the one who dealt it.

guides/workers/built-in-kinds/effect-wor.title: Effect workers | PlayForge
guides/workers/built-in-kinds/effect-wor.summary: Effect workers Kind Menu What it does AttributeChangeEffectWorker — Tells how far an attribute has moved since the effect began, for a number to read. EffectWorkerGroup — Several effect workers as one. ReviveOnRemovalEffectWorker — Revives the entity it's on as the effect ends, as a respawn timer. ThresholdDebuggerEffectWorker — Logs as its target's attribute crosses a threshold, for debugging.

guides/workers/built-in-kinds/impact-wor.title: Impact workers | PlayForge
guides/workers/built-in-kinds/impact-wor.summary: Impact workers Kind Menu What it does ImpactWorkerGroup — Several impact workers as one. LifestealImpactWorker — Heals its holder a share of each loss it deals another. RelativeOperationContextImpactWorker — Changes an attribute of its holder by a share of each impact.

guides/workers/hearing-workers-run.html.title: Hearing workers run | PlayForge
guides/workers/hearing-workers-run.html.summary: Hearing workers run An entity tells its workers' runs to whoever listens to its callbacks, and to no one else. So a worker no one hears costs nothing more. Callback What it tells OnEffectWorkerRan One of its effects' workers heard one of the effect's moments (below). OnImpactWorkerRan One of its impact workers ran for a hit it dealt, with its Execution and what it queued. OnAttributeChangeStep A step a change to one of its attributes took (below). OnEffectWorkerRan tells: its Hook: Application, Tick, Removal or Impact; its Side: the Target, or the Dealer for a hit, as the map says; the System it ran on, and the actions it Queued. A tick, which its workers hear every frame, is told only as one executes or a worker queues something. OnAttributeChangeStep tells one of three steps: an attribute worker's, with its Timing, its Execution, the change Before and After, and what it Queued; a barrier's soak; a gain's scaling. The combat log keeps each hit's steps (Entities: Combat Log). An EffectJournal hears all of it for the entities it's given (Entities: Effect Journal).

guides/workers/lifesteal.html.title: Lifesteal | PlayForge
guides/workers/lifesteal.html.summary: Lifesteal The Lifesteal worker, an impact worker, heals its holder a share of each workable loss it deals another. Property Description Share The attribute whose value is the share it heals, as 0.15 for 15%. With none, it heals nothing. Receives The attribute whose losses count. With none, the Health role's. Heals The attribute it heals. With none, the Health role's. Impact Types The types of hit that count, as attacks. With none, any. Receives and Heals are separate, so a mana burn can heal Health. An effect has no lifesteal of its own. An effect raises the holder's share while it should. A second worker on another attribute, of spells' types, makes a spell vamp. A worker that runs once for a hit, as this one, runs once however many of it its holder has, its project's and its own. The first of the kind to take the hit runs. It allocates nothing, healing or not.
